Title: An Online Algorithm for Max–Min Allocation on Hierarchical Parallel Machines
Authors: Xing Chai, Xin Zhang, Zhixin Liu, Wenhua Li, Ran Lin
Affiliations: School of Mathematics and Statistics Henan University of Technology Zhengzhou China; Department of Information & Operations Management, College of Business University of Michigan‐Dearborn Dearborn Michigan USA; School of Mathematics and Statistics Zhengzhou University Zhengzhou China
Abstract: ABSTRACT Max–min allocation and hierarchical scheduling have attracted considerable attention due to their extensive applications in computing and service domains. This article investigates the problem of online max–min allocation on parallel machines, with the objective of maximizing the minimum machine load. Jobs arrive sequentially and are categorized as either hierarchy level 1 or 2. Machines are divided into two hierarchical levels: higher‐level machines can process all jobs, whereas lower‐level machines can only process jobs labeled as hierarchy 2. We propose an online algorithm that is the best possible in certain cases, with near‐optimal performance verified numerically. This study extends and generalizes existing results on scheduling problems involving two or three machines.

Title: Behavior‐Based Price Discrimination in Elastic Demand Markets
Authors: Rosa‐Branca Esteves, Jie Shuai
Affiliations: School of Economics, Management and Political Science and NIPE University of Minho Braga Portugal; Wenlan School of Business Zhongnan University of Economics and Law Wuhan P.R. China
Abstract: ABSTRACT We study behavior‐based price discrimination (BBPD) in a two‐period Hotelling market in which consumers choose both where to buy and how much to buy, and consumers and firms may discount the future differently. For the symmetric interior solution we characterize, BBPD lowers second‐period prices, but its first‐period pricing incentives reflect two channels. The consumer‐side effect captures how consumers' anticipation of future poaching offers changes their sensitivity to first‐period price differences when choosing between firms. The firm‐side effect captures how first‐period market share affects second‐period equilibrium profit and thereby firms' first‐period pricing incentives. At symmetry, a marginal increase in that share leaves second‐period profit unchanged under unit and isoelastic demand but reduces it under strictly increasing individual‐demand elasticity. The firm‐side effect is therefore zero in the two benchmarks but gives forward‐looking firms an incentive to raise first‐period prices in our setting. The consumer‐side effect can reinforce or oppose this incentive. For any fixed positive firm discount factor, BBPD harms consumers relative to uniform pricing when consumers place sufficiently little weight on the future, despite lower second‐period prices. Such losses do not arise in the unit‐demand and isoelastic benchmarks. Holding both discount factors fixed across demand specifications, linear‐demand comparisons show that elastic demand can reverse the profit effect of BBPD.

Title: Contextual Bandits and Optimistically Universal Learning
Authors: Moïse Blanchard, Steve Hanneke, Patrick Jaillet
Affiliations: Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, Georgia 30332; Purdue University, West Lafayette, Indiana 47907; Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02139
Abstract: We consider the contextual bandit problem in general action and context spaces. This generalizes the standard multiarmed bandit to the case where side information is available—for example, patients’ records or customers’ history—which allows for personalized treatment. We focus on consistency (vanishing regret compared with optimal policy) and show that for large classes of non-independent and identically distributed (non-i.i.d.) contexts, consistency can be achieved regardless of the reward mechanism, a property known as universal consistency. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work giving consistent algorithms for any contextual bandits instance with finite action spaces and i.i.d. contexts. Further, we first give necessary and sufficient conditions on the context-generating process for universal consistency to be possible. Second, we show that there always exists an algorithm that guarantees universal consistency whenever this is achievable, referred to as optimistically universal. Interestingly, for finite action spaces, the processes admitting universal learning are exactly the same as in the full-feedback supervised setting: learning can be performed with partial feedback without any generalization cost. The algorithms balance a trade-off between generalization (similar to structural risk minimization) and personalization (tailoring actions to specific contexts). Lastly, we investigate the benefit of continuity assumptions on rewards for universal learning. Title: Predicting inflation with recurrent neural networks
Authors: Livia Paranhos
Abstract: This paper applies a recurrent neural network, long short-term memory (LSTM), to forecast inflation. This is an appealing model for time series, as it processes each time step sequentially and explicitly learns dynamic dependencies. The paper also explores the dimension reduction capability of the model to uncover economically meaningful factors that can explain the inflation process. Results from an exercise with US data indicate that the estimated neural networks present competitive, but not outstanding, performance against common benchmarks (including other machine learning models). LSTM in particular is found to perform well at long horizons and during periods of heightened macroeconomic uncertainty. Interestingly, LSTM-implied factors are highly correlated with business cycle indicators, informing on the usefulness of such signals as inflation predictors. The paper also sheds light on the impact of network initialization and architecture on forecasting performance.

Title: From Finite Data to Decisions in Stochastic Optimization: The Impossibility of Achieving Perfection
Authors: Xuecheng Tian, Shuaian Wang, Lu Zhen, Zuo‐Jun (Max) Shen
Affiliations: Faculty of Business The Hong Kong Polytechnic University Hung Hom Hong Kong; School of Management Shanghai University Shanghai China; College of Engineering University of California, Berkeley Berkeley California USA; Faculty of Engineering & Faculty of Business and Economics The University of Hong Kong Pokfulam Hong Kong
Abstract: ABSTRACT This paper studies data‐driven stochastic optimization in the finite‐sample regime, where the true distribution of the uncertain parameters is unknown and the decision maker has access only to a finite sample of observations. We assume that the true distribution belongs to a known distribution family. Each distribution in this set induces a stochastic optimization problem instance, and the collection of all such instances forms a problem class. A data‐driven policy maps an observed sample to a feasible decision. We evaluate finite‐sample policy performance through three criteria. The first is the sample‐realization‐based out‐of‐sample cost , which evaluates the expected cost of the decision induced by one realized sample. The second is the expected out‐of‐sample cost , which averages the previous quantity over all sample realizations of a fixed finite size. The third is the expected prescription bias , which compares the decision averaged over both the random training sample and any conditional randomization used by the policy with a full‐information optimal decision. In particular, we study whether a policy can match the full‐information benchmark uniformly across problem instances, problem classes, and finite sample sizes under the requirement induced by each criterion. Using the mean squared error problem and the newsvendor problem, we prove that the answer is negative. These impossibility results are consolidated in an Imperfection Theorem , which shows that no data‐driven policy can satisfy any of the three perfection requirements under the across‐class conditions studied in this paper.

Title: Optimal multi-channel pricing for perishable goods with constant price elasticity and responsive supply
Authors: Jason Z.-H. Lee
Abstract: The transition to multi-channel retailing presents a challenge for perishable goods retailers. These firms have worked to balance considerable third-party commissions and fulfillment costs against the continuous value-decay of inventory. Despite this complexity, current analytical models frequently rely on dual-channel or linear demand vs. price assumptions, leaving a gap in generalized, multi-channel optimization frameworks. This research develops an integrated profit-maximization model for multiple interconnected channels, utilizing a constant price elasticity of demand specification. Closed-form pricing rules are proposed that link fulfillment costs and platform commissions to optimal inter-channel price gaps. Unlike traditional inventory models, the pricing mechanism is discussed under a responsive and unconstrained supply logic to manage revenue and waste risk. Analytical results highlight sufficient conditions across sales channels under which channel-specific price lifting or lowering maximizes the seller’s overall profit. Furthermore, for the case of mutually substitutive dual channels, the existence of interior critical price points and conditions under which these points are not available for local maxima are characterized, where low threshold prices (determined by logistics costs) with high customer price sensitivity in a channel is one indication that optimal prices may lie at or beyond boundary points. For the case of separable multi-channels, the model defines the role of threshold prices and own-price sensitivities in each channel for optimal pricing within the price domain. By synthesizing logistics-pricing interactions across hybrid fulfillment modes, this framework provides an analytical tool for retailers in perishables markets to align prices across channels.

Title: Bilateral investment treaties and services trade
Authors: Yulin Hou, Ziqi Ye
Affiliations: School of Economics and Trade Zhongnan University of Economics and Law Wuhan China; School of Social and Political Science The University of Edinburgh Edinburgh UK
Abstract: Abstract An increasing number of bilateral investment treaties (BITs) establish a stable investment climate, which encourages both foreign direct investment and economic integration. Combining BITs data with the International Trade and Production Database and capitalizing on the latest developments in the empirical structural gravity literature, we investigate the effects of BITs on services trade. We find robust evidence of a positive effect of BITs on services trade: the presence of BITs increases services trade by 3.6%. This result is robust to an instrumental variable strategy addressing the endogeneity problem. We also find little evidence of trade diversion effects of BITs. At the industry level, there are substantial heterogeneity effects of BITs for members and non‐members.

Title: Data Market Design Through Deep Learning
Authors: Sai Srivatsa Ravindranath, Yanchen Jiang, David C. Parkes
Affiliations: Harvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences, Harvard University, Boston, Massachusetts 02134
Abstract: The data market design problem is the problem of finding a set of signaling schemes (statistical experiments) to maximize expected revenue to an information seller, where each experiment reveals some information and has a corresponding price (Bergemann et al. [8]). Each buyer chooses a downstream action based on their prior and signal, and their expected value for the information associated with a particular experiment comes from the improvement in deciding this action. In a setting with multiple buyers, a buyer’s expected value for an experiment may also depend on the information sold to others (Bonatti et al. [12]). We introduce the application of deep learning for the design of revenue-optimal data markets, looking to expand the frontiers of what can be understood and achieved. Relative to earlier work on deep learning for auction design (Dütting et al. [34]), we must learn signaling schemes (rather than allocation rules) and handle obedience constraints—those arising from modeling the downstream actions of buyers—in addition to incentive constraints on bids. Our experiments demonstrate that this deep learning framework can almost precisely replicate all known solutions from theory, expand to more complex settings, and be used to identify new designs for data markets that can be proved to be optimal as well as make conjectures in regard to the structure of optimal designs.

Title: Optimal Stopping with Interdependent Values
Authors: Simon Mauras, Divyarthi Mohan, Rebecca Reiffenhäuser
Affiliations: INRIA, FairPlay Joint Team, 91120 Palaiseau, France; Columbia University, New York, New York 10027; University of Amsterdam, 1012 WP Amsterdam, Netherlands
Abstract: We study online selection problems in both the prophet and secretary settings when arriving agents have interdependent values. In the interdependent values model, introduced in the seminal work of Milgrom and Weber, each agent has a private signal, and the value of an agent is a function of the signals held by all agents. Results in online selection crucially rely on some degree of independence of values, which is conceptually at odds with the interdependent values model. For prophet and secretary models under the standard independent values assumption, prior works provide constant-factor approximations to the welfare. On the other hand, when agents have interdependent values, prior works in economics and computer science provide truthful mechanisms that obtain optimal and approximately optimal welfare under certain assumptions on the valuation functions. We bring together these two important lines of work and provide the first constant-factor approximations for prophet and secretary problems with interdependent values. We consider both the algorithmic setting, where agents are nonstrategic (but have interdependent values), and the mechanism design setting with strategic agents. All our results are constructive and use simple stopping rules. History: This manuscript has been accepted to the Mathematics of Operations Research Special Issue on Market Design. Title: Sample average approximation for the stochastic resource-constrained project scheduling problem with flexible resource profiles
Authors: Ann-Kathrin Mendl, Julia Rieck
Abstract: Abstract Despite the availability of various decision support tools for project managers, only few methods explicitly account for uncertainty in activity durations and flexibility in resource allocation. To address this issue, we consider a stochastic resource-constrained project scheduling problem with flexible resource profiles. The problem is formulated as a mixed-integer linear program with chance-constraints, aiming to minimize the project duration while ensuring a predefined confidence level. Uncertainty is modeled through workload distributions and approximated using a sample average approximation based on discrete scenario sets. While exact solutions can be obtained for small instances with standard solvers, larger instances require heuristic approaches. For this purpose, we develop a serial schedule generation scheme to create feasible solutions and apply a scatter search to improve them. Both methods check the scenarios for feasibility with respect to the confidence level. Once a feasible schedule is identified, improvements are pursued by rescheduling activities along the critical paths. The proposed methods are evaluated in a comprehensive performance analysis, focusing on solution quality, robustness across scenarios, and scalability with respect to instance size and resource configurations.

Title: Probabilistic optimization of corrective actions for project deadline adherence in projects with stochastic activity durations
Authors: Forough Vaseghi, Mario Vanhoucke
Abstract: Abstract Project control, as an iterative process crucial for managing project uncertainties, demands continual adaptation throughout the project’s lifespan. Activity duration unpredictability, inherents in project networks, poses challenges to meeting deadlines. In response, project managers collect real-time data and employ corrective actions to ensure timely and budget-compliant project delivery. Despite extensive research on project control methodologies, explicit methods for determining the optimal size of corrective actions in stochastic environments have received limited attention. This study addresses this gap by integrating probabilistic optimization models into project control strategies, emphasizing the minimization of corrective action costs. The model ensures that a specified percentile of the project duration distribution aligns with a predefined deadline, offering a probability of meeting the promised project duration. Two control strategies are proposed: preventive, involving a one-time optimization before project initiation, and protective, with continuous re-optimization at specific tracking periods during project execution. Computational experiments on artificial datasets reveal that protective strategies outperform preventive strategies, showing faster convergence and reduced variability in project duration distribution. Results indicate that, on average, a minimum of 6 re-optimizations during project execution is required to minimize both the cumulative cost of corrective actions and the average deviations between project duration realizations and the promised deadline.

Title: Automated design of heuristics for resource-constrained project scheduling problem via regression algorithms
Authors: Jingyu Luo, Mario Vanhoucke, José Coelho, Jie Song
Abstract: Abstract The resource-constrained project scheduling problem (RCPSP) is a complex optimization problem aiming to construct feasible schedules that minimize the project makespan while satisfying the precedence and renewable resource constraints. Priority rule heuristics are prevalent approaches for solving the RCPSP, particularly in practical applications. However, these rules are problem-specific, and no rule can consistently outperform others across different projects. Designing priority rules through manual methods requires substantial expertise, time, and computational effort. This has led researchers to propose automated techniques for this purpose. Most existing research in this area focuses on unsupervised learning techniques like genetic programming hyper-heuristics (GPHH), while the investigation of supervised learning algorithms remains limited. To address this gap, this research explores the potential of supervised learning algorithms, specifically regression-based methods, for the automated design of new priority rule heuristics for RCPSP. Nine widely used regression algorithms were evaluated, and the top-performing three were further enhanced using ensemble techniques to augment their effectiveness. Computational experiments show that regression-based heuristics can outperform traditional priority rules across all primary test datasets and, in some cases, even surpass priority rules designed through GPHH. To further validate the reliability of our results, we also tested the regression-based heuristics on various supplementary datasets, including project instances with more than 1,000 activities and empirical projects. Their performance highlights the robust generalization of regression-based heuristics.

Title: Makespan service level for the flexible job-shop scheduling problem under machine-related uncertainty
Authors: Mario Flores-Gómez, Stéphane Dauzère-Pérès
Abstract: The stochastic flexible job-shop scheduling problem with random processing times is considered in this paper, where the makespan service level is maximized, i.e., the probability that a schedule is completed before a given deadline. In practice, this deadline corresponds to the scheduling horizon (e.g., a shift, a day or a week) during which the set of jobs to schedule must be completed. Compared to previous research, the uncertainty is related to the machine and the processing times of all operations processed on a machine are similarly impacted by the machine status. This helps to propose a new way of generating scenarios and deal with uncertainty. New bounds on the makespan service level are also proposed, and included in a tabu search approach. Computational experiments are conducted, that illustrate the relevance of the proposed approach. Several perspectives are proposed in the conclusions of the paper.

Title: Exact algorithms for a personnel scheduling problem in intra-hospital patient transfer with hierarchical objectives
Authors: Marco Claps, Maxence Delorme, Giorgio Zucchi, Manuel Iori
Abstract: Abstract We study a personnel scheduling problem faced by a healthcare and pharmaceutical logistics company, whose goal is to schedule a set of identical employees to transport patients within different healthcare facilities of a hospital. In addition to minimizing the total number of working hours in the schedule, we also aim to maximize shift homogeneity, where two shifts are considered homogeneous if they start and end at the same time, possibly on different days. We introduce three solution methods: two based on integer linear programming (ILP) and one using a decomposition approach in which shifts are determined in the master problem and assigned to employees in the subproblem. We show that the decomposition approach can solve all real-world instances provided by the company in a short amount of time, unlike the ILP models. We also provide managerial insights regarding the effect on the optimal solution of modifying certain instance parameters, such as varying the number of employees, allowing for shorter shifts, and imposing a mandatory lunch break in each shift. Finally, we investigate instance features that make our scheduling problem more difficult to solve for the proposed approaches.

Title: Quantitative risk prioritization. A new risk-based approach to prioritize project risks
Authors: Fernando Acebes, José Manuel González-Varona, Adolfo López-Paredes, Javier Pajares
Abstract: Abstract Several techniques have been proposed to prioritize risks identified in projects. In academia and business, the most standard use is the probability-impact matrix, also known as the risk matrix. Although widespread, this tool has specific limitations, as demonstrated in numerous studies. This article introduces a quantitative method based on Monte Carlo simulation to enhance project risk prioritization. Our proposed method quantifies the impact of each risk on both duration and total cost objectives, enabling us to determine each risk’s relative importance based on these values. In contrast to previous work, this paper proposes a methodology that integrates the effects of risk interactions and the structure of the project-defining network. We conducted two simulation studies, which are detailed in this article. The first study uses fictitious projects to examine the influence of project network structure on the effectiveness of the risk matrix, compared with our proposed methodology. In the second study, we apply our method to two distinct real-world projects and compare these findings with results from simulations of fictitious projects. The conclusions indicate that the traditional risk matrix method produces results that diverge from those generated by our proposed approach, which quantifies impacts. Moreover, it was observed that the risk matrix provides more reliable results when a project’s structure approximates a serial configuration. However, its accuracy in risk prioritization declines for projects with a more parallel structure.

Title: Simulated annealing for Max-NPV multi-project scheduling in a sharing-economy environment
Authors: Yidan He, Zhengwen He, Nengmin Wang, Erik Demeulemeester
Abstract: This paper considers a Max-NPV multi-project scheduling problem in a sharing-economy environment, where the task consists of matching project activities with joined enterprises and arranging activities’ start times to maximise the net present value (NPV) of multiple projects. First, we define the used notation, and we formulate the studied problem as an optimisation model, from which several properties of the problem are extracted. Next, due to the NP-hardness of the problem, we propose a simulated annealing algorithm, where a measure designed based on the problem’s properties is employed to improve the search efficiency. Finally, an extensive computational experiment is carried out on a randomly generated dataset to test the proposed algorithm, and based on the obtained results, the impacts of key parameters on the objective function value are analyzed. The conclusions of the research are as follows: Among the tested algorithms including simulated annealing, tabu search, and multistart iteration improvement, the proposed algorithm can obtain the best results, which are less than 1% worse than the optimal solutions for the small instances. However, varying the key parameters, the effect of the improvement measure in the algorithm changes. The NPV of multiple projects increases when the project deadline, the resource strength, the number of milestone activities or the payment proportion climb, whereas it decreases with an increased discount rate per period.

Title: Solution of a bilevel optimistic scheduling problem on parallel machines
Authors: Quentin Schau, Olivier Ploton, Vincent T’kindt, Han Hoogeveen, Federico Della Croce, Jippe Hoogeveen
Abstract: Abstract We consider the uniform parallel machines scheduling problem in the context of optimistic bilevel optimization, where two speed options are considered. In this scenario, the leader selects and assigns a subset of jobs to the follower to minimize the weighted number of tardy jobs, while the follower schedules these jobs on a set of uniform machines to minimize the total completion time. This problem has practical applications in Industry 4.0. We show that this problem is $$\mathcal NP$$ N P -hard in the strong sense by providing a reduction from the Numerical 3-Dimensional Matching problem and we provide a moderately exponential-time dynamic programming algorithm. The problem is solved by means of a concise MIP formulation and a branch-and-bound algorithm that embeds a column generation approach for the lower bound computation. Computational experiments are presented for instances with up to 100 jobs and 4 machines while larger problems are out of reach for the proposed approaches.

Title: Review of recent advances on the resource-constrained project scheduling problem
Authors: Mohammad Ghasemi, Asef Nazari, Dhananjay Thiruvady
Affiliations: Deakin University
Abstract: At the heart of project management lies the project scheduling problem, which involves arranging a set of activities within a project to ensure timely completion. The majority of works on the project scheduling problem focus on a variant called the resource-constrained project scheduling problem (RCPSP), considering limited resource availability. The standard RCPSP is known as an NP-hard problem and has attracted significant attention from researchers. Moreover, practical engineering requirements add further complexity to the problem, prompting additional assumptions and various extensions. In this survey, the PRISMA model is adopted to review recent advances on the RCPSP. The main purpose of this study is not only to provide researchers and practitioners with a comprehensive taxonomy and overview of the common extensions of the RCPSP but also to identify existing limitations and propose potential research directions in project scheduling. We investigate 268 journal articles between 2010 and 2024, and identify three main categories: multi-skilled RCPSP, RCPSPs under uncertainty, and the multi-project RCPSP. For each category, statistical analyses and summaries of model types and assumptions, solution approaches are presented. Finally, we provide insights into future research directions in the RCPSP.

Title: Multi-step newsvendors revisited: targeted marketing investment and informativeness
Authors: E. Balugani, A. M. Coruzzolo, F. Lolli, Y. Rekik, A. Syntetos
Affiliations: University of Modena and Reggio Emilia; ODAI department, Emlyon Business School; Cardiff University
Abstract: We study a retailer of short-life products facing a season with two ordering opportunities. A planned targeted marketing campaign executed immediately before the second opportunity can reduce second-period demand variance. The retailer must decide whether to invest and how much to order in each period. We formulate the problem as a two–period newsvendor and solve it with dynamic programming. A scenario analysis shows that targeted variance reduction is effective unless the first order is substantially oversized or the campaign is very costly. We also provide a benchmark comparison (no–marketing), quantify miscommunication risks, and examine how the relative lengths of the two periods affect performance.

Title: A generative artificial intelligence-driven smart factory using generative adversarial networks
Authors: Andreas Se Ho Kugele, Yechan Oh, Sumi Kar, Yejin Kwon, Jiyoung Jeon, Yeseo Kim, Biswajit Sarkar
Affiliations: Yonsei University; Lovely Professional University; Saveetha University
Abstract: This study proposes a generative artificial intelligence-driven smart factory framework that integrates advanced digital technologies with data-driven decision support across production and supply chain operations. The smart factory is structured around six core dimensions, which are smart assets, smart working, smart manufacturing, smart supply chain, smart products, and smart solution ecosystems. A smart supply chain configuration consisting of a smart manufacturer, smart retail management, and interconnected fourth-party logistics services is developed to enable real-time coordination and optimization. Generative artificial intelligence is employed to synthesize realistic demand patterns and support adaptive decision-making. The proposed model dynamically adjusts key manufacturing and logistics parameters in response to changing market conditions to enhance operational efficiency and financial performance, through which a global optimum minimum cost of $18,226,000.00 is found. The results demonstrate that the proposed framework is effective in capturing lumpy intermittent demand behaviours and supporting smart production planning.

Title: Unsupervised regime discovery from industrial multivariate time series using masked invariant information clustering
Authors: Koichi Sumiya, Sumika Arima
Affiliations: University of Tsukuba
Abstract: In industrial process monitoring, inferring the current operational regime is a prerequisite for reliable downstream tasks such as anomaly detection and maintenance planning, because normal signal patterns can vary substantially with operating context. However, discovering discrete regimes from unlabelled, high-dimensional multivariate time series (MVTS) remains challenging, particularly when dominant categorical variables induce shortcut learning and structural missingness precludes reliable interpolation. To address these issues, this study proposes Masked Invariant Information Clustering (Masked IIC), a self-supervised clustering framework that extends IIC by integrating suppression-based masking into mutual-information estimation. Stochastic masking mitigates shortcut learning caused by dominant categorical variables, while deterministic structural masking handles missing-value patterns without requiring interpolation. Quantitative validation on labelled proxy datasets and application to a real-world glass melting furnace show that the framework can recover regime-relevant structure without label supervision and reveal operationally meaningful regime transitions. A remaining limitation is that the number of clusters and the interpretation of discovered regimes require domain expertise. Nevertheless, Masked IIC provides a practical framework for exploratory regime discovery in industrial MVTS.

Title: Quality and total value optimisation in Markovian tandem queues with time-dependent quality deterioration
Authors: Yaron Yeger, Ruth Sagron, Uri Yechiali
Affiliations: Tel-Aviv University; Jerusalem College of Technology
Abstract: We consider a tandem production line consisting of n Markovian single-server sites, where a product's quality deteriorates with its traversal time. Given an overall service-rate capacity, we determine the optimal capacity allocation among the queues that maximises product's final quality. We show that under light workload, the optimal allocation is governed solely by the deterioration rates, allocating higher service-rate to faster deteriorating sites. As the system's load increases, the allocation shifts towards a balanced distribution. Further, we consider two variants of associated costs. First, we incorporate heterogeneous operating costs and find the optimal allocation maximising the product's final quality under a limited budget. Second, since quality-driven capacity allocation reduces sojourn time at one queue but increases it at others, we incorporate sojourn time costs and obtain optimal allocation maximising product's total value. Then, we quantify the trade-off between a marginal change in quality deterioration rate at site i, and a marginal change in sojourn cost rate at site j, showing that it is a function of the final quality and the deterioration rate in site i. However, as the system approaches saturation, the impact of individual deterioration or cost rates becomes negligible, and the trade-off diminishes.

Title: Integrating scenario analyses and risk preferences into carbon-regulated supply chains: a dynamic repeated game-theoretic optimisation approach
Authors: Yifan Xin, Ismail M. Ali, Yangyan Shi, Ripon K. Chakrabortty
Affiliations: UNSW Canberra at ADFA; Macquarie University
Abstract: To remain competitive while meeting sustainability goals, manufacturers' supply chain models subject to carbon regulation and serving eco-conscious markets need to adjust their production and abatement choices dynamically. However, existing models ignore how endogenous risk preferences and exogenous scenario uncertainty combine to drive these strategic shifts. This paper integrates Scenario Analyses and Risk Preferences – risk-averse, risk-neutral, and risk-seeking behaviours under optimistic, neutral, and pessimistic market scenarios – into a Repeated Carbon Game-theoretic (SA-RP-RCG) framework for a carbon-regulated supply chain model. This model applies repeated-game logic to decompose long-term dynamics into a series of non-convex Mixed-Integer Quadratically Constrained Programming (MIQCP) sub-problems, each of which performs an optimisation trade-off between profitability and emissions. Numerical results from the e-scooter industry show that production increases only when subsidies accompany moderate carbon taxes, thereby widening profit gaps in favour of carbon-efficient industry leaders, yet allowing mid-range manufacturers to narrow the gap if they invest early. Moderate risk tolerance yields stable performance, whereas excessive risk-seeking reduces returns for carbon-efficient manufacturers. Less carbon-efficient manufacturers can improve their position by adopting bolder strategies, such as risk-seeking. These findings help asymmetric manufacturers align their decisions with evolving market signals and policy interventions while selecting an appropriate risk posture.

Title: GRAPHINE: enhancing spatiotemporal supply chain forecasting using virtual node-augmented graph diffusion for improved fuel efficiency
Authors: Abdulelah S. Alshehri, Azmine Toushik Wasi, Mahfuz Ahmed Anik, MD Shafikul Islam, Mohamed Kamel Hadj-Kali
Affiliations: King Saud University; Shahjalal University of Science and Technology; Louisiana State University
Abstract: Spatiotemporal forecasting in supply chain networks demands modelling complex spatial dependencies and nonlinear temporal dynamics. Traditional models often fail to capture the heterogeneity, structural sparsity, and long-term dependencies of real-world supply chains. To address this, we propose GRAPHINE, a Virtual Node Diffusion-Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network tailored for supply chain forecasting. GRAPHINE leverages diffusion-based learning, using bidirectional random walks to model spatial relations and a recurrent encoder-decoder with scheduled sampling to capture temporal patterns. It introduces virtual nodes to aggregate global context and applies a learnable gating mechanism that allows each node to regulate global influence based on local features, preventing oversmoothing and preserving specificity. Evaluated on the SCG dataset for demand and inventory forecasting, GRAPHINE achieves reductions of 38.71% in MSE and of 21.71% in RMSE over state-of-the-art baselines, which may imply potential reductions in fuel use on the order of 5.3% in scenario-specific settings under commonly used elasticity assumptions in logistics planning. GRAPHINE thus establishes a new decision-aid framework for applying advanced spatiotemporal graph neural architectures to complex production and supply chain problems, with tangible implications for production planning, operational cost efficiency, and environmental sustainability.

Title: ALFA DT: a digital twin for assembly line fitness analytics
Authors: Omar Makke, Oleg Gusikhin, S. Ehsan Hashemi-Petroodi, Dmitry Ivanov
Affiliations: Ford Motor Company; KEDGE Business School; Berlin School of Economics and Law
Abstract: This paper presents ALFA DT, a Digital Twin (DT) designed for Assembly Line Fitness Analytics (ALFA) to support descriptive, predictive, and prescriptive analytics for assembly line performance. The paper details the digitalisation of the assembly line process, focussing on generating digital models of operator walk patterns and creating task precedence constraints. Two algorithms are proposed, one called Walk Pattern (WP) for the digitalisation of operator walk patterns in the line and another called BiDirectional Precedence Miner (BDPM) algorithm for the precedence graph generation considering quick and frequent product model evolution, which are two of main challenges in current industries. The implementation of ALFA DT is based on the UNITY game engine, leveraged for its visualisation and animation capabilities, multi-platform deployment, and collaborative environment. The proposed DT provides an efficient tool for analyzing, forecasting, and optimising assembly line performance. ALFA DT integrates real-time data and learns from aggregated system behaviour to support predictive insights and proactive decision-making. By serving as a single source of relevant data with an interactive visual interface, it facilitates advanced analytics applications, allowing users to easily validate and modify proposed solutions. ALFA DT has been applied on our real automotive assembly setting and the findings indicate that it improves operational decision-making by improving data accessibility and visualisation quality. The paper discusses several use cases of ALFA DT, including operator work pattern analysis, workcells' layout optimisation, simultaneous assembly line balancing and layout adjustment, and predicting operator overload.

Title: Demand management and forecasting in pharmaceutical and vaccine supply chains: a review and conceptual framework
Authors: Oussema Omri, Nadine Kafa, M. Zied Babai, Asmae El Mokrini, Zied Jemai
Affiliations: Université Paris-Saclay; Centre of Excellence for Supply Chain Innovation and Transportation (CESIT), KEDGE Business School; International University of Rabat; University of Tunis El'Manar
Abstract: Despite the wide range of forecasting approaches developed over the past decades, research addressing pharmaceutical and vaccine supply chains (P&VSCs) remains relatively limited compared with other industries, although recent years have witnessed more studies in this area. This article systematically reviews the literature on demand management and forecasting in P&VSCs published since 2010 to identify key methodological and contextual gaps. While traditional approaches continue to prevail, recent studies have introduced intelligent approaches to address demand volatility and data complexity. However, several important dimensions remain underexplored, including demand intermittency and aggregation, product lifecycle stages, branded versus generic dynamics, and the incorporation of external demand drivers. Moreover, existing studies primarily focus on forecast accuracy, with limited attention to forecast utility, particularly its economic implications, and a weak alignment with strategic, tactical, and operational decision-making. Fragmentation across supply chain actors and forecasting levels further limits responsiveness, especially in low- and middle-income countries. To address these gaps, the article proposes a multi-layered forecasting framework tailored to P&VSCs that supports data preparation, product segmentation, method selection, and performance evaluation. By emphasising explainability, vertical and horizontal forecast integration, and economic relevance, this article provides actionable insights for researchers and decision-makers seeking to improve P&VSCs performance.

Title: Designing urban heat logistics networks from data center thermal recovery
Authors: Imen Sakji, Nadia Ndhaief, Nidhal Rezg
Affiliations: Université de Lorraine, Metz, France; Institut en Innovation Logistique
Abstract: In a context of resource scarcity, climate change, and energy transition, this study proposes a logistics-based approach to meet residential heating needs by recovering waste heat from data centers. An optimisation framework is developed to allocate and distribute this energy within a smart urban heat network. The system integrates a heat pump and thermal storage to enhance efficiency and reduce auxiliary heating. The mathematical model manages heat flows while accounting for distance-dependent transmission losses, demand prioritisation (e.g. critical versus standard buildings), and storage operations. Heat is conveyed through an insulated pipeline network requiring coordinated control to limit losses. An illustrative case study inspired by the urban context of Metz, France, is used to demonstrate the practical applicability of the proposed framework. In this scenario, heat from a local data center is assumed to be routed via a 1,000 m insulated pipeline, a heat pump, and a thermal storage unit to supply the I2L engineering school. The parameter values are calibrated based on realistic technical and operational considerations representative of similar urban heat recovery contexts. Results show reductions in heating costs and CO2 emissions, confirming the viability of this circular energy logistics system and its contribution to low-carbon urban infrastructure.

Title: Simulation-based planning system for a power to methanol supply chain
Authors: Yohanes Kristianto, Niels Gorm Malý Rytter, Rui Goncalves, Melika Sadat Taslimi, Ali Khosravi
Affiliations: University of Southern Denmark (SDU)
Abstract: The synthesis of e-methanol (MeOH) from green H2 and CO2 using renewable electricity represents a promising pathway for sustainable fuel production. However, integrated production planning and supply chain coordination in Power-to-Methanol (PtM) systems remain largely unexplored. This study develops a simulation–optimisation framework for evaluating production planning, inventory control, and logistics coordination strategies in multi-echelon PtM supply chains. The framework captures interactions among key stakeholders, including CO2 suppliers, MeOH distributors, and logistics providers, and incorporates alternative operational strategies for hydrogen production, such as Model Predictive Control (MPC) and the Silver–Meal heuristic. The framework is applied to a real-world PtM case study to assess the techno-economic performance of alternative operational configurations. Results demonstrate that coordinated production planning and energy-aware operational strategies significantly improve economic performance by increasing Net Present Value (NPV) and shortening break-even periods (BEP). Sensitivity analysis further indicates that electricity price variability is the dominant factor influencing PtM profitability.

Title: Blood supply chain design in disaster management: a comparison of risk-averse measures in robust optimisation approaches
Authors: Komlanvi Parfait Ametana, Mehdi Amiri-Aref, Olga Battaïa, Francois Clautiaux, Boris Detienne, Laurent Facq
Affiliations: Univ. Bordeaux, CNRS, INRIA, Bordeaux INP, IMB, UMR 5251; Kedge Business School
Abstract: Disasters severely disrupt blood supply chains, challenging healthcare systems to ensure timely and equitable access to blood products. This study investigates the design of disaster-responsive blood supply chains through a two-stage, multi-period stochastic optimisation framework that explicitly incorporates decision-makers' risk aversion. The model aims to minimise unmet demand under uncertainty and budget constraints, using mean-Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) and worst-case risk measures. Computational experiments conducted on synthetic instances of varying scenario structures show that the mean-CVaR formulation outperforms alternative approaches in 95-99% of the tested cases in terms of balancing expected performance and risk exposure. To address computational complexity, decomposition-based solution methods are developed, enabling the solution of large-scale instances with up to 300 scenarios, which are otherwise intractable using monolithic formulations. A sensitivity analysis, complemented by a case instance, provides insights into the influence of risk parameters and budget levels on preparedness and response decisions. The results underline the critical role of budget availability in determining system performance, while demonstrating that risk-averse formulations allow explicit control of extreme shortages without compromising average outcomes. The study contributes to the literature on humanitarian logistics and healthcare operations by integrating risk-aware modelling and scalable solution techniques for disaster preparedness planning.

Title: An adaptive genetic algorithm with parameter control based on dynamic fitness landscape analysis for operation sequencing in CAPP
Authors: Jianping Dou, Pingyuan Wang, Muhammad Waheed Afzal, Jun Li
Affiliations: Southeast University
Abstract: In Industry 4.0, customised product volatility makes operation sequencing (OS) in CAPP frequently demanded. Solving the NP-hard OS problems requires an adaptive genetic algorithm (AGA) with robust performance and no tedious tuning, which is currently absent. Considering dynamic fitness landscape analysis (DFLA) enables measurement of GA’s parameters during search, we design an AGA with parameter control incorporating the feedback information from population fitness and DFLA. For the AGA, the direct encoding of feasible operation sequence and the precedence-constraint satisfaction method make it search in feasible solution space. In the AGA, the mutation rate is updated online by the population diversity, and four crossovers are online switched in a greedy fashion via the judgment combining population diversity and evolvability from DFLA. To improve efficiency and exploitation ability, the path-relinking local search is adaptively applied by the maximum unchanged generation of an individual’s fitness. The AGA is compared with state-of-the-art metaheuristic algorithms (MAs), including particle swarm optimisation, harmony search, two recent GAs and a self-adaptive GA, to verify its effectiveness and merits against five OS cases and six randomly generated OS problems. The comparative results show that the AGA outperforms existing MAs for solution quality, and illustrate its robust global search ability.

Title: Joint stocker placement and scheduling in automated material handling-enabled reentrant hybrid flow shops
Authors: Chun-Cheng Lin, Shi-Yu Zhang, Yi-Chun Peng, I.-Hsuan Lin
Affiliations: National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University; National Chin-Yi University of Technology; Asia University; Chung Yuan Christian University
Abstract: Automated material handling systems (AMHS) in reentrant hybrid flow shops (RHFS) are widely used in high-value manufacturing, where jobs revisit processing stages for rework or inspection, increasing the risk of work-in-progress (WIP) congestion. Existing studies commonly mitigate this issue using machine buffers and stockers but typically assume a one-to-one correspondence between stations and stockers, despite industrial evidence indicating that fewer stockers may suffice. Moreover, heterogeneity in station utilisation suggests that stocker placement decisions can critically affect system performance, yet this aspect remains underexplored. This study investigates a joint stocker placement and scheduling problem for AMHS-enabled RHFS, explicitly considering reduced stocker availability and flexible allocation across stations. The problem integrates structural resource configuration with operational scheduling decisions and is shown to be NP-hard. An improved hybrid monkey search algorithm is developed to efficiently solve the integrated problem. Computational experiments demonstrate that coordinated stocker placement and scheduling significantly reduce makespan compared with conventional uniform allocation assumptions. The results further reveal that placing stockers at stations one stage ahead of first-entry stations yields notable performance improvements, particularly under high utilisation and large-scale settings. These findings provide practical insights for configuring temporary storage resources in reentrant production systems.

Title: Investigating total closed-loop supply chain variance amplification using a Monte-Carlo system dynamics method
Authors: Shupeng Huang, Junyi Lin, Borja Ponte
Affiliations: Chengdu University of Technology; Xi’an Jiaotong-Liverpool University; University of Oviedo
Abstract: Unwanted fluctuations and instability in operations can significantly increase the operational costs of closed-loop supply chains (CLSCs). Given the coexistence of variance amplifications of order, on-hand inventory, and work-in-process inventory in CLSCs, measuring the overall system variance amplification to support coordinated production and inventory decisions can support performance improvement. However, existing research has largely focused on variance amplification in order and on-hand inventory volumes, ignoring work-in-process variance which can also have significant economic implications. Also, most relevant studies examined the behaviour of each variance separately or adopted a weighted average of inventory and order variances with fixed, predetermined weights. Motivated by these gaps, we propose a novel System Dynamics Stochastic rank Index (SDSI) approach to analyse the total variance amplification of CLSCs. The results showed that different inventory control strategies should be implemented based on different weights among variance amplifications. However, the values of manufacturing lead times, remanufacturing lead times, and return rate that minimise the total variance amplification remain similar under different relative weights. Furthermore, the lead time and yield paradox phenomena were observed under the SDSI framework, suggesting relevant trade-offs between economic and sustainable operations in CLSCs.

Title: Enhanced warehouse sustainability through material handling battery charging strategies: an economic and environmental empirically grounded analytical model
Authors: Luca Cannava, Saverio Ferraro, Filippo De Carlo, Sara Perotti
Affiliations: Politecnico di Milano; University of Florence
Abstract: The demand for efficient warehouse operations has boosted the need for improved performance in material handling activities, which still largely rely on forklifts and significantly contribute to warehouse energy consumption. Despite the interest in sustainability-related challenges, the literature still lacks analytical models based on empirical data supporting practitioners in selecting the most suitable battery charging strategy for material handling equipment (MHE). To address this gap, this study proposes an empirically grounded analytical model considering opportunity charging (OC) strategy and integration of a battery energy storage system (BESS). OC aims to utilise surplus energy generated from renewables, such as photovoltaic (PV) systems, while BESS focuses on storing PV energy surplus for optimised charging times. The methodology adopted combines the development of analytical models with empirical data obtained from publicly available reports, standards and databases. The model is applied to four industrial business cases, where economic and environmental impacts of OC and BESS are assessed. Findings suggest that OC is effective in warehouses with high PV energy surplus generation, while BESS provides benefits for warehouses low PV energy surplus. The model offers a framework and multiple real-world applications for supporting practitioners in their decision-making process towards sustainable MHE and Net-Zero energy goal.

Title: Counterfactual multi-agent reinforcement learning for causal defect analysis in manufacturing environments
Authors: Sudhanshu Srivastava, Faisal Aqlan, Pratik J. Parikh, Md Noor-E-Alam
Affiliations: University of Louisville; Northeastern University
Abstract: Effective defect management is critical for maintaining product quality in today’s manufacturing environments. However, traditional analysis often relies on correlational models that fail to capture the underlying complexity of defect causation. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel framework, Counterfactual Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Soft-Masked Vector to DAG (CF-MARL-SMV2D). The proposed framework features a collaborative multi-agent policy that explores the causal Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) space. The framework integrates a learnable domain-informed soft mask to encode expert knowledge and a counterfactual-based reward function to ensure robust causal identification. The framework was validated using a case study from a leading computer server manufacturer. Empirical results demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art causal discovery algorithms, achieving Structural Hamming Distance of 3.90 and low False Discovery Rate. Further, the resulting causal feature set enables superior downstream root cause identification with a predictive accuracy of 0.96.

Title: AI-based color-matching system for cosmetic manufacturing
Authors: Seongho Cho, Changwan Jo, Byengsu Joung, Kyungwon Kang, Jinu Im, Sangchul Park
Affiliations: Ajou University; Amorepacific Corporation; MU Manufacturing Technology Team, Amorepacific Corporation
Abstract: This study presents an AI-based automated color-matching system that uses a deep neural network (DNN) to replace manual iterative adjustments in color formulation. An on-site industrial dataset is collected from a cosmetic manufacturing system consisting of pigment and non-colorant material compositions, along with corresponding CIE L∗ a∗ b∗ (CIELAB) values. Based on this dataset, we develop a Sparsity-Aware Attention Network (SAAN) capable of predicting color outcomes under material variability and varying material combinations. By integrating the SAAN with an Automated Formulation Search Module, the proposed system is capable of automatically searching and assessing candidate formulations to match a given target color. The system is deployed in a real cosmetic manufacturing setting. Through this system, the cosmetics manufacturer reduced color-matching time and beaker-working iterations in an actual production environment. The system also reduce material and labour costs, thereby demonstrating clear practical benefits.

Title: Optimal patching policy for warrantied smart products considering user adoption and delayed installation
Authors: Le Gao, Anshu Dai, Zhaomin Zhang, Zhen He, Avinash Kumar Shrivastava, Shuguang He
Affiliations: Tianjin University; Tianjin University of Finance and Economics; Civil Aviation University of China; IMI Kolkata
Abstract: Smart products integrating hardware and software components are increasingly common. Although pre-release testing improves reliability, residual software faults often remain after launch and may cause failures in the post-release phase. To mitigate these risks, developers typically issue patches and provide warranty services. However, most existing studies assume prompt patch adoption and installation, an assumption that rarely holds in practice. This study develops a patching policy for warrantied smart products that explicitly accounts for user adoption and delayed installation behaviour. User response is modelled as a two-stage stochastic process: adoption follows Bernoulli trials with type-specific Beta-distributed probabilities, while installation delays follow user-type-dependent distributions. Users are classified into active and passive groups to capture behavioural heterogeneity. The model incorporates patch coverage effects on fault detection and hardware–software interaction in failure risk. The objective is to determine the optimal number of patches that minimises expected total warranty cost. A Monte Carlo–based algorithm is developed, with analytical results under a simplified setting. Numerical results show that user behaviour significantly affects optimal patching decisions and warranty costs, and that optimal policies may differ markedly from those under full and immediate patch installation. These findings offer managerial insights for designing robust patching policies under behavioural uncertainty.

Title: Order planning for manufacturing systems with load sequence-dependent degradation under human errors and imperfect inspection
Authors: Hongyan Dui, Hengbo Wang, Meng Liu, Rukun Wang, Nuo Zhao
Affiliations: Zhengzhou University; Beihang University; Institute of Nuclear Industry Standardisation
Abstract: Daily order planning is the core of dynamic decision-making that ensures the reliability and cost-effectiveness of manufacturing system delivery. However, order planning faces significant challenges due to the interplay of load sequence-dependent degradation, human errors, and imperfect inspection. The interplay of these factors introduces significant uncertainty, often leading to overestimated system performance and suboptimal planning outcomes. Thus, a comprehensive order planning framework is developed in this paper to optimise order scheduling. First, an Extended Stochastic Flow Manufacturing Network (ESFMN) model is introduced to characterise the dynamic interactions among processing machines, inspection machines, buffers, operators, and heterogeneous feedstocks (qualified and unqualified feedstocks) in manufacturing systems with load sequence-dependent degradation. Second, a semi-Markov model is employed to evaluate system mission performance that combines human errors and imperfect inspection. Third, a Clustering-Enhanced NSGA-II (CNSGA-II) algorithm is developed to tackle the order planning problem through the simultaneous optimisation of mission performance and cost. Comparative experimental results demonstrate that proposed order planning framework outperforms several advanced algorithms, including Memetic-NSGA-II, Reinforcement Learning-NSGA-II, Greedy algorithm-NSGA-II, and NSGA-II. Through a case study of a servo valve spool manufacturing system, the framework's effectiveness in practical applications is validated, confirming its ability to achieve reliable and cost-effective order planning.

Title: Change Begins With Us: Leveraging Cognition to Cultivate Meaning and Motivate Action
Authors: Stanley E. Fawcett, A. Michael Knemeyer, Carl Marcus Wallenburg, Mehrdokht Pournader, Matthias Klumpp
Affiliations: Logistikum at the University of Applied Sciences, Upper Austria Steyr Austria; Fisher College of Business Ohio State University Columbus Ohio USA; WHU – Otto Beisheim School of Management Düsseldorf Germany; University of Melbourne Melbourne Australia; University of Bremen, Germany and Politecnico di Milano Milan Italy

Title: Integer programming for multi-mode resource-constrained project scheduling
Authors: Nicklas Klein
Abstract: Abstract Project scheduling is a vital management task in many organizations across various industries. A project typically consists of activities that require time and scarce resources for execution. In many projects, there are trade-offs between the resource requirements and the duration of activities. These trade-offs can be represented via multiple execution modes of activities, which are considered in the multi-mode resource-constrained project scheduling problem (MRCPSP). The MRCPSP comprises determining the activities’ start times and execution modes to minimize the project completion time while respecting precedence relations and availabilities of renewable and nonrenewable resources. In this paper, we propose several discrete-time (DT) and one continuous-time (CT) mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model for the MRCPSP based on models for the single-mode resource-constrained project scheduling problem (RCPSP). We first analyze the models’ LP relaxations and show an equivalence between DT models. Then, we compare the computational performance of the models on benchmark instances. Our results indicate that the proposed CT model outperforms the state-of-the-art models on large problem instances and problem instances with relatively long activity durations, while it is competitive on smaller problem instances. A possible explanation for this outperformance is that the LP relaxations of the proposed CT model can be solved considerably faster than the LP relaxations of the state-of-the-art models.

Title: Schedule risk analysis for project control with risk interactions
Authors: Yuxuan Song, Mario Vanhoucke
Abstract: Abstract Due to the uncertainty and risks in projects, Schedule Risk Analysis (SRA) has been developed to measure the activity sensitivity for taking corrective actions during project control. With the growing complexity of projects, the interaction between risks has received increasing research attention in project management, conceptualized as a risk interaction network. In such a network, the risk can affect the project objective not only through its occurrence but also by triggering interrelated risks. However, previous studies on SRA were mostly dedicated to designing activity sensitivity metrics using the project network, ignoring the source of activity risks, which may result in inaccurate activity sensitivity information and invalid corrective actions. In this paper, we integrate the risk interaction network with the project network for schedule risk analysis and project control under risk interactions. Subsequently, a novel interaction-oriented sensitivity metric is proposed and a simulation-based control model is developed to facilitate corrective action decisions. Finally, a computational experiment is conducted to investigate the ability of the proposed metric in identifying sensitive activities under risk interaction. In addition, the experiment also tests the performance of three activity selection strategies, namely preventive strategy, interventive strategy, and hybrid strategy. The results show the proposed activity sensitivity metric not only enhances the control effectiveness but also exhibits remarkable reliability across both serial projects and parallel projects. The results also indicate that a mix of strategies is preferred depending on the project network structure and the timing of control action taking.

Title: A purely buffer-based approach to the proactive and reactive resource-constrained project scheduling problem
Authors: Yanfei Chen, Erik Demeulemeester, Jannik Matuschke
Abstract: Real-world projects frequently face uncertainties that can lead to significant delays and cost overruns. The proactive and reactive resource-constrained project scheduling problem (PR-RCPSP), introduced by Davari and Demeulemeester (Journal of Scheduling 22:211–237, 2019), integrates proactive and reactive scheduling to address activity duration uncertainties in a comprehensive manner. This paper proposes a novel purely buffer-based approach to solving the PR-RCPSP, emphasizing the practical and theoretical importance of buffer-based reactions. First, we introduce a method for generating a sufficient selection that facilitates the construction of high-quality schedule pools. Second, we develop a proactive scheduling heuristic termed the reversed starting time criticality (reversed STC), which systematically inserts buffers to enhance schedule robustness. Third, we design a reactive scheduling mechanism, the buffer-based schedule generation scheme (buffer-based SGS), which ensures that all transitions between schedules are buffer-based reactions. These innovations collectively form a unified framework for optimizing PR-policies under uncertainty. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art alternatives in terms of computational efficiency and cost reduction, particularly in scenarios with high fixed reaction costs or challenging resource constraints. The findings provide actionable managerial insights, offering project managers a systematic and efficient methodology for navigating uncertainty in complex scheduling environments.

Title: The impact of the number of preemptions in resource-constrained project scheduling problems with time-varying resources: computational experiments and a case study
Authors: Ilaria Salvadori, Alessandro Agnetis
Abstract: Abstract This paper addresses the preemptive version of the resource-constrained project scheduling problem (RCPSP), with the aim of assessing the impact of the number of preemptions on project makespan. In fact, preempting some activity can reduce the makespan, but it may have the undesired effect of requiring a surplus of coordination in the project team. Hence, we consider the bicriteria problem of minimizing makespan and number of preemptions, and using a suitable integer linear programming formulation we compute the Pareto front for a sample of 30-job benchmark instances. Resource availability can either remain constant or can vary over time (according to a known schedule), as typical of situations in which the same resources are shared among various projects. We perform a detailed analysis of the impact of preemptions on project makespan, and how it is related to structural parameters of RCPSP instances. Among other results, we find that most often very few preemptions are enough to achieve most of the benefit. Also, the utility in introducing preemptions is significantly higher when resources vary over time. The proposed solution approach is then applied to a case study in Information Technology (IT) project management, showing how preemptions and efficiency can be traded off in practice.

Title: Scheduling a shared resource among parallel dedicated machines: a red-blue knapsack modeling approach
Authors: Federico Della Croce, Andrea Grosso, Vincent T’kindt, T. Ciron
Abstract: We consider a scheduling problem with dedicated parallel machines and a shared resource. Each job to be scheduled is assigned to a specific machine and can possibly be rejected if it cannot be scheduled within a predetermined time frame. Some of the jobs need an additional shared resource to be processed: this resource has to be “conservatively” scheduled, i.e must be assigned to each machine in a single non-overlapping time window. The goal is to schedule the largest possible amount of jobs (weighted by priority) in the given time frame. The problem originates from an operating room scheduling application and can be modelled as a multiple knapsack problem with additional constraints related to the scheduling of the shared resource. We establish the complexity of the problem, develop an effective MILP model and a non standard column generation approach that considerably shorten the computation times required to compute optimal solutions.

Title: A HARQ-based framework for forecasting large covariance matrices using high-frequency data

Title: The carbon damage of services-led growth: Structure-aware baselines for the social cost of carbon

Title: Institutional race-to-the-bottom and asymmetric market synergy: Spatial linkages and carbon emissions in China's energy-intensive industries

Title: Adoption of blockchain technology and quality testing in agricultural supply chains: addressing cascade threat and moral hazard
Authors: Qing Li, Khaled Hadj-Hamou, Yacine Rekik
Affiliations: Emlyon Business School; INSA Lyon, Université Lumière Lyon 2, Université Lyon 1, DISP UR4570
Abstract: This paper studies the implications of cascade threats and moral hazard in a multi-source, multi-echelon agricultural supply chain consisting of farmers, a collector, and a buyer. Using a game-theoretic model, we analyse and compare three scenarios: one without a blockchain-enabled traceability system (Scenario N) and two with the traceability system, without and with a cost-sharing contract (Scenarios B and BS). We show that blockchain traceability expands production by mitigating cascade threats, yet it can also lower equilibrium product quality. This finding challenges the common assumption that transparency automatically improves quality. Quality declines when the cascade-threat-mitigation effect dominates the moral-hazard-mitigation effect, which occurs when testing is costly or the potential market is small. When testing is inexpensive and the potential market is large, blockchain instead improves quality. To address the quality decline, we introduce a cost-sharing contract that motivates farmers to improve quality. The contract raises all members' expected profits as the sharing ratio increases and makes adoption more attractive to the buyer. However, whether it restores quality to its level without traceability depends on the testing cost and the potential market size. The main results are robust to farmer-specific quality decisions, scenario-dependent testing intensities, and an endogenously designed contract.

Title: Forecasting US state-level volatilities with local and global EPUs: A mixed-frequency shrinkage combination approach
Authors: V. Candila, O. Cepni, G.M. Gallo, R. Gupta

Title: Does inequality harm the climate? An agent-based model with endogenous climate policy
Authors: Fiona Borsetzky, Dirk Kohlweyer

Title: Drone delivery in urban retail operations: Fulfillment competition, ground-delivery workload, and retailer–logistics provider interactions

Title: Left in charge: Political rule and the rise of local welfare
Authors: Casper Worm Hansen, Peter Sandholt Jensen
Abstract: We study how institutional constraints on executive selection shape redistributive policy using a 1919 Danish reform that allowed town councils to democratically elect mayors. Although the reform applied uniformly, it made left-wing executive control feasible, especially where prior Social Democratic support was strong. Using 1917 vote shares interacted with the post-reform period, we identify the causal effect of Social Democratic mayors on local public finance. Social Democratic rule led to substantial increases in social spending, particularly poor relief and public assistance, financed mainly through higher direct taxes, with no robust evidence of adverse effects on local economic activity

Title: Central Bank Reserves and the Balance Sheet of Banks
Authors: Hans Gersbach, Jean-Charles Rochet, Ernst-Ludwig von Thadden
Abstract: We introduce a tractable model of the two-tier monetary system with heterogeneous agents and incomplete markets. We use this model to characterize the dynamics of bank lending under general fiscal and monetary policy and derive the welfare optimal level of Central Bank reserves and the optimal interest rate on reserves. We also identify a new risk channel of monetary policy. In the model, banks have a dual role as loan providers and money creators, and cannot fully diversify credit risk. Central Bank reserves are used to settle interbank claims and serve as a safe asset, thereby buffering risks for banks. We show how the Central Bank and the Treasury can implement any desired allocation by setting interest rates, issuing a particular amount of reserves, and imposing taxes, and show that uncoordinated policy responses to shocks by the Central Bank alone may cause sub-optimal outcomes and significant instability.

Title: Optimizing Railcar Shunting Operations to Create Outbound Trains in a Stub Yard
Authors: Ruonan Zhao, Joseph Geunes, Xiaofeng Nie
Affiliations: Wm Michael Barnes '64 Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering Texas A&M University College Station Texas USA; Broadwell College of Business and Economics Fayetteville State University Fayetteville North Carolina USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT A typical freight railyard contains multiple tracks used for storage, classification, and outbound train assembly. In a railyard with a stub configuration, classification tracks are only accessible from one end of the track, requiring retrieval of railcars in last‐in, first‐out order when assembling outbound trains. Individual railcar storage locations on classification tracks are often determined before knowledge of their destination locations is known, giving rise to railcar shunting or switching problems that require retrieving subsets of cars distributed throughout the yard to assemble outbound trains. To address this combinatorially challenging problem class, we propose a large‐scale mixed‐integer programming model that tracks railcar movements and corresponding costs over a finite planning horizon. The model permits simultaneous movement of multiple car groups via a locomotive and seeks to minimize repositioning costs. We also provide a dynamic programming formulation of the problem, demonstrate the ‐hardness of the corresponding optimization problem, and present an adaptive railcar grouping dynamic programming (ARG‐DP) heuristic, which groups railcars with common destinations for efficient moves. Average results from a series of numerical experiments demonstrate the efficiency and quality of the ARG‐DP algorithm in both simulated yards and a real yard. On average, across 60 test cases of simulated yards, the ARG‐DP algorithm obtains solutions 355 times faster than solving the mixed‐integer programming model using a commercial solver, while finding an optimal solution in of the instances and maintaining an average optimality gap of 6.65%. In 10 cases based on the Gaia railyard in Portugal, the ARG‐DP algorithm achieves solutions 229 times faster on average, finding an optimal solution in of the instances with an average optimality gap of 6.90%.

Title: A data-driven machine learning approach to typhoon evacuation decision-making and system reliability evaluation of stochastic evacuation networks
Authors: Ding-Hsiang Huang, Kai-Hsiang Huang, Yi-Kuei Lin
Abstract: Abstract With the increasing frequency and intensity of typhoon disasters, developing effective evacuation decision-making systems is critical for ensuring public safety. This paper proposes a data-driven approach that integrates machine learning (ML) classification models with system reliability evaluation to support typhoon evacuation operations. We address three key challenges: (1) predicting evacuation necessity based on meteorological data, (2) modeling uncertainty in evacuation networks, and (3) quantifying evacuation feasibility under resource constraints. First, the Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE) is applied to handle class imbalance in historical typhoon evacuation data, and a Random Forest classifier is trained to automatically predict evacuation requirements. Second, the evacuation operation is modeled as a stochastic evacuation network (SEN) with multistate travel times reflecting road damage uncertainty. Third, system reliability is adopted as a quantitative performance indicator defined as the probability of successfully evacuating all affected residents within time and resource constraints. The methodology is demonstrated using Typhoon Gaemi, which struck Taiwan in 2024, in Dongshi district, Chiayi County. Evacuation commanders can dynamically adjust decisions regarding announcement timing, vehicle allocation, and route selection based on real-time meteorological data and reliability assessments. The integrated approach enables more comprehensive and data-informed evacuation planning to enhance response effectiveness.

Title: Consumer behaviour and the uptake of solar panels
Authors: Shivani Taneja, Filip Mandys
Abstract: Clean renewable energy technologies contribute towards both improving energy efficiency and reducing emissions, yet household adoption rates remain low. This paper analyses the impact of economic, household, environmental, and dwelling factors on the uptake of solar photovoltaic (PV) and thermal panels, using the Understanding Society dataset, and applying the adaptive Lasso method and a random effects logistic regression model. We find that solar panel adoption is primarily driven by electricity prices, rural location, number of rooms, and environmental factors. Living in a rural location, having one more room, and a rise in electricity prices by 10 percentage points increase the odds of PV panel adoption by 87%, 19%, and 7%, respectively. Diffusion of thermal panels is driven by similar factors, with both technologies strongly affected by environmental aspects - owners of electric vehicles are 2.4 times more likely to be interested in solar technologies. The counterfactuals and predictions made using the discrete-time hazard survival model illustrate that even modest subsidies for PV panels would significantly accelerate adoption rates, both historically and in the future. Our results highlight the need for solar technology investment, subsidies, and policy frameworks, that would encourage more optimally targeted policies and contribute to reaching net-zero emissions by 2050.
