Title: From farm to fine dining: trust is the backbone of luxury food supply chains
Authors: Kateryna Merkulova Legrand, Alessio Castello, Maria Kreuzer
Affiliations: International University of Monaco-Omnes Education , Monaco-Ville; MCI Management Center Innsbruck , Innsbruck
Abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate how trust is built, maintained and challenged along the understudied luxury food supply chain, which is characterised by more personal transactions and higher quality stakes than conventional agri-food sectors. Design/methodology/approach Using the French Riviera caviar market as the focal empirical setting, the authors conducted 21 semi-structured narrative interviews with chefs (n = 11), distributors (n = 5), and producers (n = 5) selected through purposive and snowball sampling. The authors analysed the interviews using structuring qualitative content analysis, combining main categories derived from a theory-informed interview guide with inductively developed subcategories. Findings Trust in luxury food supply chains emerges as a relational and symbolic construct, shaped by cultural capital, artisanal values and sustained interpersonal engagement. Participants relied primarily on repeated interaction, personal credibility and proactive transparency, rather than on the transactional, system-based trust models typical of conventional food sectors. Trust expectations vary systematically across supply chain roles, while luxury value is symbolically co-created through shared narratives of rarity, craftsmanship, authenticity and heritage. Trust is also particularly fragile: operational failures can simultaneously undermine relational confidence, personal credibility and the symbolic legitimacy of the product category. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this study offers the first systematic investigation of trust dynamics across the producer–distributor–chef triad in the luxury supply chain. It contributes to the supply chain management literature by empirically specifying how three interdependent trust layers, namely, operational, relational and symbolic, are activated differently in luxury than in conventional contexts, and offers managerial guidance for preserving quality, authenticity and reliability in premium food networks.
Journal: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

Title: A clustering based-approach to analyze centrality of terrorist networks using games with a priori unions
Authors: Encarnación Algaba, Alejandro Saavedra-Nieves, Paula Saavedra-Nieves
Abstract: Intelligence services need to identify the key players in terrorist networks to effectively allocate the surveillance resources according to the risk analysis in the network. Unlike of classical transferable utility games, transferable utility games with a priori unions allow for ranking terrorists in a network incorporating the affinity information through a partition of their members. However, the selection of this (in principle, non-unique) partition is not usually trivial in practice. In this work, we propose a methodological solution to accomplish this task from well-known clustering-graph techniques. Apart from briefly analyzing classical graph clustering methods, a novel and different graph clustering algorithm is introduced to capture the most natural and relevant features of these networks such as communication and hierarchical properties, which play a significant role in its performance. Moreover, with the purpose of describing the influence of the partitions determined from different clustering algorithms, including our new proposal, we compute the Banzhaf–Owen value to provide and compare the final rankings obtained for the Zerkani network. In contrast to the other clustering methods analyzed, with our new proposal, Khalid Zerkani is ranked as the first in the top-ten of the ranking.

Title: Measuring fragmentation risk in European bond markets using machine learning
Authors: Roland Bouillot, Bertrand Candelon, Clemens Kool
Abstract: This paper asks whether machine learning can forecast euro area sovereign bond spreads and whether the resulting forecasts can track financial fragmentation. Using a new high-dimensional monthly dataset of 4948 macro-financial series for ten euro area countries from December 2008 to February 2025, we run a horse race among thirteen machine-learning models and two simple benchmarks, an AR(1) process and a random walk. XGBoost is the strongest machine-learning model and is never significantly outperformed by the other learners. It is not, however, the most accurate one-month-ahead forecaster: under strict out-of-sample re-estimation the AR(1) and the random walk attain lower point-forecast errors in every country. The value of the machine-learning approach lies elsewhere. SHAP decompositions recover the macro-financial drivers of the predicted spreads. The forecasts form the basis of a fragmentation indicator built by clustering predicted spread paths. The indicator reproduces the core-periphery divide in the windows running to 2022. French spreads then decouple from the core after 2023. By 2024–2025 France and Belgium form a distinct cluster, a new source of fragmentation risk with direct implications for the transmission of a single monetary policy.

Title: Reducing perishable food loss through demand forecasting: empirical evidence from the meat industry
Authors: Mirko Mucciarini, Giulia Caselli, Manuel Iori, Marco Lippi
Abstract: Demand forecasting is a critical decision-making task, especially within the perishable food supply chain, where products exhibit highly variable demand patterns and limited shelf lives, often resulting in significant operational challenges as well as food loss and waste. Accurate forecasting is therefore essential for firms seeking to reduce food loss while improving operational efficiency performance and supply chain sustainability, with potential economic benefits. Using the real dataset of a leading company operating in the processed meat industry, this study develops and empirically evaluates a categorisation-based approach to demand forecasting, in which items are grouped by demand pattern and the most effective statistical or machine learning model is selected for each group. We evaluate the operational impact of improved forecasts through a simulation-based analysis on inventory-related indicators, measuring food loss reduction as well as warehouse inventory levels and dynamic production adjustments. Results show significant improvements in the operational and environmental performance of the company, including a 27% average food loss reduction compared to the current state.

Title: Geographic Spillover of Merger Effects Within Retail Chains
Authors: Sunmin Kim
Affiliations: Korea Institute of Public Finance Sejong Republic of Korea
Abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines the role of downstream retail chains in shaping the effects of upstream mergers. Focusing on PepsiCo's bottler acquisitions, I present evidence that the merger effects spilled over within retail chains to stores outside the territory of acquired bottlers. I find that the acquisitions reduced PepsiCo product prices by 4.3% for these outside‐territory stores, with varying magnitudes depending on retail chains' exposures, and by 7.8% for retail chains operating solely inside the territory. This study highlights that ignoring such spillovers may result in an underestimation of merger effects, both in terms of geographic reach and magnitude.

Title: Bayesian Distributionally Robust Variational Inequalities: Regularization and Quantification
Authors: Wentao Ma, Zhiping Chen, Xiaojun Chen
Affiliations: School of Mathematics and Statistics, Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an, Shaanxi 710049, China; and Department of Applied Mathematics, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hong Kong; Department of Applied Mathematics, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hong Kong
Abstract: We propose a Bayesian distributionally robust variational inequality (DRVI) framework that models the data-generating distribution through a finite-mixture family, which allows us to study the DRVI on a tractable finite-dimensional parametric ambiguity set. To address distributional uncertainty, we construct a data-driven ambiguity set with posterior coverage guarantees via Bayesian inference. We also employ a regularization approach to ensure numerical stability. We prove the existence of solutions to the Bayesian DRVI and the asymptotic convergence to a solution as sample size grows to infinity and the regularization parameter goes to zero. Moreover, we derive quantitative stability bounds and finite-sample guarantees under data scarcity and contamination. Numerical experiments on a distributionally robust multiportfolio Nash equilibrium problem validate our theoretical results and demonstrate the robustness and reliability of Bayesian DRVI solutions in practice. Title: Reconceptualizing the role of human values in sustainable transport behavior
Authors: Joanne Sneddon, Joshua Lake, Uwana Evers, Julie Lee
Abstract: Shifting people towards more sustainable modes of transport is essential for decarbonizing the mobility sector, yet the motivational mechanisms underlying these choices remain poorly understood. We draw on the Accessibility-Interpretation-Control (AIC) model to explore how the mechanisms that underlie value-behavior relations can inform sustainable transport research. We empirically explore the AIC interpretation principle to examine whether people attribute human-like values to sustainable transport modes in a manner that reflects the motivational structure of values, how modes of sustainable transport differ in attributed value prioritizations, and whether these attributions mediate relations between personal values and value-expressive reasons for choosing sustainable modes of transport. Survey data from 752 Australian adults measured personal values and, 9-months later, perceptions of sustainable transport modes, including attributed values and reasons for mode choice. Results show that values attributed to both active and public transport modes mirror theoretical trade-offs between higher-order values, consistent with the structure of human values. There is evidence of alignment between personal values and value attributions to the chosen mode; however, this is stronger for active than public transport, suggesting that active transport may be a stronger value instantiation than public transport. There is also evidence of a direct effect of the self-transcendence to self-enhancement values dimension on value-expressive reasons for taking the sustainable transport mode, and an indirect effect through attributed values. These findings highlight the importance of value interpretation processes in sustainable transport behaviour and suggest that interventions may be more effective when they align transport modes with distinct value meanings.

Title: Expertise, signaling and learning in fish auctions
Authors: Ali Vergili, İsa Hafalır
Abstract: Theoretical analyses have demonstrated that in sequential auctions, prices follow a martingale. Yet, empirical observations often indicate varied price points for comparable products. We examine sales of fresh seafood through sequential Dutch auctions at the Sydney Fish Market (SFM), presenting evidence of non-monotonic price trends and investigating the causes of price variations among homogeneous products. With the extensive data set covering over 27 years of transactions at SFM, we address potential endogeneity concerns arising from seafood diversity. Employing the lot fixed-effects approach to standardize transactions, we discern bidding patterns that differ according to bidders’ experience levels. Additionally, our findings highlight evidence of signaling and learning. We infer that the agents’ heterogeneity in the market creates an interactive environment: bidders tend to bid higher when following an experienced leader, but this trend reverses when the initial bid comes from someone not experienced, highlighting how bidders adjust based on signals from others.

Title: Store brand encroachment and manufacturer innovation under different commission design
Authors: Danyang Xu, Jian-Cai Wang, Yao-Yu Wang, Zi-Han Gong
Affiliations: School of Management, Beijing Institute of Technology, and the Sustainable Development Research Institute for Economy and Society of Beijing; Business School, and Research Center for Smarter Supply Chain, Soochow University
Abstract: Online platforms have begun to launch their own store brands while selling manufacturers’ national brands. Recognising that manufacturers often invest in product innovation, platforms have incentives to mimic and merger manufacturers’ successful innovations. Given that such free-riding behaviour may stifle innovation, this has raised serious concerns. This study develops game-theoretic game models to investigate whether store brand encroachment is harmful for manufacturers’ innovation and examine the implications for supply chain members under different commission design. Moreover, by endogenizing the platform’s store band encroachment decision, our model explicitly distinguishes between the feigning encroachment (i.e., threat) and the substantive encroachment (i.e., competition). Results show that, store brand encroachment always reduces manufacturer’s innovation level under exogenous commission scenario, while under endogenous commission scenario, store brand encroachment can motivate the manufacturer to strengthen innovation when the competition level is low and the platform introduces high-quality products. No matter whether the commission fee is exogenous or endogenous, the manufacturer facing the threat of encroachment will increase the innovation level to pre-empt the store brand encroachment as competition intensifies. We also find that, store brand encroachment definitely does harm to the manufacturer and it is detrimental to the platform to some extent under exogenous commission scenario, while under endogenous commission scenario, store brand encroachment will create a win-win situation for the two players under some conditions. The impacts of store brand encroachment on consumer and social welfare depend on the competition level and the quality of store brand products.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Can a reviewing-based contract coordinate a supply chain of mobile apps?
Authors: Priel Levy
Affiliations: Bar-Ilan University
Abstract: Nowadays, app developers perceive the commonly-used revenue-sharing contract as unjust when the sales volume is high, and thus engage in legal battles or try to bypass the platform’s billing system. To address this issue, we propose a new cost-plus contract in which the platform’s income is proportional to its expenses in reviewing the app. The cost of the app’s development, as well as the cost of the reviewing process, are correlated with the app’s quality. Following the stochastic nature of demand, and assuming risk sensitivity of the parties, we bring a game-theoretic analysis of each contract, where demand is sensitive to the app’s selling price and quality level. For the case of risk-neutral parties, we conduct an analytical comparison between the two contracts and show that all measures are higher under the new contract than under the commonly-used contract, except for the platform’s expected profit, which is higher under the latter. For the case of a risk-sensitive developer and risk-neutral platform, and the opposite case, we conduct an extensive numerical analysis and show that the new contract is preferable to the developer, whereas for the platform it is preferable only under certain conditions with regard to the parties’ risk-aversion levels.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Snowplough service area reconfiguration using workload balancing techniques with route optimisation for large municipalities
Authors: Tyler Parsons, Farhad Baghyari, Jaho Seo, Yonatan Yohannes
Affiliations: Ontario Tech University; City of Surrey
Abstract: Snowplowing is a complex, expensive, and mandatory winter fleet operation that benefits municipalities worldwide. In this research, three clustering approaches were used to create new snowplough route configurations for the City of Surrey, Canada, and the Smart Selective Navigator (SSN) method was used to optimise the routes. The three clustering approaches used are the current configuration-based dynamic clustering, static and dynamic clustering, and static and dynamic clustering with depot-to-cluster distance. The first clustering approach uses the existing configuration as a start point and makes minor changes, while the others generate new clusters from scratch with an objective of improving the workload distribution. SSN is a turn-based route optimisation algorithm that was improved by adding advanced turn-tracking methods capable of generating feasible routes in complex geographic information system (GIS) road network data. The simulation results show improvements when high-priority roads are clustered using the minor modification approach, and lower-priority roads are clustered from scratch. Overall, the clustering approaches can save 51 min of simulated travel time while significantly improving the workload balance.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Analysis of the determinants of film quality considering a risk-averse producer and consumer learning from online reviews
Authors: Chun-Yi Liu, Fernando Siciliani Oliveira, Tianhui You
Affiliations: School of Economics and Management, Yanshan University; Trade and Agriculture Directorate, OECD; Information Management and Decision Sciences, Northeastern University
Abstract: This study examines a dual distribution channel through theatres and digital platforms to understand how a producer’s investment strategy and pricing in these channels are influenced by risk aversion and the ability of Bayesian consumers to learn from online reviews. We develop a Stackelberg game model, where a risk-averse producer acts as the leader, investing in the film, which is then released sequentially in theatres and on digital platforms. Our findings show that online reviews are crucial due to the uncertainty of achieving the target movie quality. A risk-averse producer tends to invest in lower-quality movies with lower prices, while a risk-neutral producer invests in higher-quality films with higher ticket prices. Critic reviews significantly impact firms’ decisions more than audience reviews. Interestingly, increasing the precision of online reviews lessens the effect of risk aversion on quality investment. These insights provide valuable contributions to film industry stakeholders, highlighting how online reviews and risk aversion shape investment strategies in the industry.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: PNN-SOM as an alternative to PNN to enhance the performance of large bankruptcy datasets
Authors: O. Manikandan, M. Punniyamoorthy, P. Sherwin Moses, S. Srivatsav
Affiliations: Department of Management Studies, National Institute of Technology
Abstract: Among its many successful applications, probabilistic neural network (PNN) has also proved to be extremely useful in bankruptcy prediction. In our study, we have combined PNN, a supervised learning model with Self-Organising Map (SOM), an unsupervised one; aimed at developing a new model capable of efficiently predicting bankruptcy through an optimal balance between predictive accuracy and computational efficiency. The resultant, PNN-SOM has emerged as a promising solution delivering comparatively high accurate results in significantly less processing time. Various kernels like Gaussian, Triangular, Epanechnikov, Uniform, Laplacian, RBF and Exponential Kernels have been applied in this study. The robustness of our PNN-SOM model has also been evaluated across varying dataset sizes. Our work will serve as a benchmark as well as a reliable technique for decision makers in banking and finance departments for creditworthiness and performance assessments, solely intended for avoiding potential bankruptcy.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Improving the ranking position from the linear ordering problem with a limited budget
Authors: Iñigo Martín Melero, Javier Alcaraz, Mercedes Landete
Affiliations: University Miguel Hernandez
Abstract: Rankings establish comparative relationships among a set of items, such as athletes, companies, or universities. A common approach to synthesising multiple individual rankings into a single consensus ranking is through the Linear Ordering Problem (LOP). Traditionally, the LOP assumes that the input rankings are fixed; however, in practice, entities with access to financial resources may seek to strategically improve their position in the resulting aggregate ranking. This study introduces the Improvement Budgeted Linear Ordering Problem (IB-LOP), which addresses the scenario where a single item or client allocates a limited budget to enhance its standings across the criteria underlying the input rankings, aiming to achieve the highest possible position in the unified LOP-derived ranking. We develop a non-linear bilevel optimisation framework to model the IB-LOP, which we subsequently reformulate into an equivalent linear single-level problem for tractability. Furthermore, we propose two extended formulations: one that maximises the LOP objective function and another that minimises the cost incurred, conditional on a target improvement in ranking. A heuristic algorithm is also presented to efficiently address larger instances of the problem. Extensive computational experiments, including a case study on hospital rankings, validate the effectiveness of the proposed models and heuristic. Key managerial insights derived from this work include the non-trivial impact of investment allocation across criteria and the observation that being the best in a single criterion is not a prerequisite for achieving a top position in the final ranking.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Carbon footprint reduction allocations with dual-heterogeneity consumers
Authors: Siyuan Zhu, Qiang Zhou, Hui Yang, Xia Yang
Affiliations: School of Management, Jiangsu University; School of Finance, Anhui University of Finance and Economics; School of Economics and Management, Nanjing University of Science and Technology; School of Economics and Management, South China Normal University
Abstract: Our study explores a firm that reduces its carbon footprint of products in the presence of heterogeneous consumers under cap-and-trade policy. The market comprises two consumer segments, namely eco-conscious and non-eco-conscious consumers. The former considers the product’s carbon footprint when making purchasing decisions, while the latter does not. Additionally, each consumer segment exhibits heterogeneous product valuations, so the market is dual-heterogeneous. Under the cap-and-trade policy, the firm reduces its carbon footprint using two strategies. It invests in emission-reduction investment (ERI) or purchases carbon offsets (CO) in the carbon market to satisfy its emissions quota. Our findings show that the firm should not always use just one of these emission-reduction strategies but can use them simultaneously. Our findings also reveal that, regardless of whether consumer valuation and environmental preference are negatively or positively correlated, the firm adopts the ERI strategy when the initial emissions intensity per product is low. When the initial emissions intensity per product is high, the firm also chooses the ERI strategy if the gap between the initial emissions intensity per product and the per-unit quota of carbon emissions is small. However, if this gap is large, the firm may choose either the CO strategy or the ERI strategy. Our results further indicate that the firm’s equilibrium profit first decreases and then increases as the ERI cost coefficient (i.e., emission-reduction investment cost coefficient in low-carbon technology) increases, which is not entirely consistent with the intuition that the firm’s profit decreases as its corresponding cost increases. Conventional wisdom suggests that the firm should not invest in advanced technology to reduce carbon emissions when all targeted consumers are non-eco-conscious. However, our findings indicate that the firm’s equilibrium emission-reduction intensity consistently remains above zero.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Analysis of M/M/s make-to-stock queues with production start-up costs for both lost sales and backordering cases
Authors: Sinem Özkan, Önder Bulut, Mehmet Cemali Dinçer
Affiliations: Department of Industrial Engineering, İzmir Democracy University; Department of Industrial Engineering, Yaşar University
Abstract: This study considers a production-inventory system with production start-up costs and parallel production lines. Production times are independent and identically distributed exponential random variables and demands are generated according to a stationary Poisson process. Production and inventory are controlled by the extended-two-critical-number policy. The system is modelled as an M/M/s make-to-stock queue and analysed for both lost sales and backordering cases. A renewal approach is developed to calculate the expected average system cost. Furthermore, an approximation is proposed to calculate the control parameters of the extended-two-critical-number policy. An extensive numerical study is conducted to illustrate the effects of changes in system parameters and the effectiveness of the proposed approximation. The analysis shows that the proposed approximation performs well across various system conditions.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Supply chain coordination based on green subsidy
Authors: Qihang Hu, Zhimin Chen, Jiangruya Hu, Jie Liu
Affiliations: School of Economics, Peking University; Department of Mathematical Sciences, Tsinghua University; Graduate School of International Studies, Yonsei University; School of Modern Posts, Nanjing University of Posts and Telecommunications
Abstract: This article examines the coordination challenges within a supply chain comprising a manufacturer and a retailer, operating under the influence of environmental regulation instrument, namely green subsidy. A Stackelberg differential game model is developed to analyse equilibrium functions pertaining to environmental performance, retail pricing, and environmental perception levels in both integrated and decentralised channel settings. A two-part tariff contract is introduced for decentralised supply chain coordination, and a Nash bargaining model is subsequently employed to investigate the allocation of additional profits. Numerical simulations are conducted to assess the impact of the green subsidy coefficient and supply chain environmental standards on steady-state solutions and overall supply chain profit. The main findings underscore the flexible pricing strategies adopted by the supply chain in both integrated and decentralised settings. And the study indicates that the overall performance of the former surpasses that of latter. A two-part tariff contract emerges as a pivotal instrument for achieving effective supply chain coordination. Moreover, green subsidy coefficient exhibits a positive influence on enhancing coordination capability, whereas the supply chain environmental standard acts as a deactivator.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Score-driven models for inventory control of intermittent demand
Authors: Rodrigo Sarlo, Cristiano Fernandes, Denis Borenstein
Affiliations: Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro; Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul
Abstract: Inventory control for intermittent data involves overseeing inventory levels of products that experience irregular demand. These items may remain unsold for extended periods and then experience a sudden surge in orders, making it difficult to predict future demand. To effectively manage such inventory, companies need specialised strategies that ensure they have enough stock to meet unpredictable spikes in demand while avoiding excess inventory that could lead to waste or storage problems. This study aims to evaluate the performance of forecasting models based on the score-driven (SD) framework as an alternative strategy for inventory control of intermittent demand. Several models were derived using the SD framework, including Poisson, negative binomial, and their hurdle and zero-inflated variants. The SD models were compared with several traditional forecasting methods for intermittent demand using synthetic data. A simulation model was developed to emulate the dynamics associated with inventory control through an order-up-to-level policy. The models were compared using well-known service and inventory level indicators. The proposed SD models consistently achieved closer service and target levels than traditional forecasting methods. Notably, the SD negative binomial model demonstrated the most robust performance across various simulated scenarios.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: A taste for travel: improving tourism forecasts via online restaurant reviews
Authors: Konstantinos Vogklis, Evangelos Spiliotis
Affiliations: Ionian University; National Technical University of Athens
Abstract: This paper proposes a methodology for forecasting monthly overnight stays using user-generated restaurant reviews from TripAdvisor and Google Maps as timely proxies for tourism demand. Unlike delayed official statistics, online reviews provide real-time signals that enhance traditional models trained on historical data. The framework is model-agnostic and adaptable to various forecasting techniques. It is validated over a two-year period in two major Greek destinations—the Ionian Islands and Crete—demonstrating robust performance, and further replicated across four additional destinations—the South Aegean Islands, Attica, Cyprus, and Malta—thereby supporting the generalisation of the main findings. Focusing on the high season, results show significant improvements in forecast accuracy. By leveraging low-cost and scalable digital data, this approach offers an effective decision support tool for tourism planners, particularly in highly seasonal contexts where timely and accurate predictions are essential for resource allocation and operational planning.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Fixed cost allocation in two-stage systems based on robust data envelopment analysis and prospect theory
Authors: Qingxian An, Ping Wang, Wenjing Peng, Sheng Ang
Affiliations: School of Economics, Hefei University of Technology, Hefei, Anhui, PR China; School of Business, Central South University, Changsha, Hunan, PR China; School of Management, Hefei University of Technology, Hefei, Anhui, PR China
Abstract: Fixed cost allocation is a significant issue for organisations that establish common platforms. Traditional studies on fixed cost allocation based on Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) usually assume that the inputs and outputs of two-stage systems are deterministic. However, in practice, the input and output data of decision-making units (DMUs) may fluctuate around mean values due to measurement errors or changes in the market environment. Moreover, in the process of fixed cost allocation, a DMU obtains relative gain with reference to a DMU with little allocated cost and obtains relative loss with reference to a DMU with much allocated cost. Decision makers often exhibit risk-seeking behaviour towards losses, reflecting their bounded rationality. To address these issues, this study proposes a novel fixed cost allocation model for two-stage systems based on robust DEA and prospect theory. We first explore robust DEA model for two-stage systems with allocated cost and derive a novel fixed cost allocation possibility set. Building upon this, we incorporate prospect theory to construct a prospect value function for DMUs. Subsequently, a prospect allocation model is formulated by considering the non-cooperative relationship among two-stage DMUs. Finally, an empirical case study and comparative analysis are conducted to validate the proposed approach.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Ad valorem tariffs in global supply chain networks and impacts on labor
Authors: Anna Nagurney, Samirasadat Samadi
Affiliations: University of Massachusetts
Abstract: Global supply chain networks are essential to the production, trade, and consumption of commodities, including agricultural ones. Such networks have been increasingly impacted by trade policies, especially ad valorem tariffs, which are affecting commodity flows, prices, and profits. Furthermore, the labour market plays a critical role in the functioning of supply chain networks. However, the impacts of ad valorem tariffs on labour (and employment) have not yet been quantitatively examined in a competitive global supply chain network framework. This paper constructs an oligopolistic supply chain network equilibrium model that integrates ad valorem tariffs and labour. Firms compete noncooperatively in maximising their profits by determining their product flows across multiple production sites. Demand markets can be located in different countries, with production and shipment activities subject to labour upper bounds and wages. The governing Nash equilibrium conditions are formulated as a variational inequality. Through Lagrange analysis, an alternative variational inequality is derived with nice features for computations. Illustrative examples are provided along with a global soybean trade case study. Numerical results reveal how such tariffs shift trade flows, reshape labour allocation, and affect demand prices as well as profits, with labour shortages and cost disruptions further negatively compounding the effects.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Efficient assignment of flight levels: a variable neighbourhood search approach
Authors: Joaquín Pacheco, Silvia Casado, Mario Solana
Affiliations: University of Burgos, Burgos, Spain
Abstract: Air traffic management (ATM) is a complex process that includes objectives such as minimising delays, costs, and environmental impacts, with safety being a top priority. Growth in air traffic over the past few decades has increased the complexity of this process. In European airspace, ATM is more crucial because of the high traffic density. A key aspect of this management strategy is the allocation of flight levels in the planning phase to avoid conflicts before takeoff. Therefore, a model is required for the allocation of flight levels in the planning phase to eliminate all conflicts and meet objectives such as minimising cost and emissions. In the absence of conflicts, planning delays in takeoff are avoided and in-flight corrective manoeuvres (such as changes in altitude or speed during flights) are reduced, reducing the workload of the controller. This study proposed a method based on a metaheuristic variable neighbourhood search (VNS) strategy on a multistart framework. Various experiments with simulated instances demonstrated that this method improves the results obtained using commercial software. In addition, tests based on real data (both in Europe and Spain) showed satisfactory results in terms of economics and sustainability.PRACTITIONER SUMMARYIn Europe, air traffic management (ATM) is an increasingly complex task due to high traffic density and the increase in traffic in recent decades. An important aspect of this traffic management is the allocation of altitude levels to different flights during planning. The main objective is to avoid conflicts, i.e., to prevent two flights from passing through the same point at the same time. Conflicts that are not avoided in the planning phase must be avoided later through operations such as takeoff delays or corrective manoeuvres during flight, changes in direction, altitude, speed, etc. All these types of manoeuvres increase the pressure and workload on control systems. On the other hand, from an economic and ecological point of view, it is important that each flight is assigned its “ideal level” (i.e., the level where it consumes the least fuel and produces the least emissions) or at least a level close to the ideal. The article proposes and describes a method for assigning flight levels which, based on tests using real data (in Spain and Europe), manages to avoid all conflicts and assign ideal or near-ideal flight levels to over 97% of flights, even in scenarios with a high ratio of conflict potential. In short, the proposed method can improve ATM in such important aspects as increased safety, reduced stress on control systems, reduced costs, and reduced emissions.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Reselling over-supplied relief goods in secondary market
Authors: Yusen Ye
Affiliations: Business School, Sichuan University; Institute for Disaster Management and Reconstruction, Sichuan University
Abstract: The sustainable management of oversupplied relief goods is critical for minimising waste and enhancing operational efficiency in humanitarian supply chains. This study examines how aid agencies can effectively reallocate oversupplied relief goods through resale in secondary markets. Focusing on relief items that are unused, safe, but approaching expiration or removal thresholds, and thus eligible for discounted resale, we develop a loss-averse newsvendor-based model to analyse optimal allocation rules across parallel resale channels under stochastic secondary market demand. Our results indicate that the differential in the secondary-market generalised failure rate (GFR), which is a concept mathematically dual to demand elasticity, serves as the key determinant of allocation outcomes. Loss aversion further diminishes, though does not solely govern, a reseller’s competitiveness. Channels characterised by a fixed secondary-market GFR receive less favourable allocations. We also evaluate social welfare across symmetric and asymmetric channel structures, highlighting how risk preferences interact with demand characteristics. Our work extends sustainable humanitarian operations and provides actionable insights for aid agencies, resellers and policymakers on relief surplus management under uncertainty and behavioural constraints.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: The TruEnd-procedure: treating trailing zero-valued balances in credit data
Authors: Arno Botha, Tanja Verster, Roelinde Bester
Affiliations: Centre for Business Mathematics and Informatics and Unit for Data Science and Computing, North-West University; National Institute for Theoretical and Computational Sciences (NITheCS)
Abstract: A novel procedure is presented for finding the true but latent endpoints within the repayment histories of individual loans. The monthly observations beyond these true endpoints are false, largely due to operational failures that delay account closure, thereby corrupting some loans. Detecting these false observations is difficult at scale since each affected loan history might have a different sequence of trailing zero (or very small) month-end balances. Identifying these trailing balances requires an exact definition of a “small balance,” which our method informs. We demonstrate this procedure and isolate the ideal small-balance definition using two different South African datasets. Evidently, corrupted loans are remarkably prevalent and have excess histories that are surprisingly long, which ruin the timing of risk events and compromise any subsequent time-to-event model, e.g., survival analysis. Having discarded these excess histories, we demonstrably improve the accuracy of both the predicted timing and severity of risk events, without materially impacting the portfolio. The resulting estimates of credit losses are lower and less biased, which augurs well for raising accurate credit impairments under IFRS 9. Our work therefore addresses a pernicious data error, which highlights the pivotal role of data preparation in producing credible forecasts of credit risk.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Integrating buyer and supplier objectives in an iterative combinatorial auction for procurement
Authors: Bahareh Mansouri, Elkafi Hassini, Jacob Locke
Affiliations: Sobey School of Business, Saint Mary’s University; Operations Management, McMaster University; Industrial Engineering, Dalhousie University
Abstract: Combinatorial auctions face a trade-off between allocative efficiency and practicality. While achieving allocative efficiency relies on strong economic assumptions that may be difficult for bidders to meet, compromising it for practicality can raise concerns about the auctioneer’s commitment to bidders’ profit maximisation goals. Several evidence-based scenarios report that inter-organisational relationships are adversely affected due to the bidders’ increasing suspicions of the auctioneer’s opportunism. In this paper, we design an iterative procurement combinatorial auction that ensures a steady increase in the winning bidders’ profits throughout the auction process. We analytically prove the convergence of this auction and identify its termination conditions. Complementing our theoretical findings, extensive numerical experiments evaluate the convergence rate, computational costs, and the dynamic interplay between costs and profits within this auction framework. Overall, our results show a substantial increase in the winning bidders’ average profits at the cost of a marginal rise in procurement costs. We illustrate that heightened competitiveness among bidders correlates with improved profit outcomes and convergence rates. The increased profits for bidders, validated both analytically and computationally, signal the auctioneer’s commitment to their welfare which helps enhance the overall appeal of the auction and promote the auctioneer’s resilience against potential supply chain disruptions.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: A secure and dynamic trust transitivity model in decentralised trust networks of supply chain
Authors: Lijie Li, Chaoqun Ma, Liwei Zhang, Dongqing Chen
Affiliations: Business School, Hunan University
Abstract: Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) play a pivotal role in driving global economic growth and employment. Nevertheless, due to poor trust transitivity in supply chain networks, SMEs have persistently faced financing difficulties and high financing costs. Therefore, we propose a secure and dynamic trust transitivity model aimed at addressing the challenges of multi-level trust transitivity obstruction and sensitive data transmission risks in supply chain finance (SCF). The proposed model integrates the Dempster-Shafer (D-S) evidence theory for trust awareness, the graph theory method for trust path discovery, and the ElGamal encryption algorithm for privacy-preserving trust value transmission and calculation. Through this design, the model can extend the trust chain, aggregate multi-source trust information, and avoid the exposure of sensitive enterprise data. Performance analysis demonstrates that the model exhibits good performance in security, efficiency, robustness, and reliability, demonstrating its feasibility in real-world SCF applications.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Optimal timing of ESG-aligned blockchain adoption: a market-based decision and forecasting framework
Authors: Sarah Alsultan, Apostolos Kourtis, Raphael N. Markellos
Affiliations: Imam Mohammad Ibn Saud Islamic University (IMSIU); Norwich Business School, University of East Anglia; Institute for the Future, Department of Digital Innovation, School of Business, University of Nicosia
Abstract: We propose a market-based decision-support framework to guide the adoption of ESG-aligned blockchain technologies. This treats the cost of financing such technologies as a function of investor sentiment and applies sentiment forecasts to determine when adoption is economically optimal. We implement our framework using a novel set of blockchain ESG scores, data from the cryptocurrency markets and an investor sentiment proxy to identify periods when investors favour ESG features in blockchain technology. Our analysis reveals that blockchains with high ESG scores generate higher cryptocurrency returns than their lower-rated counterparts in times of optimistic market sentiment. However, they underperform in challenging market times. We also find that higher ESG scores are associated with higher market volatility. Governance and environmental factors have the strongest effect on investor preferences. On the basis of these findings, we model the adoption decision as a real-options timing problem and compute the sentiment level above which adoption is optimal. We find that delaying adoption until sentiment improves yields substantially greater value than adopting immediately. Overall, our work provides operational insights into how decision-makers can strategically integrate ESG features when introducing emerging technologies.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Optimizing scheduling performance in packaging printing systems using strategy-aware and bottleneck-guided PSO
Authors: Yuqian Wang, Zhaohua Wang, Yanping Du, Shuihai Dou, Zheng Li, Yirong Luo

Title: Market power abuse in wholesale electricity markets
Authors: Alice Lixuan Xu, Jorge Sánchez Canales, Chiara Fusar Bassini, Lynn H. Kaack, Lion Hirth
Abstract: In wholesale electricity markets, prices fluctuate widely from hour to hour and electricity generators price-hedge their output using longer-term contracts, such as monthly base futures. Consequently, the incentives they face to drive up the power prices by reducing supply has a high hourly specificity, and because of hedging, they regularly also face an incentive to depress prices by inflating supply. In this study, we explain the dynamics between hedging and market power abuse in wholesale electricity markets and use this framework to identify market power abuse in real markets. We estimate the hourly economic incentives to deviate from competitive behavior and examine the empirical association between such incentives and observed generation patterns. Exploiting hourly variation also controls for potential estimation bias that do not correlate with economic incentives at the hourly level, such as unobserved cost factors. Using data of individual generation units in Germany in a six-year period 2019-2024, we find that in hours where it is more profitable to inflate prices, companies indeed tend to withhold capacity. We find that the probability of a generation unit being withheld increases by about 1 % per euro increase in the net profit from withholding one megawatt of capacity. The opposite is also true for hours in which companies benefit financially from lower prices, where we find units being more likely to be pushed into the market by 0.3 % per euro increase in the net profit from capacity push-in. We interpret the result as empirical evidence of systematic market power abuse.

Authors: Waqas Ahmed, Jenny Bäckstrand, Vanajah Siva, Hans-Åke Sundberg, Niklas Sarius

Title: Estimating Decision Uncertainty from Preference Uncertainty: Application to Ground Vehicle Design
Authors: Chia-Ruei Liu, Yongjia Song, Qiong Zhang, Cameron Turner
Affiliations: Department of Industrial Engineering, Clemson University; School of Mathematical and Statistical Sciences, Clemson University; School of Mechanical and Automotive Engineering, Clemson University
Abstract: Engineering design problems are often modeled as multi-objective optimization tasks in which a scalarized utility function selects an optimal design from the Pareto set. In practice, preferences are imperfectly known, so uncertainty in the preference model leads to uncertainty in the resulting optimal design. This paper proposes a probabilistic framework that treats preference parameters as random variables and examines how preference uncertainty propagates to decision uncertainty. A random preference vector induces a probability distribution over optimal designs, allowing us to identify which regions of the Pareto front are most likely to be selected and to assess recommendation stability under preference variability. To explain the sources of this variability, we apply variance-based global sensitivity analysis to the induced optimal solutions, using Sobol' indices and Shapley values to quantify the contributions of individual design variables and their dependencies. We further summarize the overall dispersion of the optimal-design distribution using the Fréchet variance, which provides a scalar measure of decision stability under a given preference model. Two vehicle design case studies demonstrate how problem structure can lead to discrete versus continuous decision distributions and show how the proposed quantities support preference-aware design analysis.

Title: Forecast Accuracy and Efficiency at the Bank of England
Authors: Derrick Kanngiesser, Tim Willems
Affiliations: Independent Researcher London UK; Bank of England London UK
Abstract: ABSTRACT We propose a systematic approach for central banks to leverage past forecasts (and associated errors) with the aim of learning more about the structure and functioning of the underlying economy. Applying this method to forecasts made by the Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee since 2011, we find that its forecasts have tended to underestimate the inflationary consequences of real wage growth, while also underestimating the inflationary consequences of real GDP growth in the near term. Regarding the effects of monetary policy, our results are, for example, consistent with transmission via inflation expectations having played a bigger role than attributed to it in the forecast. This may point to a more favourable sacrifice ratio.

Title: Computational methods for bankruptcy problems
Authors: Maaike Vollebergh, Wout Dullaert, Arantza Estévez-Fernández, Yousef Ghiami
Abstract: In this paper, we discuss the computation of the most commonly used allocation rules for weighted bankruptcy problems. We extend existing recursive algorithms to the weighted constrained equal awards rule and the weighted constrained proportional rule, and prove their correctness. Moreover, we introduce novel solution methods for these rules, by providing an explicit expression for the allocations. Using duality, we extend these results to present algorithms for the weighted constrained equal losses rule and the weighted constrained proportional losses rule. The advantage of the novel solution method is demonstrated by a numerical example involving a network sharing application.

Title: Forecasting cohort mortality: Lee–Carter methods and CCP-splines
Authors: Ugofilippo Basellini, Carlo Giovanni Camarda
Abstract: Accurate mortality forecasts are central to policy, insurance, and demographic research. Yet most approaches rely on age-period models, limiting their ability to capture the real experiences of birth cohorts. We address this gap by developing and evaluating new models for cohort mortality forecasting. Specifically, we extend the Lee–Carter framework to the age-cohort setting and introduce Cohort Constrained P -splines ( C C P -splines), an age-cohort adaptation of the existing C P -splines model. In two out-of-sample validation exercises with 10- and 20-year forecast horizons across eight populations, C C P -splines generally outperform the cohort LC variants and the conventional diagonal Lexis approach, which derives cohort patterns from standard Lee–Carter age-period forecasts. By combining statistical rigour with demographic knowledge, this study provides a practical and flexible framework that positions C C P -splines as a strong competitor for cohort mortality forecasting.

Title: Top-selling product sales forecasting in the cross-border fast fashion industry: A robust attention-based deep learning approach
Authors: Guofang Nan, Caiyan Huang, Jian Luo, Tao Hong

Title: LLM time machines: Valuing digital goods over time
Authors: Avinash Collis, Felix Eggers, Erik Brynjolfsson
Abstract: Digital goods generate substantial consumer welfare, but their valuations are difficult to estimate because many are free to consumers. We investigate whether large language models (LLMs) can reconstruct these valuations over time using incentive-compatible binary choice experiments. We benchmark predictions against eight waves of representative US survey data collected between 2016 and 2024. Calibrating GPT-4-Turbo on one year, we find that it approximates the magnitude and temporal patterns of median human valuations in other years. Newer models do not necessarily improve predictions, tending to favor monetary compensation. Our findings suggest opportunities and limitations for longitudinal valuations using LLMs.

Title: Economic dynamics of flood damage: The roles of private capital, public capital, and financial accelerator
Authors: Ryuichiro Hashimoto, Kohei Matsumura, Hiroaki Shirai
Abstract: Floods can cause substantial local damage to public and private capital stock, resulting in macroeconomic losses magnified by financial intermediation channels. We propose a dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) model that synthesizes private capital stock, public capital stock, and financial intermediation channels to capture the impacts of floods. Applied to an extreme flood scenario in Tokyo, Japan, our model reveals that total GDP losses reach 149% of direct capital damage, with 19 percentage points attributed to the financial intermediation channel and 7 percentage points to the public capital productivity channel. These findings reveal that traditional flood assessments substantially underestimate total economic impact by missing key indirect channels that our model quantifies. Our results provide important implications for the cost–benefit analysis of climate adaptation projects and enhance the accuracy of climate stress testing frameworks.

Title: Disparities in climate risk-mitigation and recreation services in Grenoble (France)
Authors: Margot Neyret, Samuel Lormel, Alberto González-García, Dan Richards, Yves Schaeffer, Mihai Tivadar, Améline Vallet, Sandra Lavorel
Abstract: Summary Urban green spaces provide cultural and climate risk-mitigation ecosystem services (ES) critical for the well-being of urban residents. Yet these benefits are not equally shared across social groups, and environmental segregation - i.e., the spatial separation of population groups between areas of contrasted environmental quality - is common. For instance, environmental justice studies have shown that green space acreage and quality are typically lower in low-income neighbourhoods. However, more detailed assessments integrating a range of ES and the diverse needs of multiple groups are needed to effectively inform equitable urban planning. Here, we combine socio-demographic spatial data with ES modelling to assess social disparities in the distribution of three ES - heatwave mitigation, flood regulation, and urban recreation - in the Grenoble metropolitan area, France. Our results show that low-income households generally benefit from lower climate risk mitigation, but from equal or slightly greater urban recreation opportunities. We also identify mismatches between ES supply and demand from vulnerable groups, which are particularly acute in disadvantaged neighborhoods. These findings highlight the importance of integrating social needs and vulnerabilities into urban greening strategies. Policies that move beyond generic measures of green space provision and explicitly consider multiple ES can help ensure that urban green infrastructure delivers fair and effective benefits across diverse communities.

Title: Optimizing interdependent fourth-party logistics services in carbon-constrained global supply chains: Coordinating strategic decisions and green logistics
Authors: Yifan Xin, Ismail M. Ali, Yangyan Shi, Ripon K. Chakrabortty
Abstract: Modern fourth-party logistics (4PL) providers are evolving from logistics executors to control towers that orchestrate decisions across global supply chains. However, existing 4PL models largely treat demand forecasting, strategic decision-making, and logistics execution as separate services, without specifying how upstream strategic decisions are transferred into downstream logistics execution. This paper develops a two-stage 4PL control tower framework that integrates upstream strategic decision support with downstream logistics execution in a carbon-regulated global supply chain involving competing manufacturers and third-party logistics (3PL) providers under hybrid carbon policies. The first service, Predict–Optimize–Update (POU), couples machine learning (ML) demand forecasts with a multi-period dynamic optimization module that captures strategic interdependence among carbon-constrained manufacturers, providing decision support for supplier selection, pricing, production, and abatement decisions and updating the information set with newly observed competitor responses and market signals. These decisions feed the downstream Eco-Efficient Logistics Flow (EELF) service, which uses a multi-objective mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model to configure the international logistics network while balancing profit and emissions. By passing updated strategic decisions into logistics design, the framework connects the two services through a sequential decision process. A case study of electric vehicle shipments from China to the Netherlands shows that, compared with a traditional 4PL forecasting service, the integrated framework increases supply chain net profit by 39.86% and reduces emissions by 37.29%. Pareto and scalability analyses further show how 4PL providers can select configurations that balance profit, emissions, and computational responsiveness under changing operational, market, and carbon policy conditions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: A supervised machine learning framework to predict the request fit for rural on-demand minibus services
Authors: Simon Mader, Pirmin Fontaine, Stefan Voigt
Abstract: On-demand minibus services offer an efficient solution for enhancing public transport in rural areas through flexible routes and schedules. Public transport providers (PTPs) aim to maximize passenger service with these minibuses, yet they encounter the challenge of a dynamic booking process where requests arrive continuously over time. PTPs have to decide immediately which requests to accept but some accepted requests may tie up the resources for future requests. An informed decision on the impact of requests could enable the PTP to serve more passengers. Therefore, the problem of predicting the request fit for rural on-demand minibus services emerges. We propose a request fit predictor (RFP) framework that leverages supervised machine learning models to predict request fit from displacement labels derived via problem-specific features. A time-dependent threshold adjusts fit requirements over the booking horizon, balancing demand and uncertainty. The modular design integrates these fit predictions with either an exact solver or a heuristic method, guaranteeing feasible real-time acceptance decisions. Tested on 26 months of real data from a German PTP, we show that the RFP improves outcomes primarily by changing which requests are accepted rather than how many: the number of accepted requests increases only marginally, while served passengers rise by 15.98% compared to the status quo and by 9.32% over a sequential solver benchmark. The RFP further sustains a stable service level across the entire booking horizon, substantially outperforming a first-come-first-served solver, and does so without excluding any bus stop from service, unlike a distance-based policy. Practitioners benefit from this paper by getting evidence that in resource-constrained rural systems, acceptance composition, service-level stability, and equitable coverage, rather than raw acceptance volume, are the primary levers for improving on-demand transport. For researchers, it offers empirical evidence on a real rural case study of where an offline-learned decision rule is competitive under sparse demand and rigid time-window constraints.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Dynamic anticipatory stock repositioning framework for disaster response
Authors: Birce Adsanver, Burcu Balcik, Valérie Bélanger, Marie-Ève Rancourt
Abstract: Climate change is driving more frequent and severe weather events, which requires going beyond traditional reactive response policies to provide timely and effective aid delivery. Anticipatory action (AA), enabled by advances in early warning systems and real-time forecasting, offers a powerful opportunity to take proactive measures for better responding to predictable events. Motivated by practice and developed in partnership with the Emergency Supply Prepositioning Strategy initiative and its affiliated organizations, this study addresses anticipatory stock repositioning for cyclones, where multiple humanitarian organizations preposition relief items and adaptively reposition them as forecasts are updated. Effective AA requires integrating impact prediction with decision-making to determine how and when to reposition stocks in a dynamic environment shaped by updating forecasts and changing network conditions, as well as inter-agency collaboration to avoid duplication and improve resource utilization. We propose a new decision-making framework that integrates three key operational components of AA: predict, plan, and trigger. Specifically, we combine a linear regression model to predict demand for relief items based on wind speed forecasts and vulnerability indicators with a two-stage stochastic optimization model to determine relocation quantities and locations, embedded within an optimal stopping framework to determine the timing of action. Collaboration is facilitated by integrating the proposed framework into a logistics platform that provides shared visibility of inventories and stock movements and supports coordinated relocation decisions. Using a case study of Madagascar, we show that our approach reduces response time by up to 50% compared to a wait-and-see policy, with the largest gains achieved under coordinated planning and resource sharing enabled by the platform.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Full-truckload and less-than-truckload mixed dispatch of construction and demolition waste under a limited, class-licensed fleet
Authors: Jin Xin Cao
Abstract: Construction and demolition waste (CDW) haulage in Chinese cities combines two regimes that compete for the same trucks and night hours: bulk earthworks and demolition debris move as full truckloads (FTL) on direct site-to-sink shuttles, while small-batch renovation waste is collected through multi-stop less-than-truckload (LTL) routes. This paper formulates and solves the night dispatch problem of a carrier whose limited, class-licensed fleet must serve both regimes under catalog-fixed per-demand eligibility: truck-hour allocation and multi-stop pickup routing are decided jointly, and the problem is NP-hard by reduction from the split-delivery vehicle routing problem. The mixed-integer program with per-trip pricing, partial final loads, and shared per-vehicle time budgets is strengthened by a tonnage-flow reformulation that reduces the LP-relaxation gap from 54–74% to 8–11% and restores usable optimality certificates. An exactly aligned simulated-annealing metaheuristic, benchmarked against two structurally different searches under identical evaluation and budget protocols, returns dispatches within 2% of the exact solver’s incumbents on the larger instances (M–XL) at a 10–15-fold speedup, with certified gaps wherever the bound is informative. On a case-calibrated real road network, mode-aware dispatch lowers cost by 3–17% against naive single-mode policies and yields a certified 3.5–12.4% saving against equally optimized all-shuttle dispatch, while the all-consolidation comparison is reversed on the tightest instance, where night hours and route slots bind. These results quantify the value of mode-aware night dispatch and identify per-trip tariff design and selective deferral of remote sites as levers for carriers and regulators in access-regulated urban freight.

Title: Resource nationalism and economic outcomes: evidence from national policy interventions
Authors: Shiquan Dou, Yue Chen, Franklin Amuakwa-Mensah
Abstract: Resource-rich developing economies are once again intensifying policy intervention in their mineral sectors. Such policies, aimed at strengthening state control over resources and capturing resource rent, are collectively referred to as resource nationalism. However, their economic consequences remain empirically contested. Drawing on a multi-country database of resource policy events spanning 2000–2023, we identify three categories of high-intensity interventions and assess their effects on economic growth and household welfare, including export controls, heavy taxation, and nationalization/state equity participation. We further examine transmission mechanisms and sources of heterogeneity. The results indicate that the economic effects of resource nationalism are highly conditional. The effect depends on policy type, implementation intensity, and the fit between policy design and national governance. Countries with stronger governance capacity are more likely to translate resource control into productive expansion and economic gains. In contrast, in weakly governed or highly resource-dependent lower-middle-income countries, benefits are largely confined to fiscal and distributional channels rather than sustained output growth. Mechanism analysis shows that different policy instruments generate significant but heterogeneous adjustments through channels including fiscal revenues, trade structures, and sectoral output. Yet these changes do not systematically translate into sustained macroeconomic expansion. Sequential analysis reveals that repeated implementation of the same policy type follows a nonlinear path of diminishing marginal returns. Even in high-governance countries, repeated interventions fail to sustain stable growth dividends. These findings suggest that resource nationalism is a policy instrument highly contingent on institutional conditions with governance capacity and industrial absorptive capacity serving as prerequisites for policy effectiveness.

Title: Granular shocks and shadow banks: Concentration and real effects in mortgage markets

Title: The baby boom and the US divorce boom
Authors: Tereza Ranošová
Abstract: The United States experienced two major demographic ’booms’ during the second half of the twentieth century, in births after 1945 and in divorces 25 years later. This paper argues that the two booms are linked. As the baby-boomers were entering marriageable age, men in previous cohorts were faced with exceptionally good remarriage prospects. I find that across states people in the pre-boom generations were more likely to have ever divorced the bigger the relative supply of young women (instrumenting the size of the baby-boom with WWII mobilization rates). I construct a simple dynamic marriage and remarriage model (matched to the pre-1970s matching patterns) that illustrates how age-gap preferences can translate a cohort-size variation into a rise in divorce.

Title: The consequences of cellphone restrictions in classrooms
Authors: Ying Shi, Francisco Villarroel
Abstract: We examine teacher-level cellphone permissiveness in a setting where phones are often used for instructional support and teachers retain discretion over classroom cellphone use. Using linked Chilean administrative and survey data, we exploit variation in cellphone policy within teachers across cohorts and within students across subjects. Greater restrictiveness modestly reduces eighth graders’ cellphone use in class, but not tenth graders’. It also lowers eighth graders’ self-perceived academic capability, with no detectable effects on test scores. These findings inform settings, more common in low- and middle-income countries, involving uneven classroom enforcement within schools and where phones serve as low-cost instructional tools.

Title: Can shadow prices from energy system optimization models serve as reliable electricity price indicators?
Authors: Daniel Cäsar, Anne Neumann, Sebastian Zwickl-Bernhard
Abstract: Shadow prices from large-scale energy system optimization models (ESOMs) are widely used as long-term electricity price proxies in research and policy analysis. While their structural limitations are broadly acknowledged, no systematic empirical evidence exists on their reliability as market price proxies. We address this gap with a novel three-stage statistical framework (Kruskal–Wallis tests, t -tests, Pearson correlations) applied to ENTSO-E day-ahead prices and shadow prices from GENeSYS-MOD — one illustrative example among many cost-minimising ESOMs — across 22 European countries and four temporal resolutions. We find that shadow prices are compressed relative to observed market prices across all temporal resolutions. Volatility compression is most pronounced at the day-of-week level ( 10 × on average) and at the hour-of-day level ( 7 × on average). Month-of-year and season resolutions show smaller but still substantial compression (3– 4 × on average). Despite this, day-of-week, month-of-year, and season price patterns are structurally aligned with ENTSO-E observations. Hour-of-day alignment improves with model year but the observed market pattern is structurally shifting, making it the resolution hardest to use reliably. Independent literature projections from other LP-based models fall in the same compressed range, indicating that compression is a model-class property rather than a single-model artefact; direct empirical validation across other ESOM families remains an open task. Addressing these structural limitations is a promising avenue for future model development. In the interim, we propose resolution-conditional guidelines to support more principled shadow price applications.

Title: Urban last-mile delivery with unmanned aerial vehicles: A two-echelon vehicle routing problem with time windows and sequential cross-satellite operations
