Title: A transport–environment–receptor screening framework for ballast-water monitoring priorities in Arctic-linked shipping to Chinese ports
Authors: Yang Yang, Liehui Wang, Xin Zhao, Qiang Mei, Rongxin Song, Qin Zhou
Abstract: Ballast-water biosecurity assessments of Chinese ports typically aggregate vessel arrivals from different source regions, which may mask the distinctive environmental filtering experienced by Arctic-linked shipping. Using Automatic Identification System (AIS) data from 2013 to 2025, this study links vessel activity in six Arctic source regions to 401 independent arrivals at Chinese ports, of which 372 could be parameterized for potential ballast-water pressure (BPP). We develop a transport–environment–receptor screening framework that sequentially integrates ship type and vessel size, voyage decay based on voyage duration, temperature–salinity match and coastal ecological receptors to identify relative monitoring priority. Environmental matching substantially reduced unscreened potential pressure and concentrated high-priority exposure in a small number of arrivals reaching northern ports in winter. Tianjin and Tangshan consistently retained relatively high monitoring priority across the sensitivity analyses and all 27 exploratory scenarios, although some alternative specifications changed their exact ranking. Exposure was highly concentrated: the 10 highest-contributing arrivals accounted for 99.6 % of the receptor-weighted exposure priority index (REPI). AIS draught checks further indicated that many high-contributing arrivals did not conform to a simple “Arctic ballasting–China discharge” pattern; BPP and related indicators should therefore be interpreted as screening proxies rather than estimates of actual ballast-water discharge volumes or invasion probabilities. The results suggest that monitoring of Arctic-linked shipping could focus on northern Chinese ports in winter and prioritize verification of a small number of high-contributing arrivals.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Endogenous sunk costs and market structure in vocational higher education
Authors: Paola Bordón, Bernardo Lara

Title: Competing with Airbnb: Evidence from incumbent and entrant hotels
Authors: Hyunbae Chun, Hailey Hayeon Joo, Ian Jaeyeon Kim, Sangkon Park, Chamna Yoon
Abstract: This paper investigates how traditional hotels compete with accommodation-sharing platforms. Using detailed data on hotels and Airbnb listings in Korea, we examine the short-run and long-run effects of Airbnb on incumbent and entrant hotels, respectively. We find that Airbnb’s low-cost room supply leads to declines in incumbent hotels’ room revenue and prices. At the same time, hotels with greater Airbnb exposure experience an increase in food and beverage (F&B) revenue, such that the net effect on total revenue becomes statistically insignificant. Over a longer horizon, we find that hotels entering local markets with more Airbnb listings have an approximately 10 percentage point higher probability of choosing a high-quality level, after correcting for selection bias. Overall, our findings suggest that the rise of Airbnb may gradually reshape the traditional hotel industry through changes in revenue composition and a shift toward higher-quality accommodations.

Title: Does what goes up come back down? Pass-through of fuel-tax cuts and restorations in Korea
Authors: Taesik Kim, Yenjae Chang, Taehwan Kim

Title: An embedded boosting approach incorporating instance valuation and adaptive cleaning for imbalanced credit classification with label noise
Authors: Jianxin Zhu, Mingqi Zhang, Lean Yu, Xiaoming Zhang
Abstract: Class imbalance is a crucial problem in credit risk assessment, where model predictive accuracy is compromised not only by imbalanced data but also by challenges related to data traits (e.g., noise). Class imbalance combined with label noise aliasing can cause the model to overfit noisy instances, leading to reduced classification performance and potential economic losses. To address these issues, an embedded boosting approach incorporating instance valuation and adaptive cleaning is proposed. In this methodology, the imbalanced classification entropy (ICE) index is first designed in the Boosting with Instance Valuation (Boosting-IV) algorithm, which is used to calculate the base classifier weights of each layer iteration in the hybrid ensemble classifier (HEClassifier). Accordingly, the instance valuation and the corresponding weight of the HEClassifier on the final ensemble classifier are calculated. Subsequently, the Boosting with Adaptive Cleaning (Boosting-AC) algorithm identifies and processes noise based on the instance evaluation from the Boosting-IV stage, enhancing instance information and improving model classification performance. Finally, the ensemble classifier is constructed by combining the trained HEClassifier for testing. To verify the effectiveness of the proposed embedded boosting strategy, some experiments are conducted on three imbalanced credit datasets. The experimental results show that the proposed embedded boosting model outperforms the other benchmark models listed in this study, indicating its effectiveness as a credit risk classification tool in the presence of class imbalance and label noise aliasing.

Title: How big data analytics capability affects digital servitization: Considering the mediating effect of digital innovation and the moderating effect of environmental uncertainty
Authors: Mengxin Li, Shaobo Wei, Xiayu Chen

Title: International cooperation and the challenges of financial, environmental and social sustainability: a centre-periphery model
Authors: Chiara Grazini, Giulio Guarini, Gabriel Porcile
Abstract: This paper focuses on the role of international cooperation in shaping a sustainable growth path from a social, economic and environmental standpoint. It builds on the post-Keynesian and Structuralist traditions to include the impact of this cooperation in easing the external constraint on growth and accelerating the international diffusion of green technologies. It also highlights the potential of international Keynesian coordination as a pathway toward sustainable development. Within the conceptual framework of Ecological Macroeconomics, the paper addresses the “sustainability trilemma” faced by a peripheral small open economy and outlines a baseline scenario marked by a triple crisis arising from unsustainable debt burdens, environmental degradation, and widening social vulnerability and inequalities. In addition, the paper explores potential policy scenarios for financial, social, and environmental sustainability in the periphery, while underscoring the rise of both national and international tensions in the process of ecological transformation by discussing emerging policy proposals that link debt relief to green investment and sustainable development commitments.

Title: Unpacking open innovation in electric Vehicles: An integrated framework of Enablers, Capabilities,andOutcomes
Authors: Safiya Mukhtar Alshibani, Ankit Mehrotra, David Kalisz, Attila Kurucz, Raj V. Mahto
Abstract: The electric vehicle (EV) sector has become a cornerstone of the global transition to sustainable mobility, supported by policy incentives and rapid technological advancement. Yet, persistent challenges, including high production costs, infrastructure gaps, and regulatory fragmentation, cannot be addressed by individual firms alone. Open innovation (OI), through knowledge exchange across organizational boundaries, offers a promising pathway for addressing these challenges. Drawing on Innovation Ecosystem Theory (IET) and Dynamic Capabilities (DC), this study employs a multi-stage qualitative research design to examine how ecosystem enablers, organizational capabilities, and innovation outcomes are interconnected in EV ecosystems. Using the Gioia methodology, the analysis identifies six ecosystem-level enablers—multi-actor collaboration, resource mobilization, innovation networks, regulatory enablement, flexible business models, and open platforms and standards—and six organizational capabilities through which firms mobilize and translate these opportunities. The findings further identify six categories of innovation outcomes and show that ecosystem opportunities do not automatically translate into innovation; their realization depends on organizational capability–opportunity alignment and appropriate governance mechanisms. The study contributes theoretically by bridging IET and DC to explain how ecosystem conditions are translated through organizational capabilities into innovation outcomes, while incorporating feedback effects that shape subsequent ecosystem evolution. Practically, the study provides implications for managers, policymakers, and ecosystem orchestrators and offers a diagnostic framework for assessing OI readiness in EV ecosystems.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: The technological-financial-military linkage and the reproduction of inequality between countries
Authors: Leonardo Bargigli, Francesco Macheda
Abstract: In recent years, military power has re-emerged as a central driver of international economic relations. Economic theories have largely dismissed militarism as irrational rent-seeking that distorts efficient markets or they have focused predominantly on its impact on domestic economic performance. Both these perspectives, however, overlook the mutually reinforcing dynamic between military power and the reproduction of global economic asymmetries. Instead, this paper introduces what we term the imperialist feedback loop, which operates as follows: the technological and financial dominance of core economies provides the foundation for military dominance, which is then instrumental to reproduce the asymmetric global division of labour underpinning technological and financial dominance itself. Empirically, we employ a hidden Markov model to dynamically cluster country panel data (1988-2023), identifying a stable hierarchical world structure, wherein the stability of the imperialist core is tied to the existence of an impoverished periphery and limited upward mobility from the semi-periphery. The empirical validation of militarism's core role in reproducing imperialist structures can inform the design of policies aimed at counteracting the technological-military dependency of less-developed countries, ultimately reducing global inequalities.

Title: XEATBoost: A shape-constrained XGBoost approach for production frontier estimation
Authors: Juan Aparicio
Abstract: Estimating a production frontier with flexible learning methods requires more than accurate regression: the estimator must target an upper boundary while respecting the economic structure required for efficiency measurement. Standard XGBoost instead targets the conditional mean and does not enforce sample envelopment or monotonicity of the production function. We introduce XEATBoost, which combines Efficiency Analysis Tree partitions with XGBoost-style regularization and stagewise optimization. Given each tree partition, leaf values solve an L2-regularized strictly convex quadratic program with a unique global solution subject to monotonicity and envelopment restrictions. The method accommodates stochastic row and input subsampling, repairs envelopment violations induced by row sampling, and can convexify the fitted ensemble before calculating efficiency scores. A Monte Carlo study compares XEATBoost with Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA), Simar–Wilson bootstrap bias-corrected DEA, corrected concave nonparametric least squares (C 2 NLS), and SEATBoosting. The methods are complementary rather than uniformly ranked: C 2 NLS is particularly effective in lower-dimensional designs, whereas XEATBoost is especially competitive when inputs are numerous relative to the sample size. A paired ablation shows that convexification improves mean frontier error in every simulated scenario, although its incremental contribution diminishes with dimension. XEATBoost thus provides a production-theoretically valid route for transferring regularized boosted-tree learning to frontier estimation and a promising complementary alternative in statistically demanding, input-rich settings.

Title: Low-carbon distributed flexible job shop scheduling with AGV transport and charging under time-varying electricity prices and grid carbon intensity: an improved multi-objective evolutionary algorithm
Authors: Liao Ran, Yao Lu, Guanyu Chen, Xianming Wu, Taihua Zhang

Title: Fiscal policy in a behavioral New Keynesian model for the currency union
Authors: Sihao Chen, Jiacheng Zhang

Title: Data-driven planning of electric truck charging stations with heterogeneous driving ranges
Authors: Hailin Tong, Guangnian Xiao, Yuandong Liu, Jiapei Li
Abstract: Accelerating road freight electrification is pivotal for decarbonization, yet infrastructure deficits remain a critical barrier. This study addresses the electric truck charging station location problem by integrating driver behavioral patterns and heterogeneous driving ranges. GPS stop records from conventional trucks are used to construct candidate locations and intercity freight demand as inputs to the charging station location model. A mixed integer linear programming model is formulated, in which range heterogeneity is characterized by probability distributions. The model is solved via a hybrid multi-criterion label-correcting procedure and genetic algorithm. Empirical analysis in the Sichuan-Guizhou-Chongqing region shows that marginal cost reductions decline markedly once 25–30 stations are deployed. Results reveal that the optimal strategy exhibits high sensitivity to the unit trip failure cost, which governs the trade-off between network efficiency and service coverage. These findings provide indicative planning insights on differentiated investment strategies for improving freight electrification network reliability.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: From prediction to causality: A unified framework for two-stage MaaS subscription
Authors: Shujie Chen, Yilin Sun, Fangyuan Jia, E. Owen D. Waygood, Liwei Liu, Yifang Huang
Abstract: Mobility-as-a-Service (MaaS) supports multimodal integration and sustainable mobility, while understanding users’ subscription behavior is essential. Based on a stated-preference survey in Hangzhou, this study develops a machine learning and causal inference framework to examine MaaS subscription and bundle choices. CatBoost and GeoShapley identify correlational determinants and spatial heterogeneity, while the Bayesian network-double machine learning (BN-DML) framework estimates causal effects under stated-preference conditions and supports intervention analysis. Results show that subscription decisions are shaped by age, monthly bus pass ownership, and travel mode. Weekly bundle choice is sensitive to short-cycle travel attributes, whereas monthly bundle choice is influenced by public transport benefits and car ownership. Age, travel mode, car ownership, price, and public transport allowances exert significant causal effects on choices. The low-intensity zonal intervention scenario increases monthly subscription by 2.10% and uptake of the public transport-oriented Bundle A by 3.32%. The proposed framework advances MaaS analysis and supports targeted interventions.

Title: Coordinator or active participant? The food bank’s role in ad-hoc food rescue operations in the United States

Title: Gender quotas, political selection, and violence. Evidence from high-incidence areas in Italy
Authors: Anna Laura Baraldi, Giovanni Immordino, Erasmo Papagni, Marco Stimolo
Abstract: This paper examines the effect of Italy’s Law 215/2012, which introduced gender-balanced double-preference voting in municipal councils, on attacks against local politicians. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design focusing on municipalities with 5000–15,000 inhabitants, we find that the reform increases both the probability and the number of attacks in high-incidence regions—namely Apulia, Calabria, and Campania. We provide suggestive evidence on the underlying mechanisms. In these regions, the reform increases women’s representation in municipal councils and is associated with higher educational attainment among politicians, including mayors and aldermen, who are more exposed to violence. These changes appear to make political bodies less permeable to external pressure aimed at extracting private benefits. Consistent with this interpretation, the reform leads to an increase in both attacks characterized by criminally coded intimidation and those with broader retaliatory features. However, we find no effect on indicators of corruption risk in public procurement, suggesting that the phenomenon is unlikely to be driven by large-scale corruption.

Title: The puzzle of political ambition and prosociality
Authors: Alessandra Cassar, Jennifer Pate, Mary L. Rigdon
Abstract: We study whether embedding a redistribution opportunity in political competition alters political ambition and narrows the gender gap in willingness to run for office. Existing evidence indicates that women are more inequality-averse and less likely to enter competitive settings, but perhaps more responsive to redistributive incentives. We test whether redesigning competitive political environments to include a redistributive opportunity, more specifically the option to transfer money to the lowest earner, can mitigate gender disparities in candidate entry. We conducted a laboratory experiment with 320 participants from the University of Alabama and Loyola Marymount University using a within-subject design. We find that the Redistribute-to-Lowest treatment increases willingness to run for both women and men by nearly 5%, but does not reduce the gender gap in political ambition: women report 17.6% lower willingness to run than men. We also find a negative correlation between willingness to run and giving, revealing a paradox: those most inclined to help others are often the least likely to seek positions that would allow them to do so.

Title: The Price of Simplification: What We Miss When Hedonic Price Variation is Ignored
Authors: David Wolf, Taisuke Sadayuki, Kenji Takeuchi
Abstract: Widely applied in empirical research, the hedonic approach offers a means of valuing public goods that otherwise lack an explicit market price. These valuations become inaccurate when the hedonic price function varies, and this variation is ignored. We introduce a novel approach that allows practitioners to empirically assess the severity of this issue in any hedonic application, without imposing significant data requirements. Our methodology not only provides insight into the extent to which the hedonic price function varies but also helps identify the dimensions along which this variation is best captured. In our application, where the implicit price of seismic risk is causally identified using the Tohoku Earthquake as a natural experiment, we find the price to avoid earthquake risk ranges from 1.1% to 5.6% of a home’s value across the Tokyo metropolitan area. Out-of-sample prediction errors from cross-validation identify commuting time to central Tokyo as the preferred partition along which the hedonic price function as a whole varies. More importantly, accounting for this variation yields aggregate risk valuations that are 13.8% ($414 million) less than those derived under the assumption of a constant hedonic price schedule, with the difference being statistically significant. Our study highlights the importance of first accounting for variation in the hedonic price function before valuing a good of interest.

Title: Eurogreen+: An integrated modelling framework for analysing socioeconomic and energy transitions
Authors: David Cano Ortiz, Simone D’Alessandro, Till Heydenreich, Guilherme Spinato Morlin
Abstract: Addressing climate change, ecological overshoot and persistent inequalities requires ex-ante evaluation tools able to analyse transition pathways by integrating energy, macroeconomics, income distribution and structural change. This paper introduces the Eurogreen+ model, a substantially revised version of the Eurogreen framework, and develops an empirically grounded baseline for Italy as a reference point for policy analysis. The modelling framework combines post-Keynesian macroeconomics, stock-flow consistent accounting, system dynamics and an open input–output production structure with endogenous cost-driven technological change. Eurogreen+ widely integrates the economic and energy systems, and features a high level of heterogeneity with 100 representative households differentiated by region and income quintile and explicitly accounts for supply constraints. Rather than evaluating specific policy packages, the paper presents the baseline scenario and a set of illustrative simulations to highlight central characteristics of the model. The baseline reproduces current trends of modest growth, insufficient emissions reductions, and rising income inequality. The illustrative simulations show that Eurogeen+ captures the expansionary role of macroeconomic policy on potential output; second-order effects from consumption composition and technological change on the trade-off between inequality and emissions reductions; and the implications of electrification and renewable energy expansion, as well as rebound effects from household energy-efficiency gains. Eurogreen+ thus provides an integrated empirical framework for analysing policy mixes aimed at promoting ecological transition and social cohesion with respect to the presented baseline.

Title: The rise of refinery margins: The case of the energy tax cut in Germany
Authors: Leonard Gregor, Justus Haucap
Abstract: This paper evaluates the temporary reduction in energy taxes implemented by the German government between 1 June and 31 August 2022. Measured against the delivered cost of importing the same fuel from the Amsterdam–Rotterdam–Antwerp (ARA) region, German wholesale prices net of tax rose by 5–6 (gasoline) and nearly 4 (diesel) cents per liter during the cut, corresponding to measured pass-through of 83% and 73%. The two numbers have different economic interpretations. We separate them using heating oil, the same middle distillate as diesel but with no tax cut. We find that the diesel wedge reflects the 2022 gasoil supply shock rather than seller conduct. Therefore the diesel tax cut was passed through in full. The gasoline wedge, however, is genuine retention of about 382 million Euro, a sixth of the gasoline subsidy. We also find that retention is largest where regional buyers are affluent and locally captive. Mobile bulk-buying haulage, in contrast, disciplines diesel pricing. Lastly, we show that pass-through is enforced by the threat of imports. This arbitrage ceiling was suspended when historically low Rhine water levels physically rationed inland supply.

Title: Electricity demand without shared thermal comfort: Intra-household thermal preference heterogeneity under heat
Authors: Natalia Borzino, Samuel Chng, Harvey Neo
Abstract: Rising temperatures are increasing residential electricity demand as households rely more on mechanical cooling in hot urban environments. In much of the energy and climate literature, higher electricity use under heat is treated as evidence of successful private adaptation and preserved thermal comfort. This paper shows why that inference can fail when comfort is unevenly experienced within the household. Using linked intra-household survey data and administrative electricity records from Singapore—a dense tropical city with near-universal electricity access—we examine whether electricity demand is associated with within-household differences in reported thermal comfort that may reflect heterogeneous thermal preferences. We measure within-household variation using individual reports of comfort in unconditioned (non–air-conditioned) indoor environments, which may reflect heterogeneous thermal preferences and tolerance as well as differences in exposure. Households with greater comfort dispersion consume significantly more electricity per capita, conditional on mean comfort, income, dwelling characteristics, appliance stock, ventilation practices, and cooling behaviours. A one-standard-deviation increase in comfort dispersion is associated with approximately 5.6% higher electricity consumption per capita. By contrast, the max–min comfort gap is not significantly associated with electricity use. A complementary diagnostic analysis finds no statistically significant association between higher electricity consumption and narrower within-household comfort gaps. Together, the results are consistent with heterogeneous thermal preferences creating coordination and allocation challenges in shared cooling decisions, while highlighting why aggregate electricity use alone cannot reveal how comfort is distributed among household members—with implications for residential energy-demand modelling and the assessment of heat adaptation.

Title: Physics-informed energy-consumption prediction and charging-demand gap identification for logistics electric vehicles
Authors: Muhammad Asim Ayaz, Irfan Ullah, Quan Yuan, Chao Yang, Wei Zhao, Ali Alhawiti
Abstract: This study develops a trajectory-derived and physics-informed framework for energy-consumption prediction and charging-demand gap identification using trip-level Logistics Electric Vehicles (LEV) data from Shanghai. The analysis retained 857,697 valid trips from 1,985 LEVs. A Physics-Informed Battery-Consistency Neural Network (PIBC-NN) was developed to jointly predict trip-level energy consumption and state-of-charge (SOC) depletion while maintaining consistency between predicted energy use, SOC loss, and battery capacity. The model showed reliable performance, explaining 85.9% of the variation in energy consumption and 83.5% of the variation in SOC consumption. Charging demand was identified by combining observed charging events with low-SOC conditions, revealing an evening peak and spatial concentration in logistics activity zones. Although existing stations provided broad coverage for general demand, localized service gaps remained. Clustering identified 100 demand-oriented candidate locations for 8,945 priority-gap demand points. Under the proposed scenario, mean nearest-station distance decreased from 2.92 to 0.35 km and 2 km coverage reached 95.98%.

Title: Dynamic road-traffic noise exposure assessment for suburbs using traffic fundamental-diagram-based speed reconstruction
Authors: Zhaolang Wu, Yujie Wu, Haibo Wang, Qijun Zhang, Bin Sun, Lin Wu, Yan Liu, Hongjun Mao
Abstract: Road-traffic noise exposure in suburban areas is strongly influenced by the coupled dynamics of vehicle classes, traffic states, and population distribution, which cannot be adequately captured by conventional static assessments. This study proposes a physics-informed dynamic exposure framework integrating vehicle-class-specific traffic-state reconstruction, population dynamics, and acoustic propagation modelling. A multi-vehicle-type coupled speed network is developed by embedding traffic fundamental diagrams into neural learning to reconstruct large-, medium-, and small-vehicle speeds under heterogeneous traffic conditions. The model achieved RMSE/MAE values of 6.40/5.07 km/h on observed roads and 6.75/5.36 km/h on unseen roads. Application in suburban Beijing revealed distinct exposure mechanisms: nighttime freight activity caused critical exposure during 01:00–02:00, whereas daytime risks were governed by different combinations of traffic intensity and population presence. The proposed framework enables vehicle-class- and time-specific noise exposure assessment for refined suburban noise management.

Title: Strong Nash equilibria of core-selecting double auctions
Authors: Shuntaro Kawachi
Abstract: We study core-selecting auctions for double auctions that incorporate package bidding. Unlike in one-sided core-selecting auctions, the core may be empty in more general double auction settings, and truncation strategies need not be amongst a bidder’s best responses. Nevertheless, we establish the existence of a core-selecting auction in which every imputation in the core with respect to true preferences corresponds to a strong Nash equilibrium. Specifically, for any core imputation, there exists a profile of truncation strategies that constitutes a strong Nash equilibrium and induces precisely that imputation.

Immigration, selection, and human capital: The Venezuelan inflow and educational pathways in Ecuador
Authors: Julio Acuna
Abstract: Using a shift-share design that leverages the unanticipated Venezuelan migration crisis, I examine immigration’s impact on educational attainment in Ecuador. Immigration positively affects standardized test scores, consistent with greater effort among course takers aiming for college enrollment. Test scores show no significant effects on primary or middle schoolers. The effects lead to more college graduates and more high school dropouts, widening educational inequality. Student composition and the intensity of preparation for college admission among course takers explain the results.

Title: Building collaboration in FMCG supply chains: a time-based perspective
Authors: Claudia Colicchia, Marco Melacini, Michela Coita, Fabrizio Dallari
Affiliations: Politecnico di Milano Department of Management, Economics and Industrial Engineering, , Milan; LIUC University School of Industrial Engineering, , Castellanza
Abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how supply chain collaboration (SCC) initiatives in logistics develop and are sustained over time. While SCC is widely discussed in the literature, existing research predominantly adopts static perspectives, treating collaboration mechanisms as stable configurations rather than temporally evolving practices. This study addresses this gap by adopting a temporal, process-oriented perspective on SCC development. Design/methodology/approach The study adopts a qualitative multiple-case research design, analysing 15 collaboration initiatives across nine companies, comprising major food retailers and multinational producers, operating in the Italian Fast-Moving Consumer Goods sector. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews, pre-interview questionnaires and company documentation and analysed through within-case and cross-case analysis. Findings The findings show that collaboration mechanisms do not function uniformly across the lifecycle of an initiative: their role and relevance shift as partnerships mature. The cross-case analysis identifies two additional empirical insights: collaborative function autonomy, the degree of operational independence enjoyed by logistics teams in driving collaboration, and the dual role of time, both as an operational resource and as a relational enabler of trust. Building on these insights, the study proposes a time-based framework mapping how mechanisms are introduced, adapted and sustained across four phases: inception, development, execution and evolution. Practical implications The framework provides managers with a phased roadmap for designing and managing collaborative initiatives, supporting more realistic expectations about the pace of collaboration and the investments required at each stage. It also functions as a diagnostic tool, enabling organisations to identify gaps in their collaborative capabilities and plan targeted interventions. Originality/value The study’s central theoretical contribution is the concept of collaborative timing: the strategic alignment of mechanism introduction with the relational and operational maturity of the partnership. This concept is grounded in two supporting empirical contributions: first, evidence that established SCC mechanisms acquire different roles depending on the phase of an initiative; and second, a time-based framework that distinguishes phase-specific from continuous mechanisms across four phases (inception, development, execution, evolution).

Ancestral Distance and the Cultural Foundations of State Capacity
Authors: Trung V. Vu
Affiliations: Loughborough Business School Loughborough University Leicestershire UK; Centre for Applied Macroeconomic Analysis Australian National University Canberra Australia
Abstract: ABSTRACT This study investigates the role of long‐term population relatedness in shaping global variation in state capacity. It argues that longer periods of ancestral separation are associated with greater divergence in intergenerationally transmitted civic norms governing voluntary compliance with state institutions. Ancestral distance may also hinder the international diffusion of effective state institutions, contributing to persistent cross‐country differences in state capacity. The empirical analysis shows that countries with greater ancestral distance from the global frontier of effective state institutions exhibit lower state capacity. Dyadic regressions further indicate that ancestral distance is associated with greater divergence in state capacity. To examine a potential cultural foundation of this relationship, I exploit variation in cultural backgrounds among second‐generation immigrants residing in the same country. I find that immigrant populations with greater ancestral distance exhibit larger differences in self‐reported attitudes towards voluntary tax compliance. Taken together, the findings suggest that ancestral distance is an important historical predictor of cross‐country disparities in state capacity, consistent with a role for divergence in civic norms and barriers to institutional diffusion.

Title: Interior-Point Algorithms for Monotone Linear Complementarity Problem Based on Different Predictor Directions
Authors: Marianna E.-Nagy, Tibor Illés, Yurii Nesterov, Petra Renáta Rigó
Affiliations: Corvinus Centre for Operations Research at Corvinus Institute for Advanced Studies, Corvinus University of Budapest, 1093 Budapest, Hungary
Abstract: In this paper, we introduce two parabolic target-space interior-point algorithms for solving monotone linear complementarity problems (LCPs). The first algorithm is based on a universal tangent direction, which has been recently proposed for linear optimization problems. We prove that this method has the best-known worst-case complexity bound. We extend onto this LCP its auto-correcting version proposed by Nesterov and prove its local quadratic convergence under the assumption of the existence of a unique and strictly complementarity solution. In our numerical experiments, we compare the new algorithms with a general method, recently developed for weighted monotone linear complementarity problems. Title: A sequential foundation for two-level nested logit
Authors: Davide Luparello
Abstract: I show that the two-level nested logit model arises exactly from a sequential choice process in which group, subgroup, and product shocks are revealed in stages. The result extends to any number of levels and holds for any nesting parameters below one, without the bounds and ordering that random utility maximization requires. Parameter estimates that applied work discards for violating the standard ordering or the lower bound are consistent with sequential choice. The linear inversion and welfare formula hold. When the standard ordering fails, improving one product can raise a rival's market share in its subgroup, even with single-unit demand.

Title: Dimensions of program quality and returns to short-cycle technical education
Authors: Simona Comi, Federica Origo, Elena Villar
Abstract: This letter examines whether an external, multidimensional, high-stakes measure of program quality predicts heterogeneity in the returns to short-cycle tertiary technical education. We use student-level administrative data matched to official program-quality scores and estimate individual fixed-effects models with individual-specific linear time trends. We find that employment, earnings, and skill-match returns to the diploma are lower in low-rated programs. Delving into the different dimensions of the composite quality indicator, we find that program attractiveness and firms’ involvement in traineeships provide the strongest signals, with the traineeship gradient persisting also once controlling for program attractiveness.

Title: Hierarchical scheduling and merging control of autonomous UAV platoons in networked airspace
Authors: Yixuan Wang, Shunying Zhu, Hao Zhang
Abstract: To address collision risks and scheduling delays during air-merging and path convergence tasks involving multiple autonomous quadrotor uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs), this article proposes a hierarchical cooperative control framework for Autonomous UAV Platoons (AUPs), integrating event-triggered rolling-horizon scheduling with distributed fixed-terminal-time trajectory planning and physical-feasibility feedback. At the macroscopic level, historical flight data are analyzed using dynamic clustering and mixed integer linear programming to determine the structure of platoon formation, the optimal merging sequence, and the assigned terminal times. At the microscopic level, a distributed fixed-terminal-time trajectory-planning method is developed using analytical free and constrained trajectories, a finite constrained-arc library, and a convex-QP numerical fallback. Continuous-time feasibility validation is further introduced to verify the physical realizability of the planned trajectories, and certified temporal conflicts are fed back to the upper-level scheduler for reoptimization. The simulation results show that, the proposed framework reduces the objective value and mean UAV delay by up to 13.13% and 19.31%, respectively, while reducing online optimization calls by 93.65%.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Deep reinforcement learning for home health care routing and scheduling problem with interdependent services
Authors: Yaoxin Wu, Yuwei Gu, Ping He, Rong Cheng, Lu Zhang, Yingqian Zhang, Zhiguang Cao
Abstract: The home health care routing and scheduling problem (HHCRSP) is a highly challenging yet critical task, as it directly impacts the efficiency and quality of clinical services provided to patients at home. Due to the intricate interdependence among services, the HHCRSP is inherently complex and computationally demanding, especially for producing high-quality solutions under operational time limits. In this paper, we propose a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) method to address the HHCRSP with interdependent services. We first decompose the HHCRSP into a series of service-specific vehicle routing subproblems, and then formulate the solution construction process for each subproblem as a Markov decision process. Finally, we design an encoder-decoder-based policy network that constructs routes for healthcare staff, from which the corresponding service schedules are derived. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed DRL-based approach outperforms conventional metaheuristics and construction heuristics. Furthermore, the learned policy shows strong generalizability, achieving favorable performance across different problem sizes, distributions, and even in dynamic HHCRSP scenarios.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Dynamic transmission effects of shipping news sentiment on port congestion: A multi-regional empirical study
Authors: Haoqing Sun, Zhuo Sun, Jiaju Han, Xinrui Jing
Abstract: Exogenous shocks, including geopolitical conflicts and extreme weather events, frequently disrupt global shipping networks. The resulting port congestion threatens the stable operation of container supply chains. Existing studies of port congestion rely primarily on structured operational data, while the potential risk signals contained in shipping news remain underused. This study collects 235,860 shipping news articles from multiple sources between 2017 and 2025. A shipping specific sentiment lexicon and a large language model supported by retrieval augmented generation are combined to construct weekly Shipping Sentiment Indices (SSIs) at five analytical levels: global, cross-regional corridor, Asia-Pacific, Europe, and North America. The SSIs are then matched with weekly Port Congestion Levels (PCLs) processed from Clarksons data. A vector autoregression model is employed to examine the in-sample dynamic interaction between SSIs and PCLs, as well as regional heterogeneity. The results show a predictive relationship between shipping news sentiment and subsequent port congestion. Following a negative sentiment shock, port congestion across all regions rises rapidly, peaks within two to three weeks, and then gradually declines, with some residual effects remaining over the 12-week horizon. The explanatory power of SSI varies markedly across regions and is more pronounced in Asia-Pacific and North America than in the other regions. These findings provide a sentiment-based framework for analyzing port congestion and offer useful insights for port management and shipping policy.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Joint optimization of congestion pricing and lane reversal strategies for heterogeneous CAVs
Authors: Tongfei Li, Jiabao Yan, Min Xu, Huijun Sun, Jianjun Wu
Abstract: This study addresses the joint optimization of congestion pricing and lane reversal strategies (JOPPL) in transportation networks with heterogeneous connected and autonomous vehicles (CAVs). As CAV-based ride-hailing (e.g., Robotaxi) could reduce private vehicle ownership, we distinguish between private CAVs that minimize individual travel costs and shared CAVs that are centrally routed to minimize fleet-wide generalized travel costs. To simultaneously tackle inefficient flow distribution and imbalanced directional demand from a ”supply-demand” synergy perspective, our model minimizes total travel time by co-optimizing lane allocations and toll rates across the network while respecting multi-class user equilibrium principles. We formulate this problem as a mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) model using a link-node approach, thus avoiding the need for path enumeration. To overcome computational complexity, the original MINLP problem is reformulated as a mixed-integer linear program (MILP) via various linearization techniques, enabling an efficient solution procedure through a proposed algorithm that iteratively solves relaxed subproblems and nonlinear complementarity problems with a prescribed optimality tolerance. Variable boundary reduction further enhances computational performance. Numerical experiments demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness, achieving total travel time reductions of up to 73.24% under asymmetric demand scenarios. The results highlight the potential of integrated CAV-oriented strategies to significantly improve network performance by reallocating road resources and redistributing traffic flow.

Title: Participation, procedural fairness and policy acceptability: A quasi-experimental field study of workplace travel planning
Authors: Lucia C. Burtnik Urueta, Lorraine Whitmarsh, Kostas Iatridis
Abstract: Parking restrictions are among the most effective tools available to organisations and local authorities seeking to manage transport demand and reduce commuting emissions — yet their implementation routinely fails when commuters question their legitimacy, and the conditions under which such measures gain acceptance during the development stage remain poorly understood. This study examines whether involving commuters in the development of restrictive travel measures increases their acceptance, applying policy acceptance and deliberative democracy literatures to an organisational transport context for the first time. Using a quasi-experimental field design embedded in a real travel plan development process at a UK university generating over 20,000 daily trips (N = 486), we compare standard consultation via a travel survey with enhanced involvement via deliberative workshops. Mediation analysis shows that workshop participation increased perceived procedural fairness, which in turn increased policy acceptance, replicating and extending Liu et al.'s (2020) participation–fairness–acceptance pathway to an organisational setting. A significant negative direct effect indicates that deliberation simultaneously raised critical scrutiny, producing inconsistent mediation. Trust in the organisation emerged as a precondition of participation: deliberative engagement increased acceptance among those who already trusted the institution. Contrary to practitioner concerns, self-selection into workshops was driven by role rather than scepticism or anticipated personal costs. For local authorities and organisations developing restrictive travel policies, these findings suggest that deliberative involvement can build the legitimacy necessary for effective implementation where institutional trust has already been established, and where the process is designed to be genuinely fair and inclusive.

Title: Paving the road to prosperity: Productive government spending, takeoff and robust endogenous growth

Title: Flow-based market coupling and market integration in the Nordic electricity market: Evidence from price convergence and transmission
Authors: Kyriaki Tselika, Maria Tselika, Elias Demetriades
Abstract: This paper examines the effects of flow-based market coupling and renewable electricity generation on price convergence and transmission patterns in the Scandinavian electricity market. Using hourly day-ahead data for the Norwegian bidding zones NO1 and NO2 and the Danish bidding zone DK1 from January 2023 to September 2025, we estimate fixed-effects panel regressions to analyze how the introduction of Flow-Based Market Coupling (FBMC) in October 2024 affected cross-border and internal market integration. The results show that FBMC is associated with improved price convergence and higher exports between NO2 and DK1, while its direct effect on internal Norwegian price convergence and transmission between NO2 and NO1 is limited. Renewable generation remains an important driver of market outcomes, with Danish wind generation continuing to widen cross-border price differences and Norwegian renewable generation playing a stronger role in supporting cross-border exchange after the reform. Overall, the findings suggest that FBMC can improve aspects of market integration, but that its effectiveness depends on underlying generation patterns, network constraints, and complementary grid capacity and flexibility resources. This highlights the importance of combining market-design reforms with grid reinforcement and flexibility measures as renewable penetration increases.

Title: Road-focused flood depth and velocity prediction using deep learning for transportation resilience
Authors: Ahmad ALBarqawi, Viravid Na Nagara, Ahmad Ibrahim, Ashish Borgaonkar, Camille Kamga, Hani Nassif, Abdallah Khreishah, Michel Boufadel
Abstract: Flooded roadways threaten mobility and public safety, underscoring the need for high-resolution, road-specific flood prediction tools. This study developed a deep learning framework to predict flood depth and velocity on transportation networks using geomorphic and hydrologic features. A UNet-based Convolutional (UNet Conv) model and a UNet Convolutional Long Short-Term Memory (UNet ConvLSTM) model were implemented for flood depth and velocity, respectively. By incorporating roadway-focused weighted loss functions, the models prioritized accuracy on road pixels and achieved strong performance (Depth: R 2 ≈ 0.89, RMSE ≈ 0.07 m; Velocity: R 2 ≈ 0.93, RMSE ≈ 0.08 m/s). The framework generalized well to unseen storm conditions (R 2 > 0.75). Unlike conventional hydrologic and hydraulic models, this method eliminates the need for time- and resource-intensive modeling setups, thereby facilitating rapid flood prediction using readily available data. These results demonstrate the potential of road-focused deep learning to support flood forecasting, transportation resilience planning, and emergency response.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Evaluating unmanned courier stations for green last-mile delivery: a network psychometric analysis
Authors: Zhaotong Li, Kum Fai Yuen, Chee-Chong Teo
Abstract: Unmanned courier stations (UCS) are emerging as a green last-mile delivery option that may reduce failed deliveries and associated environmental impacts. However, limited research has examined how consumers evaluate this delivery mode as an integrated belief system. Drawing on Social Cognitive Theory, this study conceptualises consumer evaluation of UCS as a network of interrelated individual and environmental beliefs. Survey data from 612 participants in Singapore were analysed using a construct-level Gaussian graphical model and a directed acyclic graph. Results identify Trust and Response Efficacy as the most influential component in the evaluation system, followed by Green Promotion, Emotional and Epistemic Value, Green Price, and Green Product. The directed network further suggests the possible upstream positioning of Green Product relative to other evaluative beliefs. By modelling consumer evaluation as a belief system rather than isolated predictors, the study provides insights for designing interventions that promote the sustainable UCS.

Title: Sequential non-Bayesian persuasion
Authors: Yaron Azrieli, Rachana Das
Abstract: We study a model of persuasion in which the receiver's updating rule systematically distorts Bayesian posteriors. While in the classic Bayesian case providing information sequentially is never valuable, we show that the sender gains from sequential persuasion in several of the environments considered in the literature on strategic information transmission. Our proofs are constructive and reveal how properties of the bias interact with the payoff environment to make dynamic persuasion beneficial.

Title: Probabilistic selling for perishable goods: A game-theoretic framework to reduce near-expired food waste
Authors: Guoquan Zhang, Tianxin Ren

Title: Advancing the NCQG: A Fuzzy Multi-Criteria Model for Evaluating National Contributions to Climate Finance
Authors: Adel Ben Youssef, Davide La Torre, Jelena Jovović
Abstract: Climate finance is central to making the Paris Agreement work, and the New Collective Quantified Goal (NCQG) of at least USD 300 billion per year by 2035 agreed at COP29 in Baku intensifies the long-standing challenge of sharing a collective effort across countries in a way that is seen as fair. This paper proposes a fuzzy multi-criteria goal programming (FMGP) framework to allocate the NCQG across potential contributors. Building on earlier linear multi-criteria work, it treats four equity dimensions often invoked in climate finance debates – responsibility (historical or current emissions), economic capacity (total or per capita income), population and innovation effort – as fuzzy goals rather than rigid constraints. Each goal is represented by a membership function and an aspiration range, and the model searches for allocations that maximise a common satisfaction index while respecting the NCQG envelope. Using 2022 data, the analysis combines four fairness metrics (cumulative versus current emissions and total versus per capita GDP) with five contributor scenarios that gradually widen the pool from a narrow group of traditional donors to a broader coalition including the United States, Gulf states and major emerging economies. The results show that metrics linking cumulative emissions to income, in particular a hybrid specification using cumulative emissions and GDP per capita, generate more balanced and politically plausible contribution profiles than metrics based only on current emissions, and that widening the contributor base spreads the burden but reduces the degree to which equity goals can be satisfied simultaneously. Compared with a linear benchmark, the fuzzy model produces less extreme obligations and narrower contribution ranges, indicating that making “fairness” explicitly fuzzy can support the design of NCQG burden-sharing arrangements that are both transparent and negotiable in the Baku–Belém phase.

Title: Deviations from the Nash equilibrium in a two-player optimal execution game with reinforcement learning
Authors: Fabrizio Lillo, Andrea Macrì
Abstract: The use of reinforcement learning algorithms in financial trading is becoming increasingly prevalent. However, the autonomous nature of these algorithms can lead to unexpected outcomes that deviate from traditional game-theoretical predictions and may even destabilize markets. In this study, we examine a scenario in which two autonomous agents, modelled with Double Deep Q-Learning, learn to liquidate the same asset optimally in the presence of market impact, under the Almgren-Chriss (2000) framework. We show that the strategies learned by the agents deviate significantly from the Nash equilibrium of the corresponding market impact game. Notably, the learned strategies exhibit supra-competitive solution, {which might be compatible with a tacit collusive behaviour}, closely aligning with the Pareto-optimal solution. We further explore how different levels of market volatility influence the agents'performance and the equilibria they discover, including scenarios where volatility differs between the training and testing phases.

Title: Duopoly competition in a service market with strategic heterogeneous customers and servers
Authors: Gabi Hanukov, Refael Hassin
Abstract: Abstract This paper analyzes duopoly competition between service providers when the demand is segments so that each segment prefers a certain server if prices were equal. For example, a customer needs to choose between two hospitals where one of them is closer than the other. We are interested in the interaction between the service providers, the resulting price equilibrium, and conditions for each of them to act as a monopoly. The analysis consists of two steps. First, we compute the (unique) equilibrium joining (and balking) strategies of customers given the service fees set by the servers. We present five types of equilibria when customers do not balk and twelve additional types when balking is implemented. Using this customer behavior, we compute the duopoly price equilibrium.

Title: Decomposing the ideological divide in perceptions of inequality: a signal detection approach
Authors: Hannah B. Waldfogel, Daniel J. Connolly, Eldar Shafir
Abstract: A central puzzle in the social sciences is that, despite high and rising inequality, democracies consistently under-deliver redistributive policies. Research in economics and political science has documented one explanation for this puzzle: beliefs about the extent of inequality are polarized along ideological lines, with liberals believing there to be more inequality than conservatives. We decompose this ideological divide in inequality perceptions into two sources: the decision threshold applied by liberals and conservatives when classifying possible instances of inequality (‘criterion’) and their tendency to perceive inequality to begin with (‘sensitivity’). Across six studies (N = 2734), we find that liberals consistently report seeing more inequality than conservatives when exposed to identical stimuli. A formal signal detection decomposition reveals ideological differences in both the discriminability of inequality signals (‘sensitivity’) and the threshold applied when classifying them (‘criterion’). The ideological gap in perceived inequality disappears when stimuli depict inequality unambiguously— that is, when the signal is strong enough to clear even the strictest decision thresholds. Notably, we find that perceived inequality is associated with fairness concerns and support for redistributive policies above and beyond ideological orientation. These findings suggest that the everyday settings in which people encounter instances of social inequality are themselves likely to produce consequential differences in beliefs about the extent of inequality.

Title: How energy system developments affect elasticities in day-ahead electricity markets: Evidence from bid curves
Authors: Arjen T. Veenstra, Michaela Kesina, Machiel Mulder
Abstract: Since the liberalization of European electricity markets in the late 1990s, many aspects of the energy landscape have changed significantly. In this study, we investigate how the day-ahead electricity market has developed over time and how these changes are related to the growth of renewable generation, changes in fossil fuel prices and increased international integration. We do this using a rich dataset from the European Power Exchange, containing data on hourly bids that were submitted in the Dutch day-ahead market in the period 2006–2024. We use these bids to construct demand and supply curves, estimate the price elasticities of demand and supply from these curves, and examine how these elasticities have evolved over time in response to the above-mentioned developments. Our results show that both elasticities have decreased over time. The decrease in elasticities of demand is related to the growth in renewable electricity supply, as renewable production changes the number of bids and the distribution of bid prices. Supply curves are affected by renewable production via the same mechanisms, but these mechanisms now work in opposite directions such that there is no clear relationship between between renewable production and elasticities of supply. We also find that increased international trade is associated with lower elasticities as supply and demand curves shift, while the relationship between fuel prices and elasticities is less consistent.

Title: Clean vehicle incentive design and urban air quality: Evidence from Italy
Authors: Anna Laura Baraldi, Claudia Cantabene, Alessandro De Iudicibus
Abstract: Governments increasingly use financial incentives to promote electric and hybrid vehicles, yet evidence on their effects on urban air quality remains limited. This paper studies sub-national vehicle incentives in Italian provincial capital municipalities over 2013–2023. Exploiting spatial and temporal variation in regional, autonomous-provincial, and municipal policies, we implement a staggered-adoption difference-in-differences design accounting for heterogeneous treatment timing. We distinguish between direct cash subsidies, which reduce the upfront purchase price, and fiscal incentives operating through vehicle-tax exemptions or reductions. In our preferred specification, exposure to policy environments including cash subsidies reduces the maximum annual average concentration of nitrogen dioxide (NO 2 ) by about 2.5 μ g/m 3 , or 8.3 percent of the sample mean. The effect develops gradually after adoption and remains robust across alternative comparison cohorts and additional checks. By contrast, pooled and fiscal specifications provide no comparable evidence of improved air quality, while the fiscal event studies exhibit differential pre-treatment dynamics. Cash-incentive exposure is also followed by a delayed increase in electric and hybrid vehicles and a decline in the diesel component of the passenger-car fleet. The effect of local incentive programs are less clear in terms of gasoline car purchases. Overall, measurable improvements in urban air quality are more clearly identified in policy environments including upfront subsidies.

Title: Risk, time and social preferences shape cross-country support for carbon dioxide removal technologies
Authors: Chad M. Baum, Leonhard K. Lades, Livia Fritz, Benjamin K. Sovacool
Abstract: Technical innovations that remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere are gaining attention to compensate for the insufficient pace of emissions reductions. Given the scale of carbon dioxide removal (CDR) deployment envisioned, there is a notable deficit in our understanding of the underlying predictors of public support of CDR, particularly in the global South. In economic theory, risk, time and social preferences serve as fundamental predictors of judgment and decision making. The current article thus undertakes a systematic examination of economic preferences and how they predict support for three CDR technologies (direct air capture, enhanced rock weathering, afforestation and reforestation). We employ experimentally validated instruments to examine how fundamental differences in individual tendencies to take risks, be patient or act pro-socially affect CDR support. Drawing on nationally representative surveys in five countries ( n = 4000 respondents from Brazil, China, Germany, Kenya, USA), we first establish how CDR support varies between technologies and countries, with support lower for novel CDR technologies and broadly higher for global South publics. To explain such differences, we reveal the relevance of economic preferences for CDR support, notably the positive predictive effects of risk-taking, altruism, and trust. We also indicate how the relevance of economic preferences varies across technologies and countries. Risk-taking, altruism and trust have stronger effects on novel, engineered CDR support, but positive reciprocity matters more for afforestation. The results stress the importance of economic preferences as core, under-explored predictors of individual and cross-country variation in public support of CDR technologies.

Title: Strategies to minimize energy vulnerability: A machine learning assessment of the roles of artificial intelligence innovations, green investments, and energy balance
Authors: Emmanuel Uche, Ali Shadady, Mamdouh Abdulaziz Saleh AL-Faryan
Abstract: Energy vulnerability has far-reaching consequences for economic performance, climate resilience, and environmental sustainability. This study provides empirical evidence on how artificial intelligence (AI) innovation, green investments (GI), and energy balance (EB) can be used to reduce energy vulnerability. Using data from 2000 to 2022 and a combination of panel econometric and machine learning (ML) techniques, the study examines the effects of these factors on energy vulnerability across the G10 economies. It also evaluates the moderating roles of energy efficiency, energy transition, energy intensity, and governance quality. The findings show that AI has a limited vulnerability-reducing effect when the G10 countries are considered collectively. At the country level, however, AI significantly lowers energy vulnerability in Denmark, the Netherlands, and the United Kingdom. It also reduces energy vulnerability marginally in the remaining G10 economies, except Sweden, where its effect is positive and substantial. GI significantly lowers energy vulnerability in France, Japan, and the United States, while EB produces a significant reduction only in the Netherlands. The effects of GI and EB vary across other G10 countries, highlighting the need for country-specific policy responses. Results from the best-performing machine learning model, Gradient Boosting, reveal that AI is the most influential predictor of energy vulnerability. It is followed by energy efficiency, energy transition, and green investment. Based on these findings, policymakers should encourage the use of supervised AI in grid management and energy systems to limit the adverse effects associated with AI-driven energy demand. Additional measures include developing real-time vulnerability assessment metrics for green investment projects and linking energy balance to electricity tariffs through time-of-use pricing mechanisms.

Title: JUE insight: Pandemic-induced changes in service industry agglomeration economies
Authors: Naqun Huang, Jindong Pang, Yanmin Yang

Title: Breaking drug trafficking chains: digital monitoring on courier services and the decline of drug use
Authors: Pinghan Liang, Wei Zou
Abstract: Postal and courier services have become an important channel for drug trafficking worldwide. This study examines the impact of digital monitoring of mail on drug use. Based on the universe of drug arrest records in a populous province in China, the difference-in-differences analysis reveals that, after the implementation of real-identity mailing (RIM) in 2017, the number of punished drug users decreased by 5.8% in townships with any courier service points. This effect persists for at least 1 year. The number of first-time users diminishes, while the number of addicted users remains constant. These suggest that strengthening the regulation of postal and courier services may be a cost-effective approach to drug control, and courier service platforms and government could collaborate to solve public health challenges and improve social welfare.

Title: Introduction to special issue: Integrating earth observation into impact studies in agriculture and climate change
Authors: Ariel BenYishay, Karen Macours, Manjula Ranagalage, Kunwar K. Singh

Title: When Shared Manufacturing Meets the Digital Platform: Exploring the Operating Modes and Optimal Matching Policy
Authors: Xiao‐Feng Shao
Affiliations: Antai College of Economics and Management, Shanghai Jiao Tong University Shanghai People's Republic of China
Abstract: ABSTRACT The advent of shared manufacturing, driven by digital technologies, has significantly impacted the utilization of social manufacturing resources, leading to the expansion of the sharing economy into the industrial domain. Manufacturing sharing platforms generally adopt one of three operating modes: transaction (TR), supplier‐matching (SM), and requester‐matching (RM). In TR mode, the platform compensates suppliers and resells capacity to requesters; in SM mode, the platform charges requesters for matching services; and in RM mode, it collects a commission from suppliers. This study develops an analytical model of a platform that connects requesters with suppliers exhibiting heterogeneous capacity utilization and incurring different capacity‐sharing costs under each operating mode. Driven by the interaction between the platform's commission target (supplier vs. requester) and the sequence of pricing decisions in capacity sharing, we find that the RM mode maximizes platform profit, the SM mode achieves the highest capacity utilization, and the TR mode leads to the highest gross merchandise volume (GMV). Furthermore, we establish the optimality of a matching policy that prioritizes suppliers with greater capacity slack in the supply queue and requesters with larger capacity shortages in the demand queue. Numerical analyses show that, compared to a first‐come‐first‐served (FCFS) policy, priority‐based matching substantially improves average financial performance, social welfare, and consumer surplus. Overall, this research provides valuable insights into selecting operating modes and designing matching policies for manufacturing sharing platforms, with significant implications for industry practices and social welfare.

Title: Rolling-horizon reliable supply chain planning for IC design house with forecast evolution and customer order behavior
Authors: James C. Chen, Tzu-Li Chen, Po-An Chou, Dewanti Anggrahini
Abstract: In today’s highly competitive electronics market, demand for integrated circuit (IC) is increasingly uncertain due to fluctuating customer orders and continuous forecast revisions. This uncertainty challenges reliable supply chain planning (SCP), including coordinating production and resource-allocation decisions, efficiently utilizing available manufacturing capacity, and ensuring on-time delivery. In the product setting examined in this study, IC design houses manage a complex multi-stage and multi-site production network in which forecast-driven wafer production operates in a make-to-stock (MTS) mode, whereas order-driven back-end production operates in a make-to-order (MTO) mode. To improve SCP reliability under demand uncertainty, this study develops a data-driven rolling-horizon decision-support framework that integrates demand forecast evolution modeling, customer order behavior (COB), and optimization-based SCP. Two martingale model of forecast evolution (MMFE) structures, including additive and multiplicative forms, are combined with COB to construct behavior-based MMFE models that better capture realistic demand uncertainty and order dynamics. These data-driven demand evolution models are then incorporated into a rolling-horizon SCP (RHSCP) model formulated as a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP). An extended RHSCP model with stochastic lot sizing (RHSCP-SLS) is developed and solved using MILP with a piecewise-linear approximation. To evaluate the reliability and robustness of the proposed planning framework, this research establishes a rolling-horizon simulation environment and conducts experiments under different MMFE types, covariance levels, customer order behavior patterns, SCP models, and capacity utilization levels. The results provide decision-support insights into how demand uncertainty, customer ordering behavior, and capacity conditions affect supply chain performance and planning reliability.

Title: Pure-Strategy Equilibrium in the Generalized First-Price Auction
Authors: Michael Ostrovsky, Andrzej Skrzypacz
Affiliations: Stanford University, Stanford, California 94305; and National Bureau of Economic Research, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02138
Abstract: We revisit the classic result on the (non-)existence of pure-strategy Nash equilibria in the generalized first-price auction for sponsored search advertising and show that the conclusion may be reversed when ads are ranked based on the product of stochastic quality scores and bid amounts rather than solely on the bids or on the product of bids and deterministic quality scores. Moreover, the expected revenue in the pure-strategy equilibrium of the generalized first-price auction may substantially exceed that of the generalized second-price auction, although under some conditions, the relation may also be reversed. History: This paper has been accepted for the Mathematics of Operations Research Special Issue on Market Design.

Title: Uniform Value and Decidability in Ergodic Blind Stochastic Games
Authors: Krishnendu Chatterjee, David Lurie, Raimundo Saona, Bruno Ziliotto
Affiliations: Institute of Science and Technology Austria, 34000 Klosterneuburg, Austria; CEREMADE, Paris Dauphine University, PSL Research University, 75016 Paris, France; and NyxAir, 91590 Baulne, France; Toulouse School of Economics, Université Toulouse Capitole, Institut de Mathématiques de Toulouse, CNRS UMR 5219, 31080 Toulouse Cedex 06, France
Abstract: We study a class of two-player zero-sum stochastic games known as blind stochastic games, where players neither observe the state nor receive any information about it during the game. A central concept for analyzing long-duration stochastic games is the uniform value. A game has a uniform value v if for every [Formula: see text], Player 1 (resp., Player 2) has a strategy such that, for all sufficiently large n, his average payoff over n stages is at least [Formula: see text] (resp., at most [Formula: see text]). Prior work has shown that the uniform value may not exist in general blind stochastic games. To address this, we introduce a subclass called ergodic blind stochastic games, defined by imposing an ergodicity condition on the state transitions. For this subclass, we prove the existence of the uniform value and provide an algorithm to approximate it, establishing the decidability of the approximation problem. Notably, this decidability result is novel even in the single-player setting of Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs). Furthermore, we show that no algorithm can compute the uniform value exactly, emphasizing the tightness of our result. Finally, we establish that the uniform value is independent of the initial belief. Title: Strategy Complexity of Büchi and Transience Objectives in Concurrent Stochastic Games
Authors: Stefan Kiefer, Richard Mayr, Mahsa Shirmohammadi, Patrick Totzke
Affiliations: Department of Computer Science, University of Oxford, Oxford OX1 3QD, United Kingdom; School of Informatics, The University of Edinburgh, Edinburgh EH8 9AB, United Kingdom; Institut de Recherche en Informatique Fondamentale and Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique, Université Paris Cité, F-75013 Paris, France; School of Computer Science and Informatics, University of Liverpool, Liverpool L69 3DR, United Kingdom
Abstract: We study two-player stochastic games on countable graphs. Players Max and Min seek, respectively, to maximize and minimize the probability of satisfying the game objective. The Büchi objective is to visit a given set of states infinitely often. The Transience objective is to visit no state infinitely often. In Büchi games, there exist [Formula: see text]-optimal Max strategies that use just a step counter plus 1 bit of public memory. This upper bound holds for all countable graphs, but is a new result even for finite graphs. It is tight, because Max strategies that use just a step counter, or just finite memory, are not sufficient, even on finite game graphs. This upper bound follows from a slightly stronger new result: [Formula: see text]-optimal Max strategies for the combined Büchi and Transience objective require exactly 1 bit of public memory. Moreover, [Formula: see text]-optimal Max strategies for the Transience objective alone can be chosen as memoryless. Funding: Financial support from Agence Nationale de la Recherche [Grant ANR-22-CE48-0005] and the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council [Grant EP/X042596/1] is gratefully acknowledged.

Title: Inference for batched adaptive experiments
Authors: Jan Kemper, Davud Rostam-Afschar
Abstract: The advantages of adaptive experiments have led to their rapid adoption in economics, other fields, and among practitioners. However, adaptive experiments pose challenges for causal inference. This note suggests a BOLS (batched ordinary least squares) test statistic for inference on treatment effects in adaptive experiments. The statistic provides a precision-equalizing aggregation of per-period treatment-control differences under heteroskedasticity. The combined test statistic is a linear combination of heteroskedastic per-period z-statistics and can be used to construct asymptotically valid confidence intervals. We provide simulation results comparing rejection rates in the typical case with few treatment periods and few (or many) observations per batch.

Title: Climate regulation and civil society activism
Authors: Michela Limardi, Jordan Loper, Alexandre Volle
Abstract: This paper examines how climate public regulation shapes NGO activism against firms. We develop a private-politics framework where regulation alters campaign incentives through two opposing mechanisms: a cost-reducing channel lowering monitoring costs, and a value-diminishing channel where state compliance substitutes for private pressure. When the cost-reducing channel dominates, public regulation crowds in civil-society activism. Testing these predictions on a novel monthly panel of NGOs across 76 countries (2010–2023) within an event-study design, we show that executive regulations trigger a persistent increase in firm-targeted activism without pre-trend anticipation. Textual evidence shows that NGOs explicitly invoke regulatory benchmarks in their campaigns and that their use around enactment is not confined to campaigns already underway. Mobilization is strongest in weaker regulatory environments and concentrated among national NGOs targeting domestic firms. Together, these findings demonstrate that public regulation mobilizes civil society as an informal enforcement layer, extending climate governance beyond formal state action.

Title: The social–ecological system framework for farming adaptation: the influence of social capital on eco-practices
Authors: Andrea Belmartino, Marta Meleddu, Manuela Pulina, Marco Vannini
Abstract: Climate change has intensified the urgency of ecological transitions, particularly within small-scale farming systems, which are vital for food supply but highly vulnerable to environmental pressures. This study applies the Social-Ecological System framework to examine how different forms of social capital (bonding, bridging, and linking) shape ecological practices and identifies climate change as a collective action issue. Using survey data from Sardinian sheep farmers, a Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) disentangles the effects of social capital on the adoption of ecological innovations. Results show that bonding social capital reinforces traditional ecological practices, while trust in agricultural institutions ( agro-linking ) is the most consistent predictor of adoption across both traditional and innovative pathways. In contrast, bridging and institutional linking show no statistically significant effect in this context. Productivity expectations and eco-technical knowledge further mediate adoption, highlighting both economic and cognitive drivers of the adoption process. The findings provide empirical evidence of the multidimensional effects of social capital on distinct ecological pathways, offering policy-relevant insights. Sustaining traditional practices requires leveraging local networks and community knowledge, whereas innovation-oriented policies should focus on building institutional trust, technical knowledge, and closer farmer–institution linkages.

Title: Navigating the challenges of open innovation in the electric vehicle sector: a micro–meso–macro perspective on mitigation strategies
Authors: Yuanhan Chen, Reeti Agarwal, Rsha Alghafes, David Kalisz, Andreas Kallmünzer
Abstract: Open Innovation (OI) strongly influences the Electric Vehicle (EV) sector, but with its introduction comes issues such as constraint on resources, coordination problems, conflicts arising from power disparities, lack of clarity around innovation route, and threat to brand equity.. The current study applies Systems Theory and Resource Dependence Theory to conduct qualitative research using Gioia Methodology to explore employees’ views on OI challenges in the EV sector via Prolific Academic. The findings demonstrate the presence of five significant challenges related to OI application on three separate levels: (I) Micro Level – Employees experience blockages in resource usage and coordination difficulties; (II) Meso Level – Companies and partners suffer from asymmetric relations and lack clarity about innovative partnerships; and (III) Macro Level – The company and sector face systemic threats concerning their supply chains and dependence on external sources. To overcome these issues, organisations used a targeted approach that included supplier diversification, contingency planning, transparent communication, and formal agreements with stronger contractual protection. At the ecosystem level, OI firms collaborated with government and society to reduce systemic risks. Finally, the analysis indicates that OI EV firms must find the right mix of openness and control and provides several practical implications with respect to how EV firms can establish resiliency and maintain functional open innovation partnerships.
