A clique-based adaptive neighbourhood search for the vehicle routing problem with simultaneous pickup and delivery
Authors: Napoleão Nepomuceno, Victor Tiezzi Henriques, Davi Otoch Barroso
Abstract: The Vehicle Routing Problem with Simultaneous Pickup and Delivery (VRPSPD) is a challenging NP-hard problem in which each customer requires both delivery and pickup services within a single visit. This paper proposes a clique-based adaptive neighbourhood search framework (CB-ANS) for the VRPSPD. At each iteration, the method explores a large neighbourhood by solving a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model on a reduced subgraph induced by a dynamically selected customer clique. The clique size is adaptively adjusted according to the solver optimality gap, providing explicit control over the trade-off between neighbourhood size and computational effort. Computational experiments on three VRPSPD variants show that CB-ANS recovers all proven optimal solutions for the asymmetric variant and consistently outperforms reference methods for the green and heterogeneous variants, with particularly strong gains on larger instances. Additional analyses of search dynamics show that improvements are driven by the interaction between MILP-based neighbourhood exploration and local refinement, highlighting the complementary roles of diversification and intensification within the proposed framework.

Title: Blocking the blockers? Defensive investment and aggregate productivity
Authors: Iacopo Varotto

Title: Occupational choice, human capital formation and life-cycle earnings
Authors: Siyu Shi
Abstract: This paper studies how occupational choice shapes life-cycle earnings growth and inequality, and how this margin changes the effects of progressive taxation. I focus on occupational technology exposure , measured as the intensity of information technology usage, and document its positive relationship with earnings. I develop a life-cycle model with a college decision, human capital investments, occupational choices, and incomplete markets. Results suggest occupational choice incentivizes human capital formation over the life-cycle and hence affects life-cycle earnings. In particular, it accounts for 42% of life-cycle earnings growth and 45% of inequality growth. Endogenous occupational choice also amplifies the distortionary effect of progressive taxation on earnings growth by 30% relative to a model without occupational choice. This amplification also leads to a larger decline in tax revenue and a larger welfare loss when tax progressivity increases.

Title: Banking on jobs: Impact of a workfare program on formal credit
Authors: Mayuri Chaturvedi, Asad Rauf
Abstract: We study the impact of India’s National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme (NREGS) on household borrowing from banks. Exploiting the program’s staggered rollout, we find a significant increase in personal loans and bank accounts in the early-adopting districts. Using household-level data, we show that NREGS-participating households had higher confidence in banks and were more likely to borrow from banks than from moneylenders. These effects are strongest among households with the highest NREGS earnings. Banks were also more likely to approve loan applications from NREGS-participating households, suggesting that these households became better credit risks, possibly because the program provided an income floor and reduced information asymmetries. This paper provides evidence on the interactions between welfare and credit markets within the context of a large developing country. More broadly, our findings suggest that investments in state capacity (the state’s ability to design, implement, and enforce policies) support financial market development.

Title: Unraveling subjective streetscape perceptions’ impact on walking-to-school-propensity using geospatial explainable machine learning
Authors: Fangning Wu, Wenjing Li, Waishan Qiu
Abstract: Active school travel delivers substantial environmental, social, health, and well-being benefits. Existing studies have mainly examined environmental influences on walking to school using linear or nonlinear models, with limited attention to spatial variation and interaction effects. Moreover, large-scale assessment of students’ subjective streetscape perceptions remains challenging. To address these gaps, this study collected students’ perceptions through pairwise street view image comparisons and integrated CatBoost with a GeoShapley framework to investigate walking-to-school behavior in Hong Kong. Results reveal nonlinear effects of subjective perceptions, with enclosure and traffic safety emerging as particularly influential factors. Their effects varied across space, indicating context-dependent associations with walking behavior. Furthermore, interactions among perceptions showed that combined streetscape qualities could produce synergistic or counteractive effects. These findings provide evidence for context-sensitive street design strategies to promote active school travel.

Title: Changing bodies changes minds—and behavior? An economist’s guide to embodiment interventions
Authors: Nina Rapoport
Abstract: This review examines how virtual embodiment interventions can inform economic research on inequality across social groups. In these interventions, widely used in psychology and related disciplines, virtual reality is used to embody individuals in virtual bodies whose appearance (skin tone, gender, age, etc.) can be experimentally manipulated to represent a member of a distinct social group. We propose a simple framework for understanding how outgroup embodiment may affect prejudice- and identity-related outcomes through other-regarding preferences, beliefs about the represented group, and beliefs about the self. We synthesize the existing literature, provide a practical guide to designing such interventions, and discuss the methodological trade-offs involved in their implementation. The review makes a two-way contribution: embodiment interventions offer economists a promising tool to study the socio-cognitive foundations of inequality, while an economic framework provides a path toward clarifying whether “changing bodies” can change not only minds but also behavior.

Title: Dude, Where's Our Stuff? A Systematic Literature Review of Shortages in Supply Chain Management
Authors: Anne E. Dohmen, Jason W. Miller
Affiliations: Michigan State University East Lansing Michigan USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT Supply chain shortages (SCSs) arise when firms cannot access enough inputs to meet demand, and the resulting gap cannot be closed through routine operational responses or price adjustments. SCSs are practically important because they occur frequently and are disruptive, motivating this systematic literature review of supply chain management studies examining the causes and consequences of SCSs. Based on the systematic literature review, this research develops a holistic model that categorizes the sources of SCSs; recognizes the reciprocal relationship between realized and anticipated SCSs; proposes a 2 × 2 framework grouping firms' actions in response to SCSs along dimensions concerning internal versus external orientation and whether actions improve resource access versus reduce resource importance; and postulates that firm traits and product/service attributes moderate the impact that SCSs have on firms' actions. We suggest several directions for future research to extend understanding of SCSs.

Title: Issue Information
Corrigendum to “Hierarchical graph reinforcement learning for energy-efficient dual-resource distributed flexible job shop scheduling” [Comput. Oper. Res. 196 (2026) 107703]

Title: Structural Breaks in the Taylor Rule
Authors: Neil R. Ericsson
Affiliations: Department of Economics George Washington University Washington DC USA; School of Advanced International Studies Johns Hopkins University Washington DC USA; Climate Econometrics University of Oxford Oxford, England UK
Abstract: ABSTRACT Stillwagon (this issue) tests extensively for structural breaks in a dynamic Taylor rule for US data and finds no breaks over 2001–2025, whether using Bai–Perron tests or multiplicative indicator saturation. The current paper complements and builds on Stillwagon by focusing on features specific to three Fed chairs (Bernanke, Yellen, and Powell) during 2006–2025, and on the zero lower bound. The Taylor rule is chair‐specific; and the zero lower bound affects the Taylor rule for Yellen's and Powell's tenures. These economically significant structural breaks are detectable by multiplicative indicator saturation that focuses on those features, whereas the broad‐spectrum multiplicative indicator saturation in Stillwagon misses these breaks. Such structural breaks limit the interpretability and usefulness of the Taylor rule for monetary policy.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: Optimal investment in pooled maintenance resources under uncertain demand for multi-site production
Authors: Jing Li, Junkai He, Peng Hu, Miguel F. Anjos, Najat Bara
Abstract: This study investigates a novel long-term investment optimization problem involving shared maintenance resources in multi-site production systems, motivated by applications such as industrial gas production and renewable energy networks. In these systems, critical maintenance resources, including high-value backup machines and specialized technicians, are too costly and inflexible to be deployed at each individual site. To address this challenge, we develop an integrated framework that combines Remaining Useful Life (RUL)-based preventive maintenance with a centrally managed pool of backup machines and technicians across multiple sites. The objective is to minimize the total investment cost of the pool while ensuring service reliability under uncertain demand. To account for this uncertainty, we further propose a distributionally robust optimization model with a Mean-CVaR (conditional value-at-risk) risk measure to capture both the expected shortage and tail risk under partial distributional information. The proposed model allows flexible control of risk aversion while preserving robustness against demand ambiguity. It is reformulated as a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model to ensure tractability and further exploit problem-specific structural properties to improve computational efficiency. The computational results show that (i) centralized pooling reduces total investment cost, especially in larger systems and under stronger demand uncertainty; (ii) higher machine degradation rates lead to substantially higher maintenance-resource investment; and (iii) compared with benchmark models, the proposed model achieves a better trade-off between service reliability and investment cost under uncertainty.

Title: The interplay between a dual-purpose e-tailer and a manufacturer under green strategies
Authors: Xuan Jiang, Yuhe Zhang, Yanhai Li
Abstract: This paper investigates a supply chain comprising a green-product manufacturer and a dual-purpose e-tailer that values both profit and environmental benefit. To characterize their cooperation in green production, we incorporate a cost-sharing contract. We develop game-theoretic models under four scenarios—reselling and agency selling, each with and without cost sharing—and compare the equilibrium outcomes across sales models and cooperation arrangements. Our analysis yields three main findings. First, a higher level of the e-tailer's environmental concern not only improves environmental performance, but also increases the manufacturer's profit and may even enhance the e-tailer's own profit. Second, cost sharing plays distinct strategic roles across the two sales models: it is primarily investment-oriented under reselling but more compensation-oriented under agency selling. This difference in mechanism can reverse the relative ranking of the two sales models in terms of product greenness and environmental performance, and helps reconcile the conflict in the two parties' sales-model preferences. Third, an e-tailer-offered cost-sharing contract can generate a win-win-win outcome for the manufacturer, the e-tailer, and the environment, whereas this outcome does not arise under a Nash-bargained cost-sharing contract.

Title: State ownership and deposit safety
Authors: Gabriel Ramos
Abstract: Do depositors see state-owned banks as safer? The isolated, unexpected failure of Banco Santos, a private bank, in November 2004 raised the perceived risk of uninsured deposits in Brazil. Time deposits at state-owned banks grew 6.6 percentage points per month faster than at private banks, a gap of 56 percent after seven months. Excluding the largest banks leaves the estimate unchanged, separating ownership from too-big-to-fail size. Demand and savings deposits, whose clients were almost all fully insured, show no movement.

Title: Centrality crowding in asset prices: A limited-attention network model
Authors: Lei Pan
Abstract: This paper develops a one-period behavioral model of price aggregation in social networks. Investors combine noisy private signals with a centrality-weighted social feed. In the equal-precision benchmark, pricing error is summarized by M = σ 2 H , where H is the Herfindahl concentration of equilibrium signal weights. Greater centrality amplification increases H in non-uniform networks, reducing price informativeness. A Gaussian projection implies larger one-period corrections when pricing error is greater. With heterogeneous precision, centrality-based attention is efficient if and only if visibility weights align with precision weights. The model links network concentration to fragile price discovery.

Title: Air transport networks and urban economic activity: Dynamic relationships across major global airports
Authors: Kashin Sugishita, Shunsuke Kajikawa, Shinya Hanaoka, Xiaoqian Sun, Anming Zhang
Abstract: This study examines the dynamic relationships between air transport network structure and urban economic activity across the world’s top 50 airports by passenger volume in 2024, using monthly data from 2014 to 2024. As the aviation indicator, we adopt the Global Airport Connectivity Index (GACI), a composite measure of network measurements; as the economic indicator, we use Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) Nighttime Lights (NTL), providing a globally consistent, high-frequency proxy for urban economic activity. Short-run causality is assessed via the Toda–Yamamoto procedure, and long-run equilibrium relationships are tested using the Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) bounds testing approach. The Toda–Yamamoto test reveals that approximately 90% of airports exhibit no statistically significant short-run Granger causality in either direction, indicating that monthly network changes and economic fluctuations do not move in lockstep. In contrast, the ARDL bounds test detects long-run cointegration at 45 airports. The predominant pattern is aviation-led at 33 airports, with bidirectional relationships at 11 airports and economy-led at only one. Among the 11 bidirectional airports, the speed-of-adjustment analysis reveals that NTL adjusts toward equilibrium faster than GACI in every case, reflecting the structural rigidity of network reconfigurations relative to economic responses. These findings demonstrate that changes in air transport network structure predominantly precede adjustments in urban economic activity in the long run, offering policy implications for airport infrastructure investment.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: The environmental effects of forest land property rights decentralization reform: evidence from the reform of China’s collective forest rights system
Authors: Yu Qi, Aoxue Yin, Jianwei Chen, Rui Zhou, Xi Wu
Abstract: Forests are critical global ecosystems. The security of property rights and the incentives they create determine whether these resources are degraded or protected. This study evaluates the environmental and economic impacts of China's Collective Forest Property Rights Reform (CFPR), which decentralized tenure from village collectives to individual households. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design with manually compiled, county-level implementation data, as well as household-level panel surveys, we isolate the causal effects of securing individual residual claims in forested landscapes. Our findings indicate that formalizing property rights increases county-level forest cover by 0.523 percentage points. A physical decomposition reveals that the majority of this aggregate expansion is attributable to active afforestation. At the micro level, secure tenure extends investment horizons and alters household behavior. The reform stimulates a comprehensive reallocation of production factors, including local labor retention, land transfers, and capital investment. These factors collectively drive rural entrepreneurship and income growth. Concurrently, reduced household reliance on firewood is consistent with a potential mechanism through which the reform may reduce forest fire risks. Alongside forest dynamics, this intra-community privatization produces notable ecological spillovers, including increased carbon storage, improved soil conservation, reduced coarse particulate pollution, and increased wildlife biodiversity.

Title: Beyond generations: Old age allowance and girls’ educational investment in Nepal
Authors: Prashant Bhandari, Narendra R. Regmi
Abstract: Social protection programs can affect not only their direct beneficiaries but also other household members, with important implications for human capital investment in low-income settings. In Nepal, where gender disparities in educational investment remain pronounced, additional household resources may reduce these gaps if girls’ schooling is especially vulnerable to tight household budgets. This paper examines whether Nepal's Old Age Allowance (OAA), a universal non-contributory social pension for older adults, generates such intergenerational effects. Using panel data from the Nepal Household Risk and Vulnerability Survey and a fuzzy regression discontinuity design that exploits the program's age-70 eligibility cutoff, we estimate the causal effect of OAA receipt on children's educational expenditure in households near the threshold. We find a marked gender asymmetry: OAA receipt increases annual educational expenditure for female students by about Rs 3802, or roughly 56 percent of the control mean, while the corresponding effect for male students is small and statistically insignificant. The increase for girls is driven mainly by tuition, suggesting that pension income helps households cover the direct costs of formal schooling. Results by recipient gender do not support a simple female-control bargaining channel. Instead, the findings point more toward a financial-constraints interpretation, in which additional resources entering the household through older adults increase spending on daughters’ schooling. More broadly, the paper shows that an untargeted social pension can generate meaningful intergenerational spillovers in children's education even when it is not designed as an education program, especially in settings where girls’ schooling is more vulnerable to resource scarcity.

Title: Securing Nigeria’s oil pipelines: delegation and hybrid security governance
Authors: Esther Egele-Godswill
Abstract: How does delegating oil infrastructure security to politically embedded non-state actors (re)shape the political relations through which oil is governed? This article addresses this question by examining the case of pipeline surveillance contracts awarded by the Nigerian government to former militant leaders in the Niger Delta. It shows how these contracts function as delegated security arrangements, through which the state incorporates former militant leaders, with political, social, and territorial capacities, into its limited capacity to combat artisanal oil refining and secure its oil pipelines, producing a hybrid form of security governance. Drawing on ethnographic data, informal conversations, and scholarly and secondary sources, the article argues that delegation is not merely a neutral response to limited state capacity, but a form of political brokerage linking the security of critical oil infrastructure to the distribution of patronage, the cultivation of political alliances, and strategic calculations during election periods. The article contributes to debates on natural resource infrastructure management and hybrid security governance by showing that delegation can exceed formal state objectives, generating political and institutional effects that extend beyond the function being delegated.

Title: A lean expression-graph formulation for the Traveling Thief Problem and its interval bounds
Authors: Mahdi Khemakhem, Khalil Chebil
Abstract: The Traveling Thief Problem (TTP) combines the Traveling Salesman Problem and the 0/1 Knapsack Problem through a load-dependent speed function that tightly couples routing and packing decisions. Exact models fail beyond a few dozen cities, and the strongest heuristics rely on problem-specific operators. This paper focuses on the formulation and models the TTP for a general-purpose solver, Hexaly, by representing the objective as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) over a sequence variable. The main contribution is M-LEG (Lean Expression-Graph model), which replaces the conditional (iif) arcs of a direct encoding with array lookups (at) and a linear cumulative weight chain. This reduces the graph from cubic to near-quadratic size and speeds up the search. The paper also clarifies which interval bound drives the reported gap. The conditional encoding inflates the upper travel-time bound by a factor that grows quadratically with the number of cities, but the gap depends on the lower bound, so the sound gap of M-LEG is only slightly smaller. Finally, the experiments provide a reproducible baseline. On toy instances, M-LEG reaches its best solution four times faster than the direct formulation and matches or improves the Gurobi incumbent, which is proven optimal on only two instances. On the 40 smallest of 60 categorized instances, which favors M-LEG, it ranks fifth of ten up to 130 cities when all methods are scored on their mean over ten runs, and its best run beats the best CoCo+ run on five of them. Beyond that size it ranks last.

Title: Corridor-level infrastructure costs of static charging versus electric road systems in Germany
Authors: Mathias Schmidt, Grit Walther
Abstract: Heavy-duty road freight is expected to electrify through static charging at private depots, logistics facilities and public high-power sites, while Electric Road Systems (ERS) are often considered too capital-intensive. Existing comparisons cover highway sections, but not a national network, and the two technologies are costed in incompatible units. This study develops a bottom-up model that sizes and prices the static infrastructure required by battery-electric truck demand across the German highway network: electrified loading docks, public charger parks, substations, storage and grid connections. Dividing cost by edge length yields a corridor-kilometre metric comparable with an ERS benchmark. Static charging is more expensive on 37.6 percent of the modelled German and cross-border corridor length and reaches 2.6 to 3.2 times the EUR 4 million per kilometre benchmark on the busiest segments. Assigning the lower-cost technology to each edge yields an idealized investment saving of 21 percent. The model is available at https://ers.infrai.de/ .
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Spatial coopetition between shared autonomous vehicle services and metro railway
Authors: Yanan Liu, Wen Zeng
Abstract: The interaction between shared autonomous vehicles (SAVs) and metro railway exhibits coopetition which acts as both complementary feeders and competitive substitutes. The literature overlooks how these roles coexist and shift across spatial and behavioral contexts. This study employs a latent class logit model with multilevel spatial effects to analyze the stated mode shifts of 1110 respondents in Chengdu, China. The findings indicate that SAV feeders potentially enhance metro accessibility. The enhancement is primarily characterized by public transportation and active modes rather than cars. Competitive pressure from SAVs for full trip substitution accelerates across station catchment tiers and central city/suburban areas. This variation is driven by the effects of personal characteristics, SAV services, and built environment. A competition-mitigation framework is proposed, for example, implementing dedicated lanes that prioritize feeders over full-trip services, and applying strict service regulations in outer catchment where urban design alone fails to prevent metro abandonment.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Separate selling vs collaborative bundling in livestreaming with attention externalities
Authors: Ramesh Krishnan, Jagan Jacob
Abstract: Livestreaming sellers aim to earn revenue today while also expanding an audience that supports future sessions. This paper studies how two streamers choose between selling their products separately or offering them as a bundle (collaborative streaming) when their first-period decisions influence the shared reachable audience available in the next session. We develop a two-period game in which first-period prices shape both immediate demand and the shared audience capital that determines the effective market size in the following period. The analysis shows that separate selling creates an attention externality. Each streamer benefits from the future shared reach generated by current activity, yet accounts only for its own continuation value. As a result, first-period prices under separate selling can be misaligned with the level that would maximize combined long-run earnings. The direction of this distortion depends on the strength of shared-audience accumulation and on how much the streamers value future audience reach. When the audience-conversion rate is modest, or when streamers place little weight on the next session, the standard static business-stealing force dominates and independent streamers price more aggressively than a joint decision maker would. When audience conversion becomes more effective and future audience value grows, the uninternalized continuation benefit from shared-audience accumulation becomes stronger, and independent streamers may instead keep prices too high relative to the joint benchmark. Bundling eliminates the decentralized pricing externality by centralizing the pricing decision, and it can become especially attractive when the bundle regime generates stronger shared-audience accumulation. The analysis identifies sufficient conditions under which this dynamic consideration can overturn the usual static ranking of the two formats. Separate selling often appears more profitable in a one-period comparison, yet bundling can become superior when streamers place sufficient value on future audience reach and when the bundle regime supports sufficiently strong shared-audience accumulation. These results offer a rationale for collaborative bundles in the creator economy. Bundles act not only as a selling device but also as a tool for building shared reachable audience that strengthens future sessions.

Title: Editorial Board
Centralized governance, household preferences and publicly provided education: Evidence from Vietnam
Authors: Somdeep Chatterjee, David Fielding, Manhar Manchanda
Abstract: How does fiscal and administrative centralization affect the provision of public services? We address this question using a 2009 Vietnamese reform which dissolved elected district councils in some provinces and transferred authority to provincial bodies. Exploiting spatial and temporal variation in program implementation, we find that centralization reduced household education subsidies, a key public expenditure in Vietnam. Households responded by increasing out-of-pocket education spending, lowering non-recurrent consumption to offset the decline in public support and maintain enrolment levels. The replication package for this study, including the data, code, and supporting materials necessary to reproduce the reported results, is available here . The authors are responsible for the completeness and accuracy of the replication materials.

Title: How beauty affects peers: evidence and mechanisms from randomly assigned classes in China
Authors: Bing Li, Zhengwei Yan
Abstract: This paper investigates the peer effects of physical attractiveness on students’ cognitive and non-cognitive outcomes. Utilizing a nationally representative sample of Chinese middle school students with random class assignment, we find that exposure to more physically attractive peers is associated with improved academic performance, cognitive skills, and non-cognitive skills. Further analysis reveals that these effects are driven by interactions between male and female students. We provide evidence that these effects operate through improvements in the classroom environment, increased student effort, and enhanced teaching styles, as well as greater teacher responsibility and patience.

Title: Green upgrades under emission cap regulation
Authors: Zhiyuan Cao, Jianxiong Zhang, Xiaojie Sun, Zhaofang Mao
Affiliations: Tianjin University; Southwest Jiaotong University
Abstract: Manufacturers face significant uncertainty regarding green upgrade returns due to strict emission caps and their informational disadvantage relative to retailers. This paper investigates the interplay between emission caps and asymmetric market information in shaping a manufacturer’s green upgrade and pricing decisions. We develop a game-theoretic model of a supply chain where the retailer holds private demand information, resulting in a signalling game via pricing. Our analysis yields three key insights. First, we reveal a regulatory paradox: relaxing strict emission caps can incentivise upgrades by expanding effective capacity and mitigating double marginalisation. Second, information superiority becomes a strategic liability for the retailer. To credibly signal high demand, the retailer is compelled to lower her margin, which erodes her profit but benefits the manufacturer. Third, information asymmetry generates a positive welfare side effect. The retailer’s strategic margin reduction acts as a corrective mechanism for double marginalisation, leading to lower prices and higher social welfare compared to the symmetric information scenario. Our findings suggest that policymakers should balance regulatory stringency with information structures; specifically, moderate regulatory relaxation in information-asymmetric contexts can effectively stimulate corporate green transformation while enhancing market efficiency.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Pharmaceutical supply chain procurement strategies: group or decentralized
Authors: Lu Wu, Zonghuo Li, Xun Xu, Xiangfeng Chen
Affiliations: Fudan University; Jiangsu University; Soochow University; San José State University
Abstract: As drug expenditures continue to rise, healthcare systems face growing pressure to improve procurement efficiency and control supply costs. Using game theory, this study identifies optimal procurement strategies for each stakeholder in the pharmaceutical supply chain, depending on market size, discount levels, and the group purchasing organisation’s (GPO) bargaining power. Specifically, medical institutions tend to engage in group procurement to aggregate demand in smaller markets, while in larger markets, they favour diversified strategies to maintain sourcing flexibility. The pharmaceutical manufacturer is more likely to adopt low-discount group procurement in both small and large markets, but shifts towards diversified procurement under medium or high discounts to maximise profits. A further comparison between decentralised and group procurement, with the manufacturer remaining the leader and the decision sequence unchanged, shows that medical institutions benefit more from group procurement as discounts strengthen. However, the manufacturer benefits only when demand expansion and economies of scale offset price concessions. Moreover, GPO bargaining power emerges as a pivotal factor that can alter the game’s dynamics, with its relative strength or weakness even capable of reversing the strategic choices of both buyers and suppliers. Managerial implications for medical institutions and pharmaceutical manufacturers regarding their procurement strategy are discussed.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: A robust location-routing model with self-service lockers and micro-hubs for last-mile logistics under uncertainty
Authors: Fang Guo, Jingfu Liang, Tianqi Gao, Xiaofan Ding, Zhihong Huang
Affiliations: School of Management, Zhengzhou University
Abstract: The rapid expansion of e-commerce has increased the need for cost-effective last-mile delivery, particularly in regions with fragmented demand. This study develops a robust location-routeing model, termed the Vehicle Routeing Problem with Self-Service Parcel Lockers and Micro-Hub Locations (VRP-SPMH), integrating self-pickup service and en-route replenishment. The model jointly determines facility locations, customer service modes, and vehicle routes while accounting for customer willingness and finite facility capacities. Parcel-locker operating-cost uncertainty is modelled using a multi-interval robust formulation, while demand uncertainty is addressed through a protected-demand extension. Additional sensitivity analyses examine demand scale and travel-time variation. Tailored hybrid heuristics based on tabu search and modified Clarke-Wright savings are developed. Computational experiments include ablation and an independent Variable Neighbourhood Search (VNS) benchmark. The proposed heuristic achieves solution quality close to VNS with substantially less computational effort and reaches competitive solutions earlier under short-to-medium time budgets. Out-of-sample tests further reveal the trade-off between nominal cost and robustness. A rural case study in China shows that coordinating parcel lockers and micro-hubs reduces total operating cost by 7.82% relative to traditional home delivery.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Analytical Modeling and Real-Time Control for Serial Lines with Soft Residence Time Constraints

Title: How does collaboration shape supply chain resilience? Evidence from climate-exposed agri-food systems
Authors: Truong Quang Dung, Huy Truong Quang, Rajendra P. Adhikari, Kien Nguyen-Duc
Affiliations: RMIT International University Vietnam The Business School, , Ho Chi Minh City; RMIT International University School of Business and Management, , Ho Chi Minh City, , and Institute of Business Research, University of Economics Ho Chi Minh City, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam; The University of Queensland School of Agriculture and Food Sciences, , Brisbane; Hue University of Economics Faculty of Economics and Development Studies, , Hue
Abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate how supply chain resilience (SCR) emerges in agri-food supply chains under persistent climate stress. It examines the effects of specific supply chain collaboration mechanisms on SCR and evaluates whether entrepreneurial orientation (EO) serves as a behavioural enhancement pathway linking collaboration mechanisms to SCR. Design/methodology/approach Grounded in complex adaptive systems theory, the study adopts a chain-level perspective of resilience. Data were collected from 205 actors across multiple tiers of the Vietnamese smallholder coffee supply chain. Structural equation modelling was used to assess the direct effects of collaboration mechanisms on SCR and the mediating role of EO. Findings Operational collaboration mechanisms, namely information sharing, incentive alignment, decision synchronisation, communication and resource sharing, were positively associated with SCR. EO also had a positive effect on SCR and partially mediated the relationships between selected mechanisms (information sharing, incentive alignment and resource sharing) and SCR. The findings indicated that collaboration enhanced resilience through both operational coordination and behavioural adaptation pathways, while strategic alignment mechanisms showed delayed effects. Research limitations/implications The study is based on cross-sectional, perceptual data from a single commodity and regional context, which may limit generalisability. Future research should adopt longitudinal designs and examine diverse supply chain settings to further validate system-level and behavioural mechanisms of resilience. Practical implications Managers and policymakers should prioritise collaboration practices that strengthen information flows, align incentives and enable resource sharing. In parallel, fostering entrepreneurial behaviours among supply chain actors can enhance adaptive responses to climate-related disruptions. Originality/value This study contributes to SCR literature by unpacking collaboration into distinct mechanisms and identifying EO as a behavioural micro-foundation through which resilience emerges at the chain level in fragmented and decentralised supply chains.
Journal: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

Title: Data-driven supplier reliability evaluation and governance decision support in automotive supply chains
Authors: Meng Qiu, Shihao Qi, Jatinder N. D. Gupta, Tsui-Ping Chung
Abstract: The reliable operation of supplier networks is critical for automotive supply chains exposed to multi-dimensional operational uncertainties. This study develops a data-driven decision support framework for supplier reliability evaluation and governance. Supplier reliability is conceptualized across five core operational dimensions: quality, logistics, cost, sustainability, and technological capability. To process empirical performance indicators objectively under uncertainty, we propose a hybrid Entropy-TOPSIS-GRA model. This model integrates data-driven indicator weighting with distance-based geometric proximity measures and profile-based grey relational similarity into a unified supplier reliability index. The sensitivity of supplier rankings is examined through indicator-weight perturbation and fusion-parameter checks. Applying this methodology to operational evaluation records from 222 suppliers of a leading Chinese automotive manufacturer reveals distinct reliability variances. We demonstrate how these results map into percentile-based, risk-informed governance tiers coupled with prescriptive management interventions. This framework offers an empirical illustration for moving beyond static supplier rankings toward actionable, reliability-oriented supply network governance.

Title: Bayesian reliability acceptance sampling plans under adaptive accelerated type-II censored competing risks data
Authors: Rathin Das, Soumya Roy, Biswabrata Pradhan
Abstract: With modern products becoming increasingly complex and reliable, failures typically occur only after prolonged use and may arise from multiple causes. This study develops Bayesian Reliability Acceptance Sampling Plans (BRASPs) under a competing risks framework using a Simple Step-Stress Partially Accelerated Life Test (SSSPALT) with Type-II censoring. An adaptive testing scheme is also proposed, wherein the stress level is elevated at a pre-specified time if the number of failures observed is below a certain threshold. A Bayes decision function is derived under a general loss function, and the corresponding Bayes risk is evaluated. The optimal BRASP is then obtained under a quadratic loss function. An algorithm is presented to compute the optimal plan. Comparative studies are conducted against conventional accelerated and non-accelerated BRASPs to evaluate their relative performance. The proposed methodology is finally illustrated using a real dataset.

Title: PING: Physics-informed graph neural network for advection–diffusion processes with applications to solar power forecasting
Authors: Jelena Simeunović, Baptiste Schubnel, Pierre-Jean Alet, Pascal Frossard, Rafael E. Carrillo
Abstract: Advection–diffusion plays an essential role in transport phenomena such as atmospheric and cloud dynamics. Improved forecasting of cloud motion, in turn, enhances solar power production forecasts and facilitates the integration of additional photovoltaic (PV) sources into the power grid. However, both classical numerical models and emerging deep learning approaches face challenges when applied to spatially irregular sensor networks such as those formed by weather stations. In this work, we adopt a graph signal processing perspective and model advection–diffusion particles as signals on a graph to capture the dynamics of these processes. We introduce a physics-informed graph neural network (PING) for forecasting future advection–diffusion particle concentrations on irregular grids. The model incorporates a discretized advection–diffusion equation as a soft constraint in the loss function to guide learning toward physically consistent solutions. This model is on par with state-of-the-art models on synthetic and real transport phenomena datasets, including sea surface temperature and cloud index datasets. Furthermore, the PING model is successfully coupled with models for forecasting PV power production. This hybrid approach leverages data fusion from ground-based sensors at PV stations and satellite images with cloud concentration to improve the accuracy of intra-day PV power production.

Title: Modeling asymmetric risk contagion between Chinese and global commodity markets: A network quantile GARCH approach
Authors: Xiaohang Ren, Yue He, Jianxin Pan, Lulu Wang
Abstract: We propose a novel framework integrating network dependencies, volatility clustering, and quantile-specific contagion dynamics to quantify asymmetric risk transmission between Chinese and global commodity markets. Addressing limitations in existing models that isolate time and cross-sectional dimensions, our network quantile GARCH model captures heterogeneous spillover effects across quantile levels while endogenizing network synchronization mechanisms. Applied to energy, metals, and agricultural markets, the framework reveals that downward shocks propagate through commodity networks with amplified intensity compared to upward movements, and volatility clustering exhibits nonlinear interactions with network connectedness. By unifying network econometrics with quantile GARCH regression, we develop an adaptive estimator that captures time-varying volatility dynamics while incorporating network-driven contagion and tail heterogeneity through a fixed network structure. This approach enhances systemic risk forecasting accuracy by overcoming the “constant correlation” assumption prevalent in traditional methods. The findings challenge conventional views on risk contagion homogeneity, demonstrating that commodity markets form dynamic risk ecosystems where network dependencies and volatility regimes co-evolve. This work provides a framework for monitoring asymmetric risk transmission and tail-risk dynamics in Chinese and international commodity markets, offering insights for market risk assessment in interconnected commodity systems.

Title: Density forecasts and the evolution of macroeconomic uncertainty in India
Authors: Karan Bhasin, Kajal Lahiri, Prakash Loungani
Abstract: This paper estimates macroeconomic uncertainty using density forecasts from the Reserve Bank of India’s Survey of Professional Forecasters (2008–2023). These forecasts enable direct measurements of unobservable shocks to uncertainty in real time as the first difference in the second moment of the densities. In addition, we implement a bin-by-bin calibration test based on the prequential principle. We report four key findings: (i) macroeconomic uncertainty in India has been declining since 2008; (ii) shocks to uncertainty derived from density forecasts compare favorably with other popular measures, viz. the Economic Policy Uncertainty (EPU) index and the Volatility Index (VIX); (iii) uncertainty is affected primarily by negative news and is variance-rational; and (iv) it captures demand shocks even after controlling for global uncertainty shocks, in contrast to the EPU and VIX, which are primarily driven by supply shocks. Distinguishing these shocks is crucial for optimal monetary policy.

Title: Joint optimization of opportunistic maintenance and cascade utilization for homogeneous components under scheduled windows
Authors: Jiaoyang Ma, Shuguang He
Abstract: Many degradation-prone systems, such as railway freight cars, contain multiple homogeneous components maintained through scheduled inspection windows, providing institutional opportunities for coordinated maintenance under limited resources. Early intervention may waste residual service value, whereas delayed maintenance increases failure risk before the next window. This paper develops a prognosis-informed scheduled-window opportunity maintenance framework that integrates preventive maintenance, replacement, high-load continuation, and low-load cascade utilization. Remaining useful life distributions quantify action-dependent risks and costs, and a rolling-horizon optimization model determines component-level decisions under capacity constraints. By incorporating cascade utilization, moderately degraded components can be reassigned to low-load regimes instead of immediate maintenance. Numerical results show that the framework reduces expected cost by mitigating deferred failure risk while preserving residual service value.

Title: Logistics strategy selection in fast fashion cross-border e-commerce: The interplay of safety stock and environmental regulation
Authors: Guangye Xu, Jiaxuan Fang, Yongguang Zhong
Abstract: Fast-fashion cross-border e-commerce firms face a strategic trilemma among rapid trend responsiveness, cost efficiency, and environmental compliance. This paper examines how safety stock requirements and environmental regulation (specifically, take-back regulation) jointly shape logistics strategy selection. We consider a supply chain consisting of a fast-fashion e-retailer operating a cross-border platform and its supplier, and develop Stackelberg game models for three strategies: direct shipping, bonded warehousing, and a mixed strategy combining both. We derive optimal pricing decisions and compare equilibrium outcomes across four scenarios that vary safety stock and take-back regulation. The results reveal a conditional decision framework. Direct shipping is the dominant strategy when it is cost-competitive, when safety stock requirements are high, or when fashion loss under bonded warehousing is substantial. Bonded warehousing becomes increasingly attractive as safety stock decreases, take-back regulation tightens, and fashion loss diminishes. The mixed strategy is viable only in a narrow intermediate range and does not constitute a robust default. Furthermore, the mixed strategy is inherently fragile, and strategy switching is threshold-based rather than smooth, higher tariffs can expand direct shipping rather than promote local warehousing, and cost advantages are partially appropriated by the supplier through wholesale price adjustments. Safety stock and environmental regulation are complementary: a lower safety stock requirement amplifies the effect of stricter take-back regulation, whereas a high safety stock requirement locks firms into direct shipping. These findings offer managerial and policy implications, underscoring the importance of warehouse operations efficiency and tiered regulatory design.

Title: An improved approximation algorithm for the Capacitated Arc Routing Problem
Authors: Jingyang Zhao, Mingyu Xiao
Abstract: The Capacitated Arc Routing Problem (CARP), introduced by Golden and Wong in 1981, is an important arc routing problem in Operations Research, which generalizes the famous Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP). When every customer has a unit demand, the classical approximation algorithm of Jansen achieves an approximation ratio of (Formula presented), where k denotes the vehicle capacity. Based on recent progress in approximating the CVRP, we improve this result by proposing a (Formula presented) -approximation algorithm, yielding an asymptotic improvement as the vehicle capacity increases. Moreover, we show that our approach can be extended to the general CARP, where customer demands may be unequal, yielding a (Formula presented) -approximation algorithm. By combining our analysis with existing linear programming (LP) rounding techniques for the CVRP, we obtain an improved (Formula presented) -approximation algorithm in nO(k) time.

Title: The impact of connectivity on the production and diffusion of knowledge
Authors: Gustavo Manso, Farzad Pourbabaee
Abstract: We study a social bandit problem featuring the production and diffusion of knowledge. While higher connectivity enhances knowledge diffusion, it may reduce knowledge production as agents shy away from experimentation and free-ride on others’ discoveries. In the symmetric mixed-strategy equilibrium, exploration probability falls with connectivity, while expected per-capita equilibrium surplus is constant in the interior mixing region. Under finite-player pure strategies, surplus can fall discontinuously when the integer number of explorers drops. In the large-population limit these jumps vanish, and per-capita equilibrium surplus is weakly increasing in connectivity and eventually flat for intermediate beliefs.

Title: Altruistic punishment as norm-signaling: A model and experimental evidence
Authors: Kiryl Khalmetski, Axel Ockenfels

Title: Stormy futures? The impact of climatic shocks on retirement savings
Authors: Merve Kucuk, Mehmet A. Ulubasoglu
Journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

Title: Corrigendum to “Taylor rules around the world: Mapping monetary policy” [Economics Letters 232 (2023) 111275]
Authors: Makram El-Shagi, Yishuo Ma
Abstract: The authors regret errors in the original article: the output gap used in all estimations was computed with an HP filter smoothing parameter of λ = 0.25 instead of 1600, and is described in the text as GDP growth; the simulated confidence bounds of the long-run coefficients paired draws of α and β inconsistently; and the t-statistics in Table 1 were miscomputed. The main conclusion of the article is unaffected: adherence to the Taylor principle remains the exception. In Section 3, the sentence “Our starting point is a simplified backward-looking Taylor rule where the central bank responds to current growth and inflation” should read “Our starting point is a simplified backward-looking Taylor rule where the central bank responds to the current output gap and inflation”. In Eqs. (1)–(3), Δy should read y, and “y is log GDP” should read “y is the output gap (the HP-filtered log of real GDP)”.

Title: The dynamic systemic risk content of the U.S. yield curve
Authors: Abdelhamid Addi, Roqaya Diyab
Abstract: This paper examines how the U.S. yield curve relates to banking-sector capital shortfalls (SRISK). Using level, slope, and curvature factors, we find that SRISK responds differently to each dimension of the yield curve. Level is associated with a short-run increase in SRISK, whereas slope is followed by a short-run decline. The response to curvature is more persistent, and its predictive content for SRISK also persists over time. These findings point to a distinct role for intermediate maturities and show why the full shape of the yield curve matters for assessing banking-sector vulnerabilities.

Title: Does cross-regional electricity transfer reduce carbon inequality? Evidence from ultra-high voltage transmission in China
Authors: Fan Zhang, Shujie Yao, Xiyi Chen, Feng Wang
Abstract: Ultra-high voltage (UHV) transmission is a critical advancement in power grid infrastructure, enabling efficient long-distance and large-scale electricity transfer with minimal losses. Applying a staggered Difference-in-Differences approach with multiple time periods, this study examines the impact of UHV on carbon inequality, based on a panel data set of 275 cities in China from 2005 to 2023. The results show that cross-regional electricity transfer significantly reduces carbon inequality. Following the first operational UHV connection of a city's province, the Gini coefficient of county-level per capita carbon emissions within that city decreases by approximately 0.038 points on average. Further analyses provide evidence consistent with electricity accessibility and electricity supply reliability as potential transmission channels. This study provides new evidence on how technologically advanced electricity infrastructure contributes to equitable low-carbon development and offers important policy implications for regional energy integration and carbon governance.

Title: Climate policy spillovers through global value chains: Directional asymmetry and supply-chain heterogeneity in manufacturing
Authors: Minji Kim, Eunnyeong Heo
Abstract: Global value chains (GVCs) are a key channel through which climate policy shocks spill across borders. Using a panel of 40 economies and 19 manufacturing industries over 2007–2020, we construct shift-share measures of exposure to partner-country climate policy tightening by interacting pre-period bilateral trade weights with annual changes in partners' climate policy stringency, and examine whether growth in the value of GVC-linked trade is associated differently with import- and export-side exposure. We find a directional asymmetry: backward (import-sourcing) exposure is associated with slower growth in the value of GVC-linked trade (β = −0.095, p < 0.05), whereas forward (destination-market) exposure, capturing downstream supply relationships, is associated with faster growth in the value of GVC-linked trade (β = +0.101, p < 0.05), conditional on the other exposure channel. In the full sample, these associations are largely contemporaneous and do not accumulate significantly over two years. Larger point estimates are observed in sectors with both high dependence on imported low-carbon technologies (LCTs) and concentrated sourcing, where the two-year cumulative backward effect reaches −0.316 (p < 0.001) and remains robust to alternative cutoff definitions; the forward cumulative effect of +0.240 (p = 0.015) is present at the baseline specification but more sensitive to cutoff choice. The results point to supply-chain structure—especially the combination of LCT dependence and limited sourcing flexibility—as a relevant consideration in evaluating carbon border adjustments and international climate-policy coordination.

Title: Perceived Central Bank Partisanship and the Anchoring of Inflation Expectations
Authors: Hyuk An, Changkeun Lee, Soomin Lim

Title: R&D subsidies, commercialization, and growth
Authors: Daishoku Kanehara

Title: Post Extractive Afterlives through a Gendered Lens: Theorising Intergenerational Transmission
Authors: Kentse Sesele
Abstract: Post-extractive decline is commonly analysed through mine closure, employment loss, economic contraction and associated social disruption. Less attention has been given to how unresolved disruption remains socially consequential after the originating event has receded and across generations that did not directly experience it. Drawing on qualitative research with ninety-five women in Matjhabeng Local Municipality in South Africa's Free State Goldfields, this paper examines the temporal afterlife of extractive decline. It develops Complex Economic Intergenerational Trauma (CEIT) as an explanatory mechanism through which economic and institutional rupture is absorbed, normalised and transmitted through the interaction of structural inheritance and interpretive transmission. The findings show that extractive decline persists not only through diminished material opportunities but through frameworks through which institutional withdrawal and subsequent institutional encounters are understood. The paper extends Social Disruption Theory from an account of rupture and its consequences towards an explanation of how disruption can acquire an intergenerational afterlife. CEIT distinguishes this process from persistent poverty or intergenerational disadvantage by locating transmission in an unresolved economic and institutional rupture whose material consequences and social meanings remain active over time. Derived from the Matjhabeng case, CEIT is advanced as an explanatory mechanism for comparative testing across post-extractive territories.

Title: Can pollution monitors work where they do not measure? Evidence from China
Authors: Dongmei Guo, Runzhe Hu, Tingting Xie

Title: Nonlinear associations of neighborhood environments with older Adults’ travel mode by purpose
Authors: Xiangfen Cui, Lizhen Xu, Yuhan Tang, Zhenxin Li, Yongkang Chen, Senlin Tian, Haoran Yang, Yanghui Cao
Abstract: Using 2439 trip records from 745 older adults in a mountainous plateau city in southwest China, this study applied an XGBoost-SHAP framework to examine nonlinear associations between natural and built environments (NE/BE) and travel mode choice by trip purpose. A Sensitivity Difference Index (SDI) and a Bootstrap-based Directional Consistency Index (DCI) quantified purpose-specific sensitivity. NE and BE contributions were comparable (B = 2000; overlapping confidence intervals). Higher precipitation lowered walking and cycling contributions and raised those to public transit, with the transit peak shifting upward as trip necessity increased. Terrain slope and land-use mix showed pronounced purpose-specific nonlinearities. SDI and DCI identified seven directionally stable purpose-mode combinations (four recreational-dominant, three service-dominant), interpreted through an exploratory rigidity-flexibility continuum. Counterfactual simulation produced predicted responses 2.5 to 2.7 times larger for recreational than service trips in transit accessibility. These findings support purpose-differentiated planning for age-friendly mobility in topographically complex cities.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Screening, deferred compensation, and their complementarity in financial risk control
Authors: Haiqing Song, Lang Ning, Ning Wang
Abstract: Financial institutions rely on business employees to communicate project-level information for lending decisions, yet these employees possess private information and may strategically distort their reports. Two mechanisms are widely used to address this internal information asymmetry: Screening, which detects misrepresentation through selective inspection, and deferred compensation, which aligns incentives by linking pay to long-term outcomes. Despite their practical importance, these mechanisms have largely been studied in isolation. Moreover, existing Screening models typically treat screening as a binary audit decision with fixed cost, overlooking the realistic feature that its marginal detection effectiveness diminishes as effort expands. We develop a game-theoretic framework in which a financial institution jointly determines screening intensity and deferred compensation structure, modeling screening as a continuous effort variable with diminishing marginal returns. Our analysis yields three main findings. First, we characterize optimal screening effort and show how it varies with project and institutional characteristics. Second, we establish that neither mechanism universally dominates the other; the preferred choice depends on the underlying economic conditions. Third, we demonstrate that the two mechanisms can generate complementary risk-control benefits when deployed jointly and identify the conditions under which such complementarity arises. Our study contributes a unified framework for jointly optimizing Screening and deferred compensation under internal information asymmetry in financial institutions, and provides actionable guidance on when to invest in Screening, when to rely on deferred compensation, and when to combine both.

Title: The H-1B wage gap, visa fees, and employer demand
Authors: George J. Borjas

Title: Whether and how to tax a skilled temporary worker visa: comment on Borjas and Clemens
Authors: Pia M. Orrenius, Madeline Zavodny

Title: A closed loop facility layout model with an unidirectional material handling system
Authors: Arne Falkenberg, Christoph H. Glock
Affiliations: Technical University of Darmstadt

Title: Coherent forecast combination for linearly constrained multiple time series
Authors: Daniele Girolimetto, Tommaso Di Fonzo
Abstract: Linearly constrained multiple time series may be encountered in many practical contexts, such as the National Accounts (e.g., GDP disaggregated by Income, Expenditure and Output), and multilevel frameworks where the variables are organized according to hierarchies or groupings, like the total energy consumption of a country disaggregated by region and energy sources. In these cases, when multiple incoherent base forecasts for each individual variable are available, a forecast combination-and-reconciliation approach, that we call coherent forecast combination, may be used to improve the accuracy of the base forecasts and achieve coherence in the final result. In this paper, we develop an optimization-based technique that combines multiple unbiased base forecasts while assuring the constraints valid for the series. We present closed form expressions for the coherent combined forecast vector and its error covariance matrix in the general case where a different number of forecasts is available for each variable. We also discuss practical issues related to the covariance matrix that is part of the optimal solution. Through simulations and a forecasting experiment on the daily Australian electricity generation hierarchical time series, we show that the proposed methodology, in addition to adhering to sound statistical principles, may yield in significant improvement on base forecasts, single-task combination and single-expert reconciliation approaches as well.

Title: Nowcasting macroeconomic variables with a sparse mixed-frequency dynamic factor model
Authors: Domenic Franjic, Karsten Schweikert
Abstract: We propose a two-step estimation procedure for a sparse dynamic factor model in a mixed-frequency setting. A sparse factor loading matrix is estimated from sparse principal components analysis, which is then used to initialise the Kalman filter and smoother. We generalise existing theoretical results on the properties of the sparse principal components estimator. Specifically, we show that our estimator consistently recovers the true model parameters up to an orthogonal transformation, and achieves a bias-variance trade-off in finite samples. Further, we employ a simulation study to investigate the nowcasting performance and find that the sparse two-step estimator systematically outperforms the dense benchmark. A real-world nowcasting exercise with historical US GDP vintages demonstrates the empirical performance.

Title: On the Efficient Computation of Proximal Operators of Affine-Constrained Nonconvex Functions
Authors: Di Hou, Tianyun Tang, Kim-Chuan Toh, Shiwei Wang
Affiliations: Department of Mathematics, National University of Singapore, Singapore 119076; Department of Statistics, The University of Chicago, Chicago, Illinois 60637; Department of Mathematics, and Institute of Operations Research and Analytics, National University of Singapore, Singapore 119076; Institute of Applied Mathematics, Academy of Mathematics and Systems Science, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100190, China
Abstract: Proximal operators with affine constraints arise in numerous models in nonconvex projection, composite optimization, and structured regularization. However, their efficient computation remains challenging due to the simultaneous presence of affine constraints and nonsmooth, possibly nonconvex objectives. In this work, we develop a unified dual-representability framework for analyzing and computing affine-constrained proximal mappings. Specifically, we introduce a multiplier inclusion formulation that connects the primal affine-constrained proximal problem to an unconstrained convex dual problem. Based on this formulation, we prove that, whenever the associated dual inclusion problem admits a solution, strong duality holds. For convex functions and a broad class of prox-regular nonconvex functions, we establish that dual representability holds under a simple subdifferential sum rule, and further develop a hierarchy of verifiable regularity conditions that guarantee this sum rule in the convex and projection settings. In addition, we analyze the smoothness and strong convexity properties of the dual objective, providing a rigorous foundation that guarantees fast local convergence rates for efficient first- and second-order methods. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed dual reformulation enables the reliable computation of globally optimal solutions for a range of large-scale nonconvex proximal and projection problems using existing convex optimization solvers.

Title: Revenue models for social e-commerce platforms in presence of network effects
Authors: Yuting Chen, Jinpeng Wu
Abstract: Social e-commerce platforms have emerged as a new business model that combines commerce with social interaction. We use a game-theoretic model to examine the operational decisions and revenue models of these platforms in the presence of multi-sided network externalities. We compare social e-commerce platforms with pure social media and pure e-commerce platforms. We also consider two revenue models for social e-commerce platforms: a sales-only model and a sales-and-advertising model. Our results show that under monopoly, when consumer preference mismatch costs are low, sales-only social e-commerce becomes optimal only if creator promotion is sufficiently effective; otherwise, the platform remains a pure e-commerce platform. When the mismatch cost is high, the sales-and-advertising model becomes optimal. Under competition, adopting a social e-commerce model may reduce platform profitability. When two competing e-commerce platforms both switch to the sales-only social e-commerce model, they are trapped in a Prisoner’s Dilemma and earn lower profits than in the pure e-commerce model. For the sales-and-advertising model, such a dilemma arises only when the seller-to-creator monetization effectiveness is sufficiently strong; otherwise, both platforms can benefit from adopting the model. These findings provide managerial implications for platform revenue design and operational strategies under different market conditions.

Title: Who rules the battery? Optimal strategy selection of vehicle-battery separation models
Authors: Bo Liu, Yi Ding, Haoying Guo
Abstract: The vehicle–battery separation (VBS) model refers to a business model in which the ownership of the electric vehicle(EV) body and the battery is decoupled. This study examines manufacturers’ strategic choices under VBS, where the investment–utility conversion index (IU-index) and product positioning jointly shape equilibrium outcomes in the battery value chain. The IU-index captures how battery performance improvements translate into consumer utility relative to investment costs, while product positioning is measured by the vehicle-body price relative to the average battery leasing price over the usage period. Comparing the Manufacturer-Integration (MI), Supplier-Integration (SI), and Manufacturer-Cooperation (MC) models reveals how these factors shape corporate strategic choices. When the IU-index is low, the SI model is generally optimal and largely insensitive to product positioning. As the IU-index rises, strategic sensitivity to product positioning emerges: higher vehicle body prices favor the MC model for economic efficiency, whereas higher battery prices make the SI model more suitable. Consumer risk aversion can create win-win outcomes but may diminish the SI model’s advantage in low-R&D-cost settings when battery R&D costs increase. Overall, the study provides a framework for VBS strategy: technology-leading firms should adopt MI to capture value, while cost-sensitive firms can optimize efficiency through SI or MC strategies.

Title: Spatial spillovers of local climate adaptation policy: Evidence from FEMA’s Community Rating System
Authors: Yongwang Ren
Abstract: This paper examines whether FEMA’s Community Rating System (CRS) generates spillover benefits for neighboring non-participating communities. Using a newly constructed panel of National Flood Insurance Program communities from 1991–2018 and staggered difference-in-differences estimators robust to heterogeneous treatment effects, I find suggestive evidence that non-CRS communities experience lower flood claims several years after neighboring communities join the CRS. Most post-treatment estimates are statistically indistinguishable from zero, although the estimate approximately six years after a neighboring community joins the CRS is negative and statistically significant, corresponding to approximately $0.5 million in lower annual NFIP claim payments. The estimated negative effects appear to be larger among smaller and lower-income communities. The results are consistent with policy learning and the diffusion of flood mitigation practices as possible mechanisms underlying the spillover effects. These findings suggest that existing evaluations of local flood adaptation policies may underestimate their social benefits by ignoring externalities.

Title: Pre-disaster planning for emergency evacuation with social distancing under compound disasters: a multi-alternative optimization framework
Authors: Jianghua Zhang, Hongwei Shi, Zizhuo Wang, Xiangyu Yang
Abstract: Compound disasters involving a pandemic and a sudden natural hazard require evacuation plans that balance rapid clearance and infection control. We propose a Multi-Alternative Emergency Evacuation Planning Framework under Compound Disasters and formulate a multi-objective mixed-integer programming model that incorporates the capacity effects of social distancing. We develop the K Shortest Path Capacity Planning Algorithm with Social Distancing (KPCP-SD) to generate scenario-specific plans and the Simulation-Based Evacuation Path Planning Algorithm for Generating the Top- m Alternatives (SEPPm) to address road-network uncertainty. We conduct extensive numerical experiments to evaluate the proposed framework and algorithms. Across the tested instances, KPCP-SD achieves solution quality comparable to the classical Capacity Constrained Route Planner (CCRP) and Gurobi, with time savings of 78.55–98.87% and 93.12–99.89%, respectively. The sensitivity analyses reveal a nonlinear relationship between capacity loss and clearance time and clarify how the evacuation time window and objective weights affect social distancing selection. Under both log-normal and bounded Beta distributional assumptions, SEPPm accurately identifies the Top- m alternatives. Extended experiments further evaluate the framework under differentiated social distancing decisions and four non-compliance scenarios. Finally, we discuss the managerial implications of these findings for social distancing selection and pre-disaster evacuation planning.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: The cost-of-living crisis and the freedom to move: mobility, participation and wellbeing under financial pressure
Authors: Matthew J. Beck, Stephen Greaves, Andrea Pellegrini, John M. Rose
Abstract: This paper examines how rising cost-of-living pressures reshape everyday mobility, participation, and wellbeing through an integrated behavioural and psychosocial framework. Drawing on survey data from 1,532 residents of Greater Sydney, the study proposes a novel multidimensional conceptualisation of cost-of-living stress spanning housing, energy, fuel, and food pressures, while incorporating environmental concern as a comparative reference point to assess how broader long-term societal anxieties are positioned relative to more immediate financial pressures. The study also robustly examines how cost-of-stress translates to transport related behaviours. Methodologically, a comprehensive multi-stage approach combining segmentation analysis, exploratory factor analysis, latent wellbeing constructs, and hybrid ordered logit modelling is adopted. The resulting analysis identifies five distinct profiles of cost-of-living concern and examines how these differing pressures relate to behavioural adaptation, including changes in driving, public transport use, eating out, leisure participation, and household utility consumption. The findings show that essential pressures, particularly housing, food, and energy costs, dominate overall stress formation. Environmental concern remains salient across the population but operates as a comparatively less immediate source of stress relative to essential cost pressures. Behavioural adaptation to mitigate against rising cost-of-living is concentrated primarily in discretionary activities, alongside evidence of selective substitution toward public transport. Overall, the study provides a multidimensional account of how households negotiate rising living costs across everyday life, highlighting the interconnected relationships between financial stress, mobility, participation, and wellbeing.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Emissions trading and urban transportation decarbonization: Double machine learning evidence from the inclusion of China’s transport sector
Authors: Liang Zhao, Zhenggang He
Abstract: Decarbonizing urban transportation represents a pivotal challenge in global climate governance. This study exploits the phased implementation of China's carbon emissions trading system (ETS) as a quasi-experiment to evaluate the causal impacts of market-based environmental regulations on urban transportation decarbonization. We analyze panel data from 297 Chinese cities spanning 2010 to 2024. A joint nested Double Machine Learning (DML) framework with time-aware cross-fitting is employed to isolate the incremental effect of direct sectoral inclusion from general cross-sectoral spillovers. The empirical results show that the ETS significantly reduces per capita transportation emissions, with the total policy effect reaching −0.2282. Crucially, direct sectoral inclusion yields a statistically distinct incremental abatement dividend (−0.1775), whereas general ETS spillovers are statistically insignificant. Furthermore, a causal mediation decomposition reveals that policy-driven decarbonization is predominantly mediated through physical operational rationalization rather than financial asset hedging. Specifically, curbing energy-intensive road freight intensity accounts for the largest single mediating share (37.50 %). This is followed by road passenger intensity rationalization (18.67 %) and logistics modernization (9.02 %). In contrast, carbon market financial indicators contribute less than 4 %. Heterogeneity analysis indicates that policy dividends are concentrated in economically developed cities and technologically lagging cities undergoing catch-up restructuring. However, freight-intensive hubs face structural adjustment inertia. Ultimately, this study provides actionable empirical evidence for expanding the national carbon market into the transportation sector through a phased, hybrid governance framework.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Editorial Board
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Occupational exposure to decarbonization shocks: Direct and supply-chain measures
Authors: Elior Cohen, Nida Çakır-Melek

Title: Public rapid-charging infrastructure and BEV adoption: Drivers of spatially heterogeneous impacts
Authors: Prachi Singh, Chaitram Sadeek Mohamed, Takahiko Kiso
Abstract: Battery electric vehicles (BEVs) offer environmental benefits, but range anxiety remains a barrier to adoption. Public chargers help alleviate this concern. This paper provides causal evidence on how public rapid-charging infrastructure influences BEV adoption across local authorities in England. Instrumenting endogenous charger placement using the historical distribution of public car parks, we estimate that the elasticity of BEV adoption—measured as the annual net change in privately registered BEV stock—with respect to public rapid-charger stock is approximately 0.3. The effect is spatially heterogeneous—stronger in more deprived areas or those with better road-network connectivity, but weaker in rural areas or those with larger baseline charger stocks. It also weakens where on-street parking is widespread and home charging is consequently difficult, suggesting that public rapid-charging expansion may need complementary investment in non-rapid residential kerbside charging. These findings support geographically targeted public rapid-charger investment, an approach used in recent UK policies.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Multivariate perceptions of post-purchase EV ownership issues
Authors: Andrea Pellegrini, Elisabetta Cherchi, John M. Rose
Abstract: This study aims to examine how electric vehicle (EV) owners perceive a range of post-purchase issues that are relevant to EV adoption, identifying pathways to further support EV uptake, whilst reducing the risk of losing existing users. Using a nationwide sample of 1,794 Australian EV owners, we analyse the importance assigned to five post-acquisition concerns: range anxiety, public charging availability, charging duration, trust of new technologies, and battery fire safety. The empirical findings reveal significant differences across EV owners according to socio-economic characteristics, home charging infrastructure, and vehicle attributes. Post-purchase concerns are also strongly and positively interrelated, particularly those relating to charging infrastructure, technological trust, safety, and financial aspects. Finally, predictive policy scenarios indicate that ownership context influences concern levels, with home charging and solar panel ownership reducing concerns about charging availability and duration, while ownership of battery storage and SUV shifting concerns towards battery safety and emerging technologies.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Stochastic commitment in repeated games
Authors: Meichen Chen, Duozhe Li, Quan Wen

Title: Ideology or self-interest? Cross-pressures in preferences for redistribution
Authors: Roman Horvath, Eva Horvathova
Abstract: We study whether ideology can overturn the income-based prediction of redistribution preferences. Using individual-level data from the World Values Survey and the European Values Study, we compare two cross-pressured groups: poor right-wing and rich left-wing respondents. Rich-left respondents are significantly more supportive of redistribution than poor-right respondents, including within country-wave cells.
