The findings provide global evidence that ideology can reverse the income-based ranking of preferences for redistribution.

Title: Same likelihood ratio, different posteriors: Axioms for strength–weight updating
Authors: Yang Tan, Tianyu Lin
Abstract: Samples with the same likelihood ratio may induce different reported posteriors when they differ in composition and size, a pattern that Bayesian and Grether updating cannot accommodate. This motivates us to study belief updating directly over evidence samples and to separate the roles of evidence strength and weight. We characterize belief-updating rules through consistency under sample transformations. Scale invariance yields an ordinal representation, whereas relative consistency and balanced-dilution consistency jointly characterize the Griffin–Tversky strength–weight family. Within that family, translation invariance equates the two exponents, while linear replication yields Grether likelihood weighting; unit likelihood weight recovers Bayesian updating.

Title: Sequential search and oligopoly competition: A counter-example to equilibrium existence
Authors: Yue Li
Abstract: This paper revisits the consumer search and price competition model of Wolinsky (1986). When the market has a finite number of firms, and the distribution of match values has an increasing hazard rate, I provide a family of counter-examples to show that equilibrium may not exist.

Title: The global financial cycle and the trilemma: A spatial analysis of macroeconomic policy trade-offs
Authors: Piotr Adamczyk
Abstract: The Global Financial Cycle (GFC) is typically analysed through its impact on monetary policy independence, while little is known about how different phases of the GFC shape countries' positions within the Mundellian trilemma. This paper examines the effect of GFC phases on countries' positions in the trilemma triangle. The results show that the global financial cycle affects countries’ positions in the trilemma space. The empirical analysis further suggests that more benign global financial conditions are associated with movements towards regime-specific corner solutions of the trilemma.

Title: Digital transformation and corporate energy efficiency—evidence based on large language models
Authors: Jinzhe Li, Xiong Xiong, Ya Gao
Abstract: As a primary driver of competitive advantage, the impact of digital transformation on energy efficiency has become a critical research priority. This paper develops a large language model with a BERT-based transformer to comprehensively quantify a firm's digital transformation levels and determine its influence on corporate energy efficiency. The results reveal that digital transformation significantly improves energy efficiency, with mobile internet technology exerting the most pronounced positive effect among various sub-technologies. The results remain robust across multiple sensitivity tests and are relatively stronger among non-state-owned enterprises and non-energy-intensive firms. Mechanism analysis indicates that digital transformation improves corporate energy efficiency through three primary channels: technological innovation, production efficiency, and management efficiency. The effects of individual sub-technologies across these channels exhibit significant heterogeneity. Our study offers micro-level empirical evidence on the impact of digital transformation on energy efficiency and provides valuable insights into the evolution of the global digital economy and the optimization of energy structures.

Title: The psychological toll of heat: The effects of temperature on mental health in Mexico
Authors: Yumin Hong, Antonia Vazquez

Title: A Tale of Two Cities: Australian Evidence on the Effects of Lockdown on Grocery Inflation
Authors: Chew Lian Chua, Sarantis Tsiaplias
Affiliations: School of Economics University of Nottingham Ningbo China; Melbourne Institute of Applied Economic and Social Research University of Melbourne Melbourne Victoria Australia
Abstract: ABSTRACT Despite extensive research on the economic implications of COVID‐19, the inflationary consequences of lockdown remain underexplored. Prior impact assessments may be compromised due to the cross‐jurisdictional presence of lockdowns and the prevalence of the coronavirus. This study leverages a unique circumstance in Australia, where Melbourne was the only city under lockdown, to discern the impact of lockdown. By analysing granular supermarket price data and adjusting for intertemporal and geographical variation in COVID‐19 cases, policy stringency, and product availability, the study identifies a statistically significant and economically meaningful disinflationary effect on grocery prices attributable to lockdown. Excluding the specific disinflationary effect of lockdown, COVID‐19‐related stringency measures have a minimal impact on the prices of typical consumables such as food.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: Macroeconomic Effects of Public Investment in EMDEs : Nonlinear Effects of the Business Cycle, Fiscal Space, Capital Stock and Efficiency
Authors: Amat Adarov, Benedict Clements, João Tovar Jalles
Affiliations: The World Bank Washington DC USA; Universidad de Las Américas, De Los Colimes Esq Quito Ecuador; University of Lisbon‐Lisbon School of Economics and Management (ISEG) Lisboa Portugal; Research in Economics and Mathematics (REM) and Research Unit on Complexity and Economics (UECE) Universidade de Lisboa‐ISEG Lisbon Portugal; Economics for Policy Universidade Nova de Lisboa‐Nova School of Business and Economics Carcavelos Portugal; Business School Paris France
Abstract: ABSTRACT The paper examines the macroeconomic effects of public investment in emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs). To this end the analysis develops a new measure of public investment shocks based on cyclically adjusted government investment. Estimations using local projections based on a sample of 129 countries over the period 1980–2019 suggest that public investment can significantly boost economic growth, crowd in private investment, and increase productivity and potential output. Estimates suggest that an increase in public investment by 1% of GDP raises real output by 1.1% after 5 years, on average. However, the effects are much larger when public investment spending is efficient and fiscal space is ample—reaching up to 1.6% over the same period. Public investment multipliers tend to be larger during recessions and in capital scarce economies.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: Assessing International Risk Sharing in Developing Countries
Authors: Mitali Das, Hailey Ordal
Affiliations: Research Department International Monetary Fund Washington District of Columbia USA; Department of Economics Georgetown University Washington District of Columbia USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT Using an analytical decomposition to quantify the risk shared through varies channels of smoothing, this paper analyses the impact of financial integration on risk sharing in developing economies between 1994 and 2019. We establish that the omission of workers' remittances—now the largest source of financial flows to these economies—is an important factor in the limited evidence for risk sharing found previously. Of the output shocks that are smoothed, we estimate the remittance channel accounts for about 20%. We examine whether more financially developed countries—who can intermediate remittance inflows more efficiently—accrue greater benefits from sharing risk. Exploiting significant variation in the access, usage, and depth of the domestic financial sector, we show that greater financial access is associated with greater risk sharing benefits, but greater financial depth is associated with reduced risk sharing. Our results are consistent with models where risk sharing arrangements are subject to frictions in the allocation of loanable funds due in part to segmented access to local credit markets.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: A Multi‐Country Approach to Estimate the Euro‐Area Natural Real Interest Rate
Authors: Tino Berger, Daria Kazakova, Bernd Kempa
Affiliations: Chair of Empirical International Economics Georg‐August Universität Göttingen Göttingen Germany; Institute of International Economics Westfälische Wilhelms‐Universität Münster Münster Germany
Abstract: ABSTRACT We set up a semi‐structural unobserved components multi‐country model of the eurozone. The common euro‐area natural rate of interest (NRI) is identified from the joint dynamics of the national data of its 20 member countries and estimated using Bayesian methods. Relative to a univariate approach, the model offers a substantial improvement in the precision of measuring the NRI and in the reliability of its real‐time performance. The results confirm previous findings of a secular decline in the NRI, with our model generating a smoother path. Estimation of different subgroups of eurozone countries indicates convergence of regional NRIs to the euro‐area NRI in the late 2010s and early 2020s.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: Feeding Inflation: The Non‐Linear Spillovers of Global Food Commodities
Authors: Stéphane Dées
Affiliations: Banque de France and Bordeaux School of Economics Paris France
Abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines the role of global food price shocks in driving inflation dynamics, with a particular focus on non‐linear effects and heterogeneity across countries. Using a Bayesian Vector Autoregression (BVAR) approach, we identify global food price shocks and assess their impact on inflation. Quantile regressions reveal that inflation's sensitivity to food price shocks is significantly higher in high‐inflation regimes, with elasticity estimates being significantly larger for higher percentiles compared to the median. Additionally, panel estimations indicate that this sensitivity is particularly pronounced in emerging economies and developing countries, where food constitutes a larger share of household consumption. Our findings contribute to the literature on global inflation synchronisation and highlight the importance of accounting for inflation regimes when analysing the transmission of food commodity price shocks.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: Global Capital and Local Consequences: The Real and Financial Effects of Foreign Acquisitions in India
Authors: Ha V. Dang, Mi Lin
Affiliations: University of Lincoln Lincoln UK; Beijing Normal‐Hong Kong Baptist University (BNBU) Zhuhai China
Abstract: ABSTRACT This study employs firm‐level data to investigate the causal effects of foreign acquisitions on both real economic outcomes and financial performance metrics of target firms. To address potential selection bias arising from the non‐random acquisition patterns of domestic enterprises by foreign investors—a process characterized by the systematic targeting of high‐performing local firms by international entities—we employ advanced econometric methods designed to account for heterogeneous treatment effects. Furthermore, a comparative analysis between foreign and domestic acquisitions is conducted to isolate the specific effects attributable to foreign ownership, distinct from general acquisition dynamics. Empirical findings from comprehensive data on Indian firms demonstrate that foreign acquisitions yield substantial financial improvements but do not confer significant productivity advantages relative to domestic acquisitions.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: Uncovering the Inventory‐Business Cycle Nexus
Authors: Luca Rossi
Affiliations: Directorate General for Economics, Statistics and Research Bank of Italy Italy
Abstract: ABSTRACT Despite being the smallest component of GDP, inventories represent the second largest source of GDP fluctuations. Over the past decades, research in inventory management has proposed competing theories about the primary drivers prompting firms to accumulate stocks, yet consensus remains elusive on the source of inventory cycles. This paper imposes structure on US macroeconomic data and disentangles four shocks related to current and expected demand and supply conditions within a unified framework. We find that at high frequencies sales forecast errors account for the largest share of inventory investment, giving support to the buffer‐stock motive for holding inventories. Shocks to expected demand and supply—which relate to stockout‐avoidance reasons for inventory investment—dominate inventory fluctuations at business‐cycle frequencies. We show that shocks to expected costs generate the missing positive correlation between cost‐driven inventory investment and sales that the literature has struggled to find, and that forward‐looking behaviours are those that lead production to be more variable than sales. Finally, our results offer a sensible narrative around the post‐pandemic period when inventories drove a very high share of GDP fluctuations.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: Student Debt and Aggregate Consumption: Does Inequality Matter?
Authors: Berrak Bahadir
Affiliations: Department of Economics Florida International University Miami Florida USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines the role of income inequality in amplifying the macroeconomic effects of student debt. I argue that inequality captures structural differences in households' access to non‐student credit, with higher inequality reflecting a greater concentration of credit‐constrained households and thereby amplifying the adverse effects of student debt repayment on consumption. Using state‐level data, I show that the negative association between student debt and subsequent aggregate consumption growth is significantly stronger in states with higher inequality. Consistent with this mechanism, several stylized facts indicate that higher inequality is associated with lower levels of non‐student debt. Finally, I develop a simple model illustrating how income inequality increases the prevalence of borrowing constraints, thereby amplifying the sensitivity of consumption to debt repayment.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: From Shopping to Statistics: Tracking and Nowcasting Private Consumption Expenditures in Real Time
Authors: Friederike Fourné, Robert Lehmann
Affiliations: ifo Institute Munich Germany; LMU Munich Munich Germany; ifo Institute Dresden Germany; CESifo Munich Germany; TU Dresden Faculty of Business and Economics Dresden Germany
Abstract: ABSTRACT In this paper, we use high‐frequency transaction data to develop a weekly tracker for private consumption expenditures. Furthermore, we apply the transaction data in a nowcasting experiment and compare their performance with other, readily available indicators that are regularly linked to private consumption in Germany. The weekly tracker produces precise estimates and can thus be used in real time, especially in very turbulent times such as a pandemic or the high‐inflation‐phase in its aftermath. In terms of nowcast accuracy, the tracker outperforms all remaining indicators, making it a powerful tool for applied forecasting work. We intend to regularly publish the weekly consumption tracker in the future, thereby complementing the database for Germany.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: What Are The Drivers of Labour Productivity in Italy?
Authors: Josué Diwambuena, Francesco Ravazzolo
Affiliations: CREEi (ESG‐UQAM) Montreal Canada; Government of Canada Toronto Canada; BI Norwegian Business School Oslo Norway; Free University of Bozen‐Bolzano Bolzano Italy
Abstract: ABSTRACT This paper introduces a novel sign restriction identification within a structural Bayesian vector autoregression (VAR) to analyse how labour productivity responds to supply and demand shocks and to quantify the contribution of shocks to cyclical fluctuations. We apply our framework to the Italian labour market because it is characterised by several rigidities despite multiple labour reforms. Using data spanning 1984Q1–2023Q3, we show that the cyclical productivity‐output correlation has significantly declined since the late 1990s. Moreover, the relative volatility of employment to output has decreased, while that of hours per worker has increased. We estimate our specification on Italian data from 1996Q1 to 2023Q3 and disentangle three supply shocks from one demand shock. We find that automation and technology shocks generate persistent gains in productivity, while labour supply and aggregate demand shocks lower it persistently. The negative effect of demand shocks is due to the COVID‐19 pandemic. Labour supply, automation, and technology shocks are the dominant drivers of productivity both at short and long horizons. Labour supply shocks explain most of the productivity slowdown during the double‐dip recession, while all shocks contributed to its aftermath recovery during the period 2012–2019. We carry out a series of sensitivity analyses, which confirm our results.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: Issue Information
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: The externalities of private tutoring on students’ academic and noncognitive outcomes: evidence and mechanisms
Authors: Zhengwei Yan, Xu Zhang
Abstract: This paper examines the spillover effects of private tutoring on students’ academic and noncognitive outcomes. Utilizing nationally representative data on middle school students randomly assigned to classes in China, we find that exposure to a higher proportion of classmates participating in private tutoring reduces students’ academic performance and noncognitive skills. We provide evidence that these effects operate through deteriorating classroom atmosphere and reducing student effort rather than through affecting teacher or parent behaviors. Our heterogeneity analyses show that these effects are more pronounced among male students, students with a rural hukou , students from lower socioeconomic backgrounds, and students with lower ability. Furthermore, these effects are more pronounced among non-tutored students who are as academically competitive as their tutored peers, and in schools located in municipalities and provincial capitals.

Title: A model of politics and the central bank
Authors: Wioletta Dziuda, Carolin Pflueger
Abstract: We present a two-period model examining how the central bank and the elected government jointly shape elections and economic outcomes. An apolitical central bank minimizes a quadratic loss function in inﬂation and unemployment along an expectational Phillips curve, which is shifted by the government’s quality. Fully rational voters optimally choose between the incumbent, whose quality they infer from unemployment, and a challenger of unknown quality. We ﬁnd that governments prefer more inﬂation-averse central banks than the social planner, rationalizing the political success of inﬂation-targeting in practice. Inﬂation-targeting, however, has negative economic consequences by allowing lower quality incumbents to be reelected.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: Sticky Prices and Constraints to Produce
Authors: Justinas Markauskas, Morten O. Ravn, José-Víctor Ríos-Rull
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: Taxing high-skill immigration: Fundamental problems in evaluating immigrant–native wage gaps and the H-1B visa tax
Authors: Michael A. Clemens

Title: Real incentives really matter
Authors: Christoph Drobner, Sebastian J. Goerg, Orestis Kopsacheilis
Affiliations: Central European University; Nuremberg Institute for Market Decisions (NIM); Technical University of Munich; University of Crete
Abstract: Abstract Incentivizing behavior, a core principle of economic experiments, is currently under scrutiny due to a series of papers that find little to no difference in choices made under real or hypothetical incentives. We experimentally assess the effectiveness of hypothetical incentives to induce participants’ real effort – an integral aspect of reliable experimental data. We find that although linking behavior to hypothetical incentives generates modest additional effort compared to no reference to such incentives, hypothetical incentives fall substantially short of real ones, even when their nominal value is radically inflated. To understand the mechanism behind these effects, we systematically vary base pay and piece-rate magnitudes across incentive conditions and structurally estimate a model of costly effort. Although higher base pay increases effort both by increasing non-pecuniary motivation and by enhancing responsiveness to hypothetical incentives, incentive-compatible real payments are far more cost-effective.

Title: Sustaining cooperation with correlated information: an experimental test
Authors: Yongping Bao, Fabian Dvorak, Sebastian Fehrler
Affiliations: University of Bremen: Universitat Bremen; Eawag
Abstract: Abstract In infinitely or indefinitely repeated games with noisy signals about others’ actions, sustaining cooperation is difficult. Theoretical work shows that cooperation can be maintained if the signals are correlated and the degree of correlation depends on the actions. In this study, we implement such an information structure in a laboratory experiment and investigate whether subjects are able to sustain cooperation by conditioning their behavior on it. A substantial number of subjects adopt strategies accounting for the correlation, but this does not increase cooperation compared to a control treatment without correlation, as behavior with independent signals is more lenient when players can communicate, while without communication cooperation remains low in both settings.

Title: Robust process diagnosis using explainable CNNs for highly imbalanced wafer map defect classification in semiconductor manufacturing
Authors: Taehyeok Seo, Jongik Chung, Ilsuk Kang
Affiliations: Chungbuk National University; University of Central Florida

Title: A hybrid FMEA approach for risk analysis of cold chain logistics and distribution system in developing countries: the case of China
Authors: Chunyan Duan, Yuting Tan, Mengshan Zhu, Zehao Zhang
Affiliations: School of Mechanical Engineering, Tongji University, Shanghai, PR China; School of Management, Fudan University; Research Center, Suzhou Oriza Holdings Co., Ltd.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Advancing readiness and nonlinear pathways to infrastructure project success through ‘ glass box ’ machine learning models
Authors: Udechukwu Ojiako, Muzaffar Iqbal, M. K. S. Al-Mhdawi, Abroon Qazi
Affiliations: Bailey College of Engineering & Technology, Indiana State University; Hull University Business School, University of Hull; Johannesburg Business School, University of Johannesburg; Interdisciplinary Research Center for Smart Mobility and Logistics, King Fahd University of Petroleum and Minerals; School of Computing, Engineering and Digital Technologies, Teesside University; Department of Civil, Structural and Environmental Engineering, Trinity College Dublin; School of Business Administration, American University of Sharjah

Title: Channel Structure and Consumer Search: Competition Between Store and National Brands
Authors: Weiqian Lu, Lindong Liu, Xiaoshuai Fan
Affiliations: College of Business Southern University of Science and Technology Shenzhen Guangdong China; International Institute of Finance, School of Management University of Science and Technology of China Hefei Anhui China
Abstract: ABSTRACT Despite the higher profitability of store brands, retailers persistently accommodate national brands in the same category rather than excluding them from their assortments. This paper develops a consumer search model to explain this phenomenon by analyzing three selling strategies available to a retailer who simultaneously acts as a store brand owner competing with a national brand owner. Using the separate selling format (SSF) as a benchmark, we examine how the wholesale selling format (WSF) and agency selling format (ASF) alter price competition and consumer search behavior through one‐stop shopping convenience. Our analysis yields three key findings. First, both WSF and ASF soften price competition and raise product prices relative to SSF, as consumers benefit from one‐stop shopping convenience. Second, when search costs exceed a certain threshold, high retail prices and high consumer surplus coexist: the savings from one‐stop shopping convenience outweigh the losses from elevated prices, producing an anti‐intuitive win‐win‐win outcome in which both brand owners earn higher profits, consumer surplus improves, and social welfare increases. Third, selling‐format preferences depend on search costs. When search costs are sufficiently low or high, both parties prefer the WSF. At intermediate search‐cost levels, however, the store‐brand owner prefers the ASF, whereas the national‐brand owner continues to favor WSF. These findings offer actionable guidance for retail operations managers. The coexistence of store and national brands in the same category can be rationalized as a search‐cost‐driven strategy that enhances one‐stop shopping convenience and generates system‐wide welfare gains. Thus, brand owners should calibrate their selling format decisions according to the search cost and one‐stop shopping convenience conditions in their target markets.

Title: Preemptive scheduling of a single yard crane for terminal efficiency
Authors: Jeongheon Kim, Wonbeen Park, Dowon Kim
Abstract: Concentrated vehicle arrivals at limited input/output points often cause severe queuing and prolonged waiting times in automated container terminals. This study addresses a preemptive single yard crane scheduling problem in a perpendicular-layout terminal. Preemption allows the crane to temporarily interrupt a container move, stage it at an intermediate slot, serve another request, and later complete the operation. To minimize a weighted sum of makespan and total operational delay (comprising vehicle waiting and storage delays), we formulate a mixed-integer linear programming model and develop an iterated greedy framework with four preemptive variants. Extensive computational experiments confirm that at least one preemptive variant consistently outperforms a non-preemptive baseline across all problem sizes and objectives. Under the balanced objective, preemptive scheduling reduces total vehicle waiting time by 7.4–61.2%, while makespan impacts range from a 2.8% increase to a 1.7% reduction. Furthermore, average and maximum vehicle queues decrease across all operating regimes. Sensitivity analysis shows that preemption benefits scale positively with greater weight on operational delay and sufficient scheduling flexibility. These findings advocate for selective preemption policies, enabling operators to prioritize requests with substantial waiting-time savings while effectively bounding storage-delay risks.

Title: Distribution Regression for Partially Observed Discrete, Ordered Outcomes—The Case of Adolescent Substance Abuse
Authors: Daniel Gutknecht, Cenchen Liu, Jan‐Lukas Wermuth
Affiliations: Faculty of Economics and Business Goethe University Frankfurt Frankfurt am Main Germany
Abstract: ABSTRACT This paper studies Distribution Regression (DR) for ordered and discrete outcomes that are only partially observed due to misreporting. Such outcomes frequently occur in self‐reported surveys eliciting socially undesirable, illegal or stigmatised behaviours like substance abuse, domestic violence or anti‐social behaviour. We demonstrate that DR can offer a flexible way to study the distribution of these outcomes. Specifically, we analyse the asymptotic properties of the DR estimator and derive simultaneous confidence bands for unconditional ‘survival’ probabilities generated by that estimator as well as for counterfactual functionals thereof. The method is illustrated by examining possibly underreported lifetime marijuana consumption behaviour among US high‐school students. We find significant, positive differences across some consumption frequencies in lifetime marijuana use between students residing in states with and without recreational marijuana laws.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: How does artificial intelligence enhance supply chain efficiency? An information processing theory Perspective
Authors: Qiang Lu, Shiyu Cui, Yang Deng, Yu Wang
Abstract: Improving supply chain efficiency (SCE) has become a critical challenge for enterprises, and adopting intelligent technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a more effective approach. This study examines how AI affects SCE and further examines the moderating effects of business complexity and operational resilience. Our dataset consists of panel data from Chinese listed companies spanning 2012–2024, comprising 41,009 observations. Drawing on information processing theory, we construct a theoretical model and employ a fixed-effects model to analyze the impact of AI on SCE. Empirical findings show that AI has significant and positive impact on SCE. Contingently, both business complexity and operational resilience negatively moderate the impact of AI on SCE. This study expands the application scope of information processing theory and provides actionable guidance for enterprises aiming to enhance SCE.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: LLM-aided heuristic for the extended truck-drone-collection station delivery problem with dual-mode collaboration and drone multi-visit
Authors: Yixuan Zhai, Ping Chen, Jianhua Xiao, Liujiang Kang, Qianlong Wang
Abstract: Rural and low-density last-mile delivery is characterized by dispersed demand, long travel distances, and limited delivery infrastructure, which can make conventional delivery systems costly and inflexible. To improve service flexibility, this study develops the Extended Truck-Drone-Collection Station Delivery Problem with Dual-Mode Collaboration and Drone Multi-Visit (ETDCS-DMC-DMV). The model jointly considers fly-sidekick and independent parallel truck-drone operations, allows a drone to serve multiple customers within a single flight, and incorporates collection stations as optional self-pickup points. To solve the resulting integrated routing problem, an LLM-aided Large Neighborhood Search (LLMaLNS) algorithm is developed within an offline–online framework. In the offline phase, large language models (LLMs) generate problem-specific destroy and repair operators, while the online phase employs LLM-based operator selection to adaptively identify suitable operator pairs based on the current solution state and search progress. Computational experiments show that the proposed delivery model reduces total cost relative to restricted model variants that exclude collection stations, allow only single-customer drone sorties, or impose a single truck-drone coordination mode. Compared with conventional ALNS using manually designed operators, LLMaLNS improves the average best objective across medium- and large-scale instances, with the largest improvement observed on the largest test set. The ablation study further shows that both LLM-generated operators and LLM-based operator selection contribute to solution quality, while their combination yields the strongest performance. The results demonstrate the potential of combining multimodal delivery planning with LLM-aided neighborhood search for cost-efficient rural last-mile logistics.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Green and digital shipping corridors: AIS-informed infrastructure and operational coordination
Authors: Yang Liu, Kashin Sugishita, Shinya Hanaoka, Kelvin Lee, Lei Liu, Son Nguyen, Ran Yan
Abstract: Green and Digital Shipping Corridors (GDSCs) require coordinated investment in alternative-fuel and digital infrastructure to support maritime decarbonization. This study proposes an AIS-informed optimization framework for coordinated green and digital infrastructure planning in the Singapore–Japan (SG-JP) and Singapore–Australia (SG-AU) corridors. Historical 2021 Automatic Identification System data are reconstructed into end-to-end vessel trajectories and corridor networks, providing the basis for estimating fuel demand and Just-in-Time fuel-saving potential. A mixed-integer linear programming model jointly optimizes LNG bunkering deployment, interoperable digital infrastructure, and LNG/HFO fuel allocation while accounting for fuel, infrastructure, carbon-emission, and methane-emission costs. Results show that the SG-JP corridor exhibits a denser and more diversified network, whereas the SG-AU corridor is more dependent on Singapore as the dominant hub. Intermediate ports outside the officially designated GDSC contribute substantially to operational coordination in the SG-JP corridor, while restricting infrastructure deployment has only a limited impact on the Singapore-Australia corridor. Joint planning achieves lower total costs than separated planning and the single-infrastructure benchmarks, but produces slightly higher GHG emissions than separated planning. Comparisons across budget ceilings reveal differences in facility locations and composition, with no further cost reduction beyond an economic investment threshold. Sensitivity analyses show that fuel prices, methane slip, vessel tank capacity, and assumed LNG service availability influence the selected portfolios. The proposed framework provides a practical decision-support tool for planning economically efficient and operationally resilient GDSCs before implementation.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Capital flight? Do airlines move fuel-efficient planes to high-fuel-tax routes?
Authors: David R. Agrawal, Jan K. Brueckner, Quinton White
Abstract: This paper shows that airlines operate fuel-efficient planes on routes with high fuel taxes. It builds on a large data-collection effort compiling information on fuel taxes at the airport level, which is used to generate route-level taxes for thousands of nonstop airline routes in the US. The paper extends previous work exploring the connection between fuel prices and airline operations, with a new focus on the taxation of inputs. The results are used to derive the local pollution benefits from a route-specific fuel-tax increase.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Assessing response strategies for maritime chokepoint disruptions: An integrated routing–simulation framework with application to the Suez Canal
Authors: Mikhail Strukov
Abstract: This study presents an integrated routing–simulation framework to evaluate response strategies to maritime chokepoint disruptions. The framework combines disruption-route generation using the A-star algorithm with stochastic modeling of canal queuing, demand, and shipping dynamics through Monte Carlo and discrete-event simulation. The framework examines the disruption and operating conditions under which waiting, normal-speed rerouting, or increased-speed rerouting becomes the preferred response strategy. Strategy performance is assessed using a multi-perspective societal-cost framework, complemented by sensitivity analysis and random forest (RF) modeling to evaluate factor importance. A case study of container vessels affected by blockages on routes between selected European and Asian countries via the Suez Canal shows that rerouting reduces time-related costs by approximately 7–22% but increases fuel consumption, resulting in substantially higher operational (60–245%) and emissions (80–300%) costs than the waiting strategy, which serves as the baseline scenario. Overall, rerouting results in higher societal costs, making waiting the preferred strategy under most conditions. A disruption duration of approximately 25 days represents the transition point at which normal-speed rerouting and waiting yield nearly equivalent societal costs. Sensitivity analysis indicates that the preferred adaptation strategy depends on fleet characteristics. Highly energy-efficient vessels favor increased-speed rerouting in all blockage scenarios. Conversely, moderately energy-efficient vessels favor different strategies depending on market conditions, either normal-speed or increased-speed rerouting. Additionally, congestion levels influence the transition point between alternative response strategies. RF analysis further identifies the relative importance of key economic and technical parameters that shape societal cost outcomes for each strategy.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Modelling transport mode usage frequency and inter-modal relationships in Indian cities
Authors: B. Aswana, Furqan A. Bhat, Ashish Verma
Abstract: By combining the convenience and door-to-door accessibility of private vehicles with the on-demand flexibility of app-based booking, ride-hailing has emerged as a significant new layer in the urban transport ecosystem. This study uses survey data collected across four major Indian cities, namely Mumbai, Pune, Bengaluru, and Hyderabad, to jointly model the usage frequencies of public transport, private vehicles, ride-hailing services, and auto-rickshaws using a Multivariate Ordered Probit (MVOP) model incorporating sociodemographic characteristics, service attribute priorities such as comfort, safety, etc., and city-level effects. In addition, this study also analyses the inter-modal relationships between different modes. Age, education, vehicle ownership, and city are found to be the most consistent determinants of mode usage frequency across all four modes. Ride-hailing and public transport are complements rather than substitutes, while private vehicle usage is substitutive with public transport. This study provides evidence that can help policymakers design more effective and context-sensitive transport strategies. Together, these findings provide a foundation for evidence-based multimodal transport planning in rapidly urbanising Indian cities and contribute to the broader international literature on the role of ride-hailing within complex urban mobility systems.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: “Seeing is believing”: Risk, trust and technological upgrading in Peru’s artisanal gold mining landscape
Authors: Alejandra Villanueva Ubillús, Roy Maconachie
Abstract: Artisanal and small-scale gold mining (ASGM) is often portrayed as an informal, hazardous, “low-tech” activity with significant environmental risks, particularly from mercury emissions associated with traditional gold recovery methods. “Clean technologies” have long been championed as a quick “fix” solution to these challenges, yet adoption remains limited. Drawing on the concept of social embeddedness within the Global Production Networks and sociological literature, this paper critically explores how miners’ perceptions of risk and trust in gold production systems influence their technological choices. Based on multi-sited ethnographic fieldwork carried out in four mining regions in the Peruvian Andes and Amazon, we demonstrate how miners’ technological decisions in ASGM are heavily influenced by familiarity with specific methods and the predictability they offer for successful production. In Peru, three major risks – unstable formalization processes and state sanctions (regulatory risk), declining gold deposits (geological risk), and opportunistic behavior in trading (commercial risk) – affect this decision-making. While miners are not opposed to innovation, they prioritize technologies that maximize their control over value and minimize uncertainty, regardless of scientific evidence on mercury's health impacts. Our findings underscore the need for “responsible” ASGM interventions that recognize miners as pragmatic risk managers, navigating the complex social dynamics that define the realities of gold production.

Title: Resilience-oriented urban road network reinforcement and restoration with secondary disaster considerations
Authors: Shuang Yang, Bin Jia, Kai Yang, Xigui Tao, Yitao Yao, Hao Ji, Ziyou Gao
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: An experiment on social learning with information sequencing
Authors: Pëllumb Reshidi
Abstract: We test whether the order and timing of information arrival affect beliefs formed within a group. In a lab experiment, participants estimate a parameter of interest using a common and a private signal, as well as past guesses of group members. By varying the sequencing of information arrival, we find that the order and timing of information affect the groups’ beliefs, even when the information content is unchanged. We estimate a Hybrid Model that nests the Bayesian and the sequential DeGroot model while allowing for intermediate levels of sophistication. The Bayesian benchmark does a poor job predicting participants’ belief dynamics. In contrast, a version of the sequential DeGroot model that allows for flexible weights on others’ previous actions explains participants’ behavior well. Finally, participants place excessively high and fairly constant weights on their own private signals, regardless of the signal’s arrival time. I am indebted to Leeat Yariv, Roland Bénabou and Alessandro Lizzeri for their continued guidance. I have greatly benefited from discussions with Pietro Ortoleva, Guillaume Fréchette, Mark Dean, Jacopo Perego, Michael Thaler, Joao Thereze, and Mu Zhang. I am also grateful to audiences at Princeton University, “Economic Science Association Global Online Around-the-Clock Meetings ”, and “Student Workshop in Experimental Economics Techniques Princeton” for their helpful comments and discussions. Title: A collaborative framework integrating left-tail distribution forecasting and joint elicitability for risk management
Authors: Shuai Wang, Wendong Yang, Mengzheng Lv, Yang Zhao, Jianzhou Wang, Helen Lu

Title: Innovation spillovers from a mega-firm: Evidence from U.S. export controls on Huawei
Authors: Xiaoyao Yang, Sheng Fang
Abstract: We study how a mega-firm’s strategic response to foreign supply chain disruption shapes innovation by domestic upstream firms. Exploiting U.S. export controls on Huawei and the staggered county-level arrival of Huawei’s chip-related equity investments in China, we find that entry raises annual local chip invention patenting by 35.5 percent. The effect is more pronounced in places with stronger chip patent bases and prior public-fund presence and is more closely tied to proximity to Huawei-invested firms than to proximity to Huawei’s headquarters. The evidence is consistent with investee-mediated, demand-induced spillovers.

Title: The electoral disadvantage of a tie-breaking advantage
Authors: Felipe R. Durazzo
Abstract: We study tie-breaking favoritism in a costly voting model with a common fixed voting cost and Poisson population uncertainty. One candidate wins a tied election with probability greater than (Formula presented). Although this rule directly favors that candidate, it also induces an opposing strategic turnout response. At every interior equilibrium, the favored candidate receives fewer votes in expectation and, more surprisingly, wins the election with probability below (Formula presented). The strategic effect more than offsets the direct effect for any degree of favoritism. Thus, any asymmetric tie-breaking rule disadvantages the candidate it favors.

Title: The use of armed conflict as a bargaining tool against unsophisticated opponents
Authors: Santiago Sánchez-Pagés, Anıl Yıldızparlak
Abstract: This paper studies the role of conflict as a bargaining instrument and its impact on dispute termination. We explore an infinite-horizon bargaining game where limited conflicts reveal information about the contenders’ relative strength. Our benchmark assumes that the uninformed party is unsophisticated , i.e., she learns from battlefield outcomes but does not learn from diplomacy. The equilibrium of this bargaining game displays several features observed in real-world disputes. First, reducing disagreement about relative strength through battlefield outcomes is not sufficient for a peaceful dispute termination. Second, defeats lead to gambles for resurrection when limited conflicts are not too costly. Finally, disputes display non-monotonic termination probabilities over time. The main qualitative results continue to hold when the unsophistication assumption is partially relaxed and the uninformed party also learns from offers, though not from their absence.

Title: The tailoring premium: AI design, behavioral engagement, and human capital formation
Authors: Jaime Polanco-Jiménez, Kristof De Witte

Title: Tantalus curse? Multigenerational persistence of welfare dependency in Switzerland
Authors: Tamara Erhardt, Melanie Häner-Müller, Christoph A. Schaltegger
Abstract: We study welfare dependency in a multigenerational horizontal framework that exploits family links among siblings and cousins. Leveraging population-wide administrative data from Switzerland, we document how family resemblance in welfare receipt is distributed between the nuclear and the extended family. Individuals with a welfare-dependent sibling show about a 22-percentage-point higher probability of welfare receipt. Conditional on sibling receipt, having a welfare-dependent cousin is associated with a further increase of about 5 percentage points. Conditional analyses indicate that most predictive content is concentrated within the nuclear family while the cousin association remains economically meaningful given a baseline prevalence of about 4 percent. Sibling resemblance is stronger for welfare receipt than for income, while the additional predictive content of cousins is similar for both outcomes, implying that this heterogeneity is confined to the nuclear family.

Title: To auction or to give for free: Does the allowance allocation regime matter for renewable deployment in the EU ETS?
Authors: Akin A. Cilekoglu, Fatih Karanfil
Abstract: Phase III of the European Union Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) replaced free allocation with auctioning as the default method of distributing allowances in the power sector. Auctioning has generally been regarded as providing stronger incentives for renewable deployment, yet this policy proposition has rarely been tested directly. Article 10c created a unique institutional setting in which some lower-income Member States could retain free allocation, conditional on reinvesting the equivalent allowance value in renewable energy and power sector modernization. We exploit this institutional variation to test whether auctioning generated stronger renewable deployment than conditional free allocation. We combine a partial equilibrium model with an empirical analysis of EU ETS data. The theoretical model shows that under full carbon cost pass-through, auctioning does not increase carbon costs borne by power generators, while free allocation generates windfall profits. In either case, renewables gain no relative cost advantage over fossil fuels, implying that the allocation method alone does not change firms' incentives to deploy renewable capacity. Consistent with this prediction, our difference-in-differences estimates show that renewable capacity expanded and power sector emissions declined during Phase III, yet we find no statistically significant evidence that auctioning generated stronger renewable deployment or greater emissions reductions than conditional free allocation. As more countries adopt emissions trading systems, our findings suggest that, within the institutional setting examined here, their effectiveness in promoting renewable deployment may depend less on the allocation method itself than on enforceable governance mechanisms that channel allowance value toward low-carbon investment.

Title: JUE Insight: Contractual freedom versus tenancy law
Authors: Patrick W. Schmitz
Abstract: We study a two-period principal–agent model of rental housing in which a landlord (principal) offers a contract to a tenant (agent). After the first period, a cost shock may occur that increases the landlord’s cost of providing the apartment in the second period. Two scenarios are compared. In one scenario, there is full contractual freedom, while in the other scenario, there is a tenancy law requiring the landlord to continue renting in the second period if the apartment was rented in the first period. Under symmetric information, gains from trade in the tenancy law regime can never exceed those under contractual freedom. However, we show that when the tenant has private information, the tenancy law can lead to strictly higher gains from trade.

Title: Digital twin transition for intelligent and resilient industrial systems
Authors: Serena Finco, Jinsong Bao, Ilya Jackson, Yuqian Lu
Affiliations: University of Padova; Donghua University; Massachusetts Institute of Technology; The University of Auckland
Abstract: Digital twins (DTs) are a vital technology transforming industrial systems by linking the physical and digital realms through real-time, bidirectional data flow and intelligent analysis. This special issue of the International Journal of Production Research presents 14 original contributions that advance both the theoretical framework and practical applications of digital twins in diverse industrial settings, such as production control, process monitoring, human-machine collaboration, supply chains, maintenance, and value-based deployment. The articles are grouped into three key themes: (i) DT architectures, modelling principles, and trustworthy development; (ii) smart production management, process optimisation, and digital integration; and (iii) human-centered applications, supply chain support, and industrial value creation. Collectively, they offer a comprehensive overview of digital twins as a transformative technology enabling adaptive and resilient industrial operations. The editorial concludes with a discussion of major open challenges and promising research directions to promote wider adoption of digital twins across various industrial sectors.

Title: Stuck in place? Intergenerational occupational mobility in Türkiye
Authors: Meryem Türel, Ensar Yılmaz
Abstract: This study analyzes intergenerational occupational mobility in Türkiye using the 2021 Family Structure Survey. Applying mobility matrices, Altham’s statistics, and rank-rank correlations across four birth cohorts (from 1951 to 1994), we separate structural economic change from genuine social fluidity. The results reveal a clear divergence. While absolute mobility rose significantly due to de-agrarianization and service-sector expansion, relative mobility stagnated or declined after controlling for these shifts. This implies an economic transformation created movement without improving equality of opportunity. We identify asymmetric permeability: a “sticky top” where the children of professionals are protected by a “glass floor,” and a “sticky floor” where origins in agricultural or low-status positions lead primarily to manual labor. The analysis uncovers considerable heterogeneity. Mobility is highly gendered, with daughters facing stronger status persistence than sons, and spatially fractured.

Title: Intergenerational transmission of education: evidence from school construction in Indonesia
Authors: Li Li, Haoming Liu
Abstract: This paper investigates how an exogenous increase in parental schooling, driven by Indonesia’s Sekolah Dasar INPRES school construction program, affects children’s educational outcomes. Linking parents to their children aged 13–17 in the 2010 census, we estimate the effects using two-stage least squares (2SLS). Under the 2SLS identification assumptions, each additional year of parental schooling raises children’s school attendance by 1.8 percentage points and junior high school completion by 1.7 percentage points. The mechanism analysis reveals that the estimated schooling effect remains largely unchanged after considering observed candidate channels, while reduced fertility may represent an indirect channel.

Title: Digital twin-based shop-floor reconfiguration design for uncertainty management
Authors: Chenyuan Zhang, Fei Tao, Qinglin Qi, Ying Cheng, Jiangfeng Cheng, Bailing Wang, A. Y. C. Nee
Affiliations: Beihang University; Beijing Xiaomi Mobile Software Co., Ltd.; National University of Singapore
Abstract: Reconfiguration has emerged as a paradigm that adjusts shop-floor operations based on production requirements in such a way as to obtain desired performance and adapt to changes quickly. Existing research puts more emphasis on optimising the layout and configuration of shop floors based on simplified mathematical models and algorithms. However, uncertainty and complexity of shop-floor operations could diminish the effectiveness of the reconfiguration solution. This paper presents a digital twin-based design method for shop-floor reconfiguration to solve the problems. Digital twin models with dynamic fidelity are used for reconfiguration design to provide effective information of shop-floor complexity. To analyse the impact of uncertainty on shop-floor performance and then guide the shop-floor reconfiguration design, methods of shop-floor performance fluctuation identification, uncertain event extraction, reconfiguration operation domain division are proposed. The proposed method is verified with the case study of a chemical fibre silk cake packing shop floor.

Title: Improving efficiency of steel converter facility: a digital twin and reinforcement learning approach
Authors: Amit Kumar, Ramesh Kumar
Affiliations: Indian Institute of Management Mumbai
Abstract: The steel converter facility is an essential part of the steel manufacturing process and is responsible for converting molten iron into steel. The material movement within the facility depends on the effective overhead crane scheduling. However, the traditional approach of crane scheduling at these facilities leads to inefficiencies. To understand this need, we propose an integrated approach using Simulation modelling, Digital Twin (DT) and Reinforcement Learning (RL) to improve the crane scheduling operation of the steelmaking process. We developed a simulation model using discrete event and agent-based simulation and connected it with real-time data by applying the digital twin approach. Further, a Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) agent is trained in a stochastic environment with multiple feedback loops and complex interactions for crane scheduling. The DRL agent recommends the sequences of crane movement to reduce the wait time in bottleneck operation. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method gives results within 3.6% of the optimal on average. A case of the steel converter facility illustrates this approach, which is also applicable to other industries requiring complex scheduling, such as construction, automotive, and logistics, to improve operational efficiency.

Title: Digital twin-based spatiotemporal global reconstruction for industrial temperature field: a case study of the snap curing oven
Authors: Ziyuan Wang, Xiaoyue Xu, Yishun Liu, Benedict Jun Ma, Chunhua Yang
Affiliations: Central South University; City University of Hong Kong; Key Laboratory of Industrial Intelligence and Systems (Central South University); Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Abstract: Reconstruction of the temperature field for industrial processes is crucial and challenging since only sparse sensors can be deployed on-site. This paper proposes a digital twin-based spatiotemporal reconstruction method for the industrial temperature field using the computational fluid dynamics (CFD) model. First, a CFD simulation is employed to establish a digital twin of the industrial thermal process, generating high-resolution temperature field data. Considering the complex spatiotemporal dynamics, an innovative spatiotemporal decomposition strategy is adopted to extract inherent spatial modes, enhancing the accuracy and efficiency of spatiotemporal dynamic learning. Next, based on sparse observational data from the actual thermal process, the temporal evolution dynamics of the temperature field are modelled. Finally, utilising online sensor data and system control inputs, the current temperature field is reconstructed using the extracted spatial modes and temporal evolution dynamics. Furthermore, to address inevitable discrepancies between the actual thermal process and the digital twin caused by dynamic variations, an adaptive adjustment module is designed. The results of the snap curing oven case study demonstrate that the proposed method achieves 6.69% higher reconstruction accuracy than conventional counterparts with 55.0% of the computation time, indicating the superiority of the proposed method both in reconstruction precision and speed.

Title: Digital twin key technology in semiconductor manufacturing: multi-batch wafer PCD-IVM based on mixed multi-scale entropy and density clustering
Authors: Hong-Wei Xu, Shu-Xuan Zhao, Li-Lan Liu, Wei Qin, You-Long Lv, Jie Zhang, Qi-Hua Zhang
Affiliations: Shanghai University; University of Hong Kong; Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Donghua University; Hong-Qi Integrated Circuit (Zhu Hai) Corporation
Abstract: Digital twin technology provides crucial digital empowerment for semiconductor manufacturing. Aiming at the problems of high cost and low timeliness of the physical measurement method for the Post-lithography Critical Dimension (PCD) of wafers, this study proposes an Incremental Virtual Metrology (IVM) architecture that integrates hybrid multi-scale entropy and density clustering. Firstly, the temporal characteristics of the process are extracted through multi-scale entropy, the non-temporal spatial characteristics are mined by combining with density clustering, and the low-dimensional embedding mapping of high-dimensional features is realised through manifold learning. Furthermore, the adaptive partitioning of multimodal features is completed through K-Means clustering, and an incremental update mechanism driven by just-in-time learning is constructed to achieve dynamic optimisation of the model parameters. Experimental validation using empirical data from an industrial semiconductor fabrication facility demonstrates that the proposed method achieves an R² value of 0.85 for PCD real-time metrology. Compared with conventional approaches, the method demonstrates a 20% improvement in prediction accuracy while maintaining superior cross-batch generalisation capabilities. This advancement offers an efficient solution for VM-enabled digital twin systems in semiconductor manufacturing, effectively bridging the gap between physical measurements and virtual simulation environments.

Title: A digital twin-based cyber-physical system for resilient short-term equipment leasing
Authors: Kyu-Tae Park, Ju-Yong Lee, Yangho Park
Affiliations: Seoul National University of Science and Technology; Kangwon National University; Micube Solutions, Inc.
Abstract: Short-term equipment leasing (STEL) is a vital business model supporting small- and medium-sized enterprises by addressing the challenges of limited production capacities through temporary equipment leasing. To enhance the operational resilience of STEL, this study proposes a novel digital twin (DT)-based cyber-physical system (CPS), which implements service composition for leasing scheduling, dynamic prognosis, and dynamic response during type and instance phases in STEL environments. The CPS incorporates a leasing request platform for handling interactions between the STEL centre and clients and a leasing scheduling application based on the tabu search algorithm for leasing scheduling and rescheduling as elemental technical functionalities. The DT application supports virtual commissioning, prognostic simulation, and reactive simulation, minimising operational ripple effects caused by dynamic disturbances such as machine breakdowns or quality issues. The effectiveness of the CPS is demonstrated through an industrial case study in the ceramic industry, where it enhances resilience and operational efficiency. Validation experiments with industrial benchmark samples and various algorithmic comparisons showcase its capability to provide near-optimal solutions, adapt to dynamic disruptions, and maintain performance under dynamic events. This study highlights the potential of DT-based CPSs to revolutionise STEL practices and underscores the importance of resilience in ensuring successful leasing operations.

Title: Success criteria for value-oriented digital twin development and implementation: insights from an industry case study
Authors: Christian Kober, Jan Polzer, Elizabeth Kulasingham, Daniel Kulasingham, Xun Xu
Affiliations: Helmut Schmidt University; University of Cambridge; University of Auckland; Sequal Lumber Ltd.
Abstract: Digital Twins (DTs) offer transformative potential for Industry 4.0. However, the maturity of DTs in manufacturing remains limited due to various challenges. This article addresses a critical knowledge gap by examining factors that determine DT implementation success through a comprehensive case study of a pioneering sawmill. Unique for its technical complexity, proven economic impact, and complete life cycle analysis, the study provides scarce real-world evidence of a fully automated DT with tangible commercial success. It offers an in-depth examination of a real DT development process, critically evaluating it alongside a novel DT development and implementation framework. Key success criteria, such as fostering organisational trust to support DT adoption, are identified, guiding future advancements in real industrial environments. The analysis reveals unexpected commonalities between the DT framework and actual industrial practices, establishing a valuable benchmark for future DT projects. By bridging the gap between theory and practice, this work increases the likelihood of technical and economic success in DT development and implementation – an outcome rarely documented in current DT literature. Thus, this work serves not only as a practical guide for practitioners but also enriches the theoretical discourse on DTs, making it highly relevant to research and industry.

Title: Do you trust digital twins? A framework to support the development of trusted digital twins through verification and validation
Authors: Julia Bitencourt, John Osho, Ana Wooley, Gregory Harris
Affiliations: Auburn University; The University of Alabama in Huntsville
Abstract: In recent years, Digital Twin (DT) has been used to design, control, and automate decision-making in various applications. Despite advancements in DT architecture, several challenges remain unexplored. For instance, to use DTs for decision-making, it is essential to trust all components of a DT. Model credibility, or model trust, is traditionally viewed from the perspective of Verification and Validation (V&V). Although V&V concepts are well-developed and widely applied in modeling, simulation, and other fields, such as systems and software engineering, there is very little mention of V&V procedures in the context of DTs. As DTs gain prominence in many application fields, developing DTs that can be trusted and used in real-world environments is essential. This study introduces the Digital Twin V (DTV) framework as a structured approach to building trusted DTs. The DTV integrates V&V activities across the DT development lifecycle, emphasizing iterative and recursive processes tailored to the unique characteristics of DTs. A case study applying the DTV framework to a fused deposition modeling additive machine illustrates its applicability. The framework’s scalability and potential for adaptation across various DT maturity levels are demonstrated, offering actionable guidelines for practitioners and researchers to enhance the trust and adoption of DTs.

Title: A modular multi-granularity simulation modelling method for manufacturing systems oriented towards digital twins
Authors: Yangjun Sun, Zhuorui Fu, Ning Zhao
Affiliations: University of Science and Technology Beijing
Abstract: Digital Twins (DTs) are critical in advancing the development of intelligent and resilient manufacturing systems. However, general DT implementation methods often depend on high-precision simulation models, which can escalate modelling costs while constraining model modifiability and adaptability. This study introduces a modular multi-granularity simulation modelling method for manufacturing systems. The multi-granularity simulation modelling theory enables the quantitative description of detail levels and associated modelling costs through granularity analysis, thereby establishing a DT framework that accommodates different granularity requirements based on specific needs and characteristics. The modular simulation modelling approach offers a systematic methodology for partitioning manufacturing systems into modules, standardising simulation modules, performing combinatorial modelling, and constructing DTs in a modular fashion. To validate this method, we have employed a case study involving the simulation modelling of a laser cutting production system and its DT implementation process. The results indicate that the proposed method effectively reduces the cost of simulation modelling while preserving accuracy, thus fulfilling the objectives of simulation analysis and DT construction.

Title: A digital twin-enabled digital spare parts supply chain
Authors: Mirco Peron
Affiliations: NEOMA Business School
Abstract: An efficient and effective spare parts supply chain management is crucial to ensure highly available production systems. However, achieving such a spare parts supply chain management is challenging due to the intrinsic characteristics of spare parts. Traditional spare parts supply chains (TSPSCs) adopt large spare parts inventories to tackle such intrinsic characteristics, with disadvantages in terms of high inventory costs. Recently, Additive Manufacturing (AM) has shown breakthrough potential, allowing the transition from TSPSCs to digital spare parts supply chains (DSPSCs), where spare parts are no longer stored in large amounts but are stored digitally and produced only when needed. However, despite DSPSCs benefits, a complete transition from TSPSCs to DSPSCs is still far from becoming reality. Indeed, hindering such a transition is a lack of expertise in three main areas, i.e. how to design, operate, and control and monitor a DSPSC. With this position paper, we envision how a digital twin (DT) could overcome these issues, enabling a full transition to a DSPSC. Moreover, this work further concretely suggests how such a DT could be developed, providing the basis for developing both the theoretical and practical knowledge necessary to render DSPSCs a reality.

Title: A digital twin-driven human-machine interactive assembly method based on lightweight multi-target detection and assembly feature generation
Authors: Dinghao Cheng, Bingtao Hu, Yixiong Feng, Jiangxin Yang, Baicun Wang, Hao Gong, Jianrong Tan
Affiliations: Zhejiang University; Guizhou University; Beijing Institute of Technology
Abstract: In the field of industrial assembly, human-machine interactive assembly methods are frequently used. Lack of virtual and physical mapping, a convoluted guiding system, and low effect precision in the interactive process, a digital twin-driven human-machine interactive assembly method system is proposed as a solution to the mentioned issues. The YOLOv7-tiny lightweight model is used to perform accurate detection of parts. By incorporating attention modules into the backbone network, the feature extraction capability of the model in complicated assembly environments is enhanced. The assembly method proposed is validated using the assembly process of the reducer as an instance. The OpenCV method is employed to produce geometric reference features for parts. The experimental results show that the proposed assembly method can provide visual guidance for the assembly process, improve the traditional list-type assembly component retrieval method, solve the drawbacks of the pre-set assembly guidance in the guidance system that may not be able to adapt to the changes of the assembly results in the actual operation, and can accurately instruct novices how to assemble, which is characterised by easy implementation, low cost and high accuracy, and is of great significance for improving the success rate and assembly efficiency of human-machine interactive assembly.

Title: Digital thread-driven cloud-fog-edge collaborative disturbance mitigation mechanism for adaptive production in digital twin discrete manufacturing workshop
Authors: Zhiwen Lin, Zhifeng Liu, Jun Yan, Yueze Zhang, Chuanhai Chen, Baobao Qi, Jinyan Guo
Affiliations: Jilin University; Beijing University of Technology
Abstract: The collaborative capacity among various computing layers within a digital twin workshop directly impacts the handling of disturbances in discrete manufacturing processes. However, the intricate nature of the cross-space (physical and virtual space) and cross-layer (cloud, fog, and edge) interactions within a digital twin system poses challenges to construct a comprehensive data model and interoperable data flow, leading to a fragmented state of computing layers. To tackle these challenges, this study presents a digital thread-driven theory and method for cloud-fog-edge collaboration in digital twin discrete manufacturing workshops. Firstly, the five-dimensions production information that cross spaces and layers is concatenated and integrated by constructing digital thread models. Subsequently, a disturbance response model is conducted based on these digital thread models to detect, track, and evaluate disturbances. Furthermore, corresponding cloud-fog-edge collaboration strategies are devised for different types and severity of disturbances, facilitating the dynamic production tasks adjustments. Finally, a case study to discuss the performance of the proposed method regarding the maturity of the digital thread model, disturbance response capability, and production self-adaptive adjustment capability. The results demonstrate that the proposed method effectively mitigates makespan and machine idle time under gradual and abrupt disturbances, and saves 46.22% of computing processing time.

Title: Integrated optimisation of human-robot collaborative disassembly planning and adaptive evaluation driven by a digital twin
Authors: Gang Yuan, Feng Lv, Jin Shi, Guangdong Tian, Yixiong Feng, Zhiwu Li, Duc Truong Pham
Affiliations: Southeast University; Beijing University of Civil Engineering and Architecture; Zhejiang University; Macau University of Science and Technology; University of Birmingham
Abstract: With the continuous development of intelligent manufacturing and human-oriented manufacturing, human-robot collaborative disassembly is becoming a new trend in intelligent remanufacturing. The application of digital twin technology in human-robot collaborative disassembly (HRCD) can significantly increase work efficiency and improve human well-being. Herein, we propose a reference framework for digital twin-driven HRCD planning and adaptive evaluation, which integrates three modules: HRCD digital twin environment construction, HRCD sequence optimisation, and HRCD adaptive evaluation. Subsequently, based on the physiological and psychological fatigue of workers, we establish a planning model with disassembly time and disassembly complexity, and propose an improved heuristic algorithm to determine the task allocation scheme. To enable adaptive evaluation of HRCD strategies, a digital twin-driven kernel point convolution neural network model (DTKPN) and a digital twin-driven Bayesian neural network human posture estimation model (DT-BSHP) are implemented for robot recognition and human pose evaluation. The proposed model can leverage the skills of humans and robots, satisfy ergonomic requirements, improve disassembly efficiency, and reduce disassembly complexity. Finally, the method is applied to a simplified satellite disassembly case. It is shown that the proposed model significantly reduces the disassembly time and complexity and thus the effectiveness and sensitivity of the proposed model are verified.

Title: Digital twin-based multi-granularity synchronisation for production-warehousing under batch processing mode
Authors: Yongheng Zhang, Ting Qu, Mingxing Li, Zhongfei Zhang, Kai Zhang, Zhicong Hong, George Q. Huang, Zefeng Chen
Affiliations: Jinan University; The Hong Kong Polytechnic University Shenzhen Research Institute; The Hong Kong Polytechnic University; Carpoly Chemical Group Co., Ltd
Abstract: Batch production is a cost-effective way that boosts efficiency in manufacturing systems. As customer demands become increasingly customised, there is a growing need to consolidate numerous small-batch orders. However, if batch production exceeds the optimal level, it may lead to the premature completion of customer orders, causing temporary congestion in the finished goods warehouse and prolonged resource occupation. Consequently, an essential focus of this study pertains to coordinating decision-making units like workshops and warehouses within batch production setups to ensure stable system operation amidst dynamic customer demands. The proposed solution encompasses a Digital Twin-based Multi-level Synchronised Control System (DTMCS) framework, featuring the Multi-granularity Synchronised Control Mechanism (MgSCM) and a collaborative optimisation model for batch production and warehouse planning. By examining a practical case study from a paint manufacturing company, the research delves into the effects of four synchronised control patterns on various system performance metrics, such as operating costs, equipment and warehouse utilisation rates, and system stability. Overall, this study provides an adaptable and cost-effective solution for enhancing production-logistics synchronisation.

Title: The effect of climate-related disasters on inventor mobility: Evidence from China
Authors: Yu Shen, Yang Lei, Xinwei Xu
Journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

Title: A decision-aiding procedure for technology selection in the context of digital transformation
Authors: Reginaldo Carreiro Santos, Edson Pinheiro de Lima, Sergio Eduardo Gouvea da Costa, Fernando Deschamps, Elias Ribeiro da Silva, Ana Paula Cabral Seixas Costa, José Luís Martinho
Affiliations: Pontifícia Universidade Católica do Paraná; Universidade Tecnológica Federal do Paraná; University of Southern Denmark; Universidade Federal de Pernambuco, Recife, Brazil; Coimbra Polytechnic - ISEC, Polytechnic University of Coimbra; RCM2+, Research Centre for Asset Management and Systems Engineering, Polytechnic University of Coimbra, Coimbra, Portugal

Title: Balancing flexibility and robustness in operating room scheduling: the impact of resource constraints under uncertainty
Authors: Marc Chouraqui, Salma Makboul, Alice Yalaoui, Farouk Yalaoui, Lionel Amodeo, Virginie Roger
Affiliations: Université de Technologie de Troyes; Hôpital Européen; Université Paris-Saclay, Univ Evry, IBISC

Authors: Qing Feng, Dengfeng Li
Affiliations: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Forecasting global trade networks under partial disruption: a network-attack framework and machine learning benchmark
Authors: Reetendra Singh, Shivshanker Singh Patel
Affiliations: Decision Sciences, Indian Institute of Management Visakhapatnam
