Title: Aligning institutions and organizations for sustainable supply chains: the role of digital transformation and low-carbon practices
Authors: Muhammad Asim Shahzad, Xiaoxiang Wang, Muhammad Faraz Riaz, Asma Javed
Affiliations: Shenzhen Institute of Advanced Technology Chinese Academy of Sciences , Shenzhen; Shenzhen Polytechnic University Institute of Carbon Neutral Technology, , Shenzhen; Government College University Faisalabad Department of Economics, , Faisalabad; Chang’an University , Xi’an
Abstract: Purpose The transition toward carbon neutrality has become a global strategic priority for achieving sustainable development and a green economy. Despite growing interest in digital transformation among scholars and practitioners, achieving a balance between green supply chain performance and carbon performance within the context of carbon neutrality remains underexplored. Drawing on the technology acceptance model and change management theory, this research aims to provide solutions for achieving the zero-carbon target in 2060 through holistic digital transformation, and how institutional pressure and organizational readiness influence green supply chain and carbon performance through digital transformation, low-carbon operations management practices (LCOMP) and the moderating role of environmental proactivity. Design/methodology/approach Data from 442 Chinese manufacturing firms were analyzed using Smart PLS v4 to test the research hypotheses. Findings The results indicate that all three dimensions of LCOMP mediate the relationship between digital transformation, green supply chain and carbon performance. In addition, environmental proactivity strengthens the influence of digital transformation on the three dimensions of LCOMP. Originality/value The findings contribute to the literature by addressing a key gap in sustainable supply chain and digital transformation research, which has largely examined these relationships in isolation without fully explaining the mediating mechanisms and boundary conditions.
Journal: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

Title: Railway track maintenance tasks generation and assignment with considering predictive maintenance
Authors: Shao-Chi Chien, Yung-Cheng Rex Lai, Kwei-Long Huang
Abstract: A safe and efficient railway operation relies on a well-maintained system. The expenditure on railway track maintenance often contributes to approximately half of the maintenance expenditure; therefore, how to properly allocate the resources in railway track maintenance according to safety, comfort, and cost is an important task in the planning process. This study addresses the long-term track maintenance planning problem and aims to identify a set of maintenance tasks on rail networks for given horizons. In addition to the preventive maintenance strategy considered in the manual planning process, the predictive maintenance is taken into consideration to promote the performance of the railway track system. An optimization model is first established to describe the problem and a heuristic algorithm is then developed to enhance the solution efficiency based on the practical rules. Results from case studies demonstrate that the developed process can successfully identify appropriate maintenance tasks and assign them in the annual maintenance plan by minimizing the costs of expected failures (safety), irregularities (comfort), and maintenance. As a result, adopting this developed decision-support model can assist planners to identify the necessary maintenance activities and to also create long-term track maintenance plans efficiently.

Title: Leveraging statistical learning for surgery scheduling optimization under uncertainty
Authors: Jin Wang, George A. Elder, Wen Yang, Mai Zhang, Xin Li
Abstract: Operating rooms (ORs) are among the most resource-intensive and financially critical components of hospital infrastructure. Efficient surgery scheduling is of great importance to improve the utilization of ORs and reduce hospital expenditures. This paper addresses the surgery scheduling problem by integrating predictive analytics with prescriptive optimization. We first perform statistical learning to analyze the relationship between surgery duration and the volume of surgeries assigned to an operating room. Our analysis reveals an empirical predictive regularity: observed surgery durations tend to be lower in ORs assigned higher case volumes, up to a threshold of four cases. Based on these insights, we develop three optimization frameworks: a deterministic model, a stochastic programming model based on sample average approximation, and a robust optimization model. A simulation-based approach is proposed to calibrate the uncertainty budget in the robust optimization model. Numerical experiments demonstrate that models incorporating statistical learning consistently outperform those that do not. Furthermore, the robust optimization model provides superior or comparable performance to stochastic alternatives, offering a more reliable solution for high-uncertainty environments. By leveraging statistical learning, this study bridges the gap between surgical data analytics and resource optimization, providing a robust pathway for enhancing operating room efficiency.

Title: Bin packing with hierarchical item types
Authors: Leah Epstein
Abstract: Abstract We consider the following version of online bin packing. Arriving items of rational sizes in (0, 1] belong to a constant number of types denoted by $$1,2,\ldots ,k$$ 1 , 2 , … , k , and there are unbounded numbers of available bins of these types. The cost of a bin depends on its type, and the sequence of costs is monotonically increasing. Every item of type i can be packed into a bin of type whose index is at least i , and no bin may have a total size of items that is larger than 1. Items are presented one by one to be packed into suitable bins, where the information regarding bin types is known in advance. The cost of the algorithm is the total cost of used bins, and the goal is to minimize the cost. We show tight bounds on the absolute competitive ratio for the case of three types ( $$k=3$$ k = 3 ), and tight bounds for the overall bound with an arbitrary number of types k , where those bounds are 2 and 4 for $$k=3$$ k = 3 and for arbitrary k , respectively.

Title: Robust forecast evaluation under extreme shocks
Authors: Fabrizio Iacone, Andrea Viselli
Abstract: We address forecast evaluation in the presence of extreme, one-off shocks, such as the impact of Covid-19 on GDP. Conventional predictive ability tests may have no power under such brief but severe instabilities, potentially overlooking the superior accuracy of forecasts during normal periods. To remove this effect, we propose winsorizing forecast errors to neutralize the influence of extreme events. Using the US Survey of Professional Forecasters for real GDP growth, we illustrate how this approach uncovers superior performance that standard tests would otherwise fail to detect.

Title: Integrating fuzzy MCDM priors into deep reinforcement learning for sustainable and resilient supplier selection and dynamic order allocation
Authors: Ali Vaezi, Erfan Rabbani, Giulia Bruno
Abstract: Multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) offers expert-driven evaluation, but its rankings never update. Reinforcement learning (RL) adapts ordering daily, but a fresh agent knows nothing about suppliers. We combine them and contribute a prior-embedding architecture, an account of regime-dependent performance, and a multi-seed evaluation protocol. Phase I converts one expert’s judgments on 16 criteria into closeness coefficients for five suppliers via Fuzzy Best-Worst Method and Fuzzy TOPSIS. Phase II places those coefficients in a Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) agent’s observation vector throughout training. Against a PPO baseline and a base-stock heuristic, across four disruption regimes (36 main runs), the prior-informed agent’s relative performance varies by regime. In calm conditions it undercuts the PPO baseline ( d = 1.31 ), but a replicate closes the gap ( d = 0.08 ). When disruptions strike the worst-ranked suppliers, it shows higher sustainability than the PPO baseline ( d = 0.71 ), within that metric’s noise. Under supplier-agnostic volatility the PPO baseline does better. When disruptions hit the top-ranked suppliers, its sustainability falls sharply below the PPO baseline’s ( d = 2.07 ), while its observed mean cost is lower ( d = 1.09 ). All RL agents share the sustainability reward, so the ablation isolates the observation channel: its cost and sustainability effects reach at most | d | = 0.59 , while identical configurations differ by | d | above 1 on cost. Both agents undercut the heuristic by 66 to 88% under volatility and shocks; in calm conditions it is cheaper. Findings rest on synthetic, single-expert data.

Title: The Best Allocation Resource Size (BARS) problem: a bi-objective integer programming model to balance cost and complexity in resource selection
Authors: Margherita Bernabei, Silvia Colabianchi, Francesco Costantino, Marianna De Santis, Daniele Patria
Abstract: This paper introduces a variant of the assortment problem, i.e., the Best Allocation Resource Size (BARS) problem, conceived as a multi-objective nonlinear optimization model that jointly minimizes total production-related costs and input complexity by selecting the optimal subset of resource sizes, explicitly balancing cost-efficiency with scrap minimization. Unlike traditional assortment problems, the BARS adopts a manufacturer-led perspective, handling multiple characteristics of the inputs, i.e., it is n-dimensional, and it integrates multiple cost dimensions - including setup, scrap, safety stock, and non-linear purchase costs - under realistic manufacturing constraints, thus offering a flexible, producer-oriented decision-support tool adaptable to diverse industrial contexts. The problem formulation does not incorporate an ex-ante budget constraint, allowing the solution space to be retrospectively filtered by applying cost thresholds - either on aggregate expenditure or individual cost components - thus enabling targeted post-hoc analyses of feasible item sets in line with strategic objectives, including scenarios that allow for controlled increases in spending. The model proposed is solved using an adapted ε-constraint method that, unlike a generic scalarization, is provably exact for bi-objective nonlinear integer programs: a second-order cone reformulation of the safety-stock term allows to determine properly calibrated ε values, ensuring recovery of the complete Pareto front. The efficacy of the proposed model is demonstrated through validation in three real-world case studies spanning different industrial sectors. The developed model serves as a strategic decision tool for management, facilitating an understanding of the costs consequences associated with different sets of selected raw materials.

Title: Is sensitivity always beneficial? Risk perception, inventory turnover, and supply chain resilience: The roles of transparency and digitalization
Authors: Benyue Liu, Nengmin Wang, Bin Jiang
Abstract: Amid rising uncertainty in global supply chains, understanding how firms perceive supply chain risks and translate them into effective operational responses is critical to explaining the formation of supply chain resilience (SCR). Existing studies mainly explain SCR from the perspectives of external risk exposure, resources, and capabilities, while paying insufficient attention to risk cognition and its operational transformation. Based on behavioral risk theory and dynamic capabilities theory, this study uses Chinese A-share listed firms from the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges during 2013–2022 and develops a “risk cognition–operational action–resilience outcome” framework to examine the mechanisms and stage-specific boundary conditions through which supply chain risk perception (SCRP) affects SCR. The results reveal that SCRP exhibits a significant inverted U-shaped relationship with SCR; inventory turnover speed (ITS) serves as an important operational transmission mechanism; supply chain transparency (SCT) strengthens the inverted U-shaped relationship between SCRP and ITS, while digitalization level (DIG) enhances the positive effect of ITS on SCR. Dynamic QCA further shows that high SCR can be achieved through different combinations of conditions, indicating multiple equifinal pathways. This study advances understanding of SCR formation from the perspectives of risk cognition and operational response, while providing practical implications for firms to calibrate SCRP, implement dynamic inventory management, and enhance information transparency and digitalization.

Title: A note on first-order and transversality conditions in infinite-horizon continuous-time optimal control models
Authors: Stefano Bosi, David Desmarchelier, Ngoc-Sang Pham
Abstract: We provide simple and easily verifiable necessary and sufficient conditions for infinite-horizon continuous-time optimal control problems. Under standard concavity and integrability assumptions, we show that optimal paths are fully characterized by first-order conditions together with a transversality condition. Importantly, the transversality condition is derived as a consequence of the model’s structure rather than imposed a priori. Our results apply directly to standard economic models, including optimal growth and consumption–saving problems.

Title: Modeling and evaluating time-varying user preference of morning rail transit commuters with smart card data
Authors: Tian-Liang Liu, Pu Xu, Bingfeng Si, Wei Liu
Abstract: Existing studies of rail transit choice generally assume time-invariant utility preferences, although empirical evidence from morning road commuting suggests that commuters’ preferences may vary over time. Whether in-vehicle crowding perception also varies over the morning peak period in rail commuting remains unclear. Using smart card records and train timetable data, this study develops a revealed-preference framework that jointly represents time-varying scheduling preferences and in-vehicle crowding perception and evaluates alternative temporal specifications of both preference components. Because observed crowding is an outcome of passengers’ aggregate choices among train services, direct estimation may suffer from self-selection bias. To address this issue, we exploit the behavioral distinction between commuters who board the current arriving train and those who wait for a subsequent train to secure a seat, thereby differentiating in-vehicle crowding disutility across the two riding scenarios. Alternative discrete choice models are then estimated under these preference specifications to evaluate commuters’ time-varying preferences. The results show stronger empirical support for the piecewise constant and piecewise linear specifications of crowding perception than for the piecewise exponential specification, while the nested logit model provides the best overall fit and suggests lower crowding sensitivity for later arrivals among the observed regular commuters. Moreover, crowding plays a relatively greater role in commuters’ trade-offs for services arriving near their desired arrival times, whereas time-invariant specifications may smooth out temporal variation in crowding perception and understate its behavioral relevance for these services.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Analytical modeling of a stop-less modular bus line: Optimization, feasibility, and economies of scale
Authors: Haoran Zhao, Neema Nassir, Andres Fielbaum
Abstract: Conventional bus services often struggle with inefficiencies including prolonged dwell times at heavily used stops, especially for through passengers. A stop-less autonomous modular bus service (SLAM) has been proposed to reduce dwell times by decoupling the front pod to serve stops and then coupling it to the next bus. However, the optimal service design and feasibility region remain underexplored, despite their importance for planning and deployment. We propose an analytical optimization model that characterizes the optimal design, feasibility conditions, and sources of scale economies. Three novel constraints distinguish SLAM from conventional bus services: (i) a minimum headway to ensure sufficient time for decoupling, alighting, boarding, and coupling operations, (ii) a maximum headway to guarantee all passengers arriving within a headway fit in the standby pod, and (iii) a minimum bus length constraint, requiring at least two pods per bus to run in a SLAM manner. As ridership grows, the optimal design evolves through several regimes, in which headway constraints alternate between slack and binding states, while capacity constraints shift from one active form to another. Our analysis indicates that, compared with conventional services, SLAM is most suitable at intermediate demand levels: at low demand, the fixed costs of standby pods and the minimum two-pod configuration outweigh the time-saving benefits, whereas at high demand, non-stopping operation becomes infeasible. We further decompose the sources of scale economies into four components: the Mohring effect, through-capacity economies, boarding-capacity economies, and standby-pod costs, identifying under which conditions each of them is present. The numerical results validate the theoretical analysis.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: The long-run returns to rural electrification: Evidence from a randomized experiment
Authors: Matthieu Chemin, Thomas Kokossou
Abstract: We conduct a randomized controlled trial of a micro-hydro electrification project in a rural community in Kenya with staggered household connections beginning in 2016, allowing us to study effects up to eight years after connection. We find that electricity access affects economic activity, but only in the long run. Households increase time spent on non-farm work by 78 percent and reduce time on farm work, consistent with the early stages of structural transformation, yet these effects emerge only after four years. Electrification leads to business creation and expansion, higher profits, greater employment, and increased use of electricity in production. Adoption of electrical appliances follows a clear temporal pattern: lights and mobile phones are adopted immediately; smartphones with internet access spread gradually; and computers are adopted only after eight years, particularly among households with positive savings. These results highlight that measuring the returns to rural electrification requires a long time horizon to capture its full economic effects.

Title: Operational characteristics and CO2 emissions reduction effects of light-duty electric delivery trucks
Authors: Minhao Zhu, Hongjun Liu, Xiqun (Michael) Chen
Abstract: This case study analyzes high-resolution 486-day 131 million records of GPS trajectory data from 417 light-duty electric delivery trucks (LDEDTs) in Wenzhou, China. We extract valid trips from continuous trajectory data by identifying and categorizing LDEDT stops based on speed and dwell time, respectively. We then analyze the operational characteristics of LDEDTs and quantify the reduction effects on CO 2 emissions. Our results indicate a 42.6 %–58.6 % reduction in operational CO 2 emissions when replacing a light-duty gasoline delivery truck with an electric model, depending on the assumed idling behavior. We suggest considering idling control as a complementary measure to electrification, and gradually shifting policy attention toward incentivizing actual operations as a potential direction. Policy implementation should prioritize charging infrastructure planning and electric truck deployment in regions with the most favorable conditions, thereby maximizing environmental benefits. This study provides a foundation for designing targeted policies to decarbonize urban freight.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Blackout risk evolution modeling and intervention scenario simulation for battery electric ships
Authors: Ruoling Zhou, Liu Yang, Ailong Fan, Lei Wang, Chengpeng Wan
Abstract: Battery electric ships (BESs) are increasingly adopted in green shipping, while blackout risks remain a major safety concern. This paper proposes a blackout risk evolution modeling and intervention scenario simulation method. Risk factors are identified through task decomposition in the power system, followed by characterization of temporal risk evolution and propagation pathways through a dynamic Bayesian network. An improved Monte Carlo method with a risk-evolution-driven adaptive sampling mechanism is subsequently applied to multi-scenario intervention simulation. By using dynamic risk evolution to guide adaptive simulation, this method improves the efficient capture of evolving high-risk blackout trajectories under limited samples. Results reveal three blackout evolution stages: latent induction, fault propagation, and out-of-control formation. Risk progresses from early electrical failures to later amplification by emergency-response and environmental factors, potentially causing total blackout and secondary accidents. In the simulated scenario, the integrated intervention reduces blackout risk by 39.93%. The findings support stage-specific and coordinated blackout risk mitigation in BESs.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Policy making with an informed opposition
Authors: Álvaro Delgado-Vega, Wioletta Dziuda, Antoine Loeper
Abstract: We develop a model of electoral competition that captures the dynamic interaction between the incumbent’s policy making and the informed opposition’s response. An incumbent has an opportunity to introduce a reform. If the incumbent introduces the reform, the opposition can either acquiesce to it or promise to repeal it. Parties know whether the reform is partisan or common interest, but the voter does not. The voter observes the parties’ decisions and decides which party to elect for the next period. We show that parties’ platforms converge on the choice that is best for the voter only if common-interest reforms are sufficiently valuable, the incumbent is strongly office motivated, and the opposition is not. When these conditions fail, the opposition commits to policy repeal even when the incumbent’s reform is common interest. Such inefficient repeals induce the incumbent to either forego common-interest reforms (gridlock) or double down on partisan reforms (policy divergence). In the latter case, some common-interest reforms are introduced, but then are subsequently repealed with positive probability, while some of the partisan reforms survive.

Title: Robust equilibria in cheap-talk games with fairly transparent motives
Authors: Jan-Henrik Steg, Elshan Garashli, Michael Greinecker, Christoph Kuzmics
Abstract: For cheap-talk games with a binary state space in which the sender has state-independent preferences, we characterize equilibria that are robust to introducing slight state-dependence on the side of the sender. Not all equilibria are robust, but the sender-optimum is always achieved at some robust equilibrium.

Title: Rational planning and self consistency in decision problems with anticipatory emotions
Authors: Carlo Andreatta
Abstract: Belief-dependent preferences capture psychological motivations such as emotions and image concerns. To manage certain emotions, some agents may prefer not to premeditate their behavior, but to remain undecided and act spontaneously. This raises conceptual and analytical challenges. We show that a rational agent never needs to act spontaneously if, at every history, his decision utility does not depend on what he planned to do at past or counterfactual histories. Decision problems with anticipatory emotions are a common class of psychological games where this property holds. To illustrate, we study the effects of savoring and dread on intertemporal choice. We find that behavior with and without commitment only coincides if the agent’s emotions are very mild or very intense. Dynamic inconsistency arises for an intermediate range of emotional intensity.

Title: Robust optimization for shared utilization of train units in urban metro networks
Authors: Housheng Zhou, Jianguo Qi, Jianian He, Congcong Gong, Chuntian Zhang, Lixing Yang
Abstract: As urban metro networks expand, shared depots offer opportunities to reduce land use and construction costs. However, sharing a common pool of train units creates operational interdependencies among metro lines, while uncertain passenger demand further complicates service frequency and capacity planning. To address these challenges, this study proposes a robust facility-location-based modeling framework for the train-unit shared utilization problem that jointly optimizes train timetables, train compositions, and train-unit distribution among depots in a metro network. To improve the tractability of large-scale instances, three solution approaches are proposed: an equivalent integer programming model solved by commercial solvers, a standard column and constraint generation (C&CG) algorithm, and a progressive version of the C&CG algorithm that accelerates lower-bound improvements. Numerical experiments conducted on empirical data derived from the Xi'an Metro Network demonstrate that the progressive C&CG achieves near-optimal solutions with an optimality gap of 0.5%, outperforming the standard C&CG and the Benders decomposition algorithms. Furthermore, compared with operation using a fixed large train composition mode and no depot sharing, the joint use of the shared-depot strategy and flexible train composition reduces operational cost by 16.9%, the number of deployed train units by 18.2%, and passenger delay by 18.7%. The out-of-sample test further shows that the resulting robust solution remains stable under passenger-demand fluctuations.

Title: Neighborhood mismatch and visits
Authors: Jing Zhi Lim, Lucas Shen

Title: Echoes of hyperinflation: The link between past exposure and formation of expectations
Authors: Y. Emre Akgunduz, Seyit M. Cilasun, Ahmet Deryol, Semih Tumen
Abstract: This paper studies how lifetime inflation exposure shapes individuals’ inflation expectations, perceptions, and financial behavior. Using a large individual-level dataset from Türkiye spanning 2014 to 2024, combined with detailed measures of past inflation experiences, we show that individuals who have lived through higher inflation consistently report higher expected and perceived inflation. They also respond more strongly to current inflation conditions. The effects are larger for less educated and lower income individuals. In additional analysis, we find that greater lifetime inflation exposure is associated with higher use of retail loans, especially fixed rate loans. These results highlight the persistent influence of past economic conditions on expectation formation and household decisions in an emerging economy with a history of volatile inflation.

Title: The impact of fear of automation
Authors: Marta Golin, Christopher Rauh
Abstract: In this paper, we study the causal effect of workers’ perceived probability of job loss due to automation on policy preferences and workplace intentions. Using a representative sample of the U.S. workforce, we elicit individuals’ perceived likelihood of losing their job to robots or artificial intelligence within the next decade. We document strong cross-sectional relationships between automation fear and support for higher taxation, more generous government transfers, union membership, retraining, occupational switching, populist attitudes, and voting intentions. To isolate causality, we implement a randomized information treatment that provides occupation-specific job loss probabilities and generates exogenous belief shocks relative to respondents’ own priors. This design is a reduced-form approach to studying how individuals respond to perceived downside exposure to large-scale technological change. Adverse information increases demand for redistribution and government support programs. In contrast, it has limited effects on intentions to retrain or switch occupations. Treatment effects are primarily driven by individuals who receive worse news than expected. The asymmetric shifts in expressed preferences to negative belief shocks and the absence of parallel effects on closely related individual margins make a simple social-desirability explanation unlikely. By focusing on perceived employment risk as framed in public discourse, the paper highlights collective protection rather than individual adjustment as the primary margin through which workers might respond to automation risk.

Title: Integrated Production, Maintenance, and Quality Control of Unreliable Manufacturing Systems with Dynamic and Imperfect Inspections
Authors: Abdessamad Ait-El-Cadi, Ali Gharbi, Karem Dhouib, Abdelhakim Artiba

Title: Incentives and strategic behaviour: an experiment
Authors: Teresa Esteban-Casanelles, Duarte Gonçalves
Affiliations: King’s College London; University College London
Abstract: Abstract How do incentive levels affect strategic behaviour? We address this with an experiment that separately identifies own- and opponent-incentive effects in two dominance-solvable games that differ in strategic complexity. Higher own incentives favour more strategically sophisticated actions and increase best responding to stated beliefs. Beliefs shift in a parallel direction and participants expect more sophisticated opponent actions. Furthermore, although higher own incentives increase belief accuracy, opponents with higher incentives are harder to predict. Higher incentives also increase response times, and longer response times are associated with better performance and more sophisticated actions and beliefs. Taken together, the evidence suggests that incentives affect strategic behaviour through two main channels: by reducing payoff-dependent mistakes and by increasing the effort devoted to reasoning, with the returns to that effort shaped by strategic complexity of the environment.

Title: Inventory management for perishable products with a two-period shelf life when vendors face oversupply penalties and target the responsible buyers
Authors: Li-Ming Chen

Title: Improving ambulance coverage through the use of alternative return routes during vehicles' repositioning
Authors: Yulia Karpova, Fulgencia Villa, Eva Vallada, José M. Belenguer, Angel Ruiz

Title: Scalable reinforcement learning approach for scheduling customer orders with missing operations

Authors: Wenqing Xiong, Mingyao Li, Chunrong Pan, Siwei Zhang, Liangchao Chen, Cong Liu, Yan Qiao

Authors: Bo Li, Man Mi, Sen Lin

Title: Fixed cost allocation with data envelopment analysis based on lexicographical allocation
Authors: Junkang Li, Yejun Xu, Xiaoying Lai

Title: Testimonials
Time-varying explainable AI for cyber risk management in the financial sector: a Markov switching approach
Authors: Paolo Giudici, Marco Pirra, Rasha Zieni
Abstract: The growing reliance on digital infrastructure has exposed financial institutions to increasingly dynamic cyber risks. As regulatory scrutiny and capital adequacy requirements intensify, there is rising demand for models that are both adaptive and interpretable. This paper proposes a hybrid framework that integrates regime-switching econometrics with explainable machine learning to model cyber attack severity in the financial sector. Using a curated subset of global cyber incidents affecting banks, insurers, and FinTech firms, we estimate two-regime Markov Switching Models (MSMs) with autoregressive components to identify latent regime dynamics in monthly incident intensity. Smoothed regime probabilities are then used to condition event-level classification models, allowing predictive relationships to vary across structural phases. Explainability is achieved through Shapley value analysis, enabling regime-specific interpretation of severity drivers. Empirical results identify a regime transition beginning in early 2023, characterized by increased persistence of high-severity activity and a reweighting of technical and actor-related predictors. The findings demonstrate that integrating econometric regime detection with interpretable machine learning provides a coherent and regime-sensitive framework for cyber risk modeling in regulated financial environments.

Title: Multi-objective disassembly line balancing in closed-loop supply chains: Integrating supplier structure and inventory attributes
Authors: Yan Li, Zeqiang Zhang, Lei Guo, Wei Liang, Yue Han, Dan Ji
Abstract: In the context of green manufacturing and resource recycling, the disassembly industry plays a vital role in closed-loop supply chains. Compared with traditional research focusing on the internal optimization of production lines, studying the disassembly line balancing problem from a closed-loop supply chain perspective has the advantage of cost reduction and efficiency enhancement. This study proposes a multi-objective disassembly line balancing problem that integrates supply structure and inventory attributes (SI-DLBP), and a mixed-integer linear programming model is developed to quantify composite costs arising from supplier concentration, load balancing, and delayed disassembly of high-value parts. Meanwhile, a composite efficiency index evaluation system is constructed based on the analytic hierarchy process to identify the inventory attribute tasks. To address the characteristics of SI-DLBP, the task encoding and decoding mechanism is designed, and an improved multi-objective rime optimization algorithm (IMRIME) is proposed. The model's correctness and the algorithm's effectiveness are validated through a small-scale benchmark instance and comparisons with exact methods. In addition, IMRIME is compared with multiple mainstream metaheuristic algorithms across various problem scales, demonstrating its superiority in solution quality and convergence performance. Finally, an industrial case study involving electric circular saw disassembly indicates that maintaining a relatively low supplier concentration and distinguishing inventory-attribute tasks can contribute to cost reduction. The development of a composite cost function helps the company identify the optimal strategy for its medium-to long-term operations.

Title: Fuel-market reform and structural land-use lock-in in the U.S. Corn Belt
Authors: Elvis Kwame Ofori
Abstract: Biofuel-demand reform can reduce incentives for corn production, but whether it substantially changes an established production geography depends on both county responsiveness and starting specialization. We examine how much corn specialization accumulated during the U.S. Renewable Fuel Standard era would persist if corn-ethanol demand weakened. We develop the Ethanol Spatial Exposure and Agricultural Transition (E-SEAT) framework, a place-based backcasting approach applied to twelve Midwestern states across six Census of Agriculture waves from 1997 to 2022. E-SEAT estimates whether county corn-share trajectories vary with the national ethanol-demand path according to predetermined soil productivity and baseline specialization, then backcasts from observed 2022 conditions by progressively removing the estimated differential component. Higher soil productivity is associated with stronger differential responses, while the negative relationship with baseline specialization is concentrated among the most specialized counties. Because these channels partly offset, dispersion in model-implied adjustment is about 7% of the dispersion in observed 2022 corn share. Complete removal would leave 483 of 990 counties above a diagnostic 20% corn-share reference point and would close 25.5% of the mean starting gap among counties initially above it. Persistence remains under alternative reference points and reversibility assumptions. These results can inform place-based policy design by identifying where a common demand-side reform is likely to produce substantial or limited structural adjustment and where complementary measures to strengthen transition capacity may warrant closer consideration. Accounting for starting specialization, responsiveness, and the spatial distribution of adjustment can improve the targeting and sequencing of interventions while helping policymakers anticipate future transition needs.

Title: Distributionally robust operational planning for mixed charging and decentralized swapping
Authors: Jianzhi Leng, Lun Ran, Chi Xie, Cheng Hua
Abstract: This paper studies operational planning in mixed charging and decentralized swapping systems under uncertainty. We consider a two-stage distributionally robust optimization (DRO) model in which ordering decisions are subject to temporally correlated disruptions, while demand remains stochastic and distributionally ambiguous. To capture this structure, we develop a factorized joint ambiguity set that separately characterizes ordering-disruption uncertainty and demand ambiguity while evaluating their joint impact on operational decisions. Specifically, the disruption process is modeled through a marginal ambiguity set that considers all joint distributions consistent with the prescribed marginal disruption probabilities, thereby hedging against unknown temporal dependence. The associated worst-case disruption distribution is characterized by exploiting the supermodularity of the second-stage value function. Demand uncertainty is modeled via a Gelbrich distance ambiguity set, which captures mean and covariance information and enables a closed-form reformulation of the resulting distributionally robust chance constraints. The proposed model admits a tractable reformulation and can be efficiently solved using standard commercial solvers. Numerical results demonstrate that it provides robust and competitive out-of-sample performance compared with alternative optimization approaches under various uncertainty settings. Further experiments demonstrate the value of coordinating centralized replenishment with on-site charging and show that the proposed model maintains stable performance across different ambiguity and service-level settings. The optimized policies reveal a differentiated station-level structure: stations with larger inventory buffers rely more on-site charging, whereas capacity-constrained stations rely primarily on centralized replenishment. The proposed formulation also remains computationally tractable as the planning horizon and station network expand, providing a favorable balance among operational efficiency, service reliability, and robustness under joint uncertainty.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Dynamic optimization of order assignment and service pricing for urban goods delivery via crowdsourcing with uncertainties
Authors: Chunwei Yang, Andy H.F. Chow, Yang Deng, Zeyu Zhang
Abstract: Crowdsourcing offers urban logistics the potential of reducing operating costs with flexible workforce management through online service platforms. Nevertheless, such practice also introduces reliability issues due to the uncertain availability and willingness of crowdsourced couriers to take up assigned orders. This paper presents a dynamic optimization framework for joint order assignment and service pricing for urban goods delivery with crowdsourcing. The optimization framework is formulated as a Markov decision process which aims to maximize the total profit to be gained by the service platform considering the stochasticity in arrivals of delivery orders and couriers’ willingness to accept assigned orders. The selection of assigned orders by couriers is modeled by a utility based choice model. To cope with the high-dimensional state and decision spaces, the decision process is to be solved by a reinforcement learning based approach in which the state-decision mapping is approximated by an artificial neural network surrogate. The proposed framework is tested over a real-world network scenario constructed from Shenzhen, China. Results show that the optimizer could adaptively coordinate order assignment and service fees in response to the variations in order arrivals and preferences of couriers. The individualized service fees offered to the couriers could enhance the couriers’ acceptance rates and hence increase the platform revenue. The study contributes to urban logistics with use of advanced computational and modeling techniques.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: From fragmentation to coordination: open innovation in closed-loop electric vehicle battery transportation networks
Authors: Aishwarya V. M., Banu Yetkin Ekren, Vedant Singh
Abstract: The rapid growth of electric vehicle adoption is increasing the complexity of integrated closed-loop logistics. Yet, existing electric vehicle battery (EVB) transportation studies largely treat forward distribution, reverse recovery, digital enablement, and governance as separate design problems, leaving facility siting, routing and reverse-flow planning weakly integrated. This study combines a PRISMA-based systematic literature review of 95 peer-reviewed studies with the development of a coordination-embedded optimization architecture for EVB transportation network. The review reveals a clear structural imbalance: only 13.8% of studies embed governance directly, only 10.5% combine high digital embedding with substantive network redesign, and explicit network reconfiguration appears in only 1.1% of cases, while recycling dominates the literature. In response, the study develops the closed-loop innovation coordination problem (CLICP) and embeds governance mechanisms, digital deployment intensity, and circular recovery targets directly into closed-loop transportation network design. Theoretically, the study develops the CLICP as an integrative theory-building construct grounded in coordination theory, transaction cost economics, open innovation, platform ecosystem thinking and transportation network design theory. One overarching and six mechanism-level propositions specify how these established mechanisms may jointly shape closed-loop EVB transportation network design and provide directions for future empirical testing. The framework is analytically illustrated through two configurations: a conventional cost-driven system and a coordination-embedded system. The analytical illustration shows how the coordination-embedded specification can generate a more balanced closed-loop network under the stylized assumptions considered by improving reverse-logistics utilization, strengthening recovery alignment, and enabling more coordinated facility siting, routing and reverse flow allocation. Sensitivity analysis further illustrates how governance intensity and digital deployment influence network performance and adaptive recovery planning under modeled scenarios. The study therefore offers a coordination-embedded analytical perspective for examining closed-loop EVB transportation-network design.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Evolution of token-incentivized information sharing in blockchain-driven circular supply chain networks
Authors: Jia-Ying Zhao, Jingwei Guo, Zhen-Song Chen, YueJun Huang
Abstract: Recovery, remanufacturing, and secondary-resource exchange in circular supply chains require sustained, usable information sharing across firms. Greater traceability and verifiability improve information usability but do not fully address sharing costs or relationship stability. Sustained sharing therefore also requires participation incentives, adaptive adjustment of firm objectives, and relationship stability. Drawing on resource dependence theory and a complex adaptive systems perspective, this study develops an agent-based simulation to examine how blockchain maturity and token incentives shape information sharing among heterogeneous firms. Firms can adaptively adjust the weights assigned to self-interest, same-type collaboration, and cross-type collaboration. Information-sharing ties can dissolve as behavioral differences emerge, while isolated firms can form new ties. The model evaluates overall information coordination separately from network connectivity. Within the calibrated model, blockchain maturity improves the usefulness of shared information, while token incentives support sustained sharing. The two governance channels show positive interactions in both global fitness and network connectivity, although the joint condition does not perform best on every outcome. Adaptive objective weighting raises global fitness but does not consistently improve network structure. Changes in the proportions of closed-loop, open-loop, and hybrid-loop firms have limited effects on overall information coordination but more clearly reshape interfirm relationships. Robustness and sensitivity analyses further show that information coordination and network connectivity have different mechanisms and boundary conditions. Digital governance should therefore jointly address information usability, incentives for sustained sharing, and relationship stability, while evaluating information coordination and network connectivity as distinct outcomes.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Optimal menu pricing strategies for on-demand service platforms
Authors: Melina Asadi, Can Baris Cetin, Georges Zaccour
Abstract: On-demand service platforms such as Uber, DoorDash, and Lyft are increasingly adopting menu-based pricing strategies that combine a pay-per-use option with a premium membership plan. Memberships provide discounted transaction fees and enhanced service quality in exchange for an upfront fee, yet it remains unclear when these strategies are viable and how membership and per-transaction fees should be optimally set. This study develops a profit-maximization model that determines optimal membership fees and per-transaction charges while accounting for customer heterogeneity in service valuation and usage frequency. Users self-select between membership and pay-per-use under fixed discount and quality parameters. The analysis reveals that discount rates and service quality affect market structure in fundamentally different ways. For discounts, we identify a critical threshold: below it, platforms charge higher per-transaction fees than membership fees, resulting in only two customer segments (premium users and non-users) with transaction-based revenues; beyond it, platforms can effectively implement menu pricing with three segments (premium, regular, and non-users) and membership-driven revenues. For quality, the relationship is non-monotonic: moderate quality levels maximize both premium user adoption and platform profitability, while higher quality investments incur provision costs that erode margins and shift market structure toward regular-user dominance. These findings define a narrow viability zone where menu pricing can function effectively. An extension that jointly optimizes pricing and service design reveals that unconstrained platforms abandon menu pricing in favor of quality-based differentiation with per-transaction fees, confirming that menu pricing is a second-best strategy whose value arises precisely when discount and quality levels are externally constrained. The study provides a structured framework for evaluating menu pricing strategies and actionable guidance for platform managers.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: From competitors to frenemies: Strategic third-party service entry in a competitive automotive market under dual-credit regulation
Authors: Ruiying Yuan, Jianan Wang, Shiqiang Yu
Abstract: The dual-credit policy changes automakers’ production incentives and, through the installed base, reshapes demand in the automotive aftermarket. At the same time, independent third-party service providers are entering this market and competing with automakers in paid services. This study develops a game-theoretic model with a fuel vehicle (FV) manufacturer, a new energy vehicle (NEV) manufacturer, and a third-party service provider to examine how dual-credit regulation affects service entry. The results show that, as the third party’s NEV service cost increases, the policy changes the entry threshold from a conventional decreasing pattern into a U-shaped one. This U-shape is driven by a service-reallocation effect. When the NEV service cost is high, the third party shifts service effort away from NEVs. This relaxes service competition for the NEV manufacturer, encourages NEV production for credit revenue, and expands the installed base. Hence, a higher NEV service cost can eventually facilitate entry. Under the policy, the profit effects of entry on the third party, the NEV manufacturer, and the FV manufacturer also follow a three-stage pattern: win-lose-win, win-win-win, and win-win-lose as the NEV service cost increases. The final loss falls on the FV manufacturer because it faces both credit-compliance costs and stronger service competition. These findings show that environmental regulation and after-sales strategy should be considered jointly.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: On the cost-effectiveness of modular transit systems
Authors: Yuhao Liu, Mónica Menéndez, Zhibin Chen
Abstract: Modular autonomous vehicles (MAVs), due to the capability of en-route (de)coupling and in-motion transfer, have caused paradigmatic changes in transit system design and operation. A comprehensive cost-effectiveness analysis is critical for assessing the potential costs and benefits of adopting such a disruptive technology in transit services. In this study, we design an MAV-based transit system consisting of a corridor service complemented by multiple locally operated pick-up-and-delivery routes, thereby leveraging the advantages offered by MAVs while simultaneously taking into account their operational requirements. Based on the proposed MAV-based transit system, we then develop a continuum approximation (CA) model to quantify the system's performance in terms of passenger and agency costs, as well as the intricate relationship between system parameters and operation variables. Comparable CA models for a fixed-route service and an on-demand service based on the same settings are also established. We use the models to analyze the properties of these service modes and uncover the subtle interactions between the system performance and various parameters and variables. Moreover, comparisons between service modes reveal the favorable operation regime for each mode, thereby offering managerial insights and guidance for modular transit system design and operation.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Reliable real-time value at risk estimation via quantile regression forest with conformal calibration
Authors: Du-Yi Wang, Guo Liang, Kun Zhang, Qianwen Zhu
Abstract: Rapidly evolving market conditions call for real-time risk monitoring, but estimating it online remains challenging. In this paper, we study the online estimation of one of the most widely used risk measures, Value at Risk (VaR). Under the offline simulation online application (OSOA) framework, we formulate online VaR estimation as a conditional quantile learning problem with two key requirements: estimation accuracy and coverage reliability. To address the former, we employ quantile regression forests (QRF) to capture nonlinear and high-dimensional relationships between risk factors and conditional VaR. To address the latter, we adapt conformal prediction, conventionally used for prediction intervals, into a one-sided calibration procedure for the VaR estimator. We establish pointwise and 𝐿 2 consistency for the QRF estimator, finite-sample model-free marginal coverage validity for the conformalized estimator, and asymptotic conditional coverage validity. Numerical experiments on a multi-asset option portfolio show that our proposed method becomes particularly competitive as the risk-factor dimension increases, while conformal calibration substantially corrects undercoverage. The proposed estimators also enable fast online prediction, supporting real-time risk monitoring.

Title: Understanding how flooding reshapes travel behavior in coastal communities
Authors: Nafis Fuad, Xiaodong Qian, William Shuster
Abstract: Urban flooding alters travel behavior in coastal communities, yet few studies jointly examine multiple trip purposes, warning channels, and normal–flood mode choice. This study analyzes travel responses to flood scenarios using resident surveys, discrete choice modeling, and elasticity analysis. Overall trip rates declined, with discretionary and educational travel showing the steepest reductions, while essential trips such as work and shopping were largely retained but often delayed. Flooding increases travel times across all trip purposes, with smaller delays for work trips and moderate disruptions for shopping and non-home-based discretionary travel. Mode choice behavior shows reduced driving alone and greater use of carpooling and public transportation. Under normal conditions, travel is shaped by income, vehicle ownership, and employment, but during flooding, flood warnings and temporal flexibility become dominant. Interaction and elasticity results show that information access and adaptability drive resilient mobility decisions, informing adaptive transportation planning.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Economic determinants of cruise-ship operational performance: carbon tax, fuel and onshore-power price
Authors: Guozheng Liu, La Xiang, Congbiao Sui, Yu Ding
Abstract: Given the high hotel loads and complex energy demand of cruise ships, this study develops a voyage-level mixed-integer nonlinear programming model to optimize ship energy management with the objective of minimizing operating cost. The model links economic factors with cruise-specific operational decisions while accounting for life-cycle greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. The effects of carbon tax, fuel price, and onshore power price on ship speed, operating cost, GHG emissions, and the Energy Efficiency Operational Indicator (EEOI) are evaluated under marine gas oil, very low sulfur fuel oil, and liquefied natural gas scenarios. Results show that fuel price is the dominant cost driver. Increasing fuel prices from 70 % to 130 % of their baseline values raises total operating cost by 49.30 %–53.47 % across the three fuel scenarios. Increasing onshore power prices over the same multiplier range raises operating cost by 9.15 %–10.60 %, GHG emissions by 1.44 %–1.68 %, and EEOI by 3.18 %–3.58 %. Onshore power price has a smaller cost effect but produces the strongest average environmental sensitivity among the tested economic factors. Raising the carbon tax from 0 to €150/t GHG increases operating cost by 11.16 %–14.01 %, while reducing GHG emissions by only 0.76 %–1.50 % and EEOI by 1.71 %–3.15 %. Although case-specific and dependent on the selected vessel, itinerary, and economic assumptions, the findings provide support for coordinated carbon tax and onshore power pricing policies in cruise shipping.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Anchoring and cost vector design in discrete choice experiments: Testing rational choice, coherent arbitrariness, and discovered preferences
Authors: Mikołaj Czajkowski, Wojciech Zawadzki, Marek Giergiczny, Wiktor Budziński, Ewa Zawojska
Abstract: : This study tests whether cost-vector design affects welfare estimates from discrete choice experiments (DCEs), and whether repeated choice experience or a pre-DCE open-ended willingness-to-pay (OE WTP) elicitation attenuates that dependence. In a randomized survey of 5,917 Polish adults, respondents valued passive forest protection in Tatra National Park under three cost vectors, two choice-set sizes, and two OE WTP timings. Higher cost vectors consistently produced lower estimated marginal utility of cost and higher WTP. Identical posted prices were also accepted more often in higher-vector contexts, and OE WTP stated after the DCE increased with the vector encountered. Choices became more internally consistent with experience, but WTP still differed across vectors in the last choice tasks. Vector dependence was stable in the two-alternative format and weakened, without disappearing, in the three-alternative format. The pattern survives within-DCE and cross-format consistency exclusions and flexible cost specifications. The evidence rejects context-invariant valuation and shows that greater choice coherence need not imply convergence to context-independent welfare estimates. We recommend multiple cost vectors and pre-specified sensitivity checks in DCE validation.
Journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

Title: The behavioral structure of one-shot cooperation in small and large groups
Authors: Simon Gächter, Diego Marino Fages
Abstract: Cooperation is essential for realizing collective benefits in both small and large groups. In modern societies, many interactions are one-shot and differ in the magnitude of collective benefits. This paper identifies the unified behavioral structure underlying one-shot cooperation. Using online public goods games (N=2,136) and two versions of the strategy method, we examine how attitudes toward cooperation—the causal relationship between one’s own cooperation and others’—and beliefs about others’ cooperation explain cooperative behavior across group sizes (3, 9, and 30) and collective returns (low vs. high). Our ABC framework (Attitudes and Beliefs explain Cooperation) reveals a consistent structure: average attitudes toward cooperation are equally conditionally cooperative across all settings, while beliefs increase with the collective benefit of cooperation but not with group size, although beliefs become more important the larger the group. These results suggest that the ABC framework provides a parsimonious behavioral foundation for understanding one-shot cooperation.

Title: Who pays for clean power? Evidence on public support and solar adoption intentions in Mexico
Authors: Brandon García, Hector H. Sandoval, Hernán Bejarano, Pedro Hancevic
Abstract: This article examines how stated support for renewable electricity financing and stated willingness to adopt residential solar photovoltaic (PV) systems respond to experimentally varied prices, subsidies, and expected bill savings in Mexico, a country with vast solar potential but distorted electricity markets. Using randomized survey experiments, we analyze support for financing utility-scale renewables through electricity bill surcharges and stated responses to alternative residential solar incentive schemes. The results reveal a “green support gap”: support for renewable expansion declines substantially when it is framed as increasing household electricity bills. Regarding residential solar adoption, we find sub-additivity between upfront subsidies and expected bill savings, an effect that is weaker among lower-income households, consistent with the possibility that affordability constraints influence how financial incentives are evaluated. Furthermore, we find that realized bill savings reported by adopters are 152% higher than the expectations reported by non-adopters. This pattern is consistent with pessimistic beliefs regarding private financial returns to solar investment, which act as a key barrier preventing general interest in the technology from translating into near-term adoption choices and realized ownership. Overall, the results provide evidence on how households evaluate alternative financing and incentive frames for clean energy investment in an emerging economy facing fiscal and climate policy trade-offs.

Title: Global demographic change and climate policies
Authors: Reyer Gerlagh, Richard Jaimes, Ali Motavasseli
Abstract: Between 1950 and 2017, world average life expectancy increased from below-50 to above-70, while the fertility rate dropped from 5 to about 2.5. We develop and calibrate an analytic climate-economy model with overlapping generations to study the effect of such demographic change on capital markets and optimal climate policies. Our model replicates findings from the OLG-demography literature, such as a rise in households’ savings, and a declining rate of return to capital. We also find that demographic change raises the social cost of carbon, at 2020, from 28 euro/tCO2 in a model that abstracts from demography, to 94 euro/tCO2 in our calibrated model.

Title: Energy-efficient scheduling of a single resource with production requirements: a joint simulation and scenario-based mathematical programming approach
Authors: Siamak Khayyati, Oktay Karabağ, Berk Berkman, Sebnem Demirtas, Barış Tan

Authors: Hui Li, Naiming Xie, M. Zied Babai, Bo Zeng, Lili Ye
