Title: Forecasting with Hyper-Trees
Authors: Alexander März, Kashif Rasul
Abstract: We introduce Hyper-Trees as a novel framework for modeling time series data using gradient boosted trees. Unlike conventional tree-based approaches that forecast time series directly, Hyper-Trees learn the parameters of a target time series model, such as ARIMA or Exponential Smoothing, as functions of features. These parameters are then used by the target model to generate the final forecasts. Our framework combines the effectiveness of decision trees on tabular data with classical forecasting models, thereby inducing a time series inductive bias into tree-based models. To resolve the scaling limitations of boosted trees when estimating a high-dimensional set of target model parameters, we combine decision trees and neural networks within a unified framework. In this hybrid approach, the trees generate informative representations from the input features, which a shallow network then uses as input to learn the parameters of a time series model. With our research, we explore the effectiveness of Hyper-Trees across a range of forecasting tasks and extend tree-based modeling beyond its conventional use in time series analysis.

Title: Trojan Horse Hunt in deep forecasting models: Insights from the European Space Agency competition
Authors: Krzysztof Kotowski, Ramez Shendy, Jakub Nalepa, Agata Kaczmarek, Dawid Płudowski, Piotr Wilczyński, Artur Janicki, Przemysław Biecek, Ambros Marzetta, Atul Pande, Lalit Chandra Routhu, Swapnil Srivastava, Evridiki Ntagiou
Abstract: Forecasting plays a crucial role in modern safety-critical applications, such as space operations. However, the increasing use of deep forecasting models introduces a new security risk of Trojan horse attacks, carried out by hiding a backdoor in training data or directly in model weights. Once implanted, the backdoor is activated by a specific trigger pattern at test time, causing the model to produce manipulated predictions. We focused on this issue in our Trojan Horse Hunt data science competition, where more than 200 teams faced the task of reconstructing triggers hidden in deep forecasting models for spacecraft telemetry. Here, we describe the novel task formulation, benchmark set, evaluation protocol, and best solutions from the competition. We further summarize key insights and research directions for trigger reconstruction in time series forecasting models. All materials are publicly available on the official competition webpage (www.kaggle.com/competitions/trojan-horse-hunt-in-space).

Title: Anthropogenic sulfur emissions play a large role in historical declines and forecasts for sea ice in the Northern Hemisphere
Authors: Robert K. Kaufmann
Abstract: To investigate why sea ice in the Northern Hemisphere is melting and why process-based climate models underestimate this melting, I estimate a cointegrating vector autoregression (CVAR) model that quantifies long- and short-run relations among anthropogenic and natural forcings, land surface temperatures, sea surface temperatures, and sea ice in the Northern and Southern Hemispheres between 1876 and 2022. The CVAR model links sea ice extent directly to anthropogenic forcing and uses these forcings (especially anthropogenic sulfur emissions) to account for most of the observed reduction in sea ice. Using SSP1-1.9, SSP2-4.5, and SSP5-8.5, the CVAR model forecasts less sea ice melt than process-based climate models. These differences are largely associated with the ways that models simulate the effects of anthropogenic sulfur emissions. The existing focus on September sea ice may be misplaced because innovations in sea ice appear first in December and these innovations are transmitted to September and other months. The importance of December sea ice may be related to high concentrations of SO 2 in December that decline rapidly from one December to the next.

Title: Online‐optimized RAG for tool use and function calling
Authors: Yu Pan, Xiaocheng Li, Hanzhao Wang
Affiliations: Discipline of Business Analytics The University of Sydney Business School Darlington Australia; Independent Researcher
Abstract: Abstract In many applications, retrieval‐augmented generation (RAG) drives tool use and function calling by embedding the (user) queries and matching them to prespecified tool/function descriptions. In this article, we address an embedding misalignment issue that often arises in practical applications due to imperfect embedding models or noisy descriptions; such misalignment may lead to incorrect retrieval and task failure. We introduce Online‐optimized RAG (ORAG), a deployment‐time framework that adapts item embeddings from binary feedback attributed specifically to retrieval correctness. ORAG applies lightweight online gradient updates with negligible per‐query latency and requires no changes to the underlying large language model (LLM). The method supports single‐ and multihop tool use, dynamic tool inventories, and ‐retrieval with reranking. We provide a problem‐dependent theoretical analysis that quantifies how the method's performance depends on the initialization quality of the embeddings and other related quantities. Across diverse tool‐use and document‐retrieval scenarios, ORAG generally improves retrieval and tool‐selection accuracy, providing a simple, practical path toward self‐improving RAG systems. We further evaluate the method under varying query recurrence, feedback‐error patterns, learning‐rate settings, and changing tool inventories to identify the conditions under which online optimization is most appropriate.

Title: Towards integrated Material Flow Control: Dynamic SLAR
Authors: Zhiliang He, Matthias Thürer
Abstract: Delivery adherence is one of the main performance objectives of make-to-order shops in practice. It is realized by manipulating the mean and the dispersion of lateness, thereby shaping the distribution of lateness so that percentage tardy and mean tardiness are reduced. But there is an inherent trade-off, which is balanced by use of different classes in the production planning and control literature. A major means for manipulating the lateness distribution are Material Flow Control (MFC) methods. The most advanced MFC methods use different classes, such as urgent vs non-urgent and pool vs shop floor jobs, but these classes depend on static parameters that do not reflect changes in the distribution of jobs currently in the system. To account for these changes, an MFC method that dynamically determines classes is introduced and evaluated using a discrete event simulation model of a make-to-order pure job shop. Results demonstrate that the new dynamic MFC method outperforms the state-of-the-art. Moreover, the performance realized is robust to parameter settings and the method has low information requirements, which significantly facilitates implementation. A decomposition of performance contributions indicates three different mechanisms by which MFC methods shape lateness distributions. These findings have important implications for the future design of MFC methods and practice.

Title: Merger control and investment: The role of efficiency assessment
Authors: Elisabetta Iossa, Patrick Rey
Abstract: We study how the precision with which merger-specific efficiencies are assessed affects the incentives to invest in such efficiencies before the merger review. With binary investment and an exogenous cutoff, greater precision strengthens investment incentives. We then show how the analysis extends to continuous investment choice and Bayesian approval. A more rigorous merger assessment can therefore encourage efficiency creation.

Title: Women's empowerment and household resilience to climate stressors: evidence from Bangladesh
Authors: Mkupete Jaah Mkupete
Abstract: Empowering women in agriculture is widely promoted as a strategy for reducing gender inequalities and strengthening food-system resilience. Yet whether women's empowerment is associated with greater resilience to climate-induced food insecurity, and whether this relationship varies across climate shocks, remains unclear. Using nationally representative panel data from Bangladesh for 2011, 2015, and 2018, we construct a multidimensional women's empowerment score based on the five domains of the Women's Empowerment in Agriculture Index (WEAI) and examine whether empowerment moderates the associations of drought, excess wetness, and heat stress with household and women's dietary diversity. We estimate OLS, two-way fixed-effects, and correlated random-effects models. Results reveal substantial shock-specific heterogeneity. Higher empowerment significantly attenuates the adverse association of excess wetness with dietary diversity and provides suggestive evidence of attenuation under heat stress, whose adverse association becomes statistically indistinguishable from zero at high empowerment levels. In contrast, the aggregate estimates provide no evidence that empowerment moderates the adverse association of drought with dietary diversity. Season-specific estimates further show significant moderation of heat stress and excess wetness in both Aman and Boro, with heat-stress attenuation stronger during Aman and wetness attenuation somewhat larger during Boro. Drought remains unmoderated in both seasons. Overall, the findings indicate that the buffering role associated with women's empowerment is both shock- and season-specific, highlighting the importance of combining investments in women's agency with complementary structural responses to systemic climate risks.

Title: On ride-sourcing market with bundled service option and passenger’s cancellation behavior
Authors: Zhengfei Zheng, Yuming Ma, Hualing Ren, Yue Bao, Hai Yang
Abstract: The introduction of “bundled services” in ride-sourcing platforms—where riders select an option that allows the platform to strategically assign them to either a solo or a pooled ride based on the shortest expected waiting time—presents novel managerial and operational challenges that remain unaddressed in the literature. A critical problem for platforms employing this model is the need to identify diverse supply-demand scenarios and their corresponding optimal strategies for allocating both demand (those who choose “bundled services”) and supply (available vehicles). Building on our prior research, this study relaxes key assumptions, most notably by incorporating passenger cancellation behavior, a critical determinant of service quality. We propose a new modeling perspective for the bundled service option in ride-sourcing market that explicitly accounts for passengers’ cancellation behavior. First, we develop a model capturing user choice among ride-sourcing services (ride-pooling, solo ride, or bundled services) under market equilibrium conditions. By using a queuing-theoretic framework, we approximate passengers’ average waiting times at a stationary equilibrium and derive the theoretically optimal allocation strategy for bundled-service passengers. Our analysis identifies the optimal strategy assigns all such passengers who choose bundled service option to ride-pooling or to non-pooling services. Second, we analyze a more general scenario in which passenger demand is elastic to trip fare, waiting time, and in-vehicle travel time. We characterize the market equilibrium for this system while explicitly incorporating passenger cancellation behavior. Given the analytical intractability introduced by the endogenous demand and cancellation uncertainty, a full theoretical analysis is infeasible. Consequently, we numerically investigate the impact of demand allocation on both total passenger demand and platform revenue. In summary, the proposed models and our theoretical and numerical findings provide a foundational framework and actionable insights for platforms to optimize bundled-service allocation. The derived strategies guide the optimal assignment of users to ride-pooling or non-pooling options, enabling platforms to strategically balance service quality and revenue.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: A Bayesian spatio–temporal INLA framework for network-wide safety performance functions: Application to Abu Dhabi road networks
Authors: Ammar Aljasmi, Vinayak Dixit, Hamad AlJassmi
Abstract: Rapid urban growth in Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries has increased traffic exposure and crash risk, creating the need for locally calibrated safety models. This study develops a Bayesian spatio-temporal framework to estimate Safety Performance Functions (SPFs) across more than 57,000 road segments in Abu Dhabi. Police-reported injury crashes from 2013–2020 are modelled using a Negative Binomial specification within the INLA framework, incorporating roadway characteristics, exposure measures, continuous spatial dependence, and an annual effect. The results show a clear safety hierarchy: junction links (intersections and roundabouts) experience several times the crash frequency of mid-block segments, which all sit below the network average, while higher traffic volume, free-flow speed, and number of lanes are each associated with elevated crash frequency. The relationship between volume-to-capacity ratio and crash frequency is broadly increasing, with crash risk elevated under denser and over-saturated conditions. The annual effect shows a reduction in 2020 consistent with COVID-19 mobility restrictions. Using a continuous spatial field (SPDE), this study identifies a spatial influence radius of about 2–3 km, a locally calibrated screening reference for corridor bundling and control-site selection that complements, rather than replaces, existing buffer techniques. The framework delivers interpretable, locally calibrated safety parameters that support transparent and cost-effective investment decisions in rapidly motorising metropolitan networks.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Macro-financial impact of stablecoin’s demand for treasuries
Authors: Sang Rae Kim
Abstract: This paper examines how reserve-backed stablecoins influence Treasury markets and financial intermediation. Using high-frequency Ethereum blockchain data matched to intraday returns on the BIL ETF that tracks short-term U.S. Treasuries, I show that large Tether issuances are followed by an increase in BIL prices in the following hour, reflecting a combination of forward-looking market expectations of sustained Treasury demand and Tether's reserve deployment into short-term Treasuries. A complementary daily frequency analysis corroborates this pattern. A quantitative macro-finance model with capital-constrained banks and stablecoin issuers embeds this Treasury demand channel and reveals nonlinear amplification as the sector expands, highlighting how stablecoin growth can reshape safe asset pricing, bank balance sheets, and financial stability.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: Middlemen as an exchange technology in international production networks
Authors: Bernardo S. Blum, Sebastian Claro, Kunal Dasgupta, Ignatius J. Horstmann, Marcos A. Rangel
Abstract: We study the role of middlemen as an exchange technology in international production networks. Using matched transaction-level data between Chilean importers and Argentine exporters, we show that about 40 percent of imported intermediate inputs are brought in by domestic intermediaries rather than final producers. We document three important patterns: (i) even large foreign suppliers trade with few Chilean importers, implying high per-relationship costs; (ii) many suppliers sell both directly and indirectly through middlemen; and (iii) middlemen pay roughly 5 percent lower prices for identical products. These facts motivate a model where trade involves per-customer costs, and intermediation arises to economize on them. The model replicates observed patterns and indicates that removing intermediation reduces productivity by 1.8 percent, corresponding to nearly half the loss from closing the border to trade. Indirect exchange doubles the productivity effects of trade liberalization and lowers industry concentration. Intermediation thus emerges as a key, overlooked driver of efficiency in developing economies.

Title: A novel decision graph model to visualise dominance based if-then decision rules
Authors: Salem Chakhar, Simona Panaro, Salvatore Greco, Alessio Ishizaka, Sajid Siraj
Abstract: When decision makers rely on large sets of if-then decision rules to guide complex choices, information overload quickly becomes a barrier to effective use.The Dominance-based Rough Set Approach (DRSA) is a widely used preference learning method whose primary output is a set of if-then decision rules incorporating preference orders over attributes and decision classes.Although effective for knowledge representation and classification, large rule sets can overwhelm decision makers and hinder interpretation.To address this challenge, this paper proposes a new decision graph model for visualising dominance based if-then decision rules.The construction process begins with a preprocessing phase that extracts a binary decision matrix from rule descriptions.To avoid generating nonexistent rules, this matrix may require transformation through column splitting or a combination of column splitting and ordering-based strategies.The transformed matrix is then used to build a directed acyclic decision graph in which nodes represent elementary conditions and decisions, and edges denote their logical relationships.Each path from the root to a decision node corresponds to a complete decision rule.The paper introduces the core concepts of decision graphs and presents algorithms for their construction, linearisation, and exploitation.Both linearisation and exploitation algorithms are based on the Breadth-First Search graph traversal algorithm.The approach is demonstrated using real-world cultural heritage data from Europe, and expert feedback indicates that decision graphs reduce cognitive effort, improve communication, and provide a clear and accessible complement to traditional textual and tabular representations of decision rules.

Title: AI prediction: Blessing or curse for supply chain disruption?
Authors: Xiaowei Guo, Jingyan Li, Ziming Wang
Abstract: Supply chain disruptions pose substantial risks and challenges to global operations. Although multi-sourcing can help mitigate these risks, firms still face uncertainties arising from disruptions in operational processes. Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) offer transformative opportunities to improve the accuracy of disruption risk prediction. This study examines a two-tier supply chain consisting of one manufacturer and two suppliers: one reliable supplier and one unreliable supplier. We examine the manufacturer's AI adoption strategy and the effects of AI on suppliers’ pricing decisions, the manufacturer's ordering decisions, and supply chain members’ profits. First, we find that AI's effects on pricing and ordering decisions depend on whether disruption risk is underestimated or overestimated and on the magnitude of estimation bias. Notably, AI-enabled correction of a severe underestimation of disruption risk may induce the manufacturer to order more from the unreliable supplier. Second, the manufacturer does not adopt AI when the disruption probability is severely underestimated. Under moderate underestimation, AI is adopted if the reliable supplier's production cost exceeds a threshold. In contrast, when the disruption probability is overestimated, the manufacturer always adopts AI. Third, AI adoption does not necessarily benefit all supply chain members. The manufacturer and the unreliable supplier may benefit from AI under overestimation, whereas the manufacturer and the reliable supplier may benefit under underestimation. We further examine extensions involving information sharing, imperfect AI, the unreliable supplier's awareness that others’ risk assessments are biased, and the manufacturer's biased forecast of AI output, confirming the robustness of our main results.

Title: Energy shocks and the climate transition
Authors: David Comerford, Alessandro Spiganti
Abstract: We present a two-sector growth model in which a representative agent invests in fossil fuel-based energy and renewable energy. These differ in capital intensity and project duration: fossil fuel investments require lower upfront investment and have shorter duration, whereas renewables are more capital-intensive with longer-lived assets. We show that a negative economic shock (such as an energy supply shock or recession) leads to both cuts in total investment and to a shift in the composition of the remaining investment toward fossil fuel projects. This delays the clean energy transition, even if renewable energy is cost-effective on a levelised cost basis, implying a role for policies to sustain clean investment during recessions. We discuss how this mechanism can be amplified by higher interest rates, pro-cyclical climate policies, perceived risk, and financial frictions, and we relate our findings to recent empirical episodes (e.g. the 2022-23 energy crisis and post-2008 recession).
Journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

Title: Recycling, endowments, and market power in exhaustible resource industries
Authors: Weize Lin, Ruwen Tan, Chunxiang Guo

Title: Electricity supply reliability and firm productivity: A dual perspective on spatial reallocation and within-industry differentiation
Authors: Peng Liu, Xunpeng Shi, Jian Yu, Guoqin Zhao
Abstract: Reliable electricity supply is essential for firms to maintain production continuity and efficiency. Using daily newspaper text, we construct a city-level Electricity Supply Reliability Index (ESR) for China and match city-year electricity conditions to firm-level data from the National Tax Survey during 2009–2015. We find that a one-standard-deviation decrease in ESR is associated with an approximately 0.97% decline in firm total factor productivity (TFP). The relationship holds across a range of robustness tests. We further document two dimensions of structural adjustment. First, output and intermediate inputs become relatively more concentrated in cities with more reliable electricity supply. Second, deteriorating ESR is associated with greater within-industry differentiation: a one-standard-deviation decrease in ESR is associated with an approximately 0.16-percentage-point increase in the industry revenue share of firms in the top 10% of the operating-revenue distribution and a 0.003-percentage-point decrease in that of firms in the bottom 10%. Moreover, lower ESR is associated with lower TFP among follower firms, whereas the corresponding estimate for profit-defined industry leaders is statistically insignificant. These findings indicate that unreliable electricity supply is associated not only with lower average productivity but also with differences in the spatial distribution of production and firm performance within industries.

Title: Crafting mixed methods research in Procurement and Supply Chain Management
Authors: Jon Bokrantz, Árni Halldórsson
Abstract: Mixed Methods Research (MMR) appears well-suited to the broad, varied, and socio-technical nature of Supply Chain Management (SCM) research, making MMR increasingly important for advancing SCM as an academic field and empirical profession. Yet, despite its apparent relevance, MMR remains scarce and inconsistently applied in SCM. Prior reviews document low MMR prevalence but offer limited insight into how SCM scholars actually ‘do MMR’. To address this, we conduct an in-depth methodological review of 45 MMR studies in SCM published between 2005 and 2025 in leading journals. We map a diverse set of methodological elements (ways of ‘methodizing’) and theoretical elements (ways of ‘theorizing’). From this mapping, we diagnose a substantial ‘MMR slack’, evident in low explicitness, conventional interview-plus-survey data, and limited meta-inferences that integrate the qualitative and quantitative strands with rich SCM theorizing. We also identify five MMR configurations (‘conceptualize and measure’, ‘build and test’, ‘discover and confirm’, ‘test and elaborate’, and ‘explore and model’) that illustrate the current state of MMR in SCM. Further, we extend the notion of theory-method fit by distinguishing fit as intersection and fit as interaction. We use this distinction to derive two pathways and six guiding principles, together with a checklist of dos and don’ts, that seek to fix the slack through crafting MMR in SCM, i.e., proactively shaping MMR designs to firmly intersect with and interact with the SCM phenomenon under study. Overall, this article offers actionable guidance on when and how scholars can craft MMR studies to produce rigorous and impactful research in SCM.
Journal: Journal of Purchasing and Supply Management

Title: Optimal Control‐Limit Structure of Nonperiodic Inspection and Delayed Replacement Policies for Stochastic Degradation Systems
Authors: Yongchao Liu, Shuguang He, Xiujie Zhao, Zhen He
Affiliations: College of Management and Economics, Tianjin University Tianjin China
Abstract: ABSTRACT For many engineering systems, continuous condition monitoring is often infeasible due to technical and cost constraints, and system condition information is only available at inspection times. Delayed replacement, implemented after a certain waiting time, can help reduce inspection costs. Motivated by this, we study an optimal inspection and maintenance problem aimed at minimizing the long‐run average cost rate, in which system degradation can only be revealed through inspections. At each inspection epoch, the decision maker chooses whether to schedule a nonperiodic inspection, implement a delayed replacement, or perform an immediate replacement to mitigate the risk of failure. By formulating the problem as an average‐cost semi‐Markov decision process, we establish the existence and uniqueness of the optimal average cost rate and characterize an optimal stationary policy. Furthermore, the optimal policy is shown to exhibit a control‐limit structure, under which the optimal waiting times across different actions follow an ordered pattern. Numerical experiments illustrate the theoretical results and demonstrate that the proposed policy consistently outperforms commonly used benchmark strategies. A comprehensive sensitivity analysis further reveals a clear separation of roles: degradation dynamics primarily influence the length of optimal waiting times, whereas cost parameters govern the partition of inspection and replacement action regions.

Title: Forecasting seasonal changepoint models utilizing changepoint uncertainties
Authors: V. Pavlopoulos, R. Killick, E. Can, H. Pham, P. Bhatt
Abstract: Forecasting in the presence of changepoints is a challenging task. However, if changepoints occur regularly across seasons, we want to utilize that information in our predictions for the next season. In this paper, we develop a framework for forecasting seasonal data that contain within-season changepoints. In our forecasts, we account for uncertainty in the changepoint locations both within and across seasons via a weighting approach across changepoint uncertainties. The framework is very flexible across different changepoint model assumptions and approaches to identifying changepoint confidence sets. We demonstrate the improvement in forecasting performance of our framework for atmospheric pressure with a multivariate changepoint approach, and for air pollution ( PM 2.5 ) with a univariate changepoint approach.

Title: The Characterization of Clearing Payments in Financial Networks
Authors: Martijn Ketelaars, Peter Borm, P. Jean-Jacques Herings
Affiliations: Department of Econometrics and Operations Research, Tilburg University, 5000 LE Tilburg, Netherlands
Abstract: The interdependence between agents in financial networks complicates the analysis of clearing payments as the extent to which an agent can pay its creditors depends not only on its own assets but also on the incoming payments from other agents. Each financial network is endowed with agent-specific claims rules that prescribe how each agent pays its creditors. Consequently, our model also allows for general underlying payment mechanisms. A payment matrix that contains clearing payments in accordance with claims rules is a transfer scheme, which is not necessarily uniquely determined. This article is the first to provide the complete characterization of all such transfer schemes. Our characterization relies on additional cash vectors, which summarize the payments in excess of the minimum clearing payments. The set of such vectors is shown to be homeomorphic to the set of transfer schemes. We introduce a recursive procedure to compute any additional cash vector and thereby, indirectly, a corresponding transfer scheme. The characterization opens up the opportunity for a network-based axiomatic analysis of transfer rules. We show that it can be used to provide new axiomatizations of transfer rules in which each agent pays its creditors in accordance with the proportional claims rule. History: This paper has been accepted for the Mathematics of Operations Research Special Issue on Market Design.

Authors: Quoc Tran-Dinh

Title: Can information sharing eliminate greenwashing in supply chains with two-level information asymmetry?
Authors: Shichao Zhu, Yusen Xia, Jian Li, Tsan-Ming Choi
Abstract: Greenwashing may occur at multiple stages of a supply chain, as different participants possess varying levels of knowledge about suppliers (i.e., information asymmetry). This phenomenon is common in practice, yet remains underexplored in the literature. This study investigates how information sharing affects greenwashing behavior in supply chains under two-level information asymmetry, defined as a situation in which the downstream firm has more, though still incomplete, knowledge of the supplier than consumers. First, we propose a game-theoretical framework with two-level information asymmetry to investigate greenwashing behavior in a supply chain without information sharing (i.e., non-sharing). It is shown that both the supplier and the downstream firm are motivated to engage in greenwashing, albeit through different approaches. Next, we examine whether two information sharing formats, discriminatory sharing and universal sharing, can eliminate these greenwashing issues. We find that information sharing among all parties, including consumers (i.e., universal sharing), can completely eliminate greenwashing. However, if information is shared only among supply chain members (i.e., discriminatory sharing), it may exacerbate greenwashing. By comparing different sharing formats, we further find that although universal sharing can completely eliminate greenwashing, it does not emerge as the equilibrium sharing format. Finally, we propose two strategies to address this misalignment and demonstrate their effectiveness, along with the underlying mechanisms.

Title: Logistics service quality selection and digital technology investment decisions of network freight platforms considering installed base effect
Authors: Peng Han, Yanfang Huo, Weihua Liu, Jinghui Lu, Mengyu He
Abstract: Nowadays, network freight platforms serve as critical intermediaries integrating manufacturing and logistics industries. Their sustainable development hinges on the coordinated optimization of logistics service quality selection strategies and digital technology investments. Drawing on platform governance theory and the two-sided market literature, the study develops a two-stage dynamic game model for a monopolistic network freight platform to explore the interplay between these strategic levers, with a particular focus on the trade-off between openness and control and the installed base effect. Our analysis yields several key findings. First, when the quality difference between logistics service providers is small, the installed base effect is strong, and digital technology development costs are low, platforms should adopt a mixed quality selection strategy rather than a pure high-quality strategy to leverage scale advantages and enhance profitability. Second, under mixed quality selection, platforms significantly increase their digital technology investments to mitigate the adverse effects of selecting lower-quality providers, revealing a compensatory role for technology. Third, when the installed base effect is strong and technology development costs are low, the mixed quality selection strategy unexpectedly enables platforms to set higher prices than the high-quality strategy across both stages, effectively transforming network scale into sustained pricing power and maximizing overall profits. Theoretically, the study extends platform governance and platform operations research by jointly endogenizing quality selection, digital technology investment, and dynamic pricing, and by identifying conditions under which openness dominates control. Practically, our findings provide theoretical guidance for network freight platforms navigating the inherent trade-offs among scale, quality, and technology across different developmental stages.

Title: Impact of privacy-preserving horizontal retailer information sharing on the bullwhip effect in supply chains with multiple retailers
Authors: Martin Hrušovský, Emel Arikan, Lena Silbermayr
Abstract: Experiences from real-world supply chains as well as exhaustive research show that the lack of coordination within supply chains leads to bullwhip effect, in which the magnitude of fluctuations in orders increases in the upstream direction from retailer to the supplier. One potential solution for addressing this phenomenon is information sharing between supply chain actors that can reduce the impact of fluctuations in customer demand on the supply chain. However, sharing too much information might lead to higher vulnerability of stakeholders in negotiations with their partners or to an unwanted leakage of information to competitors. Therefore, relevant actors are often reluctant to share the necessary information. To overcome these problems, we propose a horizontal information sharing model where retailers share demand information in form of average values between each other without revealing the exact values of each individual partner. This could be achieved by, e.g., applying costly cryptographic methods. Therefore, we evaluate the potential effects of this type of information sharing on the whole supply chain by developing a simulation model representing a 4-echelon supply chain, which consists of multiple customers, each served by their own retailer, one wholesaler, one manufacturer and one supplier. We investigate the effect of horizontal information sharing of average customer demand among the retailers on the bullwhip effect and show its effects on the different supply chain actors. In addition, the influences of demand variability and demand correlations between customers, different forecasting methods, safety stock approaches, stochastic lead times and the number of retailers sharing the information on the bullwhip effect are analyzed.

Title: When does transparency matter for consumers’ circular decisions? Visibility and traceability in closed-loop supply chains
Authors: Benedetta Baldi, Ivan Russo, Ilenia Confente
Abstract: Markets are increasingly demanding greater supply chain transparency, yet this remains a significant challenge for many companies. Understanding whether and what type of information to disclose represents a significant challenge for companies, particularly when the information pertains to circular initiatives, such as those involved in closed-loop activities. This study, grounded in signaling theory, explores the effect of disclosing closed-loop supply chain information on consumers' intentions. We selected consumers as our unit of analysis for the active role they can play when referring to companies’ closed-loop initiatives, such as purchasing recycled products or participating in take-back programs. To test the hypotheses, two scenario-based experiments are conducted. The primary aim of the studies is to operationalize supply chain transparency through its visibility and traceability components in a closed-loop supply chain context. A second objective is to examine the effectiveness of transparency in closed-loop supply chains, analyzing how the two components influence consumer outcomes across different phases of the customer journey. The findings contribute to the growing literature on supply chain transparency, identifying the boundaries of signaling theory and offering insights for managers on strategic investments in transparency.

Title: Airport ground staff scheduling and task assignment problem with roster regularity and demand uncertainty
Authors: Si Zhang, Bo Sun, Hua Wang
Abstract: Airport ground operators need to publish staff rosters before daily task demand is fully known. They also prefer stable work patterns, since frequent changes in working and rest days may increase staff fatigue and reduce schedule acceptability. At the same time, the roster must leave enough flexibility for assigning day-of tasks under uncertain demand. Motivated by this planning trade-off, this study investigates an integrated staff rostering and task assignment problem for airport ground operations under task demand uncertainty. We formulate the problem as a two-stage stochastic integer program. In the first stage, before demand is realized, the operator selects the active workforce and assigns shifts. In the second stage, after a demand scenario is observed, tasks are assigned to the selected shifts. The model captures both operational feasibility and roster regularity through constraints on consecutive working days, short-connection task handling, and workload fairness. These constraints allow the operator to balance operating cost, assignment flexibility, and stable work patterns in a unified decision framework. To solve the resulting stochastic integer program, we develop a tailored Branch-and-Benders-Cut Decomposition (BBCD) algorithm. The BBCD generates Benders cuts from relaxed second-stage subproblems within a single-tree framework, improves upper bounds through a problem-specific recourse heuristic, and applies a post-processing step to recover exact solutions for promising first-stage solutions. Computational experiments show that the proposed BBCD algorithm obtains the same optimal solutions as Gurobi on small-scale instances where Gurobi proves optimality. For larger instances, the BBCD algorithm remains effective when Gurobi reaches the time limit. The numerical results further show that regularity policies can reduce day-to-day switching fatigue by up to about 83% with only small changes in operating cost. They also help avoid overly long work stretches and lead to a more regular distribution of rest days over time.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: UAV-enabled upstream guidance for freeway incident management: Joint location and scheduling optimization
Authors: Yuqi Shi, Jinhao Liang, Tao Wang, Xiaoguang Yang
Abstract: Adaptive large neighborhood search Rapid and effective upstream guidance is critical for mitigating incident-induced congestion and merge-risk interactions near the bottleneck. However, conventional ground-based variable message signs are often located too far away to provide timely warnings. Moreover, physical channelizing devices such as cones and tapers rely on rescue vehicles for deployment, whose arrival can be delayed by the congestion the incident creates. To address this limitation, this study proposes a UAV-enabled incident management strategy in which unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV) provide temporary and mobile upstream guidance to encourage earlier lane changes. We formulate a simulation-based joint location and scheduling optimization model. The shockwave-informed adaptive large neighborhood search (ALNS) searches guidance locations and service time windows, and a deterministic greedy assignment step allocates UAVs to the proposed tasks to produce a complete executable operating plan. Numerical experiments show that the proposed UAV-enabled strategy reduces average delay by 23.6 % relative to no management and by 15.1 % relative to rescue-vehicle taper management, while lowering the residual queue and the number of merge-risk interaction episodes. Additional algorithmic comparisons further show that the proposed ALNS can obtain better solutions under an equal simulation–evaluation budget.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Roadside unit relocation optimization with auction mechanism design: A multi-stage stochastic bi-level mixed-integer program
Authors: Yining Ren, Zhizhou Wu, Yunyi Liang
Abstract: The development of next-generation transportation systems relies on seamless vehicle–infrastructure cooperation. This study proposes a roadside unit (RSU) relocation optimization framework based on a first-price sealed-bid auction mechanism. The auction mechanism is designed to assign vehicles to execute RSU relocation plans designated by traffic authorities. The problem is formulated as a multi-stage stochastic bi-level mixed-integer program. At each stage, the upper-level model determines the RSU relocation scheme, assigns relocation tasks to vehicles, and allocates vehicles to RSUs for communication. The objective is to minimize expected total cost—including relocation expenses and vehicle-to-RSU communication delays. The lower-level model captures the vehicle bidding process, where each vehicle seeks to maximize profit from winning auctions while minimizing additional travel time incurred by performing relocation tasks. By using the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) transformation, the bi-level model is transformed into an equivalent multi-stage stochastic single-level mixed-integer program. An approximate dynamic programming approach combined with a large neighborhood search algorithm is developed to efficiently obtain high-quality solutions. Numerical experiments show that the proposed model reduces total cost by 20.04% compared to a conventional RSU relocation model without auction mechanisms.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Rural passenger-freight demand-responsive transit with reconfigurable vehicle capacity and 3D loading constraints
Authors: Jiabin Wang, Qipeng Sun, Zhen Shang, Haonan He, Ana Perić, Fei Ma, Simin Wang
Abstract: Integrated passenger–freight transport (IPFT) under demand-responsive transport offers a promising approach to improving rural mobility and logistics efficiency. However, rural passenger demand often exhibits pronounced tidal patterns, while most existing IPFT studies adopt fixed passenger–freight capacity allocation (FCA), leaving substantial seating capacity unused in counter-flow and low-demand periods. Rural freight is also heterogeneous in size and shape, making one-dimensional capacity representations insufficient to ensure physical loading feasibility. To address these issues, this study proposes a reconfigurable vehicle capacity (RVC) mechanism in which the trunk is reserved for freight and seat units can be dynamically converted between passenger and freight use. We formulate the resulting problem as SARP-RVC-3D and develop a problem-tailored ALNS-EP framework. The algorithm feeds three-dimensional loading infeasibility back into the routing search by removing only the freight requests that cannot be accommodated, while preserving feasible passenger services, freight assignments, and route structures for subsequent search. The framework is further enhanced with problem-specific neighbourhood operators and computational acceleration strategies. Computational results show that ALNS-EP closely matches Gurobi on small instances and outperforms GA-EP on medium- and large-scale instances by improving feasibility and achieving an average relative performance gain of 8.58%. The case study further shows that RVC outperforms FCA by dynamically converting temporarily unused seat units into freight space, thereby utilising otherwise idle capacity and increasing freight-carrying capability, with annual operating profit increasing by up to CNY 34,614 and annual vehicle mileage decreasing by up to 14,241 km.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Resilience assessment for China’s crude oil shipping network considering maritime chokepoint disruptions
Authors: Hanwen Fan, Lingye Zhang, Zhenming Wu, Haiying Jia, Zaili Yang
Abstract: Maritime chokepoints face increasing external disruptions from geopolitical conflicts, climate change, and sea accidents, which impose significant risks on global shipping networks and economic prosperity. This study proposes an optimization-based analytical framework to examine the dynamic behavior of network resilience across both disruption and recovery phases. Distinguished from traditional studies that rely on centrality-based indexes to determine critical nodes, the proposed framework identifies worst-case scenario by evaluating specific node failure sequences that induces the maximum resilience performance drop. A dual-optimization framework is then developed to determine the optimal recovery sequence. This framework maximizes the marginal improvement in system performance while explicitly accounting for the node-level recovery priorities. The proposed framework is empirically applied to China’s crude oil shipping network, constructed using voyage records derived from AIS that relevant to crude oil tankers serving China’s import trade. The analysis identifies a non-linear relationship between resilience loss during the recovery stage and the level of alternative capacity of disrupted maritime chokepoints. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that when critical chokepoints are disrupted, re-routing is not necessarily preferable to targeted recovery efforts. Based on these insights, this study provides a strategic decision-support tool for shipping companies to optimize routing designs and it offers a framework for national governments to safeguard energy security by identifying which chokepoints require prioritized diplomatic cooperation and infrastructure investments.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: A distributionally robust optimization model for road–rail intermodal transportation of hazardous materials with product-code conversion under demand uncertainty
Authors: Xunqing Wang, Jiaping Li, Mingliang Ma, Xiaoyu Sun
Abstract: Road–rail intermodal planning for hazardous materials must coordinate hub activation, fixed rail services, tanker availability, and product-code compatibility under uncertain demand. Incompatible residual products require tank cleaning, which consumes capacity and affects access to scheduled departures. We develop a two-stage Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization (WDRO) model with bounded demand support. First-stage decisions commit hubs, services, tankers, cleaning, and schedules; second-stage decisions adjust tonnage flows on the committed structure. Hard-capacity constraints ensure feasibility within the calibrated demand support; demands outside this set are not covered by that guarantee. An exact mixed-integer second-order cone reformulation is solved using Support-Aware Adversarial Cuts Outer Approximation (SAAC-OA) within an augmented ε-constraint procedure. Across the controlled replications, the validation-calibrated model yields mean out-of-sample violation rates of 4.37% and 4.65% for its risk and cost objective bounds, respectively. The corresponding rates under sample average approximation (SAA) are about 48%. These rates measure objective-bound reliability; capacity violations and realized tail risk are assessed separately. Relative to SAA, realized mean and 95th-percentile risks change by −0.2% and +0.1%, respectively. In the enterprise-calibrated Binzhou–Yibin case, the managerial knee reduces worst-case expected risk by 9.44% for a 1.75% increase in worst-case expected cost relative to the cost-minimizing WDRO plan. The results identify when cleaning capacity and rail-service choices affect executability and service quality, and how managers can balance expenditure and risk along the Pareto frontier.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Beyond operations: Realigning the EU’s three main decarbonization policies with a life cycle perspective and their implications on the sustainability of urban logistics
Authors: Thant Zin Aung, Adriana Saraceni, Bart Vos, Diogo Cotta, Nawatch Surinkul, Shabbir H. Gheewala, Trakarn Prapaspongsa
Abstract: Urban logistics is the least efficient mode of freight transport in Europe, and the EU has highlighted the need for more research on urban logistics in EU cities. A comprehensive assessment of sustainability across the urban logistics life cycle is essential yet remains scarce in the current literature. Based on a life cycle sustainability assessment of eight EU cities, the study examines the potential impact of the three main EU decarbonization policies on urban logistics sustainability under different policy scenarios. The results suggest that policies promoting alternative fuels and zero-emission vehicles should not yet be pursued, given current fuel and vehicle production technologies, especially advanced biofuels, which have significant negative impacts in upstream production processes. Of these three policies, the electricity grid decarbonization policy is the most appropriate in the current context. However, policy should be carefully designed to balance the benefits and impacts of the new energy mix to achieve the full potential of electricity grid decarbonization. Overall, in the current technological context, the selected EU decarbonization policies could not achieve significant sustainability benefits without controlling the life cycle impacts of upstream and downstream processes. Therefore, future EU policies on sustainable urban logistics should place greater emphasis on regulating and promoting the sustainability performance of upstream and downstream processes to realize the full potential of decarbonization policies for this sector.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Synchronizing airport check-in and security services through urban air mobility: A preference analysis of air passengers’ choices under time uncertainty
Authors: Ying Zhao, Yan Hu, Tao Feng, Anming Zhang
Abstract: This paper investigates the propensity of air passengers to use Urban Air Mobility (UAM) airport shuttle services that integrate synchronized baggage check-in and security screening traditionally performed at airports. A stated choice experiment was designed, allowing people to choose between conventional airport access modes and UAM shuttle services under varying travel conditions. To account for travel time uncertainty associated with ground access to UAM vertiports, a random parameter hybrid logit model incorporating cumulative prospect theory was estimated. The results indicate that employed individuals and frequent air travelers are more likely to be the early adopters of synchronized passenger services. Passengers traveling with companions, carrying multiple pieces of baggage, or undertaking long-distance trips, also show a stronger preference for UAM airport shuttles. In particular, streamlining baggage check-in and security screening, together with future ride incentives, significantly increase the probability of using UAM airport shuttles. These findings provide valuable insights for operators and policymakers seeking to design passenger-centered UAM airport shuttle services and enhance integration with existing air transport systems.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Incentive-based strategies for road–waterway city logistics: A single-leader multi-follower game-theoretic framework
Authors: Mingye Luan, Bilge Atasoy
Abstract: Urban freight transportation contributes substantially to congestion, pollution, and operational inefficiencies, particularly in dense urban areas where delivery activities remain strongly dependent on road transport. To address these impacts, policymakers are increasingly exploring incentive-based mechanisms that promote modal shifts toward alternative freight services within multimodal city logistics systems, while this study focuses specifically on the shift from road delivery to inland waterway transport. The effectiveness of such policies critically depends on the strategic interactions among multiple stakeholders. We therefore propose a single-leader multi-follower game-theoretic framework involving a transportation authority, logistics service providers (LSPs), and end customers. The transportation authority acts as the leader and designs the waterway subsidy policy to promote road-to-waterway modal shift under fiscal constraints. The LSPs act as followers and maximize their own profits by determining service prices and road–waterway delivery allocations. Customer demand is modeled endogenously through a discrete choice model, and the joint response of the LSPs is characterized by a generalized Nash equilibrium. Finally, three implementation strategies for deploying road-to-waterway modal-shift policies are examined and compared in a case study of Amsterdam, providing insights into their relative efficiency and practical implications.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Corporate social responsibility incentives in supply chains under pricing authority: The role of reverse factoring
Authors: Franck Moraux, Dinh Anh Phan, Thi Le Hoa Vo, Ahmad Jafarian
Abstract: Reverse factoring is a buyer-led supply chain finance mechanism that can alleviate the financial constraints faced by small and medium-sized suppliers and improve their capacity to invest in corporate social responsibility (CSR). However, improved access to financing does not necessarily translate into CSR investment, because the supplier’s incentive also depends on the allocation of wholesale-pricing authority and its ability to retain the returns generated by CSR. We develop an analytical model of a two-tier supply chain under demand uncertainty that integrates reverse factoring, endogenous wholesale pricing, order quantity, and supplier CSR effort. We compare two pricing structures: supplier-led pricing, in which the supplier determines the wholesale price and CSR effort, and retailer-led pricing, in which the retailer sets the wholesale price before the supplier chooses CSR effort. The results show that reverse factoring reduces financing-inclusive production and CSR costs, thereby improving the financial feasibility of CSR investment. Nevertheless, positive CSR effort depends on threshold conditions involving CSR effectiveness, CSR cost, production cost, and supplier margin. Supplier-led pricing generally supports CSR investment over a wider parameter region and induces higher CSR effort because the supplier can retain a larger share of the demand-enhancing value CSR generates. Under retailer-led pricing, wholesale-price compression may offset the financing benefit and reduce or eliminate the supplier’s incentive to invest. These findings demonstrate that the sustainability impact of reverse factoring depends on its interaction with pricing authority and surplus allocation. Managers should therefore coordinate financing arrangements with wholesale-pricing policies that preserve sufficient supplier incentives while maintaining overall supply chain performance.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Robust estimation of percentile travel time for transport networks using L-moments under data limitations
Authors: Ruiya Chen, Jiaoyu Liu, Xiangdong Xu, Tien-Der Han, Mingwei He
Abstract: Accurate percentile travel time (PTT) estimation is fundamental to travel time reliability (TTR) assessment, but is challenging when observations are limited, contaminated by extreme values, or heterogeneous. This study develops an L-moments-based normal polynomial transformation (LMNPT) framework for analytical PTT estimation without assuming a predefined parametric distribution. By replacing higher-order central-moment descriptors with L-moment-based characteristics, LMNPT is designed to improve robustness under data-limited conditions. Analytical monotonicity conditions define the LMNPT validity domain, covering approximately 22.72 % of the theoretically feasible L-skewness–L-kurtosis parameter space. LMNPT is evaluated against the Cornish–Fisher (CF) expansion and Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) using six theoretical distributions and empirical expressway travel-time data. Results show that LMNPT generally provides higher structural validity and greater robustness than CF under small-sample and contaminated conditions, although CF remains competitive in some settings. KDE achieves high accuracy when sufficient empirical observations are available, whereas LMNPT performs more favorably under the examined small-sample resampling conditions. Sensitivity analysis across 15-, 30-, and 60-minute windows shows broadly stable comparative patterns. Downstream analysis further indicates that PTT-estimation differences propagate differently across PTT-based TTR measures. These findings support LMNPT as an analytical PTT-estimation approach under data-limited and heterogeneous travel-time conditions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: A hierarchical generative adversarial network for traffic flow uncertainty modeling and anomalous state identification
Authors: Feng Shao, Duanduan Dong, Hu Shao, Xin Bruce Wu, William H.K. Lam
Abstract: Modeling traffic uncertainty is important for characterizing traffic variability under stochastic and non-recurrent conditions and provides a probabilistic basis for identifying unusual traffic states. This paper proposes a graph attention Transformer–Wasserstein generative adversarial network (GAT-WGAN) for hierarchical traffic flow distribution (TFD) estimation across links, point-of-interest (POI)-connected nodes, and regions. The framework is organized as a layered computational graph (CG), in which generated link flows are propagated to POI-connected nodes and regions through predefined link-to-node and node-to-region aggregation relationships. The resulting higher-layer flows are evaluated against observations or references at their corresponding layers during training, allowing TFDs at different spatial levels to be learned within a connected hierarchy rather than independently. Graph attention (GA) and high-order graph attention (HGA)-masked Transformer mechanisms are further incorporated to characterize topology-defined spatial dependencies, while temporal conditions are included in the generative learning process to distinguish TFDs under different traffic contexts. Based on the estimated conditional TFDs, a two-sided threshold-based screening mechanism is developed to identify potential anomalous traffic states by evaluating unusually low or high observations relative to their corresponding reference distributions. The framework is evaluated using data from the Caltrans Performance Measurement System (PeMS). Under the third-order graph setting, GAT-WGAN achieves a Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD) of 0.103 and a Wasserstein distance (WD) of 108.202 at the link layer, with JSD values of 0.083 and 0.066 at the POI-connected node and region layers, respectively. External comparison with California Highway Patrol (CHP) and Lane Closure System (LCS) records shows that, at the largest tested anomaly identification score (AIS) threshold, the identified anomalous states cover 71.5% of CHP records and 71.7% of LCS records, indicating a measurable correspondence between the identified anomalous traffic states and independently recorded real-world incidents.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Understanding the mechanism of gap-acceptance behavior at roundabouts: A cumulative prospect theory and drift-diffusion model framework
Authors: Congcong Bai, Cheng Xu, Donglei Rong, Xi Gao, Jiaqi Zeng, Meng Liu, Meng Sun, Xiangyu Li, Sheng Jin, Wenbin Yao
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: A deep reinforcement learning-based algorithm for regional drone routing problem with nonlinear fuel consumption
Authors: Yanfang Ma, Zheng He, Rui Qiu, Yu Gong
Abstract: With the boom of e-commerce and increasing policy support, regional logistics serving medium- and short-distance transportation have grown rapidly. Large fuel-powered drones are increasingly adopted in this field due to their flexibility and efficiency, yet their deployment has raised concerns regarding pollutant emissions and environmental sustainability. To balance logistics efficiency with environmental responsibility, this paper proposes a regional drone routing problem using large fuel-powered drones, accounting for nonlinear fuel consumption and multiple pollutant emissions. The problem is formulated as a mixed-integer nonlinear programming model to minimize the total cost, including fuel consumption cost, pollutant emission cost, and operational cost. To accurately estimate fuel consumption, a nonlinear fuel consumption function is formulated by comprehensively considering variable payload, fluctuating fuel load, empty weight, the entire flight process, and wind. A deep reinforcement learning-based algorithm, namely a double-deep Q-network with attention mechanism based large neighborhood search algorithm, is designed to solve the model. The effectiveness of the algorithm and the nonlinear fuel consumption function is validated by comparative experiments on simulated instances, and then the impacts of refueling availability and wind conditions on the total cost are further investigated. Furthermore, based on a real-world case, this paper shows that drones can reduce the total cost, while sensitivity analyses evaluate the impact of key factors on environmental and economic performance. The results indicate that the proposed model and algorithm can effectively enhance operational efficiency and environmental performance.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Topology-aware preconditioning for UAV logistics infrastructure and distributed swarm scheduling
Authors: Haoze Gu, Zhixin Qi, Yunfei Gao, Zejiao Dong, Abaho G. Gershome
Abstract: Abstract In large-scale UAV logistics systems, distributed scheduling has emerged as a key approach to overcoming the scalability limitations of centralized architectures. However, existing studies primarily focus on improving optimization algorithms, while largely overlooking the fundamental constraints imposed by the underlying communication topology. In real urban environments, heterogeneous spatial distributions often lead to poorly connected networks, which in turn become a critical bottleneck limiting distributed coordination efficiency.This paper investigates how communication topology shapes distributed scheduling performance from the perspective of coupling transportation infrastructure and information interaction. Building upon algebraic graph theory and distributed optimization, we establish a quantitative relationship between network connectivity and the convergence rate of cooperative errors, and show that, under construction cost constraints, system performance is subject to an inherent structural upper bound. To address this limitation, we propose a topology optimization method that enhances connectivity under realistic spatial constraints, and further develop a topology-aware distributed scheduling framework that enables joint design of infrastructure and coordination mechanisms.Experiments based on real-world logistics networks demonstrate that modest topology enhancements can accelerate system convergence and reduce scheduling delays under high-load conditions. Ablation studies further confirm that network connectivity plays a key role in determining overall system performance.Overall, this work reveals the mechanism linking transportation infrastructure topology to distributed coordination efficiency, and provides a principled approach to upgrading infrastructure from passive physical assets to active computational topology resources, offering theoretical support for the integration of computing and networking in future intelligent transportation systems.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Attention-based deep reinforcement learning approach for dynamic truck-drone routing with stochastic requests
Authors: Ruixue Gu, Yang Liu, Yining Ma
Abstract: Inspired by the rapid rise in demand for sustainable and cost-effective logistics services in urban areas, we introduce a dynamic truck-drone routing problem with uncertain pickup and delivery requests, aiming to optimize the total expected profits for service providers. However, the process of dynamic decision-making, including request selection, assignment, and route construction, is complex. Especially, the uncertainties, such as request time, locations, service types, deadlines, and practical constraints, such as maximum working hours, drone capacity, and endurance, pose a significant challenge in modeling and solving the problem. To address this challenge, we propose a hierarchical Markov decision process (HMDP) to formulate the problem that separates dispatch timing from route construction. The interactions between the external environment and the two levels of HMDP effectively capture the uncertainties and dynamics. Based on this formulation, we develop an attention-based deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approach with a feature extractor, self-attention module, and invalid-action mask. The policy is trained with a proximal policy optimization procedure and is applied online to select requests, assign them to the truck or drone, and construct feasible routes. Ablation analyses show the benefit of the hierarchical decision framework and the feasibility-preserving role of invalid-action masking. Comparative experiments show higher mean objective values than the basic heuristic and DRL benchmarks across the tested settings, together with substantially shorter running times than the basic heuristics. Relative to the DRL benchmarks, the approach offers improved solution quality with comparable running times. We also examine one-truck with multi-drone extensions to demonstrate the generality of the HMDP framework. Additional analyses show that our proposed DRL maintains the gap between objective values obtained in uncertain and partially uncertain scenarios below 10%. Compared to the deterministic scenarios, the gap remains below 20%. Finally, based on the experimental results, we provide insights for decision-makers to increase profits. The insights include appropriately balancing the ratio of pickup and delivery services and adjusting drone speed in relation to truck speed.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: A real-time transit signal priority control method based on stochastic shockwave profile model for multi-line bus systems
Authors: Pengjie Liu, Yanzhan Chen, Ruiguang Liu, Fan Yu, Weihua Gan
Abstract: Transit signal priority (TSP) has been widely studied to reduce bus delays at intersections and improve bus service quality. However, many existing TSP methods face challenges in real-world applications, particularly in addressing multiple priority requests from conflicting buses and mitigating negative impacts on the priority of private vehicles under traffic uncertainties. To overcome these challenges, this study proposes a novel real-time TSP control method for a single intersection based on the stochastic shockwave profile model (SSPM). Specifically, the SSPM uses a shockwave profile diagram to describe the queuing and dissipation processes of vehicles around a signalized intersection under stochastic traffic arrivals. Based on this, critical bus trajectories under three typical scenarios can be analyzed, which then contribute to deriving the probability of each conflicting bus passing through the intersection in the current cycle. On the other hand, the quantile value about the stochastic total delay of all private vehicles around the intersection in the current cycle can also be calculated at a pre-set quantile. Finally, a real-time TSP mathematical programming model is constructed and solved to maximize the sum of the passing probabilities weighted by the on-board passenger number and the schedule deviation for conflicting buses and minimize the quantile value about the total delay of all private vehicles at a pre-set quantile. A series of simulation experiments conducted on six bi-directional bus lines in Changsha, China, shows that the proposed real-time TSP control method is superior to the uncontrolled scenario and the comparative method in reducing bus stop numbers and delays at intersections, as well as decreasing passenger waiting and travel times, while remaining robust in the face of traffic uncertainties.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Optimization approaches for a fair multi-source capacitated facility location problem
Authors: Carlo Filippi, Gianfranco Guastaroba, Juan-José Salazar-González
Abstract: We incorporate a fairness measure, known as the conditional β -mean in location theory, into the Multi-Source Capacitated Facility Location Problem (MSCFLP). The conditional β -mean measures the average distance traveled by the (100 · β )% of demand units that face the longest travel distances to a facility. Minimizing the conditional β -mean results in a less conservative and more flexible approach than a standard maximum distance minimization. We term the resulting problem the Fair MSCFLP, and we develop five mathematical formulations to model it: two bilevel models, one bilinear model, and two Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) formulations. We also devise two matheuristics: a Variable MILP Neighborhood Descent ( VMND ) algorithm, and a ternary search-based approach ( Ternary ). Extensive computational experiments conducted on benchmark data sets for the MSCFLP, consisting of up to 1000 facilities and 1000 customers, show that an off-the-shelf solver can solve, in reasonable computing times, only small instances. Both matheuristics found the optimal solution to each small instance within a few seconds. The experimental analysis indicates that no matheuristic outperforms the other across all instances: depending on the size, one matheuristic generally outperforms the other when run with a time limit. Ternary usually outperforms VMND solving instances that comprise up to 500 facilities and 500 customers, whereas VMND produces solutions of considerably better quality on larger instances.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Energy-efficient coordination of mixed truck platoons using multi-agent reinforcement learning
Authors: Dan Wang, Gangyan Xu, Zhizhou Wu, Junqiang Leng
Abstract: Energy-efficient truck platooning is an important pathway toward lower-carbon freight transport, yet practical deployment will likely proceed through mixed platoons in which automated trucks operate alongside human-driven trucks. An energy-efficient decentralized multi-agent reinforcement learning framework is developed for coordinating such mixed truck platoons under human-driving uncertainty. The framework integrates freight-truck propulsion energy into the coordination objective, allowing energy reduction to be considered with stable spacing control, speed regulation, smooth motion, and safety preservation. To support cooperation in mixed platoons, a heterogeneity-aware quantized V2V communication scheme is introduced, where cooperative information exchange is organized among connected automated trucks while human-driven trucks remain part of the physical platoon dynamics. Numerical experiments are conducted in catch-up and slowdown scenarios that represent coordination recovery and speed-disturbance response in freight operations. The evaluation further examines how performance changes with automation penetration, automated-truck placement, human-driving behavior, and reaction delay. Results show that the proposed framework improves mixed-platoon coordination and reduces average platoon power with reductions of approximately 20.7% and 20.5% in the two scenarios. The uncertainty analysis indicates that fleet composition, vehicle placement, and human-response quality all shape the operational benefits of mixed platooning, providing guidance for staged automation deployment and mixed-platoon organization.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: A structured hub-corridor framework for socioeconomic performance assessment: A group fuzzy BWM approach with empirical validation in China
Authors: Liwei Duan, Zhenlang Tang, Xiyu Wang, Jian Chen, Qingru Zou
Abstract: Understanding the socioeconomic performance of transport hubs and corridors is essential for designing resilient transportation systems and effective regional development policies. Existing assessments, however, often focus on isolated infrastructure components or rely on weakly validated indicators. This study develops a hub-corridor evaluation framework that links transportation structure with regional economic dynamics and household income. Indicator weights are derived using the Type-1 Fuzzy Best-Worst Method with triangular fuzzy numbers. A panel of 12 experts provides individual pairwise comparisons. Each expert independently identifies their best and worst indicators. Individual consistency is verified through the Fuzzy Consistency Ratio with a feedback revision cycle ensuring R(FCR) ≤ 0.1. Individual fuzzy weights are aggregated using the weighted geometric mean, and a Group Consensus Index diagnoses the level of expert agreement. The framework is empirically applied to four transport hubs in China's Chengdu-Chongqing urban agglomeration. The ranking places Hub 1 first, followed by Hub 2, Hub 3, and Hub 4. Notably, Hub 1 outperforms the physically larger Hub 2 due to its balanced strengths in household transport affordability and spatial efficiency. Monte Carlo simulations with 1,000 weight perturbations confirm a completely stable ranking. The analysis reveals three resilience profiles: balanced hubs achieving synergies across multiple dimensions, economic-driven hubs generating strong agglomeration benefits but facing socio-ecological vulnerabilities, and latent hubs with infrastructure capacity underutilized by weak regional demand. Socioeconomic resilience depends less on transport scale than on alignment between hub capacity, corridor operation, and regional economic structure. These findings offer actionable guidance for policymakers to diagnose structural mismatches and prioritize resilience-enhancing investments. From a policy perspective, the proposed framework provides a transparent and replicable tool for identifying vulnerabilities and supporting context-sensitive strategies in rapidly urbanizing regions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: A note on Lagrangian underestimate cuts and domain reduction techniques for integer programs
Authors: Jixuan Feng, Jun Xia, Silong Zhang, Zhou Xu
Abstract: Integer programming formulations for combinatorial optimization problems, such as the vehicle routing problem, face significant computational challenges due to the exponential growth of the solution space. To address this, cuts and domain reduction techniques are commonly employed to reduce the search area. In this paper, we introduce Lagrangian underestimate cuts (LUCs), a novel class of optimality cuts, for integer programs. We demonstrate that LUCs can be utilized to strengthen reduced cost cuts and to derive new domain reduction techniques. Moreover, we leverage LUCs to develop new arc fixing techniques for the vehicle routing problem, based on Lagrangian duals and the tailored dual-picking strategy.

Title: Learning-oriented approach for integrated charging load prediction and mobile charging station scheduling
Authors: Ming Liu, Lutian Wang, Lihua Sun, Feifeng Zheng
Abstract: The mobile charging station (MCS) is an innovative solution for electric vehicle (EV) charging, serving as a complementary service to address the overloads at fixed charging stations (FCS). MCS scheduling is driven by EV charging demand, which exhibits spatiotemporal uncertainty. As FCS load data reflects aggregated EV charging demand patterns across time and space, data-driven load prediction can guide the strategic deployment of MCSs. However, there is no study that incorporates FCS load prediction into MCS scheduling to enable proactive and efficient decision-making. This work develops a closed-loop framework that integrates AI-driven charging load prediction at FCSs with the scheduling of heterogeneous MCSs. Within this framework, the optimal prediction model parameters are determined based on an application-specific cost function. We structure the approach as a bi-level optimization. A hybrid heuristic combining Genetic Algorithm (GA) and Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES) is designed to efficiently solve the problem in large-scale settings. Experiments on randomly generated instances of varying scales, together with a sensitivity analysis on key parameters, demonstrate the robustness and scalability of the proposed framework. Further evaluation on a real-world FCS charging load dataset from Shenzhen shows that our proposed approach outperforms benchmark methods, including the open-loop predict-then-optimize approach and an alternative gradient-free ILO baseline, on the prediction-scheduling task for MCSs.

Title: Exact and heuristic approaches for the pricing in competitive markets with unrestricted supply problem
Authors: Heloisa Reis Leal, David Sotelo, Yuri Frota
Abstract: This study addresses the problem of simultaneous price adjustments across multiple points of sale operated by the same commercial agent, with the objective of maximizing overall profit in a competitive market environment. The setting considered involves rival points of sale with predetermined prices and a consumer base whose demand levels are known in advance and assumed to be inelastic with respect to price variations. Furthermore, it is assumed that the agent’s points of sale have unlimited supply of the product in question. Within this framework, we formulate the problem mathematically as a bi-level programming model and subsequently reformulate it as a single-level mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model. We establish that the problem is NP-hard and propose a heuristic solution method based on the Iterated Local Search (ILS) metaheuristic.
