The performance of the proposed approach is assessed through computational experiments, in which the results are compared against exact solutions and a stochastic baseline, using test instances inspired by the gasoline sales market of Petrobras, the leading company in Brazil’s oil and gas sector. The computational results show that the proposed ILS consistently outperforms the stochastic baseline and provides high-quality solutions for large-scale instances in which the exact method struggles to prove optimality within the time limit. From a managerial perspective, the model can support tactical pricing decisions by estimating how price changes, logistics costs, and competitor prices affect consumer allocation and expected profit.

Title: Operational drivers of fuel performance in Ro–Ro shipping
Authors: Emilie d.L.K. Caspersen, Frederik H. Berthelsen, Ulrik D. Nielsen
Abstract: This study investigates operational drivers of fuel performance in maritime transport using 22 months of high-resolution sensor data from two Ro-Ro sister vessels. A hybrid benchmark model is developed to derive a speed-and draught-independent performance indicator, enabling consistent evaluation of efficiency and environmental impact. Results show that fuel performance is primarily governed by physical operating conditions, while hull condition and human factors are associated with variability in observed performance. Hull degradation leads to efficiency losses through increased resistance and associated operational responses, with implications for fuel consumption and emissions. Variability related to captains and crews are explained by how operating conditions are selected and managed rather than by intrinsic performance differences. A machine learning-based decision support pilot showed a 1.9 percentage-point improvement in fuel performance and reduced variability across operators. Overall, the findings demonstrate how maintenance, operational decisions, and data-driven tools can enhance transport efficiency and support maritime decarbonisation.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: The environmental cost of place-based industrial policy: Evidence from industrial zones in Vietnam
Authors: Trinh Pham
Abstract: Special economic zones are widely adopted across countries to boost growth, yet their environmental cost is far less well documented. This paper examines the local air pollution footprint of a zone program in Vietnam, which has opened more than 300 industrial zones over three decades. Exploiting their staggered establishment, I first show that a zone’s operation increases satellite-detected industrial combustion within a 5 km radius more than twofold. Firm-level data show that this rise accompanies the entry of large and high-output plants, which are likely the baseline foundation of a zone’s environmental footprint. Using wind-driven variation in downwind exposure, I find that the zones also raise PM2.5 exposure in the surrounding population by an average of 0.70 µ g/m3, a 25-day loss of life expectancy per exposed person. This effect differs substantially between zones of the same age established in different periods. The zones with the larger effect host a heavier mix of industries, and that mix changed little as the zones filled. Under weak enforcement of standards on operating firms, the composition of admitted industries therefore likely plays a decisive role in explaining these differences. A back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests that the implied health cost can be as high as the program’s local income gains for the average resident.
Journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

Title: Threshold Bayesian local projections for fiscal policy analysis
Authors: Giuseppe F. Amalfitano, Marco Lorusso, Luca Pieroni
Abstract: We develop a threshold Bayesian local-projection framework in order to estimate the macroeconomic effects of government-spending shocks across states of the economy. Our nonlinear specification allows impulse responses and fiscal multipliers to vary across regimes. We compare regime-specific and common contemporaneous impact matrices in order to distinguish state dependence in dynamic propagation from state dependence in contemporaneous shock transmission. Our results closely reproduce those obtained by Ramey and Zubairy (2018). Moreover, we show that state-dependent multipliers are sensitive to shock identification strategies, sample lengths, instrument relevance, and the available information across regimes.

Title: Pass-through with endogenous quality: An incentive decomposition
Authors: Naoshi Doi, Tetsuya Shinkai
Abstract: A cost increase can lower the price (a negative pass-through rate) or raise quality when both price and quality are endogenous. We show that the associated incentive changes decompose symmetrically into a quantity effect and a sensitivity ratio effect. The quantity effect, which depends directly on first-order demand derivatives, always pushes price and quality downward. The sensitivity ratio effect depends on second-order derivatives and can go either way. The decomposition clarifies how the demand functional form shapes pass-through and quality responses.

Title: Beyond exact match: A product-space measure of trade similarity
Authors: Charlie Joyez
Abstract: A broad class of trade-overlap measures---the similarity indices of Michaely, Aquino, Finger--Kreinin and Linnemann--van Beers, and the Grubel--Lloyd index---are the same transform [[EQUATION]] of a Jaccard coefficient, taken of trade shares or of values. Their minimum-over-matched-categories core makes them blind to cross-category relatedness and sensitive to product aggregation; cosine similarity shares the latter defect. We propose a product-space cosine index of trade proximity,[[EQUATION]], with [[EQUATION]] encoding product relatedness. It credits related cross-category overlap and is five to seven times more stable across 2-, 4- and 6-digit classifications, extending to capability similarity, structural transformation, and distance to the frontier.

Title: Adaptation through experience or description? Evidence from an experiment on efficient coding
Authors: Cary Frydman, Lawrence J. Jin
Abstract: The principle of efficient coding implies that the perception of monetary payoffs is shaped by the decision maker’s prior beliefs. Specifically, payoffs that the decision maker expects to encounter more frequently should be perceived more accurately. Most previous tests of efficient coding rely on the decision maker’s experience to shape the prior. We conduct a pre-registered experiment to test whether descriptive information about the prior affects behavior in a manner consistent with efficient coding. We randomize whether participants receive this information at the start of the experiment. We find strong evidence of efficient coding, which replicates earlier work using a similar experimental design. However, we detect only a minimal effect of information provision on behavior. Our results are consistent with the hypothesis that experience quickly crowds out any effect of descriptive information on the optimal allocation of coding resources.

Title: Learning Optimal Reprocessing Policies for Degradable Inventory Systems: A Multi‐Armed Bandit Approach
Authors: Haiqi Shi
Affiliations: Antai College of Economics and Management Shanghai Jiao Tong University Shanghai China
Abstract: ABSTRACT In this paper, we study the problem of online learning for a threshold‐based inventory control policy in degradable inventory systems with reprocessing capabilities, where the demand is unknown but independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) across periods. A key feature of our model is that degraded items can be held as inventory rather than being immediately salvaged or reprocessed, providing additional flexibility in operational decisions. Unlike traditional models that assume prior knowledge of the demand distribution, we develop an adaptive learning algorithm to determine the optimal reprocessing and production decisions without such information. Our analysis is motivated by medical supply chains where products like oxygen cylinders degrade over time but can be reprocessed through sterilization and refilling. The model incorporates key operational features including: (1) discrete quality degradation of inventory over periods, (2) the option to hold degraded items in inventory before reprocessing, and (3) the trade‐off between production, reprocessing, and inventory holding costs. Through a novel notion of generalized multi‐modularity tailored to our state‐action structure, we establish the optimality of a state‐dependent threshold policy with state‐independent threshold parameters, governing both reprocessing and production decisions. When demand is unknown a priori, we propose an online learning algorithm and prove that the algorithm achieves a cumulative regret of . This work contributes to both production‐inventory coordination and online learning literature by providing: (1) structural analysis using a generalized multi‐modularity framework to characterize the optimal policy in the setting with known demand, (2) the first learning‐theoretic framework for reprocessable and degradable inventory systems where degraded items can be strategically held before reprocessing, and (3) theoretical performance guarantees through regret analysis. The methodology applies to various industrial settings where products degrade discretely over time and can be held in degraded states before being reprocessed or salvaged.

Title: Optimal Designs and Inspection Time Decisions for Gamma Accelerated Degradation Tests
Authors: Hung‐Ping Tung, I‐Chen Lee
Affiliations: Department of Industrial Engineering and Management National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University Hsinchu Taiwan, ROC; Department of Statistics National Cheng Kung University Tainan Taiwan, ROC
Abstract: ABSTRACT This study analytically derives optimal designs for gamma accelerated degradation tests while incorporating inspection time as a design variable under both D‐ and V‐optimality criteria. Under D‐optimality, we prove that the optimal design allocates test units exclusively to the lowest and highest stress levels and adopts the longest inspection interval, resulting in only two test groups. In contrast, under V‐optimality, although test units are also allocated to the lowest and highest stress levels, the optimal inspection intervals may differ within the same stress level depending on the underlying model parameters, resulting in either two or three test groups. These results can also be applied to the optimal design for gamma‐accelerated destructive degradation tests. We further compared our proposed design with conventional V‐optimal designs that assume equal inspection intervals across all stress levels. The results demonstrate that conventional V‐optimal designs may result in a significant loss of efficiency. Two illustrative examples, an accelerated destructive degradation test and an accelerated degradation test, are provided to demonstrate the practical implementation of the proposed methods and their effectiveness in improving estimation accuracy. Finally, a sensitivity analysis demonstrates that the proposed optimal designs are more robust than the conventional V‐optimal design.

Title: Online Rebate Strategy for a Dual‐Channel Supply Chain
Authors: Peng Xu, Xuan Zhao, Tiaojun Xiao
Affiliations: School of Business, Nanjing Normal University Nanjing China; Center for Behavioral Decision and Control, School of Management and Engineering Nanjing University Nanjing China; Lazaridis School of Business and Economics, Wilfrid Laurier University Waterloo Canada
Abstract: ABSTRACT As online shopping channels become ubiquitous, consumers are faced with a vast number of digital purchasing options. To attract more consumers, many e‐shops utilize cashback websites (CWs) to provide online rebates. This study examines a dual‐channel supply chain, in which the manufacturer sells products through both its own online store and a downstream e‐tailer. Both the manufacturer and the e‐tailer need to decide whether to offer rebates via CW. We explore the rebate strategy of the two firms as well as its impacts on prices, profit, supply chain, and consumers. Our results show that (i) low‐end consumers' valuation plays a significant role on the equilibrium rebate strategy, and interestingly, a scenario where solely the manufacturer provides rebates never emerges in equilibrium. (ii) An intriguing asymmetry emerges: while manufacturer rebates invariably advantage the e‐tailer, e‐tailer rebates may benefit/hurt the manufacturer. (iii) As the valuation of low‐end consumers increases, the equilibrium rebate strategy initially enhances supply chain performance, then diminishes it, and ultimately has no effect. (iv) Low‐end consumers benefit from both manufacturer rebates and e‐tailer rebates when their valuation is at a medium level. In contrast, high‐end consumers incur losses under manufacturer rebates, while e‐tailer rebates may either benefit or disadvantage them. In addition, we extend the model to several alternative scenarios, such as simultaneous pricing, temporary rebates, product returns, and coordinated rebates.

Title: Locating Obnoxious Facilities With Variable Capacities
Authors: Zvi Drezner, Pawel Kalczynski
Affiliations: College of Business and Economics California State University‐Fullerton Fullerton California USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT The problem of locating facilities, such as garbage dumps or noisy factories, that have a negative impact on surrounding communities was initiated about 50 years ago, and intensively analyzed in the literature. In the models proposed in the literature, it is assumed that all facilities have the same capacity (size), and thus inflict the same negative impact. In this article, we propose to construct facilities of different capacities with a total given capacity. Facilities located in open areas are far from communities and can be larger without impacting the most affected community. This extra capacity allows facilities close to communities to be smaller without changing the total capacity and significantly reduces the negative impact on the most affected community. Such an important extension leads to a more complicated formulation that we were able to simplify and get much better solutions in shorter run times. In extensive computational experiments, we found in some cases that the negative impact on the most affected community is reduced by more than 50% when facilities of different capacities are established.

Title: Issue Information
Fading Away: Tropical Storms and the Decline of Internal Migrant Self-employment in China
Authors: Jiannan Wang, Wei Wang
Journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

Title: A Monte Carlo tree search guided metaheuristic for surgical cases assignment problem with no-show cases
Authors: Lei Zhu, Qiang Su, Yusheng Zhou, Jian Lin, Mingzhou Chen
Affiliations: Zhejiang Sci-Tech University; Tongji University; Zhejiang University of Technology; Zhejiang University of Finance and Economics; Shanghai University of International Business and Economics
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: A simulation-driven approach to last-mile logistics analysis considering microlevel operational sequences for efficient delivery planning
Authors: S. M. Atikur Rahman, Dana Zamorano, Tzu-Liang Bill Tseng, Md Abdul Quddus, Md Fashiar Rahman
Abstract: Abstract Supply chain management is becoming more challenging due to shifting client expectations and ongoing technological advancements. Failure to implement these changes can lead to resource mismanagement, delivery delays, and high operational costs. To address these challenges, this study presents a hybrid simulation framework combining Discrete Event Simulation (DES) and Agent-Based Modeling (ABM) for efficient decision-making. The proposed framework uses micro-level task modeling with the Maynard Operation Sequence Technique (MOST) to estimate delivery service times. In addition, Monte Carlo simulation examines output variability, and the Wasserstein distance-based double bootstrap method provides statistical validation. This holistic approach enables informed, data-driven decisions to avoid resource underutilization, ensure proper staff allocation, and maintain service consistency. Simulation scenarios revealed that incorrect planning can lead to unmet delivery commitments or excessive staffing costs. Experimental results indicate that the micro-level framework outperformed the existing simulation (Macro/Traditional) in operational efficiency. The proposed framework is benchmarked against exact MILP-VRP (Mixed Integer Linear Programming) optimization and heuristic ALNS (Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search) approaches. Compared to existing approaches, the proposed approach achieved higher efficiency by increasing deliveries by 28% with fewer fleets, increasing vehicle utilization to 98%, reducing elapsed time, and reducing delivery penalties. This approach was thoroughly validated using GIS-based data, experimentation, and performance analysis, showcasing its effectiveness in optimizing operational efficiency and profitability.

Title: Unveiling urban mobility complexities in developing nations: informal transport in a small city
Authors: Thomas E. Guerrero B., Paul Basnak, Jose Agustin Vallejo-Borda, Juan de Dios Ortúzar
Abstract: In the post-COVID-19 urban mobility landscape, transport planning has faced challenges, including shifting commuting patterns due to remote work, access inequalities, increased congestion and public transport decline. In developing countries, a prevalent issue is improving public transport service quality to provide affordable and safe alternatives that prevent modal shifts to private vehicles. In this sense, informal public transport plays a vital role, as privately owned minivans, buses, and motorcycles tend to fill gaps left by formal public transport due to socio-economic restrictions, poor urban growth planning and limited enforcement. However, while providing essential services, informal public transport services pose safety, reliability, and competition issues, in addition to taxation and insurance issues. In this context, understanding user preferences for informal public transport is crucial to developing effective public policies for its regulation. This paper evaluates mode choice in Ocaña, a small Colombian city heavily reliant on informal transportation. We designed a stated preference survey that allowed us to identify key factors explaining mode choice, to promote formal public transport and non-motorised modes while reducing private and informal transport reliance. The paper discusses mode choice models, survey design, results, and policy implications.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Analyzing the impact of high-risk recidivist drivers using nationwide automated enforcement data: policy innovations for managing habitual traffic violators
Authors: Donghyeok Park, Juneyoung Park, Minjeong Kwon, Junghwa Kim, Junhan Cho
Abstract: The widespread deployment of automated enforcement systems has significantly enhanced the capacity to detect violations. However, in South Korea, violations detected by these systems are subject only to administrative fines, with no demerit points applied to driver records. This policy limitation may overlook recidivist drivers whose frequent violations reflect persistently risky driving behavior. Addressing this gap, the present study proposes a hierarchical framework to identify high-risk recidivist drivers using nationwide plate based automated enforcement data. The analysis adopts a two-stage approach. First, statistical outlier detection using the interquartile range (IQR) identifies recidivist drivers based on violation frequency. Second, K-means clustering stratifies these drivers into low-, medium-, and high-risk groups using violation count and crash cost as input variables. To evaluate the implications of this classification, the study introduces normalized violation rate (VR) and accident rate (AR), enabling regional-level analysis across six driver groups. The results reveal that while recidivist drivers constitute only 5.3% of total drivers, they account for over 11% of all crashes. The crash rate, casualty rate, and crash cost increase sharply in the normalized metrics across the defined risk groups. General drivers show stronger region-level coupling between enforcement detections and crash outcomes, whereas high-risk recidivists exhibit sparse, localized patterns, suggesting that enforcement strategies should combine area-based deployment with targeted interventions for high-risk individuals. These findings provide empirical support for differentiated enforcement strategies. The proposed framework can help policymakers target both high-risk individuals and high-risk regions, thereby enhancing the efficiency and equity of traffic safety interventions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: A learning-augmented metaheuristic for the bi-objective generalized diversity problem
Authors: Maider Uranga, Antonio R. Uguina, Angel A. Juan, Anna Martinez-Gavara

Title: Neural and behavioral probability weighting function
Authors: Agnieszka Tymula, Hiroshi Yamada
Abstract: Recent theoretical models challenge probability weighting function as it was originally conceived in Prospect Theory in ways that are not straightforward to test using choice data. This study addresses these constraints by measuring neural responses to probability. Utilizing a unique dataset comprising 64,175 decision trials and 78,067 neural measurement trials, we pinpoint neurons whose activity (a basic biological decision processing unit) responds to probability, but does not detectably respond to payoff magnitudes, supporting the economic assumption that probabilities and utilities are in principle separable. Our observed neural probability-response functions are S-shaped, which we show can maximize earnings in our experimental environment, but diverge from probability weighting estimated from behavior under conventional assumptions. Incorporating biologically realistic, context-dependent utility in the estimation produces estimates that are more closely aligned with the independently measured neural probability-response function.

Title: Increasing healthcare usage among the homeless: Evidence from Mobile Street Clinics in Brazil
Authors: Malte Becker
Abstract: Homelessness is associated with an immense health burden and limited access to adequate healthcare. This paper studies the effects of Mobile Street Clinics on healthcare usage among people experiencing homelessness in Brazil. Exploiting unique administrative data in a staggered difference-in-differences setting, I find that Mobile Street Clinics strongly and persistently increase primary care usage and psycho-social care usage among people experiencing homelessness but do not improve tuberculosis treatment outcomes. These results suggest that MSCs expand healthcare access and utilization, but that expanding access alone is not sufficient to improve treatment continuity.

Title: Multiple criteria decision making under XORness
Authors: Amin Hocine
Abstract: How should we make decisions under XORness? XORness is a class of uncertainty arising from indeterminacy, exclusivity, and hesitancy. We develop a multiple criteria decision making framework that preserves XORness throughout the decision process. We define XOR numbers and prove their fundamental arithmetic and algebraic properties. Building on these results, we extend the deterministic decision matrix to an XOR decision matrix and introduce a compatible normalization procedure. Further, we propose an additive XOR aggregation operator, which preserves indeterminacy, exclusivity, and hesitancy inherent in evaluations. In addition, we introduce an axiomatic XORness measure that quantifies the degree of uncertainty associated with global performance scores and develop a performance–XORness index to rank alternatives. We prove that this index induces a total preorder over the set of alternatives and identify the conditions for preserving dominance. The applicability of the developed framework is demonstrated through the risk assessment of cyberthreat scenarios in energy systems, and recommendations are derived using the XOR–weighted sum method.

Title: Optimality of full effort in dynamic monitoring
Authors: Toshihiko Nanba
Abstract: I study costly inspections of a firm whose effort affects persistent quality and whose revenue depends on reputation. Full effort is globally optimal if and only if inspection costs do not exceed a computable cutoff. Above it, I construct a sequence of policies that strictly improve on the best full-effort policy. Their payoff gains and expected discounted effort losses vanish, but the gain-to-loss ratio diverges. No finite additional linear weight on quality restores full-effort optimality. The result allows nonlinear effort costs and asymmetric information losses.

Title: Motivated beliefs under delayed uncertainty resolution
Authors: Charlotte Cordes, Jana Friedrichsen, Simeon Schudy
Abstract: Experimental studies show that individuals update beliefs about ego-relevant information optimistically when they expect no resolution of uncertainty but neutrally when their ability is revealed immediately. We study belief updating and motivated memory when feedback is delayed but eventually disclosed. In a longitudinal experiment, participants receive noisy signals about their relative performance in an IQ-related task (Raven matrices) and are informed that they will learn their true rank four weeks later. Across subjects, belief updating is asymmetric: unfavorable signals are weighted less than favorable signals. We find little evidence of motivated memory, except among participants who ex post indicate that they perceive the task as ego-relevant.

Title: Multi-objective optimisation for drone allocation and routing in humanitarian aid delivery: a reinforcement learning-based approach
Authors: Ayushi Chauhan, Debabrata Das, Priyanka Verma, Ajinkya Tanksale, Shubham Singh
Affiliations: Indian Institute of Management; Indian Institute of Management Nagpur

Title: The prediction of Bitcoin price with a multi-source information fusion long short-term memory neural network model based on an attention mechanism
Authors: Zi-Xu Lv, Zhao-Cong Liu, Yinghan Zhao, Chi-Chun Zhou, Ping Zhang
Abstract: This paper investigates the advantages of leveraging multiple information sources to enhance the accuracy of Bitcoin return prediction. We propose a methodology for constructing deep learning models capable of integrating diverse inputs with a comprehensive framework that encompasses 55 determinants covering various aspects of the cryptocurrency market, blockchain technology, public attention, and the macroeconomic environment. Specifically, our study introduces an improved long short-term memory neural network (LSTM) that employs an attention mechanism and multi-source information fusion to forecast daily Bitcoin returns. Notably, our research demonstrates that this approach outperforms traditional time series models in terms of annualized return, the Sharpe ratio, and maximum drawdown. Our enhanced LSTM model, which leverages multi-source information as input, better captures the dynamic nature of Bitcoin, thereby improving its predictive power. Additionally, the model’s ability to incorporate multi-dimensional information and attention mechanisms further strengthens its reliability in predicting cryptocurrency market trends.

Title: A simple new benchmark for forecasting bond risk premia
Authors: Tobias Hoogteijling, Martin Martens, Michel van der Wel
Abstract: The standard way to summarize the yield curve is to use the first three principal components of the yield curve, resulting in level, slope and curvature factors. Yields, however, are non-stationary. We analyze the first three principal components of yield changes, which correspond to changes in level, slope and curvature. The new factors based on changes in yields have strong predictive power for bond risk premia, in contrast to the factors based on yield levels. We also provide insights into the impact this has on the added value of macro data for bond risk premia predictions and the recent conclusion that machine learning provides better forecasts than linear regression.

Title: Trade credit provision and inventory management efficiency: Evidence from the Chinese manufacturing sector
Authors: Yang Wu, Yang Xu, Ruoyu Chen
Abstract: In business practice, firms commonly provide trade credit to customers to optimize inventory management. However, empirical evidence on whether trade credit provision improves inventory management efficiency remains limited. We examine this question using a sample of Chinese A-share listed manufacturing firms. The results show that trade credit provision significantly enhances inventory management efficiency, and this operational improvement further translates into higher firm market value. Further analysis indicates that trade credit provision has a significantly positive effect on the management efficiency of raw materials inventory, work-in-process inventory, and finished goods inventory. To further strengthen causal identification, we exploit the establishment of bankruptcy courts as a quasi-natural experiment and construct an instrumental variable based on monetary policy shocks, thereby mitigating potential endogeneity concerns. Mechanism analyses reveal that trade credit provision improves firms’ inventory management efficiency by generating a demand stabilization effect and a customer concentration effect. Finally, we find that the role of trade credit provision in improving inventory management efficiency persists in firms facing greater inventory management challenges associated with product characteristics. This study provides new insights into how financial decisions serve as strategic tools for achieving operational objectives.

Title: Sales, per-use rental, or hybrid? An economic and environmental analysis of optimal business models under environmental vehicle tax
Authors: Jinyi Chen, ChenGuang Liu, Yaoqi Liu, Yongjie Dong
Abstract: In practice, firms offer vehicle usage through sales, per-use rentals, or hybrid business models. The growing demand for vehicle usage among consumers has led to a large amount of emissions. To reduce transport-related emissions, many governments implement environmental vehicle tax that is levied on vehicle ownership based on carbon emission intensity. However, it remains unclear how such a tax reshapes firms’ business model choices and whether a win-win outcome for both economic and environmental sustainability can be achieved. This paper develops a game-theoretic model comprising a profit-maximizing firm and heterogeneous consumers to investigate the firm’s optimal business model choice and corresponding environmental performance under the environmental vehicle tax. The results show the following. First, when the environmental tax is below a certain threshold, the firm prefers the hybrid model, whereas it switches to the sales model once the tax exceeds this threshold. Second, while a more stringent environmental tax generally improves environmental performance, excessively stringent taxation under the hybrid model may reduce emission-reduction effect for vehicles with relatively low production-phase emissions. Finally, when the environmental vehicle tax level and the production-phase emissions meet certain conditions, the firm’s choice of the optimal business model can achieve win-win outcomes for both economic and environmental sustainability. Furthermore, two extensions, involving production cost and a tiered tax structure, are considered to examine the robustness of the results.

Title: Estimating economy-wide mineral commodity consumption using hybrid input-output modeling: a case study of fluorspar
Authors: Miriam Stevens, Elisa Alonso, David Pineault, Nedal Nassar, Shweta Singh
Abstract: Understanding economy-wide material flows is of increasing importance as industries and governments seek to develop secure supply chains for critical minerals while mitigating negative social and environmental impacts. To advance research merging economy-wide material flow accounting with economic impact analysis, we adapt the integrated hybrid input-output analysis framework to build a mixed-unit model of mineral commodity processing in the United States. As a test case we apply the approach to fluorspar and derived fluorine-based chemicals, presenting one of a few models of fluorspar's domestic supply chain. We then estimate demand for this critical mineral that would be induced by projected sales of two emerging technologies, semiconductors and lithium-ion batteries, which are expected to contribute substantially to increasing demand. We find that near-term U.S. demand for fluorspar and its derivatives for use in semiconductors but not for use in lithium-ion batteries may surpass recent economy-wide domestic consumption of these materials. Modeling an increase in U.S. production of advanced chips in line with expressed targets results in 1% to 5% more fluorspar demand per year compared to the baseline. Global sensitivity analysis demonstrates an approach to factor prioritization applied to physical input-output table (PIOT) construction. We find the two major sources of physical flow data uncertainty, the ratios used to allocate national use to industries and the assumption used to partition exports into their domestic and foreign components, contribute about equally to uncertainty in the output. However, we also find the uncertainty in choice between several approaches to compiling the allocation ratios leads to most uncertainty in total physical output.

Title: Mapping the beyond GDP field: Canonical concentration and insular invisibility in three decades of multidimensional prosperity measurement (1995–2026)
Authors: Emilio Bonal, Serafin Corral
Abstract: Three decades after the Stiglitz Commission's call to measure “beyond GDP”, multidimensional prosperity frameworks have proliferated, yet cross-linguistic mappings of their paradigmatic and territorial composition remain scarce; existing reviews rely on English-only searches. This article characterises the conceptual, methodological and territorial structure of multidimensional prosperity frameworks published between 1995 and 2026, and tests the robustness of the resulting patterns to alternative definitions of the review scope. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020), we searched Web of Science and Scopus in English, Spanish, French, Italian and Portuguese, retrieving 23,048 unique records. Title-and-abstract screening used a deterministic rule-based classifier specified and refined by the two reviewers, who adjudicated every record it passed forward at full text, yielding 583 included studies. Paradigm was coded at two levels — the identity of the framework referenced and the analytical framing of the study deploying it — because the two do not coincide. Robustness was assessed across three nested corpora ( n = 583, 551, 503). The Human Development Index (HDI) of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and the Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) of the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative (OPHI) jointly account for 46.3–50.4% of the corpus. Frameworks with a social paradigmatic identity account for 79.0%, ecological for 8.9%, holistic for 8.3%, economic for 2.2% and two-dimensional hybrids for 1.6%. Insular contexts represent 1.0% of studies, and paradigm is not associated with territorial scale (Monte-Carlo p = 0.39), so the concentration is field-wide rather than confined to any territorial tier. Framework paradigm and study-level analytical framing diverge for 73.2% of the studies in which both are determinable: 184 of the 348 studies invoking a social-paradigm instrument (52.9%) are framed economically. Among the 162 bespoke frameworks, 58 integrate all three substantive dimensions but only one imposes an explicit biophysical boundary. All patterns are stable across the three corpus definitions. Three decades after the Beyond GDP critique, the field remains concentrated on a narrow canon of capability-based instruments that are predominantly deployed within income- and growth-centred analytical framings, while ecological-paradigm frameworks and insular territories remain marginal. Paradigmatic plurality appears to require editorial and institutional intervention rather than further conceptual elaboration.

Title: Comparing touch, voice, and gesture interaction for in-vehicle information systems: A multimodal assessment of mental workload, driving performance, and situation awareness
Authors: Qing-Xing Qu, Yiru Zhao, Zhongyang Xiao, Qiman Tan, Fu Guo, Vincent G. Duffy, Kai Tian, Wei Lyu
Abstract: The proliferation of in-vehicle infotainment systems raises critical safety concerns regarding driver distraction. This driving simulator study provides empirical evidence on how interaction modalities (touchscreen, voice, gesture) for non-driving-related tasks (NDRTs) affect driver state under varying traffic density and lighting conditions. Results showed that touchscreen interaction was associated with higher workload-related EEG activity, reduced HRV, larger eyelid aperture, lower situation awareness (SA), and less stable vehicle-control measures. Nighttime driving was associated with larger pupil diameter, while some adverse modality-related outcomes were more pronounced under high-density nighttime conditions. In contrast, voice interaction and WoZ-implemented gesture interaction were associated with lower workload-related indicators under the present controlled simulator conditions. A layered SA analysis revealed that perception-level SA was primarily impaired by visually demanding touchscreen use, while comprehension- and projection-level SA were more affected by environmental complexity. Within the scope of this driving simulator study—focusing on a music-selection task among young drivers—the proposed multimodal assessment framework contributes empirical evidence that may inform situation-aware adaptive interface design and scenario-based evaluation approaches for integrated HMI systems. These findings caution against overreliance on touchscreen interfaces for music-selection tasks in complex driving environments and suggest the potential safety relevance of lower-visual-demand modalities such as voice interaction and controlled gesture interaction, while recognizing that production-grade gesture recognition may introduce additional recognition-related costs.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Behavioral externalities and the hidden cost of fare evasion in Santiago de Chile and New York City
Authors: Bastian Henriquez-Jara, Diego Candia, Ricardo A. Daziano
Abstract: This paper introduces and empirically identifies behavioral externalities, i.e. when other users’ behavior affects utility even when operational attributes remain unchanged. We show the willingness to pay for reducing common public transport misbehaviors (social norm-deviating behaviors) in two cities, focusing primarily on fare evasion. The costs of evasion have been typically analyzed only from a revenue perspective, however, additional (hidden) social costs may arise if it impacts experienced utility, which is not immediately evident, while disutility is more readily expected from other misbehaviors, such as delinquency or informal vending, which have a direct and tangible impact on users. An online discrete choice experiment was conducted in Santiago de Chile and New York City, both of which exhibit particularly high fare evasion rates. We estimate willingness to pay (WTP) to reduce four common misbehaviors: noise from on-board informal musicians, delinquency, informal or unauthorized vending, and fare evasion. The choice experiment was framed as a hypothetical choice between public policies with different expected effects and associated costs. We estimate an Integrated Choice and Latent Variables (ICLV) model that captures: (1) heterogeneous sensitivities to the expected effects of policies on the four misbehaviors; (2) an underlying latent Misbehavior Displeasure that mediates sensitivity to each specific conduct and depends on demographic variables and latent public transport satisfaction; and (3) willingness-to-pay distributions, which allow us to economically evaluate behavioral externalities. We find that delinquency and informal vendors have a generalizable welfare impact, while the impact of fare evasion and informal musicians differs substantially across the two cities. Respondents in Santiago show a positive WTP for reducing evasion, whereas New Yorkers do not exhibit meaningful sensitivity to it. In Santiago, the WTP for reducing the current evasion rate to zero is equivalent to 7.4% of the regular fare, which is nearly half the WTP for eliminating informal vendors or delinquency. Santiago's participants valued a partial reduction of on-board musicians (against a full reduction), while in New York musicians have a positive effect on utility. We discuss the cross-sample differences, the individual characteristics that shape misbehavior disutility, and the policy implications of these results.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Asylum granted: The integration and well-being benefits of obtaining refugee status
Authors: Marine Casalis, Dominik Hangartner, Alexandra C. Hartman, Joe Kendall, Rodrigo Sanchez Sienra
Abstract: How does a person’s immigration status shape well-being, integration and opportunities? Immigration status is particularly high-stakes for people fleeing persecution and violence, who may face uncertainty in their ability to reside legally and move freely. Yet there is limited causal evidence on how obtaining refugee status affects refugees’ lives after arrival. In this study, we address this empirical gap by combining administrative UNHCR records linked to an original panel survey of asylum seekers and refugees in Greece conducted between 2022 and 2023. We use a difference-in-differences design to identify the impact of refugee status on labor market outcomes, integration into host communities, psychological distress and onward migration. We find that obtaining refugee status from the Greek state reduces psychological distress and improves overall integration, with the effects being mostly driven by navigational integration, while also increasing secondary movements within Europe. These results are robust to a variety of checks and specifications, providing evidence for the multidimensional impact of granting refugee status.

Title: Cross-country heterogeneity in potential-GDP and NAIRU hysteresis: A Bayesian approach
Authors: Julián Roa-Rozo
Abstract: This paper extends the semi-structural New Keynesian framework to estimate the potential GDP hysteresis elasticity (η) and the NAIRU hysteresis elasticity (η u ) jointly, by Bayesian methods, for 30 economies. The cross-country averages are 0.46 for η and 0.40 for η u , implying that 0.63 of a temporary demand shock remains in GDP after ten years. Regarding η u , its cross-country variation is high (0.04 in Iceland and 0.73 in Portugal) and seems to be higher in economies with stricter employment protection laws and in economies whose monetary policy spent longer at its lower bound. Cross-country heterogeneity of η is smaller in statistical terms but economically material (0.25 in Korea and 0.71 in Spain), and none of the structural characteristics considered accounts for it. Allowing for positive hysteresis elasticities yields measured output gaps that are smaller and less persistent. Using the identified demand shocks, local projections show that employment and capital respond persistently to demand shocks while measured TFP does not, a pattern consistent with accumulation-based mechanisms rather than TFP channels. These findings imply that the costs of recessions and aggressive disinflation are substantially higher than conventional frameworks suggest.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: Insights into brake wear particle emissions from a pure electric light-duty vehicle
Authors: Baoli Gong, Zhixin Zeng, Yu Lyu, Yibo Xu, Yu Gu, Yi Ma, Jiachen Li, Jianxun Tan, Qiang Lyu, Zhennan Cai, Yong Peng, Hui Xu
Abstract: In this study, an inertia dynamometer test bench system fully compliant with united nations global technical regulation No. 24 (UN GTR-24) and Euro 7 regulations was employed to systematically evaluate brake wear particle (BWP) emissions from a pure electric light-duty passenger vehicle. A critical temperature window was identified for brake emissions, beyond which PN 10 emissions increase sharply, ranging from 107.8 to 131.8 ℃ for the low-metallic (LM) material and from 106.4 to 135.1 ℃ for the non-asbestos organic (NAO) material. The uncorrected full-vehicle PM 2.5 and PM 10 emission factors are 2.459 and 4.576 mg/km/vehicle, respectively. After applying the UN GTR-24 correction factor (0.17) for regenerative braking in pure electric vehicles, the corrected PM 2.5 and PM 10 values become 0.418 and 0.778 mg/km/vehicle, which are well below the Euro 7 PM 10 limit of 3 mg/km/vehicle. Transient PN 10 emissions correlate strongly with brake disc temperature. Aggressive driving conditions (deceleration > 1.5 m/s2) trigger the highest PN 10 peaks, primarily driven by rapid temperature rise.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Integrated assessment of EU ETS, FuelEU Maritime and IMO net-zero framework: economic and emission implications of biofuel-based compliance strategies
Authors: Rukiye Ünal, Burak Zincir
Abstract: This study evaluates the economic and regulatory performance of fatty acid methyl ester (FAME)-based drop-in biofuels under the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), FuelEU Maritime, and the proposed IMO Net-Zero Framework (NZF). A container ship is analyzed over 2028–2040 under three compliance pathways: reference, minimum-cost, and proactive strategies. Annual FAME utilization is optimized through linear programming, while economic uncertainty is assessed using 1,000 Monte Carlo iterations. Deterministic sensitivity analysis examines alternative NZF targets and Remedial Unit (RU) prices under fixed fuel compositions. Results indicate that IMO NZF becomes the primary driver of FAME adoption after 2030, with utilization reaching approximately 40% in the mid-2030 s and exceeding 80% by 2040. Although FAME increases fuel costs, EU ETS savings, FuelEU pooling revenues, and NZF incentives partially offset these expenditures. Sensitivity results demonstrate that uncertain NZF targets and RU prices significantly influence long-term compliance costs without altering fuel compositions. Overall, FAME offers potential as a transitional compliance and cost-optimization option, highlighting the importance of market and regulatory uncertainties in maritime decarbonization planning.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Modeling systemic road network vulnerability and cascading healthcare disruption during urban Floods
Authors: Pritom Ray Nobin
Abstract: Flood risk management often prioritizes roads by hazard exposure alone, overlooking the network-wide consequences of localized failures. This study quantifies how flood exposure and topological importance determine systemic disruption in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Integrating a stacking ensemble machine learning model trained on an 11-year Sentinel-1 SAR flood inventory with graph-theoretic network analysis, we demonstrate that flood susceptibility and betweenness centrality are significantly but weakly associated. A composite Critical Score shows vulnerability is highly concentrated, with the top 5% of segments holding 82.6% of the network total, but only partly clustered: these segments span 143 of 187 communities, and just 43.7% lie in LISA HH hotspots. Their failure fragments the network, raising origins without hospital access 73-fold. Flood-risk-weighted Leiden detection identifies 187 vulnerability zones, where the top ten concentrate 29.1% of total vulnerability in 7.0% of segments. This framework guides limited resilience investments toward infrastructure whose failure causes the greatest city-wide disruption.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Optimal pricing for the product with matching uncertainty under social learning and cost learning
Authors: Yifan Wang, Jianxiong Zhang, Rui Dai
Abstract: As a type of product or service not yet widely accepted or utilized, new experiential products involve some uncertainty in consumers’ cognition regarding their performance, effects, and value. Consumers often know how sensitive they are to a potentially mismatching product attribute but cannot assess the product-side mismatch degree before use. Therefore, the mismatch degree remains uncertain to both consumers and the firm, and both can update their beliefs only after observing consumption-based reviews. Against this background, consumers have an incentive to strategically delay their purchases (updating their information from user reviews, i.e., through social learning), making the firm's intertemporal operational and marketing decisions particularly important. This paper examines a firm's two-period pricing strategy for a new experiential product, incorporating production cost learning and the impact of consumers’ social learning about mismatch degree. By applying rational expectations theory and the Bayesian updating rule, we analyze and compare two pricing models: preannounced pricing and responsive pricing. The findings indicate that as the influence of either social learning or cost learning increases, the firm gradually shifts from preannounced pricing to responsive pricing. Further, both social learning and cost learning have positive effects on the firm's profitability, and the strategic relationship between these two effects in enhancing profitability depends on key system parameters. It is shown that the relationship gradually transforms from complementarity to substitutability as either consumers’ strategic behavior intensifies or the firm's cost learning capability improves.

Title: Do trade deficits really de-industrialize? Manufacturing shares and trade balances
Authors: Christopher Ball, Isha Khan
Abstract: Do economies running persistent trade deficits experience faster manufacturing decline? Although prominent in contemporary policy debates, this question has not been examined systematically with global data. Using annual data for up to 172 economies from 2000 to 2022, we find no consistent relationship. Deficit countries do not experience faster declines than surplus countries and sometimes exhibit smaller declines, particularly in manufacturing employment. Results are similar using within-country changes in trade balances and employment samples with greater data coverage. These findings do not establish causal effects but suggest caution in treating trade deficits as a primary driver of deindustrialization.

Title: Monetary policy, endogenous bill supply, and the liquidity premium
Authors: Cristián Cuevas
Abstract: Liquidity premia on near-money assets (e.g. Treasury bills) co-move positively with monetary policy rates, a pattern usually read as the opportunity cost of money. I show that a cost-minimizing Treasury tilts issuance toward bills when policy eases, so part of the co-movement is issuance-mediated. A minimal model maps instrumental-variable regressions into a decomposition of the pass-through. Estimating the issuance response directly, point estimates attribute roughly one quarter of the effect of the policy rate on the premium to endogenous bill supply. The results inform the determination of US assets’ liquidity premia, an increasingly central input in macro and finance.

Title: Chance constrained optimization of hub transport systems
Authors: Max Bourgeat, Öykü Naz Attila, Rémy Chevrier, Quentin Cappart, Antoine Legrain
Abstract: Railway transportation offers an efficient and reliable service between stations. However, in remote areas, reduced accessibility due to large distances between stations and passengers’ origin/destination points presents a significant challenge for railway companies. In low-density areas and in the countryside in particular, the supply of complementary transport to the train is often limited, or even nonexistent during off-peak hours, and does not always allow for an intermodal journey. For the French railway operator (SNCF), it is desirable to be able to provide a complementary offer to transport service in order to make a typical passenger journey as seamless as possible. A key aspect to operate this service successfully is to ensure that shuttles arrive at the train station before the time that passengers are due to take their train. Consequently, finding an optimal routing plan for shuttles is a highly time-sensitive problem. Besides, an inaccurate representation of travel times can easily lead to infeasible routing decisions with respect to meeting the due date that passengers are required to be at the train station. Given this context, the main contribution of this paper is the formalization of this problem, that we refer to as the hub transportation problem with chance constrained due dates . The problem involves optimizing routing decisions for shuttles while ensuring their timely arrival at the train station under uncertain travel times. The second contribution is an algorithm based on column generation to solve it. The pricing problem incorporates chance constraints, deeming a route feasible if the shuttle can reach the train station before the passengers’ due date. Travel time uncertainty is modeled using a discrete and finite uncertainty set to represent various travel time scenarios. The chance constraints ensures that the final decision remains feasible by meeting the passengers’ due date in at least a specified proportion of the travel time scenarios. Because solving the chance-constrained pricing problem exactly on a large scenario set is intractable, the proposed heuristic algorithm samples a finite scenario set, accelerates the labelling algorithm in the pricing problem with reduced dominance and feasibility sets, and recovers an integer solution by re-solving the master problem with the generated columns. Experiments on 100 instances built from real transit and census data, with synthetic travel-time scenarios generated from a calibrated multimodal distribution, show that the chance-constrained approach consistently meets the desired empirical feasibility rates while achieving cost savings compared to deterministic counterparts, which tend to be either overly conservative or insufficiently reliable.

Title: Optimizing long-term charging management for warehouse robots using average reward reinforcement learning
Authors: Yongjin Mu, Jianqi Gao, Yanjie Li, Qi Liu, Xiaoqing Yang, Yunjiang Lou
Abstract: Efficient charging management of Automated Guided Vehicles (AGVs) is crucial in automated warehouses, where continuous order arrivals necessitate a long-term charging strategy focused on maximizing benefits. Traditional methods struggle with dynamic workloads, and discounted reward-based reinforcement learning (RL) is short-sighted. To address these limitations, we formulate the AGV charging problem as an average reward Markov decision process and propose a novel Unified ARTD3 Framework (U-ARTD3) to emphasize long-term operational efficiency. U-ARTD3 integrates two complementary average reward RL algorithms: ARTD3-Episode-Based, which captures system-level temporal workload dynamics for robust adaptation to peak surges, and ARTD3-Batch-Based, which utilizes historical data for low-bias, stable reward estimation to accelerate learning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed algorithms significantly outperform baseline charging strategies, achieving average performance gains of a 14.9% improvement in order completion ratio, a 526-second reduction in mean order processing duration, and a 448-order decrease in peak backlog, thereby enhancing warehouse operational efficiency.

Title: (Un)intended consequences of extreme heatwaves for air pollution and its social cost: Evidence from the power sector in China
Authors: Pin Sun, Yu’an Wang, Yang Wang, Wei Dai, Qingchen Chao, Bowei Guo, Chenpeng Wang
Abstract: Extreme heatwaves can undermine the efficiency of fossil-fuel power generation, amplifying air pollution and health risks. Using plant-level operational data and high-resolution weather data from China, we find that during the 2022 extreme heatwave in Guangdong Province, exposed plants experienced approximately 21.4% higher PM 2.5 emission intensity relative to unexposed plants, an increase attributable to heatwave-induced efficiency losses. Coal-fired plants exhibited an additional 12.3% increase relative to gas-fired plants. Similar patterns are observed for other combustion-related pollutants. We estimate that heatwave-induced pollution from power-sector efficiency losses imposes an annual social cost of USD 4.21 billion in China, which could be reduced by USD 1.42 billion under a complete coal-to-gas substitution scenario. Looking ahead, under the high-emissions SSP5-8.5 scenario, which is associated with approximately 4.4 °C of warming by 2100, annual costs in China could rise to USD 20.41 billion. The impacts are highly uneven across provinces, with coal-dependent and industrial coastal regions disproportionately affected. Our findings highlight how extreme heatwaves can amplify air pollution and health damages through an overlooked energy-sector efficiency channel, underscoring the broader societal costs of continued fossil-fuel dependence in a warming world.

Title: Age Discrimination in the Labour Market, Depression and Coping Strategies
Authors: Jinglin Wen, Luigi Siciliani, Xuezheng Qin, Prateek Chandra Bhan, Yingying Zhang

Title: When does smart manufacturing pay off? a configurational investigation based on necessary condition and fuzzy set qualitative comparative analysis
Authors: Matteo Podrecca, Francesco Arcidiacono, Michela Bearzi, Florian Schupp
