Title: Challenging assumptions in supply chain management accounting and reporting: a metamodern sustainability transformation
Authors: Stefan Schaltegger, Roger L. Burritt
Affiliations: Leuphana University Lüneburg Centre for Sustainability Management (CSM), , Lüneburg; Australian National University Fenner School of Environment and Society, College of Science, , Canberra
Abstract: Purpose This paper aims to use a metamodern approach and a problematization lens to challenge the assumption that transparency driven accounting of historical social and environmental harms is sufficient to achieve the scale of sustainability transformation of supply chains required by scientific evidence. It argues that sustainability measurement, accounting and reporting must also encompass future orientated, positive and absolute sustainability contributions enabled by transformative product, business model and supply chain redesign. Design/methodology/approach A metamodern approach is introduced and used in the paper. Drawing on metamodernism, the paper develops a framework for oscillating between incremental, transparency-based measurement and more fundamental assessments of business development. Through problematization of existing literature, it identifies limiting assumptions and advances accounting and reporting for sustainable supply chain transformations. Findings The analysis reveals four dominant assumptions in sustainability accounting and reporting that constrain sufficiently far-reaching sustainability transformations of supply chains: backward looking transparency, supplier assessment logics, harm reduction framing and incremental improvements. The proposed metamodern framework broadens the role of accounting by integrating multiple intelligence sources to support monitoring of existing supply chains and identification of redesign opportunities aligned with planetary boundaries and the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. Research limitations/implications The paper provides a metamodern foundation for future empirical development and testing of transformative sustainability measurement and accounting that embraces different intelligence sources. Practical implications Measurement and accounting informed by metamodern theory oscillates between different intelligence sources, comprising data, information and knowledge, to support both monitoring of existing supply chain relationships and identification of transformative redesign opportunities. Social implications The argument supports development of supply chain strategies and designs capable of addressing the easing of social and environmental harms as well as development of transformative sustainability opportunities. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this is the first paper to apply a metamodern lens to sustainability accounting and reporting for supply chain management. It shows how oscillation between modernist and postmodern logics opens new pathways for theorizing transformative measurement and positions accounting information as a catalyst for strategic redesign rather than incremental optimization.
Journal: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

Title: Putting all your eggs in one basket? A mathematical analysis of attack strategies
Authors: Yahel Giat, Irit Nowik
Abstract: In fields such as cyber operations, management, medicine, and military strategy, the choice between sequential and parallel strategies is critical for optimizing success rates and minimizing completion time. This study examines a hacker using multiple attack tools to destroy a rival system, assuming that each tool has an equal and independent probability of success. Attack execution is time-consuming, with the required time increasing concavely as more tools are used simultaneously. We analyze two protocols of attack strategies: one beginning with a multi-tool strike followed by single-tool strikes, and the other following the reverse sequence. We study the system’s expected survival time as a function of attack duration and the single-tool success probability, and for each parameter configuration we identify the strategy that minimizes expected survival. Our analysis yields two main results. First, hybrid strategies can be strictly optimal, depending on the success probability of each tool and the concavity of the setup-time function. Second—and more importantly—although one might expect the optimal hybrid policy to depend delicately on the model parameters, we prove a structural invariance result: within the class of strategies studied in this paper, whenever a hybrid strategy is optimal, the simultaneous strike must occur before the sequential phase. This finding provides a unified analytical principle for timing and coordination decisions for structuring resource deployment under uncertainty.

Title: Mixed financing strategies and coordination analysis under a partial trade credit contract
Authors: Qiang Yan, Wen Ding, Zhiyuan Zhen
Abstract: This paper studies a financing and coordination problem in a capital-constrained supply chain consisting of one supplier, one electronic business (EB) platform, and one financially distressed retailer under stochastic demand. We formulate a three-tier Stackelberg game to analyze a partial trade credit (PTC) contract, under which the supplier provides only partial trade credit, while the EB platform finances the retailer’s remaining capital requirement. The model jointly characterizes the operational decisions such as the supplier’s wholesale price, the platform’s interest rate, and the retailer’s order quantity. We derive the equilibrium strategies of all supply chain members and examine how the trade credit ratio and the commission rate affect equilibrium outcomes. The results indicate that a high commission rate may incentivize the EB platform to provide interest-free financing. We further compare the proposed mixed financing scheme with pure trade credit financing and pure platform financing to identify the retailer’s financing preference. Additionally, we characterize the conditions under which the PTC contract coordinates the decentralized supply chain and yields Pareto improvements for all members. Finally, we extend the model to examine how debt priority affects operational decisions and profits in a multi-creditor setting. When the retailer has no initial capital, both the supplier and the EB platform can benefit from debt priority; however, when the retailer has positive initial capital, debt priority is not always advantageous to creditors.

Title: AI-driven ESG investing: robust portfolios with dynamic ensemble learning
Authors: Nico Rosamilia, Irene Ferrari, Edoardo Pariani, Daniele Marazzina
Abstract: The increasing relevance of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) factors in portfolio optimization requires advanced methodologies capable of handling data heterogeneity and non-linear interactions. This study introduces the Dynamic Ensemble Learning Strategy (DELS), a machine learning-based framework that enhances firm selection for sustainable portfolio construction. DELS integrates a modified Random Forest algorithm ensuring an adaptive decision making process based on a two-stage consensus mechanism, optimizing risk-adjusted returns while aligning with sustainability objectives. The methodology is applied to Euro STOXX 600 stocks over the period from 2021 to 2024, demonstrating improved robustness against market fluctuations and enhancing ESG adherence. By combining different splitting measures, we also propose a volatility based recalibration strategy able to outperform iShares STOXX Europe 600 UCITS ETF and a passive buy-and-hold investment based on DELS, which demonstrates the practical implications of the model into Socially Responsible Investing.

Title: Deadlock detection and resolution in queueing networks with blocking
Authors: Tim Rens de Boer, René Bekker, Rob D. van der Mei
Abstract: Queueing networks with after-service blocking and limited or no buffer space are prone to deadlocks, a situation in which jobs become directly or indirectly blocked by themselves. Such networks are frequently used to model real-world scenarios, particularly in healthcare. This paper addresses deadlock detection and resolution in queueing networks with blocking, as a resolution mechanism is essential to prevent permanent deadlocks. We derive closed-form expressions for the number of customers in a single-node network to illustrate the effect of resolution frequency. For more complex settings, we propose a dynamic deadlock resolution strategy based on Integer Linear Programming (ILP), which adaptively determines job transitions. The effectiveness of the ILP is demonstrated using a system dynamics model, and its impact on blocking probabilities is evaluated through simulation. This approach substantially improves system performance: increasing the resolution frequency reduces job rejections and blocked servers, especially in systems with few servers or coarse time discretization. A case study on elderly care in Amsterdam shows that coordinated deadlock resolution can reduce patient rejections by up to 10% and wrong-bed days by up to 20% over a ten-year horizon, improving patient flow without expanding capacity.

Title: Forecasting atmospheric ethane
Authors: Marina Friedrich, Karim Moussa, Yuliya Shapovalova, David van der Straten
Abstract: This paper considers several methods to forecast the atmospheric ethane burden above three measurement stations across the world. Ethane data are characterized by a large fraction of missing observations and a strong seasonal pattern. We therefore use a selection of time series forecasting methods that can handle these properties: discounted least squares, damped exponential smoothing, a structural time series model, local linear kernel regression, and Gaussian process regression. Their performance is investigated and compared against a set of benchmarks in a forecasting experiment. The results are overall encouraging regarding the forecastability of atmospheric ethane. Among our proposed methods, the Gaussian process regression appears to perform best. Across the different forecast horizons, it also generally produces stable results. We further provide out-of-sample forecasts for the next three years. These are mainly driven by the seasonal component, consistent with the strong degree of seasonality observed in the data.

Title: RIDKA: Normalization-free multi-criteria framework for large-scale evaluations with mixed data
Authors: Saad Ahmed Javed, Jun-Liang Du, Arjab Singh Khuman

Title: Who pays for decarbonizing homes?
Authors: Teresa Lackner, Stefan Nabernegg
Abstract: The decarbonization of the residential building sector requires large upfront investments in heating system replacement and thermal renovation that fall disproportionately on lower-income households. Faced with political constraints on carbon pricing and technology mandates, investment subsidies have become the main policy instrument.This paper analyzes the distributional effects and fiscal costs of this policy approach for Austria. We develop a microsimulation model that links household-level investment needs to landlord wealth distributions,allowing us to assign the incidence of subsidies and financial burden across homeowners and landlords within a unified empirical setting.We find total investment needs amount to 78–92 billion euros over the transition period to 2040 (approximately 1% of GDP annually), implying fiscal costs of 33–40 billion euros under the 2023 subsidy scheme. Despite a targeted low-income component, approximately 45% of subsidy outlays accrue to the top three income deciles. Net investment burdens remain strongly regressive when thermal renovation is required, exceeding three annual incomes for low-income single-family homeowners. We further document substantial horizontal disparities within income groups and show that Austria's fragmented housing law is a first-order determinant of investment feasibility in the multi-apartment (rental) sector.Addressing distributional and feasibility concerns under fiscal constraints may require a policy mix combining mandates, income-contingent transfers, liquidity-support instruments and housing law reform.

Title: Do the trophic impacts which jaguars have on wildlife communities matter to farmers? Diverging farmer preferences for jaguar-associated benefits and costs
Authors: Alejandro M. Bellon
Abstract: Farmers who live near jaguars (Panthera onca) can experience various benefits and costs associated with both the jaguars themselves (direct impacts) and the ways jaguars alter wildlife communities (indirect impacts). In order to understand the trade-offs farmers face in communities that are important for maintaining jaguar population connectivity, I conducted a Discrete Choice Experiment (DCE) in the corridor communities of the Montes Azules Biosphere Reserve in Mexico. This DCE quantified the relative value placed on: (i) maintaining jaguars inside and surrounding these communities; (ii) avoiding maize losses caused by herbivores that jaguars may prey upon; (iii) avoiding livestock losses caused by jaguars and other predators with which they interact; and (iv) gaining additional income through ecotourism. The indirect benefit of jaguars helping prevent maize losses was valued by a majority of respondents, but not by those who most highly valued jaguar conservation for other reasons. Understanding the magnitude of jaguars' indirect impacts on agriculture would likely affect choices regarding jaguar conservation among a minority of respondents. In contrast, all respondents valued jaguar conservation in the reserve, and a majority would prefer jaguars in their communities, all else equal. A dislike of attacks on livestock and of having jaguars nearby are negative impacts of jaguars on human welfare. Jaguar conservation can broadly benefit the welfare of neighboring farming communities, and the benefits are potentially more evenly spread among households if the indirect benefit of maize protection is considered.

Title: The power of tolerance: First environmental violation exemption and air quality
Authors: Shiyi Chen, Juan Lu, Jidan Yao
Abstract: Responsive regulation emphasizes adaptive discretion and graduated enforcement to improve compliance. Using China's First Environmental Violation Exemption (FEVE) policy as a quasi-natural experiment, this study examines the environmental consequences of flexible enforcement. FEVE significantly improves urban air quality. Theoretical analysis identifies two complementary mechanisms: conditional penalty exemptions increase the expected returns to timely rectification and compliance investment, while risk-based enforcement and public oversight strengthen expected losses from subsequent violations. Consistent with these predictions, FEVE is associated with adjustments in green and digital innovation, green firm entry, polluting firm exit, regulatory resource allocation, and public oversight, with stronger air-quality effects where pre-policy conditions allow greater scope for such adjustments. The effects are also stronger in regions without a fixed first-violation identification period, non-border areas, smaller cities, and more densely populated areas. FEVE reduces average PM₂.₅ concentrations by approximately 3.20%. Under specified exposure–risk relationships and epidemiological parameters, and using the first full year after implementation in each province as a common evaluation window, the model estimates approximately 504,508 averted disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) nationwide. Descriptive comparisons with more stringent regulatory instruments show environmental improvements across different levels of enforcement intensity. Overall, the findings support a risk-tiered regulatory framework in which enforcement intensity is matched to firm behavior and environmental risk, combining flexible correction with credible escalation.

Title: Factors influencing aircraft ground delays in passenger air transport: Evidence from China
Authors: Yuwei Zhou, Lei Bian, Hanjun Wu
Abstract: This paper investigates the determinants of aircraft ground delays, defined as excess time spent during taxiing and turnaround, using a dataset of domestic flights in mainland China in 2023. As one of the first studies to examine aircraft ground delays in China's regulated aviation market, we use a two-stage least squares (2SLS) model to analyze flight-, airline-, and airport-level factors, with a focus on scheduling buffers (outbound flight buffers and ground buffers). The results show that longer outbound flight buffers are associated with longer ground delays, whereas longer ground buffers reduce ground delays. The outbound flight-buffer effect operates partly through increased gate holding and is stronger on longer-haul flights; it is also more pronounced when the inbound flight arrives late and when daily aircraft utilisation is lower. Ground delays are further higher for full-service airlines, larger aircraft, longer routes, and more congested airports. Component analyses indicate that earlier legs in an aircraft's daily rotation tend to have longer boarding times, while late-arriving inbound flights are associated with longer taxi-out times. Regional heterogeneity is evident: the outbound flight-buffer effect is most pronounced in eastern China, where an additional outbound flight buffer more often translates into extra ground time due to boarding and gate holding. Within the Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei cluster, airlines with larger market shares experience longer delays, with longer gate hold and taxi-in times, indicating a shift in waiting from taxiways to gates. These insights inform both airline scheduling strategies and airport policies aimed at mitigating ground delays.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Differentiated port fees and efficiency: evidence from Sino–U.S. liner shipping
Authors: Kevin X. Li, Xinping Zhao, Guanqiong Ye, Zoey Yi Xiao
Abstract: The U.S. Section 301 investigation against China's maritime industry and the resulting differentiated port service fees constitute a novel trade policy intervention with potential implications for Sino–U.S. shipping routes. To examine this policy shift, this study constructs a policy intensity index (PII) based on official policy documents and evaluates the evolution of logistics efficiency on Sino–U.S. liner routes over the 2023–2025 period. The DEA-BCC model and Malmquist index are applied to evaluate logistics efficiency from both static and dynamic perspectives, while a rolling-window VAR model is employed to examine the association between efficiency fluctuations and exports to seven major trading partners. The results show that comprehensive efficiency (Crste) varies with policy intensity, reaching its sample-period low of 0.667 in November 2025 following the formal implementation of port service fees. Scale efficiency (Sech) is the primary source of variation, while pure technical efficiency (Vrste) remains stable throughout the sample period. Furthermore, the rolling-window VAR results reveal a positive and significant association between efficiency changes and exports for the EU and ASEAN, a finding that remains robust even after controlling for tariff rates. These findings highlight that route efficiency varies with policy intensity and that the efficiency–export linkage differs across trading partners.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Tradable credit schemes to decarbonize commuting trips: Insights from a field trial in a university setting
Authors: Isabella Waldorf, Erik Verhoef, Klaus Bogenberger
Abstract: Tradable Credit Schemes (TCS) are a promising policy instrument for reducing transportation externalities. Their political feasibility may be higher than that of taxes, since policymakers can steer distributional outcomes through the initial allocation of credits, which may in turn increase acceptability. However, TCS require complex decision-making by participants, making empirical evidence on user behavior essential. We conducted a multi-week randomized controlled trial with over 600 participants in a university setting to evaluate the effects of a TCS on commuting emissions. Specifically, we implemented the MobilityCoin system, which prices CO2 emissions. While 18% of the treatment group reported changes in their commuting behavior, compared to 10% in the control group, econometric analysis shows only weak evidence of emission reductions in the full sample. Significant effects are found for specific subgroups, such as public transport users. We find no evidence that participants respond to variation in the price level. Our distance-based allocation leads to progressive outcomes: low-income participants benefit financially on average and do not appear to bear a disproportionate behavioral burden. In terms of acceptability, a majority of treated participants evaluate the system favorably, with more than one-third supporting its implementation at the university. Overall, our results highlight the potential of TCS as a policy instrument: they can induce behavioral change in specific populations while achieving progressive distributional outcomes and relatively high public acceptance.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: A machine learning-driven heuristic for an integrated lot-sizing, production–distribution and hub location problem
Authors: Jingwen Zhang, Xiaoning Zhang, Zhe Liang, Tao Wu
Abstract: This study investigates an integrated lot-sizing, production–distribution, and hub location problem in hub-and-spoke logistics networks (LSPDHL). We formulate a multi-period optimization model to jointly optimize facility location, production–distribution, and inventory management decisions, with the objective of minimizing total costs. To enhance computational performance, we propose a path-based formulation that provides a tighter linear programming relaxation lower bound compared to traditional formulations. Since the LSPDHL problem is a multi-period problem, a rolling horizon (RH) heuristic is adopted as the foundational framework. Within this framework, we develop several learning-based heuristics to reduce problem complexity by eliminating integer and continuous variables. Specifically, a random forest-based RH (RFRH) heuristic is first designed to predict the opening probabilities of hub and warehouse variables, eliminating low-probability facilities before problem decomposition. To further address large-sized instances, additive-structured statistical regression models—including logistic regression (LR) and generalized additive models (GAMs)—are integrated into the RFRH heuristic to capture both linear and nonlinear patterns between instance features and setup decisions. These models guide the reduction of the setup variable space. Additionally, for scenarios featured with demand-concentrated commodities, we define demand-concentrated and non-demand-concentrated commodities by adopting different value intervals of the Gini coefficient, and an enhanced transportation variable elimination (ETVE) method is proposed to prune continuous transportation variables. Computational experiments demonstrate that the proposed formulation yields tighter lower bounds. Results show that the RFRH heuristic outperforms the greedy-based RH, and CPLEX. Furthermore, the integration of GAMs yields the better solution quality by effectively capturing non-linear relationships between features and setup decisions, outperforming the LR model and heuristics without machine learning-guided reduction of setup decision variables. Finally, the ETVE method significantly improves computational performance for instances featured with demand-concentrated commodities.

Title: Heterogeneous trends of animal product consumption in the US: Evidence from grocery purchase data
Authors: Zach Freitas-Groff, Carl Meyer, Trevor K. Woolley
Abstract: Over the past two decades, U.S. meat consumption has remained high while purchases of plant-based alternatives have grown, raising questions about whether consumer behavior is shifting. Answering this question is difficult. Survey measures may overstate meat avoidance because stated identities and reported behavior do not always match purchases, a gap that may partly reflect social desirability. Aggregate data also obscure differences across households and regions. To address these challenges, we use a U.S. household grocery panel (2004–2020) linked with ingredient-level product data and develop a machine-learning-based classification of grocery purchases. We show that, despite modest growth in meat’s grocery-weight share, the share of screened household-months with no recorded meat grocery purchases rises from about 5.6% to about 7.5% by the end of 2019, and the share with no recorded animal-product grocery purchases rises from about 0.4% to about 1.2%, revealing growing polarization in grocery-purchase behavior. These increases partially reverse in 2020, when pandemic conditions shift consumption back toward food at home, consistent with declining food-at-home grocery purchasing accounting for part of the pre-pandemic rise in non-purchasing. Heterogeneity across demographic groups is consistent with cohort and demographic composition contributing to these patterns, though the grocery panel cannot cleanly separate composition, food-away-from-home substitution, and within-household behavior. By contrast, the extensive-margin patterns begin before modern plant-based meat alternatives (PBMAs) become prominent; PBMA spending shares are too small to account mechanically for much of aggregate meat-purchase changes, and their timing and limited penetration make them unlikely to explain the broader non-purchasing patterns on their own. Our findings reconcile persistently high aggregate meat consumption with the increasing visibility of meat avoidance.

Title: When immigrants meet exporters: A reassessment of the migrant-native wage gap
Authors: Léa Marchal, Guzmán Ourens, Giulia Sabbadini
Abstract: We show that exporting reshapes the migrant-native wage gap. We develop a model with heterogeneous firms and directed search, showing that high-skilled immigrants lower fixed export costs by leveraging destination-specific knowledge. The model generates an information premium for these workers in exporting firms that can offset immigrant-specific labour-market disadvantages. Using Portuguese employer-employee data linked to customs records, we observe a closing of the migrant-native wage gap among high-skilled workers in exporting firms, so that high-skilled immigrants earn wages comparable to those of high-skilled natives. We find no such results for low-skilled workers. To test the information premium hypothesis, we exploit differences across immigrants’ origin countries and firms’ export destinations. Our results indicate that destination-specific exporting can help reduce the wage gap, especially for high-skilled occupations. We thus provide micro-level evidence that immigrants’ export-facilitating role translates into wage premia within firms.

Title: China’s fiscal stimulus, global financial intermediaries, and international spillovers
Authors: Guangyu Nie, Dongling Su, Yifan Wang
Abstract: In this paper, we investigate the international spillovers of China’s fiscal policy and identify the financial channel as a pivotal transmission mechanism. Using monthly data from 2001 to 2019 and a sign-restricted Bayesian SVAR model, we document three stylized facts: First, China’s fiscal expansion crowds in domestic consumption and investment while inducing a mild trade deficit. Second, it triggers a persistent real appreciation of the Renminbi, despite systematic monetary accommodation. Third, it generates positive spillovers to the global economy, boosting commodity prices, output, and asset prices. These findings are robust when the global risky-asset factor is replaced with alternative measures of global bank balance-sheet activity. To rationalize these patterns, we develop a two-country New Keynesian model featuring financially constrained global intermediaries. We demonstrate that a balance-sheet channel underpins these positive spillovers: fiscal expansion, supported by accommodative monetary policy, improves global intermediaries’ net worth, relaxes their leverage constraints, and lowers credit spreads, culminating in a “prosper-thy-neighbor” expansion. This mechanism acts as an international financial accelerator, amplifying the domestic stimulus, yielding a fiscal multiplier above one and generating a sizable foreign spillover multiplier. Counterfactual analysis shows that removing this financial channel reverts the economy to a “beggar-thy-neighbor” outcome where foreign output declines. Furthermore, we show that in a monetary union, these positive spillovers are amplified when the common central bank accommodates the fiscal expansion, leading to larger stimulus effects for both countries.

Title: Risk-sharing with a central authority: Free-riding, lack of commitment, and bail-outs
Authors: Matthias Kredler, Rubén Veiga-Duarte
Abstract: Agents with independent risks ( regions ) often create unions and delegate re-distributive power to a central institution ( center ) that provides risk-sharing through costly transfers. However, there is the risk that regions free-ride on each other; this risk may be exacerbated when the center cannot commit to future policies. We study a differential game of two regions that make savings decisions and a benevolent center that sets transfers but lacks commitment. We show that this fully dynamic savings game of high complexity can be characterized and computed. One region always ends up bankrupt and the center provides a bail-out : as the poor region enters bankruptcy, there is an upward jump in transfers to the poor region that coincides with a downward jump in the poor region’s consumption. Delegation to a center is Pareto-improving provided that the center’s welfare weights reflect initial wealth differences between regions. However, once regions’ wealth and the center’s welfare weights tilt sufficiently, the dynamics turn unstable, hastening impoverishment and bail-outs.

Title: Flexibility at a cost? Required price reductions in dynamic EV charging tariffs
Authors: Paul Fabianek, Ayse Tugba Atasoy, Reinhard Madlener
Abstract: Congestion at charging stations during peak hours limits their optimal utilization hindering the adoption of e-vehicles by restricting user mobility. This study examines how dynamic pricing schemes can incentivize users to modify their charging behavior and alleviate charging station congestion. Through a survey-based experiment, we quantified users’ willingness to pay across different pricing schemes with variations in time, location, and duration. Results demonstrate that average price reductions required for demand shifting were: 23.9% to change charging time (day to night), 24.1% to change location (by 1 km), and 29.7% to accept a prolongation of charging duration (by 100%). Responsiveness to dynamic pricing varied based on e-vehicle driving experience, mobility patterns, and socio-demographic characteristics. Our findings indicate that sufficient financial incentives can effectively reduce charging station congestion. We recommend policymakers to establish regulatory frameworks for dynamic pricing for electric vehicle charging and further investigate the effectiveness of various pricing schemes.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Port alliance and information disclosure under disasters: a distributionally robust optimization approach
Authors: Shan Lyu, Ruisi Yang
Abstract: The uncertainty of natural disaster damage poses considerable challenges for port throughput and adaptation investment decisions. In practice, governments typically hold more accurate disaster information and choose whether to disclose it to ports, while ports may form alliances to mitigate such risks. This paper considers two competing ports that know the mean and variance of disaster damage but not its distribution. Using a distributionally robust optimization approach, we derive optimal port decisions and reveal three effects of alliances: the spillover effect, the competition-mitigation effect, and the Matthew effect. When the market size gap is small (large), the competition-mitigation (spillover) effect dominates, thereby reducing (increasing) total disaster damage. The alliance consistently benefits the stronger port but may harm the weaker port due to the Matthew effect. Furthermore, information disclosure increases expected throughput, profit, and the adaptation investment willingness, but may increase disaster damage when the adaptation investment cost is excessively high.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: A law of large numbers for quadratic forms in near-epoch dependent random fields and its application
Authors: Xing-Ao Li, Mingxi Wang, Ming-Yu Deng
Abstract: This article establishes a new law of large numbers (LLN) for quadratic forms in near-epoch dependent (NED) random fields where existing LLNs are inapplicable due to unboundedness of pairwise distances between locations. The regularity conditions impose suitable moment and dependence-decay restrictions for NED random fields and their α[jls-end-space/]-mixing bases. Our proposed LLN just requires weighting matrices in the quadratic forms to be uniformly bounded in both row and column sum norms in absolute value, without imposing the localized spatial structure typically required to preserve the NED property after row filtering. As an application, we demonstrate the stochastic convergence of the sample moment functions used in efficient GMM estimation with α[jls-end-space/]-mixing regressors.

Title: Simple closed form Anderson–Rubin confidence sets
Authors: Christian N. Brinch
Abstract: This note provides simple rules and formulas for deriving closed form confidence sets by inverting the Anderson-Rubin (AR) test in the important case of one endogenous covariate and one instrument. I demonstrate that these confidence sets can be easily constructed using standard output from three regressions: the first stage, the reduced form, and a modified reduced form. The procedure is the same for a wide variety of standard error estimators. Furthermore, I provide graphical intuition for the confidence sets that we get from inverting the AR test using instrumental confidence regions within the coordinate system of the first stage and reduced form slope coefficients.

Title: A Cauchy MESS
Authors: R. Kelley Pace
Abstract: The matrix exponential spatial specification (MESS) recovers its dependence parameter when disturbances exhibit large impulses, as occur under Cauchy and log-Cauchy distributions. The zero diagonal of the weight matrix W eliminates the leading contamination term from the gradient, leaving an (Formula presented) bias under standard constructions. Monte Carlo experiments without regression signal show the standard deviation under Cauchy errors is 24% smaller than under (Formula presented) errors, with robustness across weight matrices and gradual degradation under nuisance regressors and spatial fixed effects.

Title: Short-sale constraints and the non-monotonic ambiguity–crash risk relation
Authors: Binsheng Qian, Chi Thi Mien Tran
Abstract: Can firm-level ambiguity reduce crash risk when short selling is constrained? Ambiguity facilitates bad-news hoarding, raising crash risk, but also discourages ambiguity-averse investors from sustaining overvaluation when pessimistic beliefs cannot be expressed. During China’s market-wide short-sale ban, the ambiguity–crash risk relation is U-shaped among firms with limited analyst coverage but not among better-covered firms, though the cross-group difference is imprecise. The U-shape survives volatility and illiquidity controls and lower-tail trimming. After stocks become eligible for short selling, firms with higher pre-treatment ambiguity show more negative crash-risk responses, with no detectable differential pre-trend. Short-sale constraints and information production are boundary conditions.

Title: Signaling with burned money and transparent motives
Authors: Arseniy Samsonov
Abstract: This paper studies how an informed Sender communicates with an uninformed Receiver by visibly burning money. The Sender prefers higher Receiver actions, while the Receiver wants to match the true state. I characterize the full set of equilibrium payoff pairs and show that its Pareto frontier is generated by lower-censorship equilibria. In these equilibria, the Sender burns no money when the state is low and uses costly signals to disclose higher states.

Title: Predicting food waste from dynamic inconsistency
Authors: Alexander M. Danzer, Helen Zeidler
Abstract: Household food waste imposes substantial economic and environmental costs, yet its behavioral determinants remain imperfectly understood. Because food consumption unfolds over multiple stages, it creates scope for dynamically inconsistent choices that may turn good intentions into waste. We investigate this relationship using a nationally representative survey from Germany that combines targeted measures of food purchasing, consumption, and waste with individual present-bias parameters elicited from monetary intertemporal trade-off questions. More present-biased individuals waste significantly more food: a 10% increase in dynamic inconsistency is associated with roughly 2% more waste. This relationship is robust across specifications, replicated using a self-reported procrastination proxy, and stable several weeks later in a second survey wave. We also identify and empirically validate the mechanism linking present bias to food waste: dynamically inconsistent individuals are more likely to deviate from their own consumption intentions, and these deviations are strongly predictive of food waste. Our findings identify present bias as a systematic and previously overlooked driver of avoidable household food waste, suggesting that food policies need to address behavior along the full consumption chain.

Title: A phase-aware scheduling heuristic for sparse multi-queue multi-server service networks with switching frictions
Authors: Yu Bo, Zhanyou Ma
Abstract: Dynamic scheduling in multi-queue, multi-server-pool networks becomes difficult when bursty phase-modulated arrivals, sparse compatibility, heterogeneous service rates, and reconfiguration frictions interact. We develop a generalized phase-aware heuristic, an interpretable and training-free policy that processes server pools sequentially. Its operational edge score combines current backlog, a short-horizon arrival forecast, service efficiency, coverage scarcity, already assigned load, and switching cost and delay. Computational experiments span multiple network topologies, arrival regimes, compatibility densities, service conditions, loads, and system scales. Across this benchmark, the heuristic provides a favorable balance between congestion, switching cost, and overflow risk relative to the strongest tested structured scheduling rules on most instances. Conditional ablations show that backlog is the essential base signal, while forecast, service, scarcity, and switching terms provide mechanism-dependent corrections. The learned-policy comparisons are limited to the tested implementations and fixed training budgets. Finite-buffer stress tests do not establish infinite-buffer stability, and no claim of universal optimality or instance-wise dominance is made.

Title: Policy design and firm-level energy efficiency: Evidence from emissions trading versus command-and-control in Korea
Authors: Inseok Park, Donggyu Yi
Abstract: This study investigates how differences in climate policy design—emissions trading versus command-and-control regulation—affect firm-level energy and carbon performance. Exploiting the coexistence of the Korea Emissions Trading Scheme (K-ETS) and the command-and-control Target Management System (K-TMS), we examine whether market-based regulation reduces firms' value-added-based energy and carbon intensity relative to direct regulation. Using firm-level panel data from 2011 to 2023, we implement a staggered difference-in-differences framework and a separate event-study design to trace dynamic treatment effects. Because regime eligibility is determined by emissions thresholds, we focus on firms near the regulatory cutoffs and construct a unified measure of policy stringency to account for differences in reduction requirements across schemes. The results show that K-ETS participation is associated with significant reductions in both energy and carbon intensity for firms in the first-entry ETS cohort, but these effects are concentrated in the early post-entry years. Comparable reductions are not consistently observed for later-entry cohorts, suggesting that the effects of emissions trading are heterogeneous across cohorts and over time. Heterogeneity analyses further indicate that intensity reductions are more persistent among larger or higher-revenue firms, while stronger policy stringency alone does not guarantee sustained improvements. Overall, the findings underscore the need for market-based policy design that accounts for cohort-specific responses, regulatory stringency, and firms' financial capacity.

Title: Impact of artificial intelligence adoption on quality management in service organisations: a multi-case study
Authors: Guilherme Luz Tortorella, Paolo Gaiardelli, Jose Moyano-Fuentes, Juan Manuel Maqueria, Moacir Godinho Filho, Daniel Nascimento
Affiliations: The University of Melbourne; IAE Business School, Universidad Austral; Fundacao Dom Cabral; Universita Degli Studi di Bergamo; Universidad de Jaen; EM Normandie Business School; Universidade Federal de Sao Carlos; Aalborg University; Universidad de Barcelona
Abstract: This study empirically examines the effects of artificial intelligence (AI) integration into quality management (QM) processes of service organisations. A multi-case study in service organisations of different types was conducted. We utilised multiple sources of evidence to analyse and triangulate findings, yielding the development of propositions in light of the Dynamic Capabilities theory. Our findings indicated that AI adoption positively supports QM, especially in terms of the organisation’s ability to quickly learn and create new quality control and assurance solutions/procedures from this learning (sensing), and to integrate them into organisational processes and routines (seising). The identification of the impact of AI adoption on QM helps service organisations anticipate potential issues and address adequate countermeasures to reinforce their QM processes towards superior performance results.

Title: Action researchers’ competence-in-use in operations management research
Authors: Peter E. Johansson, Andreas Wallo
Affiliations: Department of Health Sciences, Innovation and Design, Mälardalen University; Department of Behavioural Sciences and Learning, Linköping University
Abstract: Action research (AR) has become increasingly established as a methodology in operations management (OM), yet limited attention has been paid to the competence required to perform AR skilfully. This paper examines the qualities of OM action researchers’ competence-in-use in terms of how they are enacted and represented in published AR studies within top-ranked OM journals. Drawing on a literature review of 28 empirical AR papers, and a competence-theoretical framework, the study analyses researchers’ working practices, self-understanding, and understandings of work. The findings show that AR in OM is predominantly characterised by task-oriented competence, reflected in instrumental use of established AR models and tools. In contrast, ideological-normative and development-oriented competences—such as reflexivity, ethical sensitivity, and methodological innovation—are less visible. The paper contributes by shifting the discussion from methodological design to researcher capability, highlighting how the quality and impact of AR depend on competence-in-use. Implications are discussed for developing AR capability, reviewer practices, and future research on collaborative methodologies in OM.

Title: Lean accounting practices in Chinese listed companies: a Contingency Theory perspective
Authors: Kunyu Yang, Qiong Wu, Kathryn Cormican
Affiliations: School of Business, Macau University of Science and Technology; Enterprise Research Centre, School of Engineering, University of Galway
Abstract: Lean Accounting (LA) is increasingly adopted as a means to embed operational relevance into financial measurement systems, thereby improving the visibility of waste, flow, and value creation from an accounting perspective. However, its performance outcomes remain inconsistent and under-explored, particularly in the Chinese context. Drawing on Contingency Theory, this study develops and empirically tests a conceptual model to examine how LA practices influence firm financial performance, with overproduction costs acting as a mediating variable and internal control quality as a boundary condition. Using panel data from 27,991 individual company-year observations across multiple industries in China (2014–2023), we found that LA practices are positively associated with financial performance and negatively associated with overproduction costs. Further analysis confirms that overproduction costs partially mediate this relationship, while strong internal controls amplify both the direct and indirect effects of LA on performance. The study contributes to the production control literature by validating the role of LA in reducing costs and enhancing performance under specific contextual conditions.

Title: Lean Management and Industry 4.0: a dynamic capabilities framework for an integrated transformation
Authors: Tim Komkowski, Jiju Antony, Fabiane Letícia Lizarelli, Leopoldo Gutierrez, Michael Sony, Daryl Powell, Tanawadee Pongboonchai-Empl, Jose Arturo Garza-Reyes, Luis Ignacio Araos Acharan
Affiliations: Edinburgh Business School, School of Social Sciences, Heriot-Watt University; Operational Excellence, Newcastle Business School, Northumbria University; Department of Production Engineering, Universidade Federal de Sao Carlos; Department of Business Administration, Business Management Faculty, University of Granada; Oxford Brookes Business School, Oxford Brookes University; Department of Business, Strategy and Political Science, USN School of Business, University of South-Eastern Norway; Department of Manufacturing, SINTEF Industry; Centre for Supply Chain Improvement, University of Derby; Department of Management Studies, Graphic Era Deemed to be University; Faculty of Engineering, Christian-Albrechts-Universität zu Kiel
Abstract: This study addresses the ongoing challenge of concurrently integrating Lean and Industry 4.0, a critical need for companies striving to enhance operational capabilities in increasingly digital environments. While past research focused on sequential approaches or high-level conceptualizations, this research delves into the level of ‘how’, applying Dynamic Capabilities theory through a deductive, four-stage mixed-method design, focused on large German manufacturing firms. First, expert interviews underwent thematic analysis to identify strategies and courses of action for integration. Next, an exploratory survey refined these results statistically. Third, the findings were validated and triangulated via a Delphi study, from which a structured integration framework emerged. Finally, confirmatory composite analysis of 236 managerial responses confirmed the reliability and validity of the framework. The study presents 44 validated actions grouped into six dimensions: Initiating, Sensing, Seizing, Transforming, Resources and Capabilities. Notably, it introduces the new ‘Initiating’ dimension, expanding the Dynamic Capabilities theory. While the study’s focus on large German manufacturers is a limitation, the resulting framework offers practical pathways for companies unable to pursue sequential integration due to time pressures. Ultimately, this research provides both theoretical advancement and practical tools for successfully managing the simultaneous transformation towards Lean and Industry 4.0.

Title: Strategic alignment of big BIM data for production management in the AEC industry: a cross-domain analysis anchored in organisational strategy
Authors: Apeesada Sompolgrunk, Hamed Golzad, Henry J. Liu, Saeed Banihashemi
Affiliations: School of Design and the Built Environment, University of Canberra; School of Built Environment, University Technology Sydney (UTS)
Abstract: The Architecture, Engineering and Construction (AEC) sector has entered a data-driven era, necessitating an integration of building information modelling (BIM) with big data (Big BIM data). However, current data-management practices within the industry are underdeveloped, constraining AEC’s capacity to meet Industry 4.0. We address this challenge by developing a Strategic Alignment Framework to optimally integrate big BIM data into organisational strategies. A Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling is employed to examine it. Emergent results reveal the pivotal role and pathways of aligning business strategy with BIM-data processes to enhance operational efficiency and competitiveness. Discussion on facilitating future practice and epistemological development is also presented. The contribution of this study is threefold viz: (1) expanding strategic alignment paradigms; (2) providing empirical insights into how big BIM data drives business process automation and cognitive insights/engagement; and (3) setting forth an agender for research on advancing business-IT alignment to better leverage BIM.

Title: Virgin or recycled powder for producing additive manufacturing spare parts? An economic analysis
Authors: Mirco Peron, Luigi Panza, Mohammad Arbabian, Srinivas (Sri) Talluri
Affiliations: Department of Information Systems, Supply Chain Management & Decision Support, NEOMA Business School; Department of Management and Production Engineering, Politecnico di Torino; Pamplin School of Business, University of Portland; Department of Supply Chain Management, Michigan State University
Abstract: Additive Manufacturing (AM) is used for spare parts production, but its adoption is limited by high costs, driven by expensive AM machines and raw materials. While machine costs are hard to reduce, raw material costs can be lowered by using recycled powders instead of virgin powders. However, recycled powders can affect part quality and reliability, potentially increasing costs for inventory and backorders. This study investigates whether using recycled powders is cost-effective when factoring in these management costs. We develop a mathematical model that includes purchasing, holding, and backorder costs, accounting for the cost and reliability differences between recycled and virgin powders. The model identifies break-even points for recycled powder use. Our results show that recycled powders are cost-effective only if their quality remains high. As AM machine costs decrease, using recycled powders becomes more attractive. This research provides a framework to guide managers on when to use recycled powders for AM.

Title: Artificial intelligence in supply chain management: enhancing customer engagement through real-world cases
Authors: Sudipendra Nath Roy, V. Kumar, Ashutosh Dixit, Ashutosh Ramesh Patil
Affiliations: Herberger Business School, St. Cloud State University; Goodman School of Business, Brock University; Monte Ahuja College of Business, Cleveland State University
Abstract: Supply chain disruptions, such as those triggered by the COVID-19 pandemic, have exposed vulnerabilities in customer engagement due to delays in communication and delivery. This study investigates how artificial intelligence (AI) can address emergent challenges in supply chain management (SCM) and enhance customer engagement across multiple supply chain functions. Drawing on twenty-six real-world cases, we develop an integrative framework that maps AI applications to seven key SCM operations and identifies their impact on customer engagement parameters including trust, convenience, satisfaction, personalisation, connectedness, profitability, and loyalty. The study also examines five AI failure cases to highlight potential risks and mitigation strategies. Interpreting the findings through a Dynamic Capabilities lens clarifies how AI-enabled sensing, decision making, and process reconfiguration translate operational gains into customer engagement outcomes. Findings suggest that AI-augmented supply chains can improve automation, resilience, and efficiency, but require careful implementation to avoid unintended consequences. The paper contributes a holistic blueprint for AI integration in SCM and offers practical recommendations for managers seeking to enhance customer engagement through intelligent technologies.

Title: Seeding Circular Supply Chain 5.0: essential factors for building the future supply chain
Authors: Sachin Kumar, Vinay Singh
Affiliations: Institute of Bussiness Management, GLA University Mathura; Department of Management Studies, ABV-Indian Institute of Information Technology and Management
Abstract: Depletion of natural resources, environmental concerns, and stricter regulations necessitate a shift from linear supply chain to Circular supply chain 5.0 (CSC 5.0), a smart, regenerative, and resilient model. CSC 5.0 integrates digitalisation, sustainability, and adaptive processes addressing disruptions, resource scarcity, and carbon emissions. This study identifies the essential factors facilitating CSC 5.0 seeding through literature review and examine its dimensions and interrelationships using Grey influence analysis (GINA), followed by Exploratory and Confirmatory factor analysis, and SEM (AMOS) to explore relationships. Data were collected from 17 experts shaped the GINA and framework, while responses from 41 industry professionals validated it. The findings reveal ‘Smart Digital Infrastructure’, and ‘Zero Waste management’ being the most influential essential factors. These factors define CSC 5.0 dimensions: Eco-intelligent infrastructure, Smart Circular Supply chain, Smart Resilient Process, and Adaptive and Sustainable Supply Chain. The study provides actionable insights to develop sustainable, intelligent, and adaptable supply chains.

Title: Collaborative innovation with suppliers: how to deal with openness, power, and cohesion paradoxes in purchasing and supply management
Authors: Oihab Allal-Chérif, Marie-Anne Le Dain, Hugues Poissonnier
Affiliations: NEOMA Business School; Grenoble INP-UGA Industrial Engineering and Management – G-SCOP Lab; Grenoble Ecole de Management
Abstract: This article draws on paradox theory to: (1) understand paradoxes in the context of collaborative innovation with suppliers; and (2) develop strategies to manage these paradoxes. We explored the manifestations of three major paradoxes identified in the literature: openness, power, and cohesion. For each paradox, we formed three focus groups of five practitioners from different sectors to stimulate peer discussion and elicit different opinions. Based on the results of these nine focus groups, we conduct a thematic content analysis using the classical framework of paradox resolution strategies: either-or, both-and, and more-than strategies. Our results reveal that the relevance of the paradox resolution strategy depends not only on the paradox, but also on the context. The three strategies are not mutually exclusive and can be combined according to contingency factors. The paradoxical mindset, considered as a micro-foundation of dynamic capability, must be integrated as an essential skill for managing collaborative innovation with suppliers.

Title: Harnessing Generative Artificial Intelligence for predictive maintenance: a case study in the tyre manufacturing industry
Authors: Ashish Jagdish Sharma, Bhawana Rathore, Rohit Gupta, Mahadeo Jaiswal, Baidyanath Biswas
Affiliations: Information System Area, Indian Institute of Management Sambalpur; Operations Management Area, Indian Institute of Management Sambalpur; Trinity Business School
Abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is a promising enabler of predictive maintenance in capital-intensive manufacturing. However, there is limited empirical evidence on how it can be effectively embedded in production planning and control and on the performance gains it delivers. This paper reports an in-depth case study of ABC Tyres Limited (ABC), a tyre manufacturer that introduced a GenAI-enabled predictive maintenance solution for its curing presses. The solution combines a domain-adapted large language model (LLM) with the plant’s process data lake, allowing engineers to query historical production cycles in natural language and generate diagnostic insights. Using before-and-after operational data, we assess the impact on key performance indicators. The intervention reduced the mean dry cycle time from 106 to 80 seconds, stabilized the curing process, increased daily curing capacity by 304 tyres, reduced steam consumption by 0.3 MT per day, and shortened the turnaround time for complex root cause analyses from around 10 days to roughly 2 hours.

Title: Supply chain resilience: a multi-level framework
Authors: Guoqing Zhao, Mar Vazquez-Noguerol, Denis Dennehy, J. Carlos Prado-Prado
Affiliations: School of Management, Swansea University; Grupo de Ingeniería de Organización (GIO), Escola de Enxeñaría Industrial, Departamento Organización de Empresas e Marketing, Universidade de Vigo
Abstract: Grounded in middle-range theory (MRT), this study explores supply chain resilience (SCRes) during the 2021 Henan floods through 54 interviews with agri-food industry practitioners. The findings reveal SCRes to be a multi-level framework determined by individuals, organizations, supply chains, and broader environments collectively. The environmental level, comprising political, economic, social, technological, environmental, legal, and cultural (PESTELC) factors, functions as the resource layer, providing critical resources. The supply chain level is the direction layer, setting goals for preparation, response, recovery, and adaptation by the organizations and individuals involved. The organizational level is the transmission layer, disseminating resilience objectives both horizontally and vertically. Finally, the individual level is the implementation layer, operationalizing organizational and SCRes strategies. Organizational employees’ personal attributes, such as openness, persistence, and extraversion, should be carefully considered when implementing SCRes strategies. China’s hierarchical culture, chain leader system, and accountability mechanisms ensure coordination across all levels.

Title: A maturity model for sustainable servitization in manufacturing
Authors: Elena Beducci, Antonio Masi, Anna De Carolis, Ali Bigdeli, Marco Taisch
Affiliations: Department of Management, Economics, and Industrial Engineering, Politecnico di Milano; Aston Business School, Aston Triangle, Aston University
Abstract: Despite increasing managerial interest, many firms struggle to scale sustainable servitization initiatives beyond pilot projects, facing capability misalignments, measurement challenges and governance complexities. This paper proposes a maturity model to assess and support manufacturing firms’ transition towards sustainable servitization. We structure and populate the model through a systematic literature review complemented by 19 interviews with managers, consultants and academics, and we subsequently test and deploy it in four companies. Our analysis shows that sustainable servitization is enabled by 11 capabilities, which we articulate into 62 items. These items populate 7 maturity dimensions and can be evaluated on five-level scales. The resulting model consolidates the fragmented sustainable servitization literature by identifying the capabilities that enable this transformation. In practice, it can be used to identify structured maturity profiles, support both internal analysis and cross-company benchmarking, guide targeted capability-development roadmaps and raise awareness of sustainable servitization opportunities, even in low-maturity contexts.

Title: A Better Cycle-Breaker for Direct Democracy?
Authors: Hans Gersbach, Rodrigo Casado Noguerales, Samuel Schenk
Abstract: When a counter-proposal is made to an initiative to change the Swiss constitution, the citizenry makes three binary majority choices: the initiative versus the status quo, the initiative versus the counter-proposal, and the status quo versus the counterproposal as a tie-breaker. If there is a cycle, the alternative that beats the status-quo wins. This system invites strategic voting, as exemplified by the 2010 case of the “Ausschaffungsinitiative”. We suggest to break cycles differently by choosing the middle alternative in case of a cycle, which will normally be the counter-proposal. More precisely, we show that there always exists a strong Nash equilibrium in which all citizens vote sincerely. Moreover, the outcome of all alternative strong equilibria with strategic voting is the same as if everybody votes sincerely. We also show that other common cycle-breaker rules cannot achieve the same result.

Title: Scheduling coupled tasks with flexible gap for minimisation of makespan
Authors: Danyu Bai, Chenbo Zang, Tianyi Liu, Zhixin Wang, Zhi-Hai Zhang, Chengbin Chu, Hu Qin
Affiliations: Dalian Maritime University; Tsinghua University; Univ Gustave-Eiffel; Huazhong University of Science and Technology
