Title: Improving Affordability and Accessibility of Modern Energy: Tax‐Cut or Direct Subsidy?
Authors: Jing Wang, Yanfei Lan, Hongyang Zou, Kuishuang Feng, Ying‐Ju Chen, Huibin Du
Affiliations: School of Economics and Management Beijing Jiaotong University Beijing China; College of Management and Economics Tianjin University Tianjin China; Laboratory of Computation and Analytics of Complex Management Systems (CACMS) Tianjin University Tianjin China; Department of Geographical Sciences University of Maryland College Park Maryland USA; School of Business and Management (ISOM) The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Hong Kong China
Abstract: ABSTRACT Promoting off‐grid solar (OGS) products is a cost‐effective way to expand access to modern energy. However, limited purchasing power in energy‐deficit regions creates an affordability gap, leaving the households most in need unable to afford it. This paper investigates the effectiveness of two key policies for promoting OGS adoption: direct subsidies providing financial support to consumers and tax cuts reducing firms' tax burden. We employ a three‐echelon game model comprising a government, an OGS firm, and consumers with heterogeneous affordability to delineate the applicability conditions of the two policies and identify their underlying mechanisms. Our analysis reveals that both policies can expand OGS coverage and generate a win‐win‐win outcome for the government, the firm, and consumers. The optimal policy choice is jointly determined by both consumer affordability and the tax environment. Under high‐tax environments, the optimal policy shifts from subsidies to tax cuts as consumers' affordability improves; under low‐tax environments, subsidies can unlock latent demand even when intervention would otherwise be unnecessary. The core difference stems from their price pass‐through efficiency. Contrary to the intuition that subsidies act directly on consumers and therefore achieve full pass‐through, we show that tax cuts deliver complete pass‐through, while subsidies are partially captured by the firm through strategic price adjustments.

Title: Embracing control tower for disruption forecast to enhance dual-sourcing resilience
Authors: Qiyang Li
Abstract: Many firms have experienced high-impact supply chain disruptions events such as China–United States trade war, Suez Canal blockage, and COVID-19 pandemic, driving them to seek more effective tools to enhance supply chain resilience. Control tower, a disruptive technology that can generate updated disruption forecast information, has the potential to be useful, but it has yet to be widely adopted. We develop a dual-sourcing model comprising a brand-owner, a reliable supplier, and an unreliable supplier, where the unreliable supplier is exposed to disruption risk. We study firms’ strategic decisions regarding control tower adoption considering three scenarios: (1) no control tower adoption (Scenario N), (2) only the brand-owner adopts control tower (Scenario B-A), and (3) both the brand-owner and unreliable supplier adopt control tower (Scenario BU-A). Comparing Scenario N and Scenario B-A, we find that the brand-owner is better-off in Scenario B-A due to control tower’s core function of reducing uncertainty through improved forecast accuracy, which triggers two key interactive effects: a procurement cost effect (lowers suppliers’ pricing power leading to lower costs) and an order allocation effect (flexible quantity adjustments to mitigate risks and avoid competition). However, comparing Scenario N and Scenario BU-A, we find that the two effects mentioned above do not have purely positive or negative impacts on the brand-owner and the unreliable supplier, resulting in intriguing shifts in their preferences towards control tower adoption.

Title: Low-carbon e-commerce platform supply chain operations driven by blockchain technology: Sales mode selection and decision optimization
Authors: Shuaishuai Fu, Zhengyi Li, Jia Shu
Abstract: Motivated by the collaboration between e-commerce platforms (EPs) and manufacturers in utilizing blockchain technology (BT) to boost the sales of low-carbon products (LCPs), this paper considers a low-carbon e-commerce platform supply chain (LESC) consisting of a manufacturer and an EP, the manufacturer produces LCPs and sells them via EPs through either the marketplace or reselling modes. The study investigates how BT implementation impacts sales mode selection and decision optimization for the LESC. Results indicate that in marketplace mode, BT enhances consumer market recognition and the added value of LCPs, enabling EPs to offer manufacturers preferential terms. However, whether BT improves carbon emission reduction level and increases market demand depends on the consumers' trust levels and preferences level for LCPs. In the reselling model, LESC's decision to implement BT is more sensitive to blockchain costs compared to the marketplace mode. Nonetheless, LESC members are more likely to reach an agreement on BT adoption in the marketplace mode. Interestingly, regardless of BT implementation, compared with the reselling mode, the LESC adopting the marketplace mode can improve environmental impact, increase consumer surplus and profits. The adoption of BT in the LESC does not affect Eps' preference for sales mode selection, manufacturers should conduct market research on the unit cost of BT, consumers' trust levels, and preferences levels for LCPs to choose a more suitable sales mode.

Title: Enjoying more years of good life while reducing resource use and emissions? A global panel analysis 1990–2019
Authors: Helmut Haberl, Juan Antonio Duro, Benedikt Grammer, Alejandro Perez-Laborda, Paul E. Brockway, Matthew K. Heun, Shonali Pachauri, Claudia Reiter, Erich Striessnig, Fridolin Krausmann, Jan Streeck, Dominik Wiedenhofer
Abstract: Abstract Achieving a good life for all within planetary boundaries is essential for sustainability. But analysing this goal is hindered by problems of definition, measurement, and the large number of potentially relevant factors. The indicator ‘years of good life’ (YoGL) is defined as the number of years a person can expect to live above absolute poverty, enjoy good physical and cognitive health, and experience positive life satisfaction 1. YoGL has been quantified 2, but how it depends on resource requirements and other potential determinants has not yet been studied. We analysed this question for ~110 countries from 1990 to 2019, revealing that the relationship between YoGL and resource use (materials, energy) and emissions follows saturation curves. YoGL/resource use ratios improve over time, which we analyse in fixed effects and between-effects panel analyses considering factors hypothesized to affect this ratio. We find that education, health expenditures, and per-capita GDP covary with YoGL, whereas ambient air pollution and income inequality are negatively related to YoGL. In panel analyses considering all factors simultaneously, resource and emission indicators lose importance and are often negatively related with YoGL. In countries with high-YoGL (upper three deciles), income becomes insignificant, while other factors remain important. Reducing income inequality and air pollution, as well as promoting education and healthcare, while minimizing the use of physical resources and emissions hence emerge as essential strategies for raising social wellbeing sustainably.

Title: IoT-enabled packaging recycling adoption in circular packaging 4.0 supply chains under policy mechanisms
Authors: Qingyu Liu, Devika Kannan, Kannan Govindan
Abstract: Achieving a circular economy (CE) is a critical societal challenge as packaging waste surges while recycling rates remain low. Internet of Things (IoT) technologies, such as RFID tracking and smart sorting, offer tools to improve recycling efficiency. The manufacturer can choose between the traditional packaging recycling (TPR) and IoT-enabled packaging recycling (IPR) modes, which differ in cost structure, operational efficiency, and environmental impact. Government subsidies for Packaging 4.0 further influence recycling adoption decisions. This paper evaluates the effectiveness of the IPR mode and subsidy impacts, yielding three key findings. First, while the IPR mode generally increases the recycling rate, it may unexpectedly lead to higher landfill volumes under certain conditions, highlighting unintended environmental consequences of technological adoption. Second, incorporating government subsidies into the decision framework demonstrates that uniform subsidies fail to account for industry cost differences, whereas targeted subsidies lead to more efficient resource allocation and enhanced social welfare. Finally, a case illustration of Australia’s B2C packaging industry explores how the interaction of IoT adoption and environmental subsidies optimizes the IPR mode. The findings provide actionable insights for policymakers and industry leaders to design adaptive policies that balance financial and environmental goals.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Reducing car use to support local climate goals: The potential role of small and medium-sized employers
Authors: Jesse Wise, Lorraine Whitmarsh, Sam Hampton
Abstract: Widespread adoption of Transport Demand Management (TDM) would significantly reduce congestion, pollution, and carbon emissions. Employers can implement some TDM measures more quickly and acceptably than measures which must be implemented by authorities. This study evaluates the role of employers in achieving TDM targets, including small and medium employers (SMEs). The role of SMEs in implementing TDM strategies has been under-researched despite them comprising most private-sector employment. We evaluated demand for employer-led TDM measures using a Travel to Work survey from the West of England (n=20,017). Employees commuting by car reported which measures would facilitate walking, cycling, public transport, car-sharing to work, and purchasing a battery electric vehicle (BEV). We categorised these ‘enablers’ based on whether they could be implemented by employers (e.g., lockers) or required government action (e.g., cycle lanes). Results suggest authority-led measures, like improved infrastructure and public transport provision, are the primary enablers of modal shift. However, employers can meaningfully support shifts to walking, cycling, car sharing, and purchasing a BEV. Employers should prioritise the adoption of showering facilities, drying rooms, storage lockers and secure cycle parking to achieve modal shift. SMEs could enable an equal, if not greater, proportion of their employees to cycle as their larger counterparts. Results invite a re-assessment of the impact of area-based workplace travel plans. Overlooking the role of SMEs in TDM risks missing a rapid and acceptable approach to decarbonisation. Constrained authorities could re-assess area-based travel plans to capitalise on this opportunity to influence commutes through these trusted middle actors.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Ranking transport projects in benefit–cost analysis: A welfare–consistent profitability measure under general and sectoral budget constraints
Authors: James Odeck
Abstract: Cross-country evidence shows that transportation project appraisal systems apply profitability measures derived from benefit–cost analysis (BCA) inconsistently. Some countries rely on benefit–cost ratios (B/C), defined as discounted benefits divided by total discounted social costs; others rank projects by net present value (NPV) per unit of total cost; and some use NPV per unit of government budgetary expenditure. In several institutional settings, transportation investment funds are allocated on a sectoral basis and must largely be spent within the sector, even when available projects yield negative welfare-adjusted NPVs, including cases involving toll-financed infrastructure. Although the welfare-theoretic foundations of BCA are well established, transportation appraisal practices differ substantially in how BCA results are translated into operational ranking rules under alternative budget regimes. This study applies standard welfare economics and constrained optimization to derive welfare-consistent investment criteria for transportation projects under three institutional settings: (i) unconstrained budgets, (ii) binding general public budgets, and (iii) sectoral mandatory-spend regimes. Assuming benefits and costs are correctly measured, three main results follow. First, under unconstrained budgets, all projects with positive NPVs should be undertaken. Second, under binding public budgets, welfare-adjusted NPV per unit of government budgetary expenditure provides the optimal marginal ranking criterion for divisible projects and an operational ranking heuristic for indivisible projects, for which exact portfolio selection may require comparison of feasible project combinations. Third, under mandatory-spend regimes, the same profitability index governs project prioritization; when all feasible welfare-adjusted NPVs are negative, ranking implies selecting projects with the least negative welfare-adjusted return per unit of unavoidable public expenditure in order to minimize welfare loss. The analysis distinguishes explicitly between total discounted social resource costs and publicly financed budgetary costs, incorporates the marginal cost of public funds, and clarifies the distinction between ranking independent projects and selecting among mutually exclusive alternatives under fiscal scarcity. By explicitly linking BCA to institutional budget constraints, the paper provides a coherent welfare-economic benchmark for transportation project ranking under fiscal scarcity.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Electrified cross-carrier platooning for long-haul freight: Charging coordination and stable cost allocation
Authors: Rui Zheng, Yu Zhou, Chuan Ding, Mi Gan, Xiaobo Liu, Xuedong Yan
Abstract: Electrification and truck platooning can reduce long-haul freight’s environmental burden, but leader–follower energy-cost differences complicate cross-carrier coordination and cost sharing. We develop an integrated operational and cooperative-game framework for electric heavy-duty trucks. A mixed-integer linear programming model optimizes charging, departures, and platoon roles under battery, station, dwell, and delivery constraints. Coalition-specific solutions and optimization bounds assess cooperative cost allocations and their stability. Experiments examine a four-carrier aggregate benchmark, individual charger feasibility, emissions, robustness, and scalability. Coordination reduces generalized operating cost by 1.89%; platooning reduces en-route charged energy by 20.41%. The electric plan emits 24.59% less operational CO 2 than a matched diesel plan under a full-corridor accounting boundary and a uniform grid emission factor. Individual charger scheduling reveals service conflicts in the aggregate grand-coalition plan at the stated capacity. Under a conditional capacity scenario, all 15 coalition incumbents admit feasible charger schedules, with cooperation savings bounded between 1.86% and 2.64%.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Low-emission zones in urban freight: Tailpipe and life-cycle impacts
Authors: Cristian Aguayo, Jorge Amaya, Fernando Arenas-Araya, Sabine Limbourg
Abstract: Urban low-emission zones (LEZs) aim to improve air quality but can shift environmental burdens across space and accounting boundaries. We propose a three-echelon location-routing model with candidate satellites, heterogeneous fleets, and explicit LEZ accessibility constraints, jointly optimizing satellite use, multi-product flows, and vehicle routes. Using a scenario analysis calibrated on Belgian data (Brussels and a four-city network), we compare No-LEZ, Mild-LEZ, and Full-LEZ settings with and without mandatory consolidation. Mild restrictions can be non-binding under the prevailing fleet and network configuration. Full-LEZ triggers fleet substitution toward eligible last-mile modes and eliminates tailpipe emissions inside the zone, apart from marginal residuals on exempt segments, while operational costs and life-cycle indicators may increase depending on demand and consolidation. At high demand, satellite activation becomes a compliance requirement once in-zone demand exceeds the payload capacity of the LEZ-eligible depot fleet.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Assessing pre-earthquake preparedness through multi-system simulation of post-earthquake medical rescue
Authors: Pengshun Li, Bingyu Zhao, Tracy Becker, Ziqi Wang, Kenichi Soga
Abstract: Earthquakes pose a constant threat to human life and civil infrastructure. Effective rescue depends on the coordination of three systems: search and rescue (SAR) operations, road network, and hospitals. Most existing studies analyze these systems separately, limiting holistic assessment of regional preparedness. This study develops an efficient multi-system simulation framework to examine how pre-earthquake preparedness affects post-earthquake rescue. We evaluate a wide range of preparedness scenarios involving SAR team capacity, bridge retrofitting, and hospital upgrades. A multi-fidelity Monte Carlo approach accelerates computation, and SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) analysis quantifies preparedness contribution. Applied to the San Francisco Bay Area under a magnitude-7.0 HayWired scenario, the multi-fidelity approach runs ten times faster than high-fidelity simulations. Results show that, in this case, hospital upgrades provide greater benefits than bridge retrofits, while adding SAR teams substantially reduces rescue and hospital travel times. Findings highlight the value of coordinated system-level preparedness and targeted resource allocation.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: When should firms promote consumer learning? An experimental study
Authors: Eric Schmidbauer, Brock Stoddard, Lan Zhang
Abstract: We experimentally examine firms’ incentives to provide information that enables consumers to learn about product valuations. In our design, firms make take-it-or-leave-it offers to consumers who are uncertain about their own valuations. Firms can choose to facilitate learning without observing what consumers learn. Consistent with theory, firms are more likely to provide information when ex-ante gains from trade are low, particularly when marginal costs are high. Consumers, however, depart from the benchmark model: acceptance rates are lower when the absence of learning is chosen by the firm than when exogenously imposed, even though the firm’s choice conveys no information about valuation. Firms that permit learning charge higher prices, but, relative to theory, low-cost firms oversupply information while high-cost firms undersupply it. These patterns are consistent with consumer responses to intentional nondisclosure influencing firms’ pricing and information provision.

Title: Rounding in data deposits distorts meta-analytic heterogeneity
Authors: Yossef Tobol
Abstract: Meta-analysis is standard in economics, and its reporting guidelines ask for data deposits without saying at what precision. Effect sizes are computed from rounded statistics; coding files record counts formed by rounding estimated shares. Treating them as exact distorts the between-study variance through two channels: an added variance and an effect-dependent systematic shift. It is easily missed: a plug-in within-study variance from the same inputs absorbs part of it. On two dishonesty data sets whose exact counts survive, it absorbs 72 to 88 percent; correcting only the first channel recovers about seventy percent, and on a plug-in variance it overshoots.

Title: Strait of Hormuz crisis and euro area financial market spillovers: An event-targeted approach
Authors: Jakub Cery, Martin Alexy
Abstract: The closure of the Strait of Hormuz during the U.S.-Israel-Iran conflict disrupted global energy trade and repriced euro area financial markets. Using a daily event-targeted vector autoregression, we estimate the effects of Hormuz-related geopolitical shocks on equities, sovereign yields, inflation expectations, and core–periphery spreads. A negative shock comparable to the initial closure reduces the Euro Stoxx by over 4%, raises German one-year yields by about 30 basis points and inflation swaps by 15 basis points, and widens spreads. Historical decompositions show these shocks explained much of the initial market response, though other factors became increasingly important as markets adapted.

Title: Is Chinese inflation still too smooth? New evidence from Engel curves
Authors: Yuanpei Liang
Abstract: Official inflation statistics in transitional economies often suffer from measurement biases. This paper extends the Nakamura–Steinsson–Liu Pooled Engel Curve Methodology to estimate bias-adjusted annual inflation rates in China up to 2024. To overcome the 2013–2015 household survey reform, we derive the subcategory equation’s dependent variable as the logarithm of quantity, splicing estimates into one bias-adjusted inflation series (1996–2024). The results reveal China is still smoothing its CPI inflation reality. Furthermore, we find the inflation dynamics pattern has shifted away from the hog cycle since the COVID-19 pandemic.

Title: Tax audit expectation updating: Direct and indirect effects of an audit
Authors: Yulia Kuchumova, Suriya Kumacheva
Abstract: In recent years, an emerging body of empirical research has shown that tax audits, in addition to recovering unpaid taxes (the direct effect), increase future tax compliance (the indirect or dynamic effect). This literature also suggests that the revision of expectations about future audits induced by audit experience plays an important role in explaining this indirect effect. However, how exactly taxpayers form their beliefs and adjust them based on audit experience remains an open question. This paper extends tax evasion theory by introducing a novel framework embedded with a Bayesian audit belief updating mechanism. This allows us to formally model how taxpayers internalize past audit experiences to dynamically adjust their perceived probability of an audit. Applying this model to analyze the dynamic impact of audits on tax evasion behavior, we find that our predictions align with all patterns of the indirect effect observed in the empirical literature: it is positive for non-compliant taxpayers, and it persists but attenuates over time.

Title: Accelerating the solution of sparse test collection problems with a virtual null item
Authors: Yao Qi, Qi Cao, Gang Ren
Abstract: The Test Collection Problem (TCP) asks for a minimum-cardinality subset of binary tests that distinguishes every pair of items. Two items are distinguishable if at least one selected test gives different outcomes for them. The standard TCP formulation contains one pairwise distinguishability constraint for each item pair, so the number of such constraints grows quadratically with the number of items. This paper considers sparse TCP instances arising in network sensor placement, where items represent possible system states or fault locations and tests represent candidate sensors. We introduce a virtual null item and develop a null-item augmented TCP (NA-TCP) framework. Distinguishability from the null item requires each actual item to be covered by at least one selected test. Under this coverage requirement, two items covered by disjoint sets of tests are automatically distinguishable, and their explicit pairwise distinguishabilityconstraint can be omitted. Under unit costs, requiring full coverage leaves the minimum test-set size unchanged or raises it by one, and at least one optimal NA-TCP test set contains an optimal TCP test set. Motivated by this result, we develop a restoration procedure that searches optimal NA-TCP test sets in the solver solution pool to recover an optimal TCP test set. Computational experiments on water distribution network instances and synthetic instances indicate that the proposed method generates fewer constraints and requires less solution time on the tested instances. Additional experiments examine sensitivity to network scale and density, solution pool size, and heterogeneous test costs.

Title: Leveraging surplus electricity: Profitability of Bitcoin mining as a national strategy in South Korea
Authors: Yoonseul Choi, Jaehong Jeong, Jungsoon Choi
Abstract: This study examines the feasibility and profitability of utilizing surplus electricity for Bitcoin mining. Surplus electricity refers to the remaining electricity after net metering, which can be repurposed for Bitcoin mining to improve Korea Electric Power Corporation's (KEPCO) energy resource efficiency and alleviate its debt challenges. Net metering (or net energy metering) is an electricity billing mechanism that allows consumers who generate some or all of their own electricity to use that electricity when they want, rather than when it is produced. Using the latest Bitcoin miner, the Antminer S21 XP Hyd, the study evaluates daily Bitcoin mining when operating at 30,565 and 45,439 units, incorporating Bitcoin network hash rates to assess profitability. To examine profitability, the Random Forest Regressor and Long Short-Term Memory models were used to predict the Bitcoin price. The analysis shows that the use of excess electricity for Bitcoin mining not only generates economic revenue, but also minimizes energy loss, reduces debt, and resolves unsettled payment issues for KEPCO. This study empirically investigates and analyzes the integration of electricity surplus in South Korea with bitcoin mining for the first time. The findings highlight the potential to strengthen the financial stability of KEPCO and demonstrate the feasibility of Bitcoin mining. In addition, this research serves as a foundational resource for future advancements in the Bitcoin mining industry and the efficient use of energy resources.

Title: External reference pricing versus price controls under endogenous product quality
Authors: Difei Geng, Kamal Saggi
Abstract: Motivated by the high prices of branded/patented pharmaceuticals in many parts of the world, this paper analyzes price regulations in a two-country (home and foreign) model where a single home firm serves both markets and its R&D investment determines product quality. We study two types of price regulations: direct price controls (PCs) and external reference pricing (ERP) under which the price that the firm is permitted to charge locally depends upon its price abroad. We show that although ERP undermines R&D incentives, its implementation can raise home welfare. However, home's optimal ERP policy is too restrictive from a joint welfare perspective. Furthermore, if the foreign market is subject to a PC, home prefers ERP to a PC due to strategic considerations that come into play due to the international price linkage created by ERP.

Title: Managing acceptability and eliciting weights for hesitant fuzzy preference relations with additive consistency
Authors: Yejun Xu, Yihua Chang, Lei Qiu
Affiliations: Laboratory of Computation and Analytics of Complex Management Systems (CACMS), Tianjin University; Guangdong Research Center for Rural Policy; College of Management and Economics, Tianjin University; Business School, Hohai University

Authors: Stefan Silva, José Crispim
