Title: Order retrieval in a compact storage system with side access
Authors: Malte Fliedner, Julian Golak, Yağmur Gül, Simone Neumann
Affiliations: Institute of Operations Management, University of Hamburg Business School; Institute of Sustainable Logistics and Mobility, University of Hamburg Business School

Title: Capacity investment with inventory: a path-dependent real options model under multi-factor demand process
Authors: Anna Maria Gambaro, Ioannis Kyriakou, Gianluca Fusai
Abstract: In this paper, we develop a stochastic optimization framework for production capacity planning that integrates inventory management and demand backlogging in a discrete-time, dynamic newsvendor-type setting. Our model explicitly accounts for both inventory storage and demand shortage, incorporates revenues and costs within the plant’s cash flow structure, and treats profit as a function of stochastic factors, including commodity prices and demand, with the latter evolving according to a Markov multi-factor process. We contribute to the literature in two key ways. First, we develop a joint capacity and inventory optimization problem to capture the dependence of inventory levels on both the system state and the time-weighted sum of values along the demand path. Second, to efficiently address the resulting path-dependence, we introduce a tree-based method. Subsequently, using empirically calibrated models, we evaluate profitability under different scenarios, with and without inventory management, for varying holding and backlog cost parameters. By recasting the joint problem as a real options model that depends on cumulative demand, we provide a unified and tractable framework that captures both the operational complexity and the financial flexibility involved in capacity investment decisions under uncertainty.

Title: The individual‐team discontinuity effect on institutional choices: Experimental evidence in voluntary public goods provision
Authors: Kenju Kamei, Katy Tabero
Affiliations: Faculty of Economics Keio University Minato‐ku Tokyo Japan; Department of Politics and International Relations University of Southampton Southampton UK
Abstract: Abstract A laboratory experiment finds that teams acting as a decision‐making unit through communication behave more efficiently than individuals. Decision‐making units vote on formal and informal sanctions in a repeated public goods dilemma. When a formal scheme is selected, teams vote for deterrent sanction rates more frequently than individuals. When an informal scheme is selected, teams inflict costly punishment more frequently toward low contributors. As such, teams sustain cooperation more efficaciously than individuals. The results underscore the effectiveness of utilizing teams as a decision‐making unit in organizations in combating moral hazard, such as free riding.

Title: Ecological macroeconomics models? Caveat emptor
Authors: Lieke A. Melsen, Andrea Saltelli
Abstract: Ecological Macroeconomic Integrated Assessment Models (EM-IAMs) have emerged as tools for exploring post-growth narratives and challenging the dominant discourse of continuous economic growth. Their use may be strategically advantageous: by employing modelling approaches that are epistemically legitimate within economics, EM-IAMs can contest the growth paradigm with their own tools. Yet, the framing of socio-ecological processes in EM-IAMs, through quantification and evaluative logics, risks interfering with the other goal of EM-IAMs; to address social inequality and injustices. As such, EM-IAMs risk operating as what ecologist Langdon Winner coined as ‘conceptual Trojan horse’. We question whether EM-IAMs may truly provide “robust modelling tools to explore alternative future scenarios, enabling the ex-ante evaluation of direct and indirect effects of policies on well-being, employment, and the ecosystem” (Ecological Economics, 2025). Our doubts rest upon complexity that does not reduce uncertainty, the politics of model simplification, the limitations of EM-IAM models for aspects that resist quantification, the reinforcement of historical power imbalances, and, ultimately, the performative effects of models themselves. We suggest that, rather than extending EM-IAMs to incorporate well-being analysis, we should adopt a different approach to modelling, learning from ecological values; appreciating diversity, variability in space and time, self-regulation, and entanglements.

Title: Economic impacts of pasture degradation at the municipal level: Evidence from Minas Gerais, Brazil
Authors: Amanda Camargos de Moura, Diogo Nepomuceno Cosenza, Rafael Faria de Abreu Campos, José Marinaldo Gleriani, Talles Bhering de Matos, Vivian Silva Santos, Mikaely Vasconcelos Paulo
Abstract: Pasture degradation represents a major challenge to the sustainability of Brazilian livestock production, with impacts that go beyond environmental damage and extend to economic and social dimensions. Few studies have sought to assess the magnitude of these impacts, particularly at the municipal level. Accordingly, this study aimed to quantify the effects of pasture degradation on municipal economies between 2000 and 2022. The case study focused on municipalities in the state of Minas Gerais, which is known for its long-standing tradition in livestock production. We used a methodological approach combining fixed-effects panel data econometric models to assess economic impacts and local Moran's I spatial autocorrelation analysis to identify spatial patterns of degradation. The econometric analysis indicated that pasture degradation had a negative impact on key economic indicators, such as GDP per capita and production values in major agribusiness sectors. The spatial analysis revealed critical clusters of high degradation and low economic productivity, especially in eastern Minas Gerais. Overall, the findings suggest that the restoration of degraded pastures, supported by public policies such as the Low-Carbon Agriculture plan (“ABC Plan”) and the 2012 Forest Code is essential not only for meeting environmental targets but also as a strategy to enhance municipal economic and productive performance.

Title: Column-and-row generation for integrated berth allocation and quay crane assignment considering crew scheduling
Authors: Xueting He, Jianyi Zhao, Bingying Zhao, Lu Zhen
Abstract: This study investigates the integrated scheduling problem of berth allocation, quay crane (QC) assignment, and crew scheduling in container terminals. The problem incorporates crew-related operational characteristics, including crew assignment constraints, shift requirements, heterogeneous handling rates, and administrative inspection time windows. A mixed-integer linear programming model is developed to jointly optimize vessel berthing decisions, QC assignment, and crew scheduling, with the objective of minimizing vessel departure penalty costs. To solve the proposed large-scale optimization problem, a tailored column-and-row generation algorithm is developed to address the computational challenges arising from the integrated decision structure and continuous berth positioning decisions. Computational results based on practical terminal settings demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of the proposed algorithm. Further analyses reveal that crew scheduling decisions significantly influence QC utilization and vessel departure delays, highlighting the importance of integrating crew team considerations into terminal resource planning.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Train rescheduling under unidirectional disruptions: A status-driven dynamic rolling optimization framework
Authors: Xiaoyu Hao, Fangsheng Wang, Rudong Yang, Ruihua Xu, Andrea D’Ariano
Abstract: Unidirectional disruptions in metro systems often evolve dynamically, with uncertain duration and continuously updated operational status, posing significant challenges for real-time train rescheduling. Conventional time-driven rolling-horizon optimization methods update rescheduling plans at fixed intervals, which may delay responses to irregular status changes and cause unnecessary recalculations. To address these limitations, this study proposes a status-driven dynamic rolling optimization framework that transforms the rolling optimization paradigm from time-driven to status-driven, where recalculation is triggered immediately by disruption status updates. Within this framework, a coordinated timetable-rolling stock rescheduling model is developed based on the reconstructed train-service structure, with explicit consideration of limited turn-around capacity and fine-grained modeling of train routing conflicts during the turn-around process at origin stations. To achieve real-time computational performance, a Time-Domain Decomposition and Overlapping (TDO) algorithm is proposed as a fast solution approach. A real-world case study based on peak-hour operations of Shanghai Metro Line 2 demonstrates that the proposed framework can rapidly generate complete and globally coherent rescheduling plans following each disruption status updating. The results confirm that the proposed framework provides a resilient, adaptive, and practically implementable decision-support tool for metro rescheduling under dynamically evolving unidirectional disruptions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Integrating circular economy strategies enhances carbon mitigation in China’s passenger vehicle electrification
Authors: Yijing Zhu, Haotian Zheng, Zhencheng Xing, Xiang Liu, Yifan Liu, Bowen Chu, Fengqi You, Haikun Wang
Abstract: As passenger vehicle fleets turn over, lifecycle emissions shift from road transport to the energy and manufacturing sectors, posing new environmental and resource challenges. We propose a fleet-level framework, incorporating dynamic material flow analysis with lifecycle assessment to capture regional and temporal dynamics behind electrification in China. Relative to the baseline scenario, early circular economy implementation could reduce ∼ 50% lifecycle CO 2 emissions in 2030. By 2060, integrated strategies could reduce annual fleet lifecycle CO 2 emissions by 33%–38%, while recycled lithium could meet 89%–100% of battery demand, complementing the 349.9 Mt CO 2 annual reduction achieved by energy-related actions. Substantial regional variations reflect differences in electricity mix, fleet turnover, and local conditions, with Northeast China benefiting more from energy-related actions due to coal-based electricity, whereas the Southwest favors circular economy strategies. Overall, while energy-related actions are effective long-term countermeasures, ambitious circular economy strategies are critical to advancing environmental and resource synergies.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: From commitment to implementation: policy pathways for green shipping corridors
Authors: Hanwen Fan, Zaili Yang
Abstract: Despite rapid growth in green shipping corridor (GSC) commitment, the translation of policy ambitions into operational practice remains deeply uneven across regions. Addressing this policy-critical gap, this study investigates the structural bottlenecks that impede GSC implementation through a comparative analysis of global and regional development trajectories. By integrating text mining with complex network analysis, the study systematically identifies and maps how bottleneck configurations diverge across institutional and geographic contexts. The findings reveal that GSC development is not a uniform transition process, but a regionally differentiated and stage-dependent system requiring targeted policy responses. Critically, the study derives evidence-based, region-specific policy insights that are difficult to capture through conventional approaches, offering actionable guidance for policymakers seeking to close the gap between regulatory ambition and corridor-level realization. The findings will support stakeholders in designing differentiated policy interventions and advancing the transition of GSCs from conceptual commitments to practical implementation.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Optimizing battery management in drone delivery under uncertainty: a decomposition-based Markov decision process approach
Authors: Ali Tolooie, Ashesh Kumar Sinha
Abstract: This study addresses the operational challenges in drone logistics, focusing on the optimization of recharging stations, which are essential components of efficient drone delivery systems. We develop strategies for efficient battery management, optimal charging times, and effective inventory control under variable conditions such as fluctuating demand and variable flight and charging times. Our methodology is based on Markov decision process (MDP) models that optimize operations at drone recharging stations, taking into account factors such as battery charging strategies, inventory management, and operational conditions. We provide structural action-comparison conditions that interpret the optimal charging policy and its threshold-type switching behavior. To scale the resulting high-dimensional MDP, we develop a problem-structured decomposition based on steady-state coupling, implemented as an iterative fixed-point procedure. The method partitions the model into interacting lower-dimensional subproblems (MDPs and/or Markov chains) and updates their linking quantities to consistency. We analyze its convergence, showing that the coupling reduces to a one-dimensional fixed-point map and identifying the condition under which the iteration reaches a unique solution at a geometric rate. Benchmarks against the full MDP (where tractable) quantify the solution gap and show substantial computational savings while preserving the threshold structure of the charging policy. Additional experiments characterize how demand intensity, flight dynamics, and holding/backorder costs shift the optimal charging mix and steady-state congestion. The analysis provides practical guidance for battery management at drone-delivery recharging stations, together with a tractable decomposition framework for analyzing similar large-scale systems that couple inventory control with queueing dynamics.

Title: On dynamic income taxation and absolute inequality
Authors: Oriol Carbonell-Nicolau
Abstract: This paper evaluates income tax schedules by their ability to reduce absolute inequality in a dynamic setting. Classical static absolute-equalization criteria permit a broad class of nonlinear tax schedules, but they do not assess whether a tax system mitigates changes in inequality over time. We introduce Dynamic Absolute Equalization and show that a continuous tax schedule satisfies this criterion if and only if it is affine, with a marginal tax rate between zero and one and a nonpositive intercept. Dynamic equalization thus imposes a substantially sharper restriction than static absolute equalization.

Title: I Want My Country Back! British Euroscepticism after the Eastern European Enlargement
Authors: Edoardo Cefalà
Abstract: Did immigration from Eastern Europe increase Euroscepticism in Britain? This study examines how this migration wave influenced British Euroscepticism. Using longitudinal survey data and an instrumental variable strategy, I provide causal evidence that the inflow of Eastern European migrants led to increased Eurosceptic attitudes. The migration inflow also increased comparative national attachment and perceived crime risk.

Title: School timing, sleep, and adolescent behavior: Evidence from lottery-assigned start times
Authors: Nicolás A. Roig
Abstract: Double-shift school systems assign some adolescents to early-morning and others to afternoon schooling, yet causal evidence on the consequences of such large timing differences remains limited. I study a selective public middle school in Argentina, where the outcome of a public lottery determines a 7:30 a.m. or 1:15 p.m. start time for up to three years. Unlike the relatively modest schedule changes studied in most prior work, the lottery shifts the school day by nearly six hours while holding curriculum, facilities, and school-day length fixed, identifying reduced-form effects of school timing. Afternoon schooling increases self-reported night sleep by nearly an hour and reduces the share sleeping at most seven hours by 34 percentage points from a 65% baseline. Boys also gain total daily sleep, whereas morning-shift girls offset their shorter nights with longer naps, leaving total daily sleep unchanged. These differences largely disappear before non-school days. Behavioral responses diverge sharply by gender: afternoon assignment reduces boys’ aggressive or delinquent behavior, especially vandalism, but increases girls’ substance use initiation. Together with changes in extracurricular and social activities, these contrasting responses caution against interpreting school timing through a single channel such as sleep. In double-shift systems, school timing is thus a behavioral design choice, not merely a capacity tool.

Title: Beyond GDP: Quantifying heterogeneous impact of climate change on social progress
Authors: Naveen Kumar
Abstract: This study examines the relationship between well-being and temperature across 167 countries from 1990 to 2019, employing the Social Progress Index (SPI) as a measure of well-being and social progress. Using a fixed-effects panel data framework, I study temperature impacts on social progress by modelling local and global weather anomalies simultaneously, capturing both within-country temporal and global climate variation. First, a statistically significant negative relationship exists between annual temperature anomalies and well-being, with a 1 °C global (local) mean temperature deviation leading to a 0.8068 (0.0929) point decline, respectively. Second, annual precipitation anomalies have no statistically significant effect on the SPI. Third, an increase in temperature anomaly has a more adverse impact in winter and spring than in other seasons. Fourth, poorer regions, hotter climates,global south, and countries with weak institutions are disproportionately affected by temperature deviations. Fifth, the impact of temperature on well-being persists over the medium term, most clearly through the global temperature anomalies.

Title: Do crises integrate or fragment energy transition metals markets? Evidence from a connectedness-based crisis typology
Authors: Abdulla Al-Haddad, Azzam Abu-Rayash
Abstract: This paper develops a two-dimensional crisis typology that classifies the impact of major crisis episodes on return spillover connectedness across energy transition metals (ETM) markets. Using daily data for 17 metals, spanning base metals, precious metals, battery metals, and technology metals, and the rolling-window Diebold–Yılmaz (2012) connectedness framework, the paper classifies 11 crisis events between 2017 and 2025 along two orthogonal axes: the direction of the connectedness shift (integration vs. fragmentation) and the stability of the response (volatile vs. stable), with the latter benchmarked against a bootstrap-derived threshold from pre-crisis markets. The typology reveals a fragmentation paradox: supply-side shocks (armed conflicts and bilateral trade restrictions) consistently decrease market connectedness, while demand-side shocks (pandemics, monetary tightening, and financial crises) consistently increase it. This dichotomy, which is robustly preserved across all 25 event-study window specifications, challenges the prevailing assumption in the connectedness literature that crises uniformly amplify systemic risk through heightened spillovers. The mechanism is grounded in the distinction between common-factor and idiosyncratic transmission channels: supply disruptions affect individual metals asymmetrically based on their geographic exposure, fragmenting the co-movement structure, while demand shocks operate through common macroeconomic channels that drive all metals together. The typology has implications for strategic reserves policy, portfolio hedging, and energy transition risk assessment, suggesting that geopolitical risk to critical minerals supply chains is more modular than the contagion hypothesis predicts.

Title: Sustainable railway maintenance and renewal planning using lexicographic optimization under uncertainty
Authors: Malak Saiem, Faicel Hnaien, Hichem Snoussi, Brice Nelain, Anaïs Menetrier
Abstract: Sustainable maintenance planning in railway infrastructure requires balancing safety, cost, and carbon emissions, while accounting for uncertainty in asset degradation and limited track access windows. Existing optimization approaches typically handle cost and reliability but rarely integrate explicit CO 2 objectives or provide scalable uncertainty treatments. This study develops a mixed-integer linear programming framework that lexicographically prioritizes emissions reduction over maintenance cost and enforces safety via joint chance constraints derived from predictive degradation distributions. Two tractable formulation were developed and compared: a cumulative-distribution-function (CDF) based model and a Bonferroni approximation. Experiments on industrial maintenance instances across multiple reliability levels show that the CDF model yields lower total cost at comparable emissions, whereas the Bonferroni approach substantially reduces computation time, enabling near-real-time re-planning. The results offer clear guidance for practice: use the CDF model when cost efficiency is critical, and the Bonferroni scheme when rapid decision-making is required. The proposed framework is compatible with standard solvers and provides a scalable, data-driven decision-support tool for sustainable rail maintenance planning.

Title: Monopolistic Data Dumping
Authors: Kfir Eliaz, Ran Spiegler
Affiliations: Tel Aviv University and King's College London (email: ); Tel Aviv University and University College London (email: )
Abstract: A profit-maximizing monopolist curates a database for users seeking to learn a parameter. There are two user types: “Nowcasters” wish to learn the parameter's current value, while “forecasters” target its long-run value. Data storage involves a constant marginal cost. The monopolist designs a menu of contracts described by fees and data-access levels. The profit-maximizing menu offers full access to historical data, while current data are fully provided to nowcasters but may be withheld from forecasters. Compared to the social optimum, the monopolist keeps too much historical data, keeps too little current data, and may store too much data overall. (JEL C53, C80, D42, L12, L86)

Title: Strategic Limit Orders and Intertemporal Price Dispersion
Authors: Suman Banerjee, Ravi Jagannathan, Kai Wang
Affiliations: Stevens Institute of Technology (email: ); Northwestern University and NBER (email: ); Northwestern University (email: )
Abstract: We study a two-period commodity market with competitive consumers and Cournot sellers. Without speculation, equilibrium is stationary. A storage-capable, strategically large speculator can profitably create deterministic intertemporal price dispersion using standard order types. A period-1 limit buy order flattens residual demand, induces higher output, and yields a low purchase price. With mandatory liquidation, resale remains below the no-speculation price but above the purchase price, so the speculator profits; consumers gain and sellers lose. With free disposal and a stop-loss, the period-2 price can exceed the benchmark, benefiting sellers but harming consumers. (JEL D43, G12, G14, G41, Q02)

Title: Learning in the Marriage Market: The Economics of Dating
Authors: Yair Antler, Daniel Bird, Daniel Fershtman
Affiliations: Coller School of Management, Tel Aviv University, and CEPR (email: ); The Eitan Berglas School of Economics, Tel Aviv University (email: ); Tel Aviv University, Emory University, and CEPR (email: )
Abstract: This paper develops a search-and-matching model where potential partners can learn about their compatibility as a couple by spending time together (interpreted as dating). We show that a steady-state equilibrium exists and characterize its induced dating patterns. In equilibrium, highly attractive individuals are more selective. We derive conditions under which equilibria induce positive assortative matching and show that even when these conditions hold, the socially optimal outcome can exhibit negative assortative matching. Finally, the framework is applied to study the effect of recent advances in search technologies on dating patterns and the connection between dating and interracial segregation. (JEL C78, D83, J12)

Title: Competing Diffusions in a Social Network
Authors: Arthur Campbell, C. Matthew Leister, Philip Ushchev, Yves Zenou
Affiliations: Monash University, Australia (email: ); ECARES, ULB, Belgium (email: ); Monash University, Australia, and CEPR (email: )
Abstract: We develop a model of competing diffusions of goods on a social network. There are two types of goods and individuals: mass-market and niche-market. There is a unique stable steady state, and the adoption of a mass-market good is greater than its population share. Greater connectivity and homophily will concurrently increase the prevalence of niche-market goods. If there is a strategic agent who wants to promote a niche good, she will invest more in influencing activities than one promoting mass-market goods. When individuals choose their degree of homophily, niche-market individuals exhibit greater homophily than mass-market ones. (JEL D83, D85, L86, Z13)

Title: Symmetric Equilibrium in Pre-auction Investment
Authors: Daniel Quint, Fuhito Kojima
Affiliations: Department of Economics, University of Wisconsin-Madison (email: ); University of Tokyo (email: )
Abstract: We characterize the symmetric equilibria of a pre-auction game of investment in an internet ad auction environment. For a wide class of auction formats, we show a symmetric equilibrium exists for the pre-auction investment game, is essentially unique, and is the same for all auction formats in the class. We give sufficient conditions for the symmetric equilibrium to be in pure strategies and to achieve the efficient level of investment. Finally, we show comparative statics results with respect to a variety of parameters. (JEL D44, D82)

Title: Reputation and Competitive Selection
Authors: Joyee Deb, Jack Fanning
Affiliations: Department of Economics, New York University (email: ); Department of Economics, Brown University (email: )
Abstract: We demonstrate how selection in competitive markets can impede long-run reputational incentives. In our model, competent firms can exert costly effort to improve expected product quality, but inept firms cannot. With low entry barriers, we show competent firms cannot persistently exert effort, despite bounded memory. Such effort would cause consumers to select firms based on reputations for competence, eventually selecting a monopolist with an arbitrarily high reputation, which has no incentive for effort. More generally, reputation-based selection rules out long-run effort, which undermines the basis for such selection. Intermediate entry barriers provide stronger reputational incentives than low or high barriers. (JEL D21, D40, D82, L15)

Title: Optimal Procurement Design: A Reduced-Form Approach
Authors: Kun Zhang
Affiliations: Auburn University and University of Queensland (email: ).
Abstract: Standard procurement models assume that the buyer knows the quality of the good at the time of procurement; however, in many settings, the quality is learned only long after the transaction. We study procurement problems in which the buyer's valuation of the supplied good depends directly on its quality, which is unverifiable and unobservable to the buyer. For a broad class of procurement problems, we identify procurement mechanisms maximizing any weighted average of the buyer's expected payoff and social surplus. The optimal mechanism can be implemented via an auction that restricts sellers to submitting bids within specific intervals. (JEL D44, D82, H57, L15)

Title: The Perils of Overreaction
Authors: Konstantin von Beringe, Mark Whitmeyer
Affiliations: Arizona State University (email: )
Abstract: To study updating rules, we consider the problem of a malevolent principal screening an imperfectly Bayesian agent. We uncover a fundamental dichotomy between underreaction and overreaction to information. If, for some signal realization, the agent's updating rule produces a posterior that lies outside the convex hull of the Bayesian posteriors induced by the signal structure, she can be exploited by the principal without bound: Her ex ante expected loss can be made arbitrarily large. In contrast, an agent who underreacts—whose posterior after each signal realization lies between the prior and the corresponding Bayesian posterior—cannot be exploited at all. (JEL D82, D83)

Title: Land, Wealth, and Taxation
Authors: Roberto Brunetti, Carl Gaigné, Fabien Moizeau
Affiliations: LEMMA, Université Paris-Panthéon-Assas (email: ); INRAE, SMART, Rennes, France; Laval University, CREATE, Quebec, Canada; and CNRS-TEPP, France (email: ); Univ Rennes, CNRS, CREM-UMR6211, F-35000 Rennes, France (email: )
Abstract: This paper examines the role of land in wealth dynamics and its consequences for efficiency and inequality. We focus on the interplay among agents’ bidding for location, mortgage market imperfections, and inheritance in a model in which agents leave to their heirs financial bequests and their housing wealth. The borrowing constraint generates a housing return premium and spatial wealth sorting, which translate into persistent wealth inequality. Since altruism and the borrowing constraint distort land price formation, we show that taxing land rent transmitted between generations is optimal. Land taxation cannot be disconnected from taxation on intergenerational wealth transfers. (JEL D31, D64, H71, Q24, R23, R31, R52)

Title: Electoral Campaign Attacks: Theory and Evidence
Authors: Marcos Y. Nakaguma, Danilo Souza
Affiliations: Sao Paulo School of Economics, FGV (email: ); University of Sao Paulo (email: )
Abstract: This paper studies the determinants of electoral campaign attacks. We first propose a model to examine the main factors that influence candidates' decisions to attack. Our theoretical analysis yields a number of predictions that we test using information from “right of reply” lawsuits filed in Brazil. Our empirical analysis exploits a regression discontinuity design based on virtual ties between second- and third-place candidates to show that candidates with an electoral advantage are more likely to receive an attack. We then exploit another discontinuity to show that the patterns of campaign attacks differ significantly under single- and dual-ballot plurality systems. (JEL D72, D74, K16)

Title: Cognitive Ability and Perceived Disagreement in Learning
Authors: Piotr Evdokimov, Umberto Garfagnini
Affiliations: University of Surrey (email: ).
Abstract: Do agents believe they agree more with others over time? This paper explores how individuals perceive the belief-updating behavior of others and the resulting disagreement in a sequential experiment with public information. We uncover a persistent gap in the perception of disagreement as a function of cognitive ability. Higher cognitive ability correlates with less perceived disagreement, although the average subject underestimates the extent of actual disagreement. Information about a partner's cognitive ability only impacts perceived disagreement when the partner has a low test score. Our findings highlight the roles of overconfidence and cognitive projection in shaping these perceptions. (JEL C91, D12, D83, D91)

Title: Degree-Weighted Social Learning
Authors: Chen Cheng, Xiao Han, Xin Tong, Yusheng Wu, Yiqing Xing
Affiliations: School of Economics, Renmin University of China (email: ); School of Management, University of Science and Technology of China (email: ); Faculty of Business and Economics, the University of Hong Kong (email: ); Department of Mathematics, University of Southern California (email: ); China Center for Economic Research, NSD, Peking University (email: )
Abstract: We study social learning in which agents weight neighbors' opinions differently based on their degrees, capturing situations in which agents place more trust in well-connected individuals or, conversely, discount their influence. We derive asymptotic properties of learning outcomes in large stochastic networks and analyze how the weighting rule affects societal wisdom and convergence speed. We find that assigning greater weight to higher-degree neighbors harms wisdom but has a non-monotonic effect on convergence speed, depending on the diversity of views within high- and low-degree groups, highlighting a potential trade-off between convergence speed and wisdom. (JEL D83, D85, Z13)

Title: Targeted Advertising in Elections
Authors: Maria Titova
Affiliations: Department of Economics, Vanderbilt University (email: )
Abstract: How does targeted advertising influence electoral outcomes? This paper presents a one-dimensional spatial model of voting in which a privately informed challenger persuades voters to support him over the status quo. I show that targeted advertising enables the challenger to persuade voters with opposing preferences and swing elections decided by such voters. Ex ante commitment power is unnecessary—the challenger succeeds by strategically revealing different pieces of verifiable information to different voters. Publicizing all political ads would mitigate the negative effects of targeted advertising and help voters collectively make the right choice. (JEL D72, D82, D83, M37)

Title: Innovation and Competition on a Rugged Technological Landscape
Authors: Steven Callander, Nicolas S. Lambert, Niko Matouschek
Affiliations: Stanford Graduate School of Business, Stanford University (email: ); Department of Economics, University of Southern California (email: ); Kellogg School of Management, Northwestern University (email: )
Abstract: We integrate innovation into Hotelling's classic model of spatial competition. Potential entrants arrive sequentially and choose whether and where to innovate. They can innovate beyond the frontier, expanding the boundary of the market, or within a niche between incumbent products. Product quality is learned only after introduction, and uncertainty increases with novelty. Innovation on a rugged technological landscape is irregular, with frequent changes in direction and cycles between frontier and niche innovation. The ruggedness of the technological landscape itself deters innovation, generating fewer entrants, less product differentiation, narrower markets, and more intense competition than under certainty. (JEL D11, D21, D83, L11, L25, O31)

Title: Recurring Auctions with Costly Entry: Theory and Evidence
Authors: Shanglyu Deng, Qiyao Zhou
Affiliations: Department of Economics, University of Macau (email: ); Department of Economics, Wilfrid Laurier University (email: )
Abstract: Recurring auctions are widely used to sell durable assets, with follow-up auctions held for unsold items. We investigate such auctions theoretically and empirically. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that recurring auctions outperform single-round auctions when buyers face entry costs, enhancing efficiency and revenue due to sorted entry of potential buyers. Optimal reserve price sequences are characterized. Empirical findings from home foreclosure auctions in China reveal significant annual gains in efficiency (US$3.40 billion, 16.60 percent) and revenue (US$2.97 billion, 15.92 percent) using recurring auctions compared with single-round auctions. Implementing optimal reserve prices can further improve efficiency (3.35 percent) and revenue (3.06 percent). (JEL D44, D82, R31)

Title: Competitive Bottlenecks and Platform Spillovers
Authors: Tat-How Teh, Julian Wright
Affiliations: Division of Economics, Nanyang Technological University (email: ); Department of Economics, National University of Singapore (email: )
Abstract: We provide a general framework to analyze competition between oligopolistic platforms in competitive bottleneck settings, allowing for pricing and nonprice design choices by platforms, and post-participation buyer-seller decisions. We show that equilibrium choices by platforms are distorted against sellers’ interests in a way harmful to welfare (e.g., setting excessive commission fees), and that an increase in the number of competing platforms can exacerbate this distortion. We also characterize how buyer-side heterogeneity in interaction benefits, partial market coverage, platform asymmetry, and cross-platform spillovers further amplify or mitigate welfare distortions. Based on our findings, we discuss policy implications for mobile app platforms. (JEL D43, L13, L25, L96)

Title: Front Matter
A beta-binomial algorithm for forecasting the price of crude oil
Authors: Nima Nonejad
Abstract: I combine the Bayesian beta-binomial model with the dynamic forecast rotation methodology analyzed in depth in Zhu and Timmermann (2022) to suggest an algorithm for forecasting the price of crude oil out-of-sample. The algorithm performs real-time selection between the benchmark’s point forecast and a combination of point forecasts produced by predictive regressions employing economic variables. In terms of both population-level predictability and finite-sample point forecast accuracy, the algorithm outperforms the end-of-month price of crude oil random-walk model of Ellwanger and Snudden (2023) , as well as other commonly applied point forecast combination techniques. Further analysis attributes this success to the suggested algorithm’s ability to identify periods (windows) of relative predictability ex ante. While heterogeneous in their frequency, duration, and magnitude of the afforded net predictive gains, these windows tend to emerge in the wake of business, macroeconomic, financial, and geopolitical shocks.

Title: The Effect of a Miscarriage Compared to a Completed Pregnancy on Mental Health Care Use, Labour Market and Family Outcomes
Authors: Pieter Bakx, Pilar García‐Gómez, Sara Rellstab
Affiliations: Erasmus School of Health Policy and Management Erasmus University Rotterdam Rotterdam the Netherlands; Erasmus Center for Health Economics Rotterdam Rotterdam the Netherlands; Erasmus School of Economics Erasmus University Rotterdam Rotterdam the Netherlands; Tinbergen Institute Rotterdam the Netherlands; Università Della Svizzera italiana Lugano Switzerland
Abstract: ABSTRACT Miscarriages occur in about 15% of recognised pregnancies and often cause grief and stress. We investigate the effect of a miscarriage on mental health care use, labour market and family outcomes of women and their partners using an event study framework applied to Dutch linked administrative data. After a miscarriage, women's use of mental health care temporarily increase compared to before the miscarriage, while their partner's use is unaffected. Furthermore, miscarriages affect labour market trajectories and reduce the probability of living together. Results are similar when comparing the effects of a miscarriage with the effects of having a child using a matched sample of women with a completed pregnancy.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: Prophet Secretary Against the Online Optimal
Authors: Paul Dütting, Evangelia Gergatsouli, Rojin Rezvan, Yifeng Teng, Alexandros Tsigonias-Dimitriadis
Affiliations: Google Switzerland GmbH, 8004 Zürich, Switzerland; University of Wisconsin–Madison, Madison, Wisconsin 53706; University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas 78712; Google Research, USA, New York, New York 10011; Universidad de Chile, Santiago 8330111, Chile
Abstract: We study the prophet secretary problem, a well-studied variant of the classic prophet inequality, where values are drawn from independent known distributions but arrive in uniformly random order. Upon seeing a value at each step, the decision maker has to either select it and stop or irrevocably discard it. Traditionally, the chosen benchmark is the expected reward of the prophet, who knows all the values in advance and can always select the maximum one. In this work, we study the prophet secretary problem against a less pessimistic but equally well-motivated benchmark: the online optimal. Here, the main goal is to find polynomial-time algorithms that guarantee near-optimal expected reward. Our main result is a polynomial-time approximation scheme for this problem. The approximation scheme builds on careful discretization and bundling arguments, in combination with a novel “front-loading” technique that helps reduce the number of decisions the algorithm has to make.

Title: Public Signals in Affine Network Congestion Games with Uncertain Free-Flow Times
Authors: Svenja M. Griesbach, Martin Hoefer, Max Klimm, Tim Koglin
Affiliations: Department of Computer Science, RWTH Aachen University, 52074 Aachen, Germany; Institute of Mathematics, Technische Universität Berlin, 10587 Berlin, Germany; and Department of Economics, Sciences Po, 75007 Paris, France
Abstract: Travel times in road networks are subject to stochastic uncertainty resulting from various parameters. A benevolent mobility service provider observing the actual travel times from data may use its informational advantage to steer the traffic equilibrium in a favorable direction through a processs known as signaling or Bayesian persuasion. Previous work has shown that the underlying signaling problem can be NP-hard to approximate better than [Formula: see text], even for static Wardrop flows with affine cost functions with stochastic offsets. In contrast, we show that in this case, the signaling problem is easy for many networks. First, we tightly characterize the class of single-commodity networks in which full information revelation is always an optimal signaling strategy. Second, we construct a reduction from optimal signaling to computing an optimal collection of active edges for the Wardrop equilibrium. For two states, this allows us to efficiently compute an optimal signaling scheme whenever the number of different active edge sets is bounded by a polynomial in the input size. Using a cell decomposition technique, we extend the approach to a polynomial-time algorithm for multicommodity parallel-edge networks provided that both the number of commodities and states are constant. Funding: This work was supported by Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft EXC-2046/1 [Grant 390685689] and Ho 3831/9-1 [Grant 514505843].

Title: Reducing carbon emission from the source. Green purchasing response to environmental regulation: How executives’ perceptions of incentives, executive age, and ownership type matter?
Authors: Hesong Ren, Nengmin Wang, Zhengwen He, Bin Jiang
Abstract: Green purchasing (GP) serves as a crucial pathway for reducing supply chain carbon emissions; environmental policies such as command and control (CAC) and market-based incentive (MBI) are implemented to promote GP. However, it is still unclear whether CAC and MBI enhance GP. Based on the stimulus-organism-response theory, this study addresses this issue and proposes that CAC and MBI influence executives' perceptions of incentives that increase GP. Our results from structural equation modeling and artificial neural network show that CAC and MBI positively influence perceptions of political incentives (PPI) and perceptions of wealth incentives (PWI), both PPI and PWI positively affect GP. Executive age strengthens the effects of CAC on PWI and MBI on PPI. The multigroup analysis between state-owned enterprises (SOEs) and private-owned enterprises (POEs) reveals that parts of the above relationships differ between SOEs and POEs. By revealing the “black box” of how environmental regulation impacts GP, our research findings provide a perspective for reducing supply chain carbon emissions by enhancing firms’ GP. Furthermore, by highlighting the importance of PPI in SOEs and PWI in POEs, our findings provide nuanced support for effectively enhancing GP in different ownership-type firms. From a managerial perspective, this study provides guidance for firms to tailor executive incentive strategies that drive them to implement GP when responding to environmental policies.

Title: Government positions and climate change: paradigmatic conflict versus consensus in environmental performance
Authors: Detlef Jahn
Abstract: Historically, environmental policy was framed as a fundamental trade-off between economic growth and ecological preservation. Since the mid-1980s, however, this dichotomy has been largely replaced by the paradigm of ecological modernization, which posits that economic growth and environmental protection are mutually reinforcing through concepts like "green growth" and "sustainable development." This shift was accompanied by the assumption that a broad political consensus on these concepts would lead to superior environmental outcomes. Yet, the persistent gap between climate targets and actual emission trends necessitates a critical re-evaluation of this "consensus" approach.,This study empirically examines the impact of ideational positions on climate performance across 36 advanced industrialized democracies from 1990 to 2021. Contrary to the consensus hypothesis, the results demonstrate that governments adopting antagonistic positions on the environment-growth dimension achieve significantly faster reductions in greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions than those holding moderate or consensus-oriented positions. These findings suggest that the depoliticization of climate policy may hinder transformative action, whereas ideological contestation—specifically regarding growth-centric paradigms—appears to be a key driver for effective emission reduction.

Title: Optimising toll prices and speed limits for minimising emissions in Zealand, Denmark, using a dynamic multi-region MFD SUE traffic model
Authors: Lawrence Christopher Duncan, Thomas Kjær Rasmussen, David Paul Watling, Ravi Seshadri
Abstract: Reducing emissions from road traffic is important for public health and the environment. One way of reducing emissions is electrifying the vehicle fleet. Full electrification, however, will take many years due to constraints on the production of electric vehicles to meet demand. Another effective way is to encourage or legally enforce travellers to drive fossil fuel cars at desirable intermediate speeds. Few studies, however, have explored the combined optimisation of policy schemes aimed at both increasing vehicle speeds where/when speeds are too low and decreasing speeds where/when speeds are too high. This paper addresses this by, for the first time, exploring the joint optimisation of a tolling scheme and fixed speed limit reduction policy for the minimisation of emissions, in a large-scale case study. A joint travel-time-based toll-price and speed limit optimisation framework is developed that minimises CO 2 and NOx emissions, with a constraint that social welfare is no worse than in the do-nothing scenario. Traffic behaviour is modelled using the dynamic multi-region Macroscopic Fundamental Diagram (MFD) Stochastic User Equilibrium (SUE) model recently introduced in Duncan et al. (2025, 2026), where the elastic demand and departure time choice components are updated to improve behavioural realism. Aggregate emission functions are applied to outputs of the traffic model to estimate dynamic emission levels. The optimisation framework is applied in a large-scale case study of Zealand, Denmark where motorways are treated separately, allowing for the targeting of speed limits where speeds are highest. Results find that both tolling the main area of Copenhagen during peak-hours at 2.62 DKK/min and lowering the maximum speed limit to 91.12 km/h on motorways could yield a 10 % and 5 % reduction in CO 2 and NOx emissions, respectively, without a loss in social welfare from the do-nothing scenario. The speed limit reduction reduces CO 2 emissions the most (achieving a 7 % reduction on motorways), while tolling reduces NOx emissions the most (achieving a 4 % reduction within the tolled urban area). Synergistic effects of the joint policy enforcement are uncovered. Numerical experiments illustrate the joint policy’s impact on car travel demand, departure time choices, route choices, vehicle speeds, and travelling costs. It is also explored how results are affected when considering unequal redistribution of toll revenues, the marginal cost of public funds, increasing the social cost of emissions, specifying inner and outer tolling areas, and adopting a distance-based tolling scheme. Tolling is also compared to increasing fuel tax.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Managing urban transportation carbon emissions through integrated personal and corporate carbon trading systems
Authors: Yong Lyu, Tiande Mo, Fangni Zhang
Abstract: This paper develops a novel emission trading system (ETS) framework for the urban transportation sector that jointly regulates travelers and public transit operators through two interconnected markets: a Personal Trading Platform (PTP) for travelers and a Corporate Trading Platform (CTP) for operators. In the proposed system, the transportation authority allocates carbon credits for a transit operator and three traveler groups: conventional internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicle owners, electric vehicle owners, and vehicle-less travelers. The transit operator determines fares, service frequency, and fleet composition consisting of conventional and electric buses, while travelers choose between private driving and public transit. Travelers’ and the transit operator's credit requirements are determined by the emissions associated with their travel and operational activities, respectively; and credits can be traded in the PTP or CTP markets. We formulate a non-cooperative Stackelberg game in which the transportation authority leads by deciding credit allocations; the transit operator responds with optimal fare and transit service frequency decisions; and travelers make mode choices under user equilibrium with carbon trading. We then extend to a cooperative Nash bargaining game in which the transportation authority and the transit operator jointly optimize allocation and operational decisions against a disagreement point. The existence and uniqueness of the user-PTP equilibrium are examined. The outcomes of these two games are analyzed and compared analytically and numerically. The sensitivity analyses on PTP transaction costs, EV penetration rate, and baseline credit price in CTP are conducted to derive additional insights. The results show that the proposed dual-market PTP-CTP emission trading framework is effective in lowering overall transportation system emission, enhancing transit operator profits and promoting the electrification of public transit.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Human rights economics
Authors: Jose Cuesta, Leja Ejury, Paola Fajardo-Heyward, Natalia Pecorari, Harper Schwab, Bryce Wijesekara
Abstract: This article proposes a theoretical framework that systematically integrates human rights and economic analysis, addressing gaps in previous attempts linking theory and policy. Rather than developing a new theoretical approach, we work within a standard social planner setting in which a social welfare function embeds both fiscal constraints and rights-based valuations, ensuring Pareto-efficient outcomes while guaranteeing minimum rights. Conceptually, we link principles, policy instruments, and outcomes, highlighting shared structures across disciplines and enabling policy design that balances efficiency, equity, and transparency. Empirically, a case study of universal social protection strategies in South Africa illustrates how economic, human rights, and integrated approaches produce different priorities: targeted basic income maximizes fiscal efficiency, the universal transfer maximizes equality and rights, and the integrated perspective favors the expansion of the existing system as the second-most rights-consistent and most cost efficient option. This fully integrated framework demonstrates that human rights economics is not a slogan, nor merely the economics of human rights or rights within economics, but a true integration of both—practically applicable, context-sensitive, and offering a pathway to fiscally sustainable, socially inclusive, and administratively feasible policies.

Title: Estimation of agent-based models using the Wasserstein distance
Authors: Sebastiano Manzan, Lulu Wang
Abstract: We propose a Simulated Minimum Distance (SMD) estimator based on the Wasserstein distance for estimating parameters in economic models with intractable likelihoods, such as Agent-Based Models (ABM). This approach avoids the need for complex likelihood approximations and is robust even when model and data distributions have non-overlapping support. Simulating the two- and three-type Brock and Hommes (1998) asset pricing model, we show that the estimator is more accurate than a likelihood-based Bayesian benchmark, in particular in the estimation of the behavioral parameters. We conclude with an empirical application of the Brock and Hommes (BH) model to S&P 500 data. Overall, the Simulated Wasserstein Minimum Distance Estimator (SWMDE) offers a flexible and computationally efficient tool for structural estimation in models where likelihood-based inference is infeasible or unreliable.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: Reassessing the benefits of European integration and the European Union’s ability to achieve strategic autonomy
Authors: Lionel Fontagné, Yoto V. Yotov
Abstract: European integration is now faced with the question of strategic autonomy. Against this backdrop, this paper has three objectives. First, it uses disaggregated trade data and established empirical methods to assess the benefits of European integration on trade among the members of the European Union (EU) as well as on trade between EU members and non-member countries, including non-members that are part of the Single Market. Second, it evaluates the costs of EU strategic autonomy — implying not trading with “riskier” partners. Third, it asks whether deeper integration within the EU can alleviate these costs. The paper shows that the gains from European integration are substantial, albeit heterogeneous across Member States, non-members, and sectors, and that the costs of strategic autonomy can be offset by deeper, but comparatively more modest, integration efforts within the European Union.

Title: Do black politicians matter? Political leadership and racial composition in top public sector positions
Authors: Fernanda Estevan, Thiago de Lucena, Marcos Y. Nakaguma, Alexandre Rabelo
Abstract: Non-white leaders remain underrepresented in top public-sector positions, and their absence has been linked to persistent racial gaps in the bureaucracy. This paper investigates whether electing a non-white mayor affects the share of non-white managers in the Brazilian public sector. We leverage a close-election regression discontinuity design combined with a novel dataset on candidates’ race, constructed by applying face-classification algorithms to the photographs of all candidates in Brazil's 2004–2016 municipal elections. On average, electing a non-white mayor does not significantly increase the share of non-white managers, although positive effects emerge in elections where the racial contrast between candidates is especially pronounced. We develop a search-theoretic framework of public-sector hiring and document limited differentiation in the observable recruitment pools of white and non-white mayors, together with little systematic evidence of race-contingent hiring standards. Our findings suggest that evidence from the United States may not readily generalize to settings with more fluid racial boundaries and greater overlap in recruitment networks across racial lines.

Title: A Fenchel-Moreau conjugation-based approach for computing the pre-kernel/pre-nucleolus
Authors: Holger I. Meinhardt
Abstract: Computing the (pre-)nucleolus of a coalitional game with transferable utility (TU game) is generally NP-hard. Therefore, no universal polynomial-time algorithm exists. However, polynomial-time algorithms exist for specific game classes. The most general approach in the literature is based on the ellipsoid method and Maschler’s approximation scheme. In contrast, we propose polynomial-time solvability by using a Fenchel-Moreau conjugation-based approach from convex analysis that applies the method of Meinhardt (2013) to compute a pre-kernel element. This method not only allows the computation of the pre-nucleolus for game classes with a singleton pre-kernel with a runtime complexity of 푂(푛 3 ). It also works for game classes with a set-valued pre-kernel whenever the pre-nucleolus is a vertex or a separated point within the pre-kernel set. Finally, we focus on the replication of the pre-nucleolus in the sense of Meinhardt (2024) for a class of related games to demonstrate the versatility of the Fenchel-Moreau conjugation-based approach while referring to group algebra.

Title: Revisiting the price elasticity of charitable giving: Meta-analysis of tax incentives and matching donations
Authors: Gwen-Jiro Clochard, Shubham Dey, Shusaku Sasaki, Taisuke Imai
Abstract: This paper presents the first quantitative meta-analysis of the price elasticity of charitable giving under both rebate and matching schemes. We compile 137 elasticity estimates from 26 experimental papers and synthesize them using random-effects and multilevel models. Charitable giving is highly price-responsive: the pooled meta-analytic mean elasticity of total donations is −1.75, indicating that lowering the effective price of giving substantially increases charitable revenue. Although we observe considerable between-study heterogeneity and some evidence of publication bias, bias-adjusted estimates remain negative. Furthermore, elasticity is substantially more negative under matching (−2.44) than under rebate (−0.73), contradicting the theoretical prediction of equivalence but aligning with the original experimental findings in this literature. The rebate-matching difference is attenuated when moving from laboratory to field settings, although it persists.

Title: A time-expanded network exact algorithm for solving escape interdiction games on transportation networks
Authors: Peter E. Gill, Andreas T. Ernst
Abstract: Consider the problem of optimally coordinating vehicles of the police force of a city in order to capture a suspect fleeing from a recent crime scene. Such a scenario is naturally modelled as an escape interdiction game on a transportation network, where the criminal (attacker) desires to escape to some exit and the police force (defender) desires to interdict them before they reach the exit. An optimal strategy for either player therefore entails a Nash equilibrium, and thus computing one in a timely manner is of interest for law enforcement. Unlike utilising static roadblocks for the duration of the scenario, we allow dynamic movement of multiple police resources throughout the road network but we assume that neither the attacker nor defender has access to real-time location information on the other player, and that the defender may only interdict at nodes. We present theoretical analysis of the game to show that the natural continuous-time version of escape interdiction games cannot be reduced to one using discrete-time without additional assumptions, and that the previously published mixed integer programming formulation of the attacker & defender oracles produces incorrect results in some cases. We also develop new attacker and defender oracles that utilise network flow on a time-expanded network for computing Nash equilibria in a double oracle algorithm. Computational results show our new oracles outperform the existing exact approach from the literature and often finds a provable Nash equilibrium in less time than that of the current state of the art heuristic.

Title: The effectiveness of statutory environmental disclosure: The roles of regulatory supervision and climate risk awareness
Authors: Jinfan Zhi, Yuchen Gao
Abstract: Mandatory environmental disclosure has become an increasingly important policy instrument in global environmental governance, yet evidence on its real effects remains limited. Using China's 2021 statutory environmental disclosure (SED) reform as a quasi-natural experiment, this study examines the impact of the SED policy on corporate environmental governance investment. We use panel data from Chinese A-share-listed firms from 2017 to 2023 and apply a staggered difference-in-differences approach. The results show that the SED policy significantly increases corporate environmental governance investment. The effect is stronger when formal government regulation and informal media oversight operate synergistically and for firms with greater chronic physical risk awareness. It is also more pronounced in cities with weaker local environmental law enforcement or higher local economic growth pressure and among firms with lower financing constraints. The SED policy further improves substantive environmental disclosure and promotes firms' attainment of environmental certification and official recognition. These findings provide new evidence on the governance effects of SED and inform the design of mandatory environmental disclosure as an instrument of information-based environmental regulation.

Title: Women’s missing mobility and the gender gap in higher education: Evidence from Germany’s university expansion
Authors: Barbara Boelmann
Abstract: This paper examines how local universities can help close the gender gap in higher education arising from women’s greater geographic mobility barriers. Using the opening of new universities in the 1960s and 1970s in West German regions which previously lacked universities and individual-level survey data from the National Educational Panel Study (NEPS) for cohorts born 1944–1960, I examine how proximity to universities affects women’s educational decisions. First, I descriptively document women’s low regional mobility in post-war West Germany along with their low educational attainment. Second, in the main causal analysis, I exploit the university expansion in a difference-in-differences (DiD) strategy, comparing regions which experienced a university opening within commuting distance to those where no university was opened. Women benefited more than men from nearby openings, reducing the local gender gap in university education by about 74%. Local universities also affected women’s pre-tertiary education decisions, increasing high school graduation rates. Third, I provide descriptive evidence that universities increased participation not only by reducing moving costs but also through other channels, likely including greater visibility of and information about higher education. This paper highlights how public policy can reduce regional inequality and foster higher education participation, demonstrating that higher-education-stage interventions can influence pre-tertiary decisions and expand the policy toolkit beyond early childhood.

Title: Failures of contingent reasoning in screening decisions
Authors: Gonzalo Arrieta, Maxim Bakhtin
Affiliations: University of Zurich; Analysis Group Inc
Abstract: Abstract Screening decisions—choosing a costly action that reveals information about an unknown quality—can be crucial in various situations, such as hiring workers or designing policies. Choosing whether to screen can be difficult because it requires recognizing and trading off the benefits of information with the costs of getting it. We investigate whether people recognize when the benefits of screening dominate its costs and what causes them to choose otherwise. Our online experiment simulates a hiring scenario with an initial trial task. Participants can first reveal candidates’ quality at a small cost and then choose which candidate to hire. Most participants choose the dominated task that does not reveal the candidates’ quality, and this mistake persists even with experience and feedback. We show that this insufficient screening is driven by failures to anticipate inference and plan the full strategy.

Title: Brave new cities? Governance configurations for sustainable city logistics
Authors: Hugo de Tarragon, Christina Theodoraki
Affiliations: University of Limoges Department of CREOP, , Limoges; Aix-Marseille University IAE Aix-Marseille Graduate School of Management, CERGAM, , Aix-en-Provence, , and Department of Management, School of Business, University of Nicosia, UNIC Athens, Athens, Greece
Abstract: Purpose Despite extensive research and policy efforts, there is still no consensus over the aspects that must be influenced to mitigate the environmental and social impact of city logistics. Existing approaches have primarily focused on optimizing urban freight operations but have struggled to generate lasting and systemic improvements. Building on recent supply chain management (SCM) calls to conceptualize supply chains as socially embedded systems, this study aims to investigate why cities implementing broadly similar collaborative governance initiatives produce different sustainable city logistics outcomes. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative configurational analysis was conducted across twenty French city logistics initiatives. Drawing on Furnari et al.’s (2021) configurational theorizing toolkit, governance conditions were iteratively identified and combined to explain variation in sustainable city logistics outcomes. Findings The analysis identifies five governance configurations. Rather than depending on collaborative governance alone, high-impact outcomes emerge from the interaction among governance structure, stakeholder representation, structural commitment and intervention scale. Research limitations/implications The governance configurations identified are grounded in French city logistics initiatives and should be further strengthened through fieldwork, and then examined in other institutional contexts. Future research should investigate how governance configurations evolve over time and across different socially embedded supply chains. Practical implications Managers and public authorities should focus less on replicating individual governance practices and more on assembling governance configurations that combine broad stakeholder representation, collaborative decision-making, structural commitment and coordinated ecosystem-level interventions. Originality/value The study advances SCM research by reconceptualizing sustainable city logistics as a governance and coordination challenge embedded within socially embedded supply chains. By doing so, it further demonstrates how configurational theorizing explains wicked sustainability problems in SCM by shifting attention from isolated governance mechanisms toward governance configurations as the appropriate unit of analysis.
Journal: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

Title: Manufacturer's Agency Selling and Reselling Choices and Online Intermediary's Information Sharing: The Role of Product Quality Decisions
Authors: Xiaojie Wu, Xin Liu, Xiaogang Lin, Ying‐Ju Chen
Affiliations: School of Management Guangdong University of Technology Guangzhou China; School of Business and Management (ISOM) Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Clear Water Bay Hong Kong
Abstract: ABSTRACT Meeting consumers' product‐quality demands is essential. Online intermediaries typically possess more accurate demand information than manufacturers and may share it to support quality adjustments. Manufacturers can adopt two selling formats: agency selling, in which they sell directly to consumers through intermediaries and pay commissions, and reselling, in which intermediaries purchase products from manufacturers at wholesale prices and then resell them to consumers. Manufacturers may also sell to downstream resellers who distribute through intermediaries. We develop a game‐theoretic e‐commerce supply chain model in which a manufacturer adjusts product quality in response to realized demand and chooses between agency selling and reselling, while the intermediary decides whether to disclose demand information to the manufacturer, the reseller, or both. Our results yield several insights. First, sharing demand information only with the manufacturer may reduce product quality under both selling formats. Second, under agency selling, the intermediary may disclose information either only to the manufacturer or to both parties; endogenous quality decisions increase full disclosure while reducing manufacturer‐only sharing. Under reselling, with exogenous quality, the intermediary either shares information only with the reseller or withholds it. However, when quality improvement is sufficiently efficient, it may disclose information to both parties despite higher wholesale‐price uncertainty. Furthermore, anticipating the intermediary's disclosure strategy, the manufacturer may still choose higher product quality under agency selling even when this results in a lower expected wholesale price than under reselling. Thus, the manufacturer's preferred selling format depends on which format better induces the intermediary to restrict information disclosure to the intended party. Finally, we show that agency selling can improve consumer surplus and social welfare and may also benefit all supply chain members with endogenous quality decisions.

Title: Optimizing Multi‐Fuel Operations for Green Container Shipping: Models, Analysis, and Solution Approach
Authors: Xuecheng Tian, Yidan Shangguan, Shining Wu, Shuaian Wang
Affiliations: Department of Logistics and Maritime Studies The Hong Kong Polytechnic University Hung Hom Hong Kong
Abstract: ABSTRACT This study investigates the optimization of multi‐fuel operations for container shipping in the context of evolving environmental regulations. Faced with increasing pressure to reduce emissions, particularly of sulfur oxides and carbon dioxide, the maritime industry must navigate a complex regulatory landscape in terms of energy use. Key policies include Sulfur Emission Control Areas, the European Union's (EU) Maritime Emissions Trading System, and the FuelEU Maritime Regulation. We propose a novel mathematical programming model to minimize total operational costs, including fuel and carbon emission costs, while maintaining regulatory compliance. Our model integrates three fuel types (very low‐sulfur fuel oil, marine gas oil, and renewable energy) to determine optimal fuel selection and sailing speed in different regulatory zones. To reduce computational complexity, we transform the model from a shipping leg‐wise formulation to a segment type‐wise formulation by categorizing all shipping legs of a route into six segment types, leading to a more efficient representation. Through a comparative analysis of the cost competitiveness and environmental effectiveness of the three fuel types, we derive four possible fuel selection strategies that determine the candidate or optimal fuel types for each segment type. We then develop an exact condition‐based sequential optimization algorithm to evaluate the feasibility of each strategy and identify a globally optimal multi‐fuel operations solution for a given container shipping service. Extensive computational experiments validate the efficacy of our approach, offering practical insights for shipping companies to strategically manage multi‐fuel operations and achieve cost‐efficiency while complying with environmental mandates.

Title: Even flow in dynamic networks for wastewater treatment
Authors: Antton Kasslin, Jeremias Berg
Abstract: Abstract Network flow allocation is a central problem within operations research. Arguably, the most classic setting of flow allocation problems is a static one in which the arcs of a directed graph need to be assigned flow values in a way that respects the capacities of each edge and, for example, maximizes the amount of flow that arrives at a sink node. The numerous applications of flow problems have resulted in several variants being proposed and studied. In this paper, we study a variant of dynamic network flow. Dynamic network flow generalizes the static setting by introducing a notion of time and allowing the flow to move over time in the network. In our setting, the sink of the network also has a maximum capacity of flow it can receive at each timestep, and we are interested in computing flow allocations that distribute an even amount of flow to the sink of the network over all timesteps. Additionally, we assume that new flow can be generated at each non-sink node in each timestep, and that the nodes can temporarily store a limited amount of the flow. In a central instantiation of the problem, the non-sink nodes of the network are pumping stations that need to transfer wastewater to a treatment plant, which is the sink of the network. To evaluate our solving approaches in practice, we worked with the Helsinki Region Environmental Services Authority to collect and create a new open-source benchmark set based on wastewater quantities in the Helsinki region. More precisely, we study the applicability of linear programming for solving real-world benchmarks of this dynamic network flow optimization problem. As our main contributions, we: (i) extend and modify a previously proposed constraint model for computing feasible allocations to the dynamic setting and allow more flexible allocations, (ii) introduce several different approaches to even the workload arriving at the sink at each timestep, (iii) collect a new open-source dataset based on real-world wastewater flow quantities, and (iv) report on an extensive experimental evaluation of our model on three differently-sized time spans of the new dataset using state-of-the-art solvers. Our evaluation demonstrates that, among our evenness approaches, minimizing the difference between the maximum and minimum hourly incoming water to the treatment plant consistently yields the highest evenness in the flow arriving at the treatment plant. Additionally, we demonstrate the flexibility of our model by incorporating additional constraints aimed at reducing the energy consumption of the pumps.

Title: Assessing comprehensive impact of autonomous electric taxis via an integrated modeling framework
Authors: Junxin He, Jialin Tang, Huan Zhang, Libo Zhang, Qunwei Wang
Abstract: Autonomous electric taxis are a crucial technology for the sustainable urban transport transition, yet the multidimensional impacts of large-scale deployment and differentiated policy effects remain insufficiently assessed. This paper proposes a framework integrating BERTopic, Bass diffusion, parameterized binary Logit and system dynamics to analyze autonomous electric taxis’ penetration in the on-demand mobility market of Guangzhou, a representative Chinese megacity, and their accident-related economic, environmental and employment impacts. Results show that autonomous electric taxis will reach approximately 70% penetration by 2050, and save roughly 88.4 million yuan in socioeconomic costs from fewer traffic accidents. However, new travel demand will lift cumulative carbon emissions by around 760,000 tons and displace about 61% of traditional mobility jobs. Moreover, policy trade-offs emerge: price subsidies best promote penetration and promotional campaigns best lower accident costs, but both exacerbate carbon emissions and employment impacts; opening operating areas has limited market effects yet mitigates environmental impacts.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Large-Scale pavement deterioration analysis considering climate, surface-material, age, and traffic in Japan
Authors: Chunliang Xue, Kai Xue, Boyu Zhao, Tomonori Nagayama
Abstract: Climatic conditions may accelerate road deterioration, but multi-factor mechanisms remain poorly understood owing to limited large-scale field data. This study integrates Japanese national road inspection records, meteorological reanalysis and traffic census data into a dataset of 13 climate variables, 58 asphalt mixture types, 19 binder categories, service years and traffic volumes, covering 90 regions and 16,934 km of roads. Interpretable machine learning quantifies factor contributions to the crack index, International Roughness Index and rutting index, and identifies deterioration tipping points. Long-term climate-associated factors, especially freeze–thaw cycles, contribute more to deterioration than short-term extremes, traffic volume or material type. Abrasion and deformation resistance are key material properties, whereas recycled materials show limited association with deterioration while offering sustainability benefits. As maintenance records are unavailable, these climate-related findings reflect the combined effect of climate exposure and maintenance response rather than purely physical climatic effects.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Implementation via political parties
Authors: Luis C. Corchón, Guadalupe Correa-Lopera
Abstract: We address the implementation of public policies (alternatives) when the feasible set is unknown to the planner. The implementing agents are the political parties, who know the feasible set. They care about the implemented alternative, which reflects their ideology, and their share in parliament and office. They face a mechanism that, given the alternatives proposed by all parties, asks the voters to rank them and determines the chosen alternative and the shares in parliament and office. We identify conditions on parties’ preferences that guarantee the socially optimal policy is the outcome of the unique pure strategy Nash equilibrium of the electoral game played by the parties. The existence of the equilibrium does not require any assumptions about the parties’ ideology. To ensure uniqueness, shares must prevail over ideology: office or parliamentary shares in two-party systems, and strictly office shares in systems with more than two parties.

Title: Editorial Board
Bi-level stochastic optimisation of integrated bed allocation and inpatient scheduling in dedicated inpatient systems with overflow capability
Authors: Xuran Gong, Jianjun Zhou, Jiajun Dai, Na Geng
Affiliations: Sino-US Global Logistics Institute, Antai College of Economics & Management, Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Shanghai University of Finance and Economics
Abstract: Inpatient beds serve as the cornerstone of efficient care delivery and timely access to medical services. Managers typically allocate beds to individual departments. When a department’s dedicated beds reach full capacity, inpatients are often transferred to non-primary departments. This practice is termed ‘patient overflow'. Furthermore, uncertainties in inpatient arrival rates and length of stay hinder bed management optimisation, undermining efficiency and increasing care delays. This paper proposes a collaborative solution for bed allocation and inpatient scheduling.
