A two-stage stochastic programming (TSP) model is developed to optimise bed allocation while integrating daily patient scheduling to minimise patient waiting, diversion, and overflow costs. The first-stage determines bed allocations, whereas the second-stage then optimises scheduling decisions under sampled demand scenarios. To support the evaluation and implementation of these allocation decisions, two inpatient scheduling policies are proposed. The first is a rolling horizon scheduling policy, that updates a TSP model on a daily basis using real-time data on current hospitalisations/waitlists. The second is a threshold-based policy, that regulates patient queue lengths and bed reservation quantities through simulation-based optimisation. Computational experiments demonstrate the superiority of the proposed bed allocation and scheduling approaches over conventional benchmarks, and yield practical, actionable managerial insights for healthcare operations management.

Title: Nonlinear trade-offs in GenAI application pricing: a game-theoretic analysis of API and psychological costs
Authors: Liaoliao Li, Yali Zhang, Jun Sun, Zhaojun Yang
Affiliations: Northwestern Polytechnical University; University of Texas Rio Grande Valley; Xidian University
Abstract: In the rapidly evolving generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) ecosystem, downstream application providers face persistent challenges in designing optimal pricing strategies. These challenges arise from dual cost pressures: application programming interface (API) costs imposed by upstream model platforms and psychological frictions experienced by end consumers. This study develops a game-theoretic model to analyze application providers’ strategic choice between subscription-based and usage-based pricing under both monopolistic and duopolistic market structures. The analysis reveals that the optimal strategies are shaped by a nonlinear interplay among psychological costs, model API costs, and consumer valuation. Under low psychological-cost conditions, API costs exert an inverted U-shaped effect on competing providers’ profits. By contrast, under high API-cost regimes, subscription-based and usage-based models exhibit asymmetric sensitivities to psychological costs: profits under usage-based pricing decline with rising psychological costs, whereas subscription-based profits stabilise. Fthermore, elevated API and psychological costs attenuate competitive intensity, driving duopolistic equilibria toward monopoly-like outcomes. These findings remain robust after incorporating a broad set of realistic market frictions. The results provide actionable insights for GenAI application providers balancing cost pass-through, user engagement, and competitive positioning in pricing decisions.

Title: Improvement of steel strip quality based on reinforcement learning with offline data constraints
Authors: Yue Huang, Zhen Chen, Di Zhou, Ershun Pan
Affiliations: Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Donghua University
Abstract: In hot-rolling finishing stands, control parameters are numerous and diverse, and quality metrics are tightly coupled. Optimising parameters to improve product quality requires high precision, safety, and fast response. Offline reinforcement learning (RL) is a promising approach for parameter optimisation, but out-of-distribution (OOD) issues undermine its effectiveness. To address this, we propose a new offline RL framework for control-parameter optimisation. First, we construct an offline dataset for four key quality metrics, comprising 1,048,576 state transition processes. Second, we introduce an offline RL algorithm. The policy update adapts to constraints derived from the state and action distributions of the original dataset, thereby reducing incorrect generalisation to OOD samples. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the method can mitigate OOD risk. Moreover, we develop an offline policy-evaluation technique that combines the neural predictive model with the system state-space equations to simulate the rolling environment with reduced approximation error. Extensive experiments show that the proposed approach, evaluated within the simulation framework and supported by temporal-split validation, improves quality metrics by more than 10% on an independent test set compared to existing control methods. Moreover, it reduces convergence time steps by over 50%, yielding more conservative policies and enhanced decision support for production.

Title: Orchestration of Organisational Technologies: Synergies, Challenges, and Contingencies
Authors: Mohamad Ali Mezher, Indra Gunawan, Sajad Fayezi
Affiliations: Adelaide University; Flinders University
Abstract: Rapid technological advances create a pressing challenge for firms: coordinating diverse organisational technologies. Companies must balance and integrate emerging and established technologies, notably Industry 4.0 technologies (I4T) and Lean technologies (LT). Yet guidance on how to integrate these systems remains limited. This study addresses this gap through a systematic literature review (SLR) of I4T (as emerging technologies) and LT (as established technologies). We synthesise evidence on synergies, challenges, and contingencies, and translate these insights into guidance for operational excellence. Grounded in the Resource-Based View (RBV) and Contingency Theory (CT), we argue that combining I4T and LT yields synergistic resource bundles that can potentially deliver sustained competitive advantage. Unlike past research that treats these technologies separately, we introduce an ‘Orchestrated VRIO' perspective that conceptualises value, rarity, inimitability, and organisation as emergent properties of sociotechnical bundles formed through managed orchestration, rather than as static attributes of discrete resources. Building on this framing, we extend CT via a Contingency Bundling Framework that specifies internal and external factors shaping whether bundles deliver value. The review culminates in an integrative framework linking bundle configurations to expected benefits and trade-offs, and highlights implementation risks that can erode advantage.

Title: Single-machine batch scheduling with split jobs and a maintenance activity
Authors: Junyi Zhang, Juan Zou, Ran Ma
Affiliations: Qufu Normal University; Qingdao University of Technology
Abstract: Motivated by batch-dependent processing constraints in semiconductor testing and other time-critical industrial applications, we consider a single-machine batch scheduling problem with a fixed maintenance activity, where jobs have equal processing time but different sizes. Each job can be split and processed in two consecutive batches if necessary. For the objective of minimising the makespan, we prove the NP-hardness of the problem and provide an approximation algorithm with a worst-case ratio of 32, which is the best possible polynomial-time approximation algorithm under the assumption that P≠NP. For the objective of minimising the total completion time, we prove that the problem is NP-hard, and then present a pseudo-polynomial time dynamic programming algorithm and a 32-approximation algorithm. Moreover, through computational experiments, we demonstrate that the approximation algorithm performs very well in practice, achieving an average relative error of only 0.36%.

Title: Machine learning in feature recognition for manufacturing: taxonomy, analytical review, comparisons, trends, challenges, and outlook
Authors: Peizhi Shi, Yuchu Qin, Fanlin Meng, Paul J. Scott, Xiangqian Jiang
Affiliations: University of Leeds; University of Huddersfield; University of Exeter
Abstract: Feature recognition is an important topic in the area of intelligent manufacturing and production research. This technique is utilised to extract and recognise functional components and geometric shapes, such as slots, holes, and pockets, from solid models. The term ‘learning-based feature recognition’ refers to the feature recognition methods implemented based on machine learning. This topic was examined three decades ago but has been growing quickly in the recent five years. In this paper, a taxonomy and review of learning-based feature recognition methods are presented. This paper categorises the literature, examines basic components of a learning-based feature recognition method, identifies the technical evolution of these components, examines their impact on the overall feature recognition process, provides a broader overview of existing methods, identifies the milestone learning paradigms, makes comparisons among different approaches, assesses their practical capabilities, and identifies the gaps between research and real-world applications. By reading this paper, researchers and industry professionals can understand different learning-based feature recognition methods and their underlying principles, gain insights into design decisions made in a learning-based system, and understand their applied situations.

Title: Generative models for energy modelling and management: a structured framework for technology adoption in energy systems
Authors: Leonardo Fontoura, Daniel Luiz de Mattos Nascimento, Julio Neto, Guilherme Luz Tortorella
Affiliations: Fluminense Federal University; University of Barcelona Business School; The University of Melbourne; Universidad Austral; Fundacao Dom Cabral
Abstract: The growing complexity of modern energy systems demands intelligent, adaptable, and theoretically grounded approaches to modelling and management. Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen-AI) and Deep Learning Models (DLMs) configured for generative tasks offer significant potential for scenario simulation and rare-event modelling; however, their adoption remains constrained by conceptual ambiguity and the absence of structured, theory-informed frameworks. To address this gap, this study proposes the Generative Models for Energy Modelling and Management (GM-EMM) framework. By establishing a functional taxonomy of generative approaches, the research addresses critical analytical challenges, including counterfactual reasoning and data scarcity in decentralised energy systems. A multi-method research design was employed, integrating a scoping review, expert elicitation via the Fuzzy Delphi method, and non-parametric statistical prioritisation using Friedman and Nemenyi tests to evaluate six core technologies (RNNs, GANs, GNNs, TNNs, VAEs, and CNNs). Based on expert consensus and statistical differentiation, technologies were positioned across four analytically defined phases: Deployment, Validation, Exploration, and Monitoring. To enhance practical relevance, an interpretive validation stage with industry experts confirmed the roadmap’s coherence and decision-support value.

Title: Farming contract design with random yield and private farmer information
Authors: Xinyan Cao, Xiang Fang, Yuanjie He, Wei Hu, Xiao Xiao
Affiliations: Northern Illinois University; University of Colorado Denver; California State Polytechnic University, Pomona; Nankai University; California State University Stanislaus
Abstract: We study an agricultural supply chain in which a distributor purchases products from a farmer who holds private information regarding their own random yield and costs. We develop an efficiency index to streamline the farmer's three pieces of private information and categorise the farmer as either efficient or inefficient. Following the principal-agent model, we design the optimal forward contract menu for the distributor. Our findings indicate that when the probability of an efficient farmer is low, the distributor will engage both types of farmers. Conversely, when this probability is high, a contract is exclusively offered to the efficient farmer. Interestingly, while improvements in the farmer's efficiency consistently benefit the distributor, they may either increase or decrease the farmer's expected profit. Additionally, the farmer's production cost has a more substantial impact on both parties' profits and values of information than the backup cost. Finally, we analyse the contract design problem with risk-averse farmers to highlight the impact of the farmers' risk aversion on the agriculture supply chain.

Title: Construction and application of a multimodal knowledge graph for machining deformation uncertainty analysis
Authors: Zhaoze Sun, Xiaoyue Li, Guangyuan Si, Erpeng Wang, Hui Xu, Deguo Yao, Yuanqing Sun
Affiliations: Qingdao University; College of Economics and Management, Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics; Ltd.; .; Shandong North Binhai Machinery Co., Ltd.
Abstract: Uncertainty analysis of machining deformation is crucial for improving product quality, reliability, and manufacturing efficiency. Current machining deformation uncertainty problems still face many challenges, such as complex mechanism, scattered information, and high dependence on expert experience. In order to solve the aforementioned problems, the paper constructs a multi-modal knowledge graph for machining deformation uncertainty analysis, and designs a large model-augmented intelligent system driven by a multimodal knowledge graph. The constructed multi-modal knowledge graph realises the multi-integration of text information, chart information and finite element simulation information, and covers key links such as ontology construction, knowledge extraction, knowledge fusion, knowledge inference, and knowledge storage. Aiming at the knowledge inference link, the principal component analysis (PCA) and multi-head self-attention mechanism (MHSA) are innovatively introduced to enhance feature extraction, proposing a new knowledge inference method. Additionally, through multi-stage large model enhancement strategies and expert large model training approaches, the generalisation ability and multimodal interaction capability of the intelligent system have been effectively improved. Finally, a multimodal knowledge graph of machining deformation uncertainty is constructed, and an intelligent system is developed to provide multimodal decision support for machining deformation uncertainty analysis from a full life-cycle perspective, with its performance validated.

Title: Reconfiguring a mixed-model robotic assembly line considering lifespan, obsolescence, and retrofit in a manufacturing 4.0/5.0 environment
Authors: Daniel Schibelbain, Milton Luiz Polli, Luiz Carlos De Abreu Rodrigues, Leandro Magatão
Affiliations: Federal University of Technology – Paraná (UTFPR)
Abstract: This paper addresses the challenges of reconfiguring mixed-model robotic assembly lines to face volatile market demand, new products, and technological innovations from the Manufacturing 4.0 and 5.0 Industries. The literature extensively studies designing new manufacturing systems or balancing reconfigurable ones. However, to adapt existing lines to these issues, considering lifespan and obsolescence remains an underexplored domain, along with the emerging trend of retrofitting in-house resources. A multi-step MILP-based method is proposed to bridge this gap. An exhaustive set of scenarios is compared with exact and heuristic benchmarks. The method’s effectiveness is evaluated in a large-scale industrial case study, assessing the influence of flexibility on the system. This real-world industrial case is optimised, achieving an average improvement of 4.69% over the conventional approach and better results in more than 82% of instances. Furthermore, a statistical analysis is conducted and reveals the correlation between robots’ task accessibility and their assignments. In a complementary way, a financial assessment and bottom-up analysis from Process Engineering have also been explored. Therefore, this research provides a method to reconfigure manufacturing lines considering variable operational conditions and practical issues. This leads to several managerial insights and contributes to more sustainable and profitable assembly systems.

Title: A multi-level modelling approach for magnesium-carbon brick die-casting digital twin workshop oriented to production anomaly detection
Authors: Dengli Yi, Xinfeng Wang, Chuanqi Li, Lu Bai
Affiliations: Institution of Mechanical and Power Engineering; Beijing Gangyan Hydrogen Metallurgy Technology Research Institute Co., Ltd; Automation Research and Design Institute of Metallurgical Industry
Abstract: The manufacturing process of magnesia-carbon bricks involves complex equipment and dense workflows, leading to frequent production anomalies that are hard to diagnose. Traditional modelling methods struggle with multi-level anomaly detection and process awareness. This paper proposes a digital twin-based multi-layer modelling framework for anomaly detection in magnesia-carbon brick production. The framework unifies equipment behaviour and workshop logic through three layers: equipment twin, workshop twin, and system decision-making. It addresses modelling gaps by dividing equipment into five component types, creating a three-level twin structure (unit, chain, and equipment) to map structure-action-state relationships. For workshop logic, a complex event processing method models process events using behaviour correlation matrices and directed graph adjacency matrices, capturing time evolution and path dependencies. A prototype system was developed, integrating data collection, state mapping, anomaly detection, and visualisation. Initial tests in a pilot workshop confirmed its feasibility and scalability. This research offers a structured, multi-level modelling approach for anomaly detection in complex manufacturing, enhancing digital twin expressiveness and workshop intelligence.

Title: Risk propagation modelling and resilience assessment of supply chain networks based on an improved SIS model
Authors: Yu Wang, Yufeng Sun, Zhining Zhang, Fulin Zhang, Zihan Wang
Affiliations: School of Reliability and Systems Engineering, Beihang University; School of Information Resource Management, Renmin University of China
Abstract: Traditional assessment methods fail to capture the dynamic interplay between risk propagation and managerial interventions, and cannot precisely quantify the evolutionary mechanisms underlying Supply Chain Network Resilience (SCNR). This study proposes a decision-embedded SIS dynamics model that explicitly integrates performance-state-triggered intervention detection, dynamic resource mobilisation, and topology-aware resource allocation into the modelling framework, enabling intervention behaviours to be endogenously activated by real-time system performance dynamics. Grounded in the complete life-cycle trajectory of disruption–intervention–recovery–adaptation, this study constructs a comprehensive four-dimensional resilience assessment framework encompassing absorptive, recovery, adaptive, and structural dimensions. The findings demonstrate that, while physical topology integrity governs SCNR under low-intensity shocks, the contribution of dynamic performance resilience metrics significantly surpasses that of structural factors under extreme shocks inducing large-scale structural fragmentation, thereby emerging as the decisive determinant of system viability. By breaking the autonomy constraint inherent in classical risk propagation models, this study provides a quantitative decision-making benchmark for differentiated resilience governance of SCNs under resource constraints.

Title: Resilience analysis of supply chain networks under cascading failure model considering tolerance state and competitive recovery
Authors: Bin Hou, Xinyu Wang, Jiafu Tang
Affiliations: Dongbei University of Finance and Economics
Abstract: Stability and resilience of supply chains are crucial for enterprise operations. Supply chains are vulnerable to disruption risks, potentially resulting in cascading failures (i.e. the ripple effect). This study aims to delve into the dynamic characteristics of cascading failures and explore effective approaches to enhancing supply chain resilience (SCR). We propose a cascading failure model named CFM-TSCR, which incorporates tolerance state and competitive recovery. The tolerance state represents the manifestation of an enterprise's willingness to tolerate risk, thereby influencing the timing of its execution of recovery measures. Competitive recovery acknowledges that recovery is a process of bilateral selection among enterprises within a competitive environment rather than unilateral efforts. Essentially, the tolerance state and competitive recovery reflect when enterprises initiate the recovery process and how enterprises respond to the recovery process, respectively. Additionally, we investigate the effects of modelling parameters and diverse disruption scenarios on SCR. These findings play a significant role and hold substantial value in identifying critical nodes within supply chain networks, refining enterprises' recovery strategies and enhancing SCR.

Title: Jointly optimising assembly line feeding and supermarket layouts
Authors: Ebenezer Olatunde Adenipekun, Veronique Limère, Nico André Schmid
Affiliations: GhentUniversity, Ghent, Belgium; Flanders Make@UGent–core lab CVAMO; Univ. Lille, CNRS, UMR 9221 -- LEM -- Lille Economie Management
Abstract: Customised products increase the complexity of managing assembly systems efficiently, particularly when multiple part variants are required for assembly, necessitating adept handling of limited space within assembly lines. Leveraging diverse feeding policies efficiently optimises space utilisation and minimises logistical complexity in part feeding. Moreover, strategic decisions regarding the placement and sizing of preparation areas are crucial for smooth intra-logistics flows. Precise cell placement facilitates efficient transportation between preparation areas and assembly lines, reducing transportation costs, while optimal sizing minimises spatial costs. In response to these challenges, we propose a mixed-integer optimisation model that determines a feeding policy for each part and assigns parts requiring preprocessing to either regular or line-integrated cells. The collection of these cells forms the supermarket. Exploiting a callback procedure, the model ensures that navigating regular cells sharing the same delivery frequency and assembly station sequence is done by the dedicated automated guided vehicle. We enhance model efficiency using valid inequalities and symmetry-breaking constraints and validate the approach through extensive experiments on artificial instances. The results demonstrate that our cell-design optimisation approach is more cost-effective than both a simplified supermarket-based planning strategy that omits detailed cell structures and an operational simplification case restricted to line-integrated cells.

Title: Tri-objective based scalable balancing of reconfigurable manufacturing systems subject to resource constraints and task processing time uncertainty
Authors: Siwar Arbi, Audrey Cerqueus, Evgeny Gurevsky, Alexandre Dolgui, Ali Siadat
Affiliations: IMT Atlantique; CNRS; University of Nantes; LCFC, Arts et Métiers Institute of Technology; Arts et Métiers Institute of Technology
Abstract: This article studies reconfigurable manufacturing systems and their ability to efficiently evolve (or scale) through the use of a limited number of additional resources to improve two analysed system characteristics: productivity and robustness against task processing time uncertainty. The goal is to find an initial system configuration (or balancing) representing the best potential for scalability. To this end, we propose a multi-step based multi-objective approach, where productivity and robustness are considered as two objectives to be maximised and the number of used additional resources as the third objective to be minimised. Thus, for a given balancing, we first explore the set of its non-dominated (in the sense of Pareto) configurations, reflecting relevant possibilities for additional use of resources. Then, we calculate its corresponding tri-objective hyper-volume and suggest to consider it as a scalability metric. Finally, to find the most scalable balancing, we develop an efficient simulated annealing algorithm, where the proposed metric is used as a fitness function. The algorithm is tested and analysed on small- and medium-sized instances, extracted and adapted from the well-known benchmark dataset. The numerical results obtained demonstrate the stability and efficiency of the developed algorithm and confirm the relevance of the proposed scalability metric.

Title: Process intervention decisions in biomanufacturing under lead time constraints
Authors: Yasemin Limon, Tugce Martagan, Ananth Krishnamurthy
Affiliations: Bilkent University; Northeastern University; Indian Institute of Management Bangalore

Title: Labour assignment with convergent product structures: an assessment by simulation
Authors: Matthias Thürer, Nuno O. Fernandes
Affiliations: Chemnitz University of Technology; Instituto Politécnico de Castelo Branco; Universidade do Minho
Abstract: Most labour in practice is somehow flexible, and most shops in practice use some form of labour flexibility to cope with varying demand. A large literature on labour assignment rules that decide when and where to shift or reassign workers has consequently emerged. But this literature typically neglects convergent assembly structures. There is the implicit assumption that results from other shop structures are directly transferable. Results from discrete event simulations show that this is not the case. Although previous literature indicates that shifting workers to the station with the longest queue and considering critical parts improve performance, these results are not confirmed in our study. In assembly systems, the flow of jobs is constrained by synchronisation requirements and capacity availability, determining both waiting times overall performance. Labour assignment has a direct impact on both if workers are shared among assembly stations, which has direct implications for the rule to adopt. In terms of research, we confirm the literature on inventory diagnosis and highlight its importance for labour assignment. In terms of practice, we contribute by supporting managers in finding the appropriate labour assignment rule for their shop.

Title: Healthcare network resilience analysis under equipment failure and patients’ preferences
Authors: Claudia Piffari, Alexandra Lagorio, Roberto Pinto
Affiliations: University of Bergamo
Abstract: We propose a resilience analysis framework to assess the resilience of an elective healthcare network subject to low-impact-high-frequency (LIHF) disruptions, thereby identifying the most critical facility, considering both the impact of disturbances and the probability of their occurrence. The proposed framework combines agent-based simulation with design of experiment (DOE) and patient behaviour modelling. The framework has been tested with data from a real case, demonstrating its usefulness for conducting resilience analyses and prioritising resilience-enhancing actions to improve network performance. Two resilience-enhancing actions with different characteristics have been tested. The distinctive feature of the framework is the consideration of patient preferences in the simulation, allowing patients to be considered as active actors who can influence the behaviour of the system during a disturbance.

Title: Robust real-time optimisation for train rescheduling and platforming in high-speed railways under a route-locking sectional-release mechanism
Authors: Huimin Zhang, Wenhui Qi, Zebin Chen, Shukai Li
Affiliations: Qingdao University; Beijing Jiaotong University; Shantou University
Abstract: The route-locking sectional-release (RLSR) interlocking mechanism has been shown to significantly improve operational efficiency and station throughput in large stations. However, most existing studies rely on simplified interlocking rules, particularly in real-time rescheduling problems. To address this gap and enhance operational efficiency and resilience under dynamic perturbations, including dwell disturbances, running disturbances, and disruptions, this paper proposes a robust real-time optimisation framework for the train rescheduling and platforming problem (TRPP) in high-speed railways, with RLSR explicitly incorporated into the model formulation. Dwell and running disturbances are characterised by uncertainty sets, and the resulting model is reformulated into a tractable robust counterpart, while disruption-related uncertainty is handled through a rolling horizon framework with real-time feedback. To reduce computational complexity and meet real-time requirements, a Lagrangian relaxation-based decomposition algorithm is embedded within the rolling horizon framework. At each rolling horizon stage, the problem is decomposed into two parallelizable subproblems: the train timetable rescheduling problem (TTRP) and the train platforming problem (TPP). Numerical experiments using real-world data validate the effectiveness and computational efficiency of the proposed approach. Furthermore, several managerial insights are derived for practitioners.

Title: Estimation of process capability indices for high-dimensional data
Authors: Shuai Wang, Mengying You, Yi Li, Jyun-You Chiang
Affiliations: Hainan University; Shanghai University of International Business and Economics; Chengdu Technological University; Southwestern University of Finance and Economics
Abstract: In high-dimensional manufacturing environments, quality assessment must account for multiple correlated characteristics, posing significant challenges for multivariate process capability indices (MPCIs). This study focuses on identifying and improving MPCIs suitable for such settings. Among several candidates, volume-ratio-based indices are found to retain interpretability and sensitivity under high dimensionality. However, their practical applicability is hindered by instability in covariance matrix estimation. To address this issue, a modified adaptive thresholding approach is developed, incorporating a positive-definiteness constraint to ensure reliable and bounded MPCI estimation. Theoretical analysis establishes the consistency of the proposed estimator. We further develop interval estimation procedures for high-dimensional MPCIs and evaluate their coverage and length properties via bootstrap-based and asymptotic approaches. In addition, we propose a diagnostic variable-ranking strategy to identify and prioritise the characteristics most responsible for capability degradation, providing actionable guidance for process improvement. Simulation studies across various sample sizes, sparsity levels, and dimensions confirm the superior accuracy of the proposed framework over existing methods. A semiconductor manufacturing case study further demonstrates its practical relevance for high-dimensional process capability analysis.

Title: Nonparametric change-point detection for unstructured 3D point cloud data with an application in additive manufacturing
Authors: Zhiqiong Wang, Pingping He, Yangyang Zang, Shuguang He, Zhen He
Affiliations: Tianjin University of Technology; AVIC China Aero-Polytechnology Establishment; Tianjin University
Abstract: In contrast to key product characteristics, unstructured 3D point cloud data with coordinates at random measurement locations can be collected from 3D scanning systems to reflect product geometry entirely. However, challenges such as high dimensionality, registration complexity, and sensitivity to small process changes hinder effective modelling and monitoring of such data. Furthermore, there is very limited research on Phase I analysis of unstructured point cloud data in the literature. To this end, this paper proposes two novel nonparametric change-point detection methods for unstructured 3D point cloud data to identify the presence and location of a change point in a historical dataset. Specifically, we first introduce the Laplace-Beltrami (LB) operator spectrum as an intrinsic geometrical property of unstructured 3D point clouds by leveraging tools from differential geometry. Then, we develop two nonparametric control charts for detecting a change point among the LB spectra. Finally, we provide an effective procedure to determine critical values for the control charts. Extensive numerical simulations demonstrate the superiority of the proposed methods in detecting and estimating the change point while maintaining in-control performance. In addition, an application in additive manufacturing illustrates the implementation of the proposed methods and validates their effectiveness to pinpoint the change point.

Title: Trade war shocks and the reconfiguration of global maritime networks: Evidence from trade flows and vessel movements
Authors: Xinyue Pu, Jingyang Du, Xiwen Bai
Abstract: Trade-policy shocks may reshape maritime logistics not by physically disrupting shipping routes, but by reallocating cargo demand across countries and routes. This paper examines how the 2025 U.S.–China trade-war escalation is reflected in bilateral trade flows, vessel operations, and global maritime-network structure. We combine U.S. import and export shipment records from Panjiva with AIS-based vessel trajectory data to construct monthly trade-flow measures, port-to-port shipping links, realized bilateral routes, and network centrality indicators. The results show that the escalation is associated with a contraction in U.S.–China trade and selective reallocation toward Vietnam. However, the vessel-movement evidence does not indicate widespread disruption of China–U.S. shipping links. Instead, China–U.S. links remain broadly intact, while Vietnam-related route activity expands relative to China–U.S. routes. At the network level, China–U.S. port pairs experience a modest relative increase in shortest-path length, whereas core accessibility and overall network concentration remain stable. A notable network-level change in the baseline specification is the rise in Vietnam’s betweenness centrality, consistent with a stronger intermediary role after the shock. These findings suggest that trade-war shocks are reflected in changes in how maritime networks are used rather than in a fundamental alteration of network topology. The evidence points to route reallocation and intermediary-role shifts as key features of maritime network reconfiguration under geopolitical trade disruptions, with implications for how resilience is understood in policy-driven shocks.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Newsworthy workplace deaths
Authors: Vincenzo Carrieri, Mattia Filomena, Francesco Principe
Abstract: Using high-frequency administrative data from Italy, this study examines how workplace fatalities and related media and public attention affect safety outcomes. Our empirical strategy combines event-study and difference-in-differences designs with variation in newspaper circulation, article-level reporting, and exogenous shifts in public attention from unexpected football results. We find that “newsworthy” deaths—those involving young, female, or foreign-born workers—reduce non-fatal injuries, especially where media exposure and coverage are higher, but the effect weakens when attention is diverted by competing football events. These results highlight media salience, shaped by public attention, as an informal mechanism for improving workplace safety.

Title: How energy transmission infrastructure affects production strategy? Evidence from China’s UHV projects
Authors: Boqiang Lin, Jie Xu
Abstract: Ultra-High Voltage projects represent a critical shift in energy logistics from physical fuel transport to efficient “power-by-wire” transmission. Using UHV construction as a quasi-natural experiment and matching the National Tax Survey with China’s Customs trade records, this paper examines how improved electricity transmission reshapes firms’ production and product portfolios. The results show: (1) UHV operation significantly increases firms’ electricity use and output; (2) greater electricity reliability induces firms to drop non-core products, narrow their product range, and concentrate resources on core products; and (3) production gains occur in both electricity-sending and electricity-receiving regions and are stronger in electricity-dependent industries, whereas product-range adjustment is more pronounced in receiving regions and among firms with lower electricity dependence. Further analyses show that product adjustment is concentrated among non-state-owned, large, and export-intensive firms. These findings provide micro-level evidence that clean energy transmission infrastructure improves resource allocation and supports sustainable industrial development.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: University shocks and research productivity inequality: Evidence from the COVID-19 pandemic
Authors: Yuxiang Jiang, Ruijie Liu, Dominik Rösch, Cristian I. Tiu
Abstract: Using data on more than 36,000 authors at 1000 business and economics departments, we study how the COVID-19 pandemic reshaped the distribution of research productivity. The pandemic widened pre-existing gaps: relative to the rest, output rose for top-50 departments and for senior and male scholars, while it fell for lower-ranked departments, women, and Ph.D. students. This widening is robust to restricting the sample to authors already active before the pandemic, to excluding scholars who changed institutions, and to using peer-reviewed publications rather than Social Sciences Research Network (SSRN) postings. Institutional slack appears to explain who absorbed the shock: larger departments, prior online-teaching experience, continued hiring, and closure policies matched to local severity are each associated with smaller losses. This episode illustrates how a common organizational shock can deepen inequality by favoring the already well-resourced.

Title: Long-term impacts of climate change on electricity demand and household expenditure in Saudi Arabia
Authors: Ansir Ilyas, Puneet Kamboj, Fahad Alswaina, Pavithra Kumar Shetty, Mohamad Hejazi, Yoshihide Wada
Abstract: With regional warming across the Arabian Peninsula occurring at twice the global average and driving summer peak electricity loads to nearly 80% of total system capacity, understanding long-term energy implications is critical for Saudi Arabia's national climate resilience. Consequently, this study assesses the impacts of climate change on thermal comfort, energy demand, and household electricity expenditure through 2100. Using the multi-sectoral Global Change Assessment Model for the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (GCAM-KSA), we integrated three regionally updated Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP1–3) with two climate pathways: RCP7.0 (high impact) and RCP2.6 (low impact). Our results indicate a shift in thermal conditions by 2100 relative to the 1981–2014 baseline. Cooling Degree Days (CDD) are projected to increase up to 28% and 85% under the low and high-impact pathways, respectively, while Heating Degree Days (HDD) remain negligible. Furthermore, the temporal distribution of CDD expands significantly, representing a substantial lengthening of the summer season beyond mid-century. By isolating socioeconomic and climate drivers, we find that high socioeconomic development (SSP3) initially drives a 33–53% rise in cooling demand through 2060 compared to 2025. However, climate impacts emerge as the dominant accelerator between 2060 and 2100, independently driving cooling service demand up by an additional 38–49% (RCP7.0) and 13–16% (RCP2.6). Consequently, annual average household expenditures attributable to climate impacts are projected to increase by 32–45% (RCP7.0) and 7–11% (RCP2.6) in 2100. These findings highlight the importance of integrating climate adaptation strategies into long-term energy planning to mitigate rising household expenditure.

Title: Effects of trade barriers on foreign direct investment: Evidence from Chinese solar panels
Authors: A. Oriana Montti
Abstract: Trade barriers can affect firms’ international investment decisions, not only the trade flows they directly target. This paper studies the anti-dumping and countervailing duties (AD-CVDs) imposed by the United States in 2012 on Chinese solar panel imports and examines how affected Chinese firms adjusted their foreign direct investment decisions. Due to their differential exposure to U.S. trade policy, Chinese firms are granted different AD-CVD rates. I leverage this variation to develop a difference-in-differences design. Using monthly greenfield FDI announcement data from 2009 to 2018 and a Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood estimator, I find that targeted firms increased FDI by 145 million dollars in 2012, relative to a pre-policy average of 9 million dollars. The effects are larger and more persistent among firms already active in FDI before the policy. The greenfield FDI response does not carry over to cross-border mergers and acquisitions. Location choice analysis suggests that targeted firms shifted investment toward Asia, especially after a second round of AD-CVD measures in 2015. Descriptive trade and investment data provide suggestive evidence consistent with production relocation and export-platform FDI. These results document FDI diversion that modifies investment patterns in the short run and is consistent with trade-barrier avoidance in the medium run.

Title: Financial contagion of climate risk: evidence from cross-industry complex networks and machine learning
Authors: Xiao-Li Gong, Xiu-Chao Zhang, Xiong Xiong
Abstract: Identifying the financial linkages associated with climate risk is crucial for preventing systemic risk. Based on annual reports of listed firms, this paper constructs physical and transition climate risk indices reflecting firms' attention and disclosure of climate risks, and characterizes their interdependencies with cross-industry financial risks. We adopt complex network analysis to map risk-linkage networks and measure industry resilience, apply econometric models to examine linkage characteristics, and use Random Forest (RF), XGBoost and CatBoost to predict systemic risk contagion. The results indicate that brown industries feature stronger index-financial risk associations than green industries. Physical risk linkages are short-term, whereas transition risk linkages are more persistent. Linkage characteristics vary with industries' positions in the industrial structure and are moderated by climate policy. Disaster losses, management's climate perception and investor sentiment drive the observed heterogeneity. The RF model delivers the best prediction performance for risk contagion. In conclusion, there is a significant systemic association between China's climate risk indices and industry-level financial risks, and risk prevention efforts should focus on industry-level structural linkage features.

Title: The efficiency of the performing arts industry in China: An application of the Post-view Model
Authors: Hong Chen, Dariush Khezrimotlagh, Shiuh-Nan Hwang
Abstract: China's performing arts industry has expanded rapidly, with substantial investment from local governments. Yet evidence remains limited on whether these public inputs generate efficient outcomes or how efficiency findings can translate into concrete policy choices. This study models the industry as a unified two-stage system consisting of infrastructure construction and economic transformation. Using the post-view unified two-stage DEA model, we evaluate the overall and stage-specific efficiency of 31 provinces, autonomous regions, and municipalities in China from 2015 to 2019. We then apply truncated bootstrap regression to identify the factors associated with efficiency in each stage. The results show that infrastructure construction is generally more efficient than economic transformation. Bootstrap estimates indicate that market structure is significantly associated with infrastructure construction efficiency, whereas audience size and venue attributes are significantly associated with economic transformation efficiency. To move beyond interpretation alone, the study also compares a baseline budget allocation rule with a DEA-informed allocation rule and quantifies how incremental public resources would be redistributed across representative regional types. The comparison shows that DEA-based evidence directs additional support toward regions with clear capacity or transformation bottlenecks and away from benchmark or relatively efficient regions. These findings suggest that improving the performing arts industry requires coordinated management of both linked stages and that DEA can inform not only efficiency diagnosis but also measurable policy design. This study develops a new representation of the performing arts industry, selects a DEA framework appropriate to that representation, produces a new diagnosis for each stage, and translates the analytical results into policy decisions.

Title: Channel coordination on exclusive vs. non-exclusive content under endogenous consumer homing
Authors: Malin Arve, Ole Kristian Dyskeland, Øystein Foros
Abstract: We analyze competition between two digital platforms selling subscriptions for unlimited access to their content catalogs. An upstream content provider offers additional content and chooses between a per-consumer wholesale price and a non-marginal contract, modeled as revenue sharing. The platforms independently decide whether to buy this additional content, so that exclusive or non-exclusive distribution arises endogenously. With low initial exclusivity, the content provider and both platforms prefer per-consumer wholesale pricing, yielding non-exclusive distribution and full consumer singlehoming. With high initial exclusivity, all parties prefer a non-marginal contract, yielding exclusive distribution and partial multihoming. Allowing contracts contingent on exclusivity does not change these predictions.

Title: Uncovering economic policy uncertainty during conflict
Authors: Sophie Brochet, Hannes Mueller, Christopher Rauh
Abstract: The correct measurement of economic policy uncertainty (EPU) plays a critical role in many policy settings - in particular where economic policy decisions need to be taken in response to large shocks. One such large shock is armed conflict. But, counterintuitively, the standard text-based EPU index systematically declines during armed conflict periods. Using a global news corpus covering 192 countries and over 5 million articles, we show that this decline is driven not by reduced uncertainty, but by a crowding out of reporting on economics and policy. We show that a combination of topic modeling and two-way fixed effects can be used to adjust the measurement of EPU, providing a new view on political risk during armed conflict. After adjustment, the EPU aligns more closely with firm perceptions, political risk insurance and investment during armed conflict.

Title: Inequality matters: A systematic review of heterogeneity in integrated assessment models
Authors: Sara Pavesio, Jaime Nieto, Mercedes Molpeceres, Óscar Carpintero
Abstract: Integrated Assessment Models (IAMs) are among the most widely used tools for informing climate policy, yet their capacity to represent social and economic heterogeneity remains limited. This paper presents a systematic literature review of IAMs to examine how inequality and heterogeneity are addressed within these models. Using the PRISMA framework, 115 IAMs were initially identified, of which 34 featured an endogenous economic component; only 15 incorporated any form of socioeconomic disaggregation. The analysis reveals that heterogeneity is predominantly captured through income, education, and labour-market variables, while dimensions such as gender, age, and health remain largely underrepresented. Although several models—such as MEDEAS, EUROGREEN, and GEM-E3—have advanced the integration of income distribution and labour-market differentiation, only a few explicitly assess inequality outcomes in their scenario analyses. The results highlight the persistent gap between social reality and model representation: most IAMs continue to rely on representative-agent assumptions, neglecting key feedback loops between inequality and environmental change. The paper concludes that expanding the inclusion of multidimensional heterogeneity—particularly gender and time-use dynamics—would enhance the capacity of IAMs to evaluate the distributive and behavioural effects of transition policies, thereby contributing to a more just and socially grounded ecological transition.

Title: Optimizing freight rail electrification: A framework for charge station selection and battery charge/swap scheduling
Authors: Jia Guo, Elnaz Irannezhad
Abstract: Battery-electric freight trains are promising for decarbonization by providing zero-emission transportation alternatives. Successful adoption of battery-electric freight trains depends on an efficient electrification strategy, involving infrastructure setup and charging scheduling. The study presents a comprehensive model for the optimal design of charging infrastructure and charge scheduling for trains. To provide greater recharging flexibility, we allow a battery to be either charged or swapped at a deployed station, and each train can carry multiple batteries. This problem is formulated as a mixed-integer linear programming model with a Rectangle Piecewise Linear Approximation (PLA) technique. To obtain strategic and tactical solutions, we develop two algorithms to solve the optimization problem: (1) a Fix Algorithm (FA), and (2) Benders Decomposition (BD) algorithm with extra feasibility cuts to speed up the procedure. In computational experiments, we use the original model with the PLA technique, and the two proposed algorithms. Statistical analysis verifies the modified BD algorithm with extra feasibility cuts performs best with respect to the objective function value in larger instances, closely followed by FA, and the PLA technique provides the least optimal solutions. Specifically, compared with the standard BD, the modified BD can reduce the objective function value by 11.73%, 30.92% and 51.58% on large, extra large and high-frequency instances, respectively. Sensitivity analysis is implemented to investigate the impact of delay penalty weight, charge rate, demand pattern and battery inventory. Finally, a case study is conducted to demonstrate the application of the proposed framework in a representative freight rail planning setting.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Which bike-train integration strategy is most suitable in a city? A cost comparison using continuous approximation
Authors: Regine Tejada, Andrés Fielbaum
Abstract: This paper studies which bike–train integration strategy minimizes total cost under varying city conditions. Assuming a uniform service area where travelers access a single train station, we develop continuous approximation models for three strategies: (i) shared bikes, (ii) private bike parking near stations, and (iii) boarding bikes on trains. Key decision variables depend on the modeled strategy, including the bike parking location, the number of bike-sharing stations, and the number of slots. The formulations show how demand, values of time, cycling and walking speeds, egress distance, land cost, truck speed, service-area size, and rail capacity affect optimal design and cost. Analytical comparisons are complemented by case studies in Parramatta (Australia) and Pasig City (Philippines). Results indicate: at low demand, boarding bikes on trains is attractive if there is enough train space and space cost is low; otherwise, parking private bikes is more favorable. At high demand, shared bikes dominate through reuse and smaller fleets. High time values make shared and private bikes costly due to rebalancing and security, making boarding bikes strategy favorable unless rail operating costs or crowding are high. Faster walking speeds mainly affect the shared bikes and private bike strategy. Faster cycling and long egress distances favor biking the last leg which is done when boarding bikes. High land costs favor smaller parking areas (from shared bikes). Slower streets and larger service areas result to avoiding shared bikes, and boarding can be infeasible under tight rail capacity. The framework guides cities on selecting cost-effective bike–train integration.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Air quality and noise exposures near an urban freight railyard in Canada
Authors: Angelos T. Anastasopolos, Keni Mallinen, Phillip Pham, Ryan Kulka, Mathieu Rouleau, Marianne Hatzopoulou, Tor Oiamo
Abstract: Growing demand for freight rail alongside trends in residential land use can lead to increased railyard activity near populations. Railyard locomotive and train movements generate air and noise pollution associated with adverse health effects. We sampled gaseous and particulate pollutants and measured sound levels over 15 months in a Toronto (Ontario, Canada) residential neighbourhood surrounding an active freight marshalling railyard. Analyses showed that both air pollutant concentrations and noise levels were higher in the railyard neighbourhood compared to non-railyard-influenced urban locations, notably during overnight hours. The composition of fine particulates in the railyard neighbourhood was enriched in elements consistent with railyard-relevant sources, such as wheel and rail abrasion, soil dust, and diesel fuel combustion exhaust. Railyard neighbourhood concentrations of toxic polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons were also elevated. Noise modeling showed that railyard sources contribute to locally elevated noise levels and noise characteristics. Thus, railyard neighbourhoods may have comparably high combined multi-pollutant exposures, inclusive of noise exposure. These findings can inform mitigation strategies for reducing air pollutant and noise exposure health risks for populations living near freight transportation hubs.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Setting boundaries and thresholds in transportation research and policy: Between principles of sufficientarianism and limitarianism
Authors: Ignacio Tiznado-Aitken, Jaime Soza-Parra
Abstract: This paper rethinks transport research and practice by integrating two distributive justice principles: sufficientarianism and limitarianism. While sufficiency has shaped debates on minimum accessibility, basic needs and mobility rights, the notion of upper thresholds or limits, central to limitarian thinking, remains underexplored. Drawing on transport, environmental, and political philosophy scholarship, we propose a normative mobility-accessibility-wellbeing corridor that guarantees accessibility to fulfill basic needs while curbing resource-intensive travel that exacerbates environmental degradation and undermines collective wellbeing. Combining features of a narrative and critical review, we examine cross-disciplinary frameworks on boundaries, critically discuss the main challenges when defining and navigating trade-offs between lower and upper thresholds in transportation, and illustrate how these principles are associated with established and emerging transport policies. We conclude with a discussion of further conceptual, empirical, and policy-oriented research directions opened up by this approach.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: The geometric adjudication of water rights in international rivers
Authors: Ricardo Martínez, Juan D. Moreno-Ternero
Abstract: We study the adjudication of water rights in international rivers. We characterize allocation rules that formalize focal principles to deal with water disputes in a basic model. Central to our analysis is a family of geometric rules that implement concatenated transfers downstream. They can be seen as formalizing Limited Territorial Sovereignty, as suggested in the Rio Declaration on Environment and Development. We apply our rules to the case of the Nile River, with a long history of disputes between downstream and upstream nations

Title: Urban bias in capital allocation: Evidence from China
Authors: Piyusha Mutreja, Abdulaziz B. Shifa, Wei Xiao
Abstract: Urban bias in resource allocation is central to development debates, yet direct evidence on differential access to capital remains limited. Using firm-level data from China, we infer the cost of capital from returns and compare urban and rural firms within the same prefecture. We find that urban firms have significantly lower returns, indicating cheaper access to capital. This gap is large for state-owned enterprises (SOEs) but negligible for nonstate firms, and is robust across specifications. The results suggest that urban bias in capital allocation is primarily driven by state-directed investment rather than private-sector constraints.

Title: Imperfect certification and endogenous quality provision
Authors: Mingyuan Ban, Yuyi Wang, Chan Zhou
Abstract: Existing studies on imperfect certification typically assume exogenous quality. This paper studies endogenous quality in a duopoly with certification subject to false negatives. Firms are either strategic or bad types. We show that, without bad types, imperfect certification cannot sustain high-quality provision in pure-strategy equilibrium. Introducing bad types disciplines strategic firms into choosing high quality when investment costs are sufficiently low. Thus, adverse selection can support, rather than undermine, quality investment incentives. Beyond the direct information effect, more accurate certification may reduce welfare by triggering an inefficient quality investment race.

Title: Thou shalt not fear: Crime drama and safety concerns
Authors: Dariia Mykhailyshyna, David Zuchowski
Abstract: Does prosocial television reduce safety concerns? Using daily municipal-level data before and after broadcasts of the Polish crime drama Ojciec Mateusz (Father Matthew), we exploit distance from Sandomierz, the town where the show is set, as a source of variation in the psychological salience of the broadcast. Reported safety concerns decline near Sandomierz the day after a broadcast, with the effect fading with distance. The effect is driven by low-violence episodes and police-substantiated reports, consistent with the show’s prosocial content improving actual safety.

Title: The incidence and distributional effects of electric vehicle subsidies in China
Authors: Jing Liang, Chao Wang, Junji Xiao
Abstract: This study investigates the pass-through and distributional effects of electric vehicle (EV) subsidies in China, offering insights for effective environmental policy design. Using a structural demand-supply model with detailed sales and survey data, we find that EV subsidies are more than fully passed through to consumers, yet disproportionately benefit high-income buyers. This regressive distribution undermines the subsidies’ effectiveness in promoting broader EV adoption. To address this, we propose an equitable alternative subsidy model that prioritizes innovation while being progressive—redistributing resources towards low-income households. Simulations demonstrate that, under the same budget, this scheme increases both consumer and producer surplus. Manufacturers pass on a larger share of the subsidy, and price-sensitive low-income buyers gain access to larger subsidies, expanding EV sales and yielding overall welfare gains through reduced market distortions. These findings underscore how subsidy design—particularly its distributional impact—is crucial to the success of clean vehicle policies in accelerating green technology adoption and mitigating environmental externalities, providing a blueprint for equitable, welfare-enhancing policies.

Title: Climate impacts on economic growth: Evidence on structural heterogeneity and state-dependent adaptation
Authors: Chueh-Yung Tsao
Abstract: Although climate change affects countries unevenly, the structural sources of this heterogeneity and the effectiveness of adaptation remain incompletely understood. This study develops a semi-parametric varying-coefficient framework that extends the anomaly-based climate–growth model of Kahn et al. (2021), allowing the economic effects of temperature anomalies to vary continuously with countries' structural characteristics. Using an unbalanced panel of 177 countries spanning 1965–2017, we examine six potential sources of heterogeneity and identify income, baseline temperature, and agricultural dependence as the primary structural determinants of climate vulnerability. The results reveal distinct nonlinear patterns across these structural dimensions. Climate impacts exhibit a piecewise-linear relationship with income, an inverted-smirk relationship with baseline temperature, and a threshold-like relationship with agricultural dependence. Extending the analysis to joint heterogeneity further demonstrates that the effectiveness of conventional adaptation strategies is inherently state dependent. Economic development reduces climate damages primarily in economies with relatively low agricultural dependence, whereas structural transformation is most effective in relatively high-income economies. By contrast, in persistently hot and highly agriculture-dependent economies, neither strategy alone is sufficient to substantially reduce climate damages. These findings suggest that effective climate policy should adopt differentiated adaptation strategies that account for countries' structural characteristics while integrating structural transformation with measures that reduce future climatic exposure.

Title: Uncovering household carbon emissions in a lower-fertility, shrinking society
Authors: Kaitong Yang, Jun Wu, Ling Li, Ling Tang
Abstract: Societal shifts such as shrinking households and lower fertility, profoundly affect household consumption patterns and emissions, posing challenges to climate mitigation goals. Using Japan, one of the countries with smaller household size and fertility rate than the global average, as a reference, we investigate long-term carbon footprints from household consumption and its intertemporal gaps based on household size and structure, by using an environmentally extended input–output model and Japan's household consumption survey from 2012 to 2022. The findings reveal that per capita household carbon footprint decreases with increasing household size. However, even within households of the same size, per capita carbon footprint varies by household structure, with households having fewer children typically generating lower emissions. Moreover, the carbon footprints of households with children show a greater intertemporal reduction gap than those without children. This study emphasizes that carbon reduction policies should be formulated with a deep understanding of household characteristics under social shifts, and these results have broad applications in other nations undergoing demographic transitions.

Title: Interviewers as instruments: estimating the wage penalty of drug use
Authors: Sergey Alexeev, Mark Wooden
Abstract: Abstract We exploit quasi-random interviewer assignment in the Australian HILDA Survey to instrument for self-reported drug use and estimate its effect on wages. Applying the optimal formula IV framework to six substance categories, we find that IV estimates largely mirror WLS for cannabis, ecstasy, and hallucinogens but diverge sharply for methamphetamine and inhalants — notably, the meth estimate reverses sign, indicating a wage penalty of 10% for frequent users, equivalent to the earnings loss from forgoing a high school diploma. Point estimates under IV suggest a larger premium for high cocaine use, but remain statistically similar to WLS. Romano-Wolf multiple-inference adjustment confirms substance-level significance for five of six drugs; the methamphetamine result, while just outside conventional thresholds after adjustment, is substantively large and clinically plausible. These findings demonstrate the empirical value of interviewer-driven variation for studying the labour-market effects of sensitive behaviours.

Title: How can firms implement smart manufacturing through supply chain collaboration? A multiple-case study from China
Authors: Weihua Liu, Jiahe Hou, Yang Cheng
Affiliations: College of Management and Economics, Tianjin University; Center for Industrial Production, Department of Materials and Production, Aalborg University; School of Business Administration, Jiangxi University of Finance and Economics
Abstract: The complex system characteristics of Smart manufacturing (SM) require firms collaborating with supply chain members to implement SM transformation. However, the motives, methods, and influencing factors of such collaboration remain unclear. Addressing this gap, we conduct a multi-case study of four manufacturing firms and obtain three findings based on complex adaptive system theory. First, the motives of supply chain collaboration include the adaptation to the environment of high customisation, technical complexity, policy, and horizontal competition. Second, firms collaborate with supply chain members in terms of equipment customisation and information interconnection, to establish the data and equipment foundation of SM. This process is affected by the scale and volume of invested resources. Based on these, firms further build collaborative platforms to realise the integrated management of all supply chain links and improve the SM capability through the iteration of solutions, which are affected by the degree of security in data sharing. Third, supply chain collaboration improves the quality and satisfaction, reduces the cost, and shortens the cycle of SM implementation. This study not only addresses whether and how supply chain collaboration influences SM implementation, but also provides guidance to help companies implement SM through a gradual multi-stage collaboration in supply chain.

Title: The impact of LLM-based recommendations on decisions under uncertainty
Authors: Marty Haoyuan Chen, Emel Filiz-Ozbay, Erkut Y. Ozbay
Affiliations: University of Maryland, College Park
Abstract: Abstract We study how large language model (LLM) based recommendations affect evaluations of uncertainty. We elicit certainty equivalents for (i) lotteries that share the same reduced-form winning probability but vary in cognitive demands because they are compound, and (ii) an Ellsberg-style ambiguous lottery. Across all lottery types, valuations from participants who receive LLM-based recommendations before each valuation exhibit second-order stochastic dominance relative to valuations from participants who do not. Hence, LLM-based recommendations leave mean valuations unchanged but compress the distribution, reducing the incidence of extreme valuations. Consistent with this pattern, LLM-based recommendations reduce the intensity of risk, complexity, and ambiguity aversion, while leaving the fraction of participants classified as averse unchanged.

Title: Borrowed plumes: the gender gap in claiming credit for teamwork
Authors: Klara Kinnl, Jakob Moeller, Anna Walter-Dockx
Affiliations: Vienna University of Economics and Business: Wirtschaftsuniversitat Wien; Institute for Advanced Studies Vienna
Abstract: Abstract Teamwork is prevalent in many forms of production, but individual contributions to team output are often ambiguous. We use a large-scale online experiment with an interactive team task to investigate gender differences in claiming credit for contributions to teamwork with misaligned incentives: Team members have an incentive to exaggerate their contribution, but this harms the other team member. In this setting, we observe that men claim to have contributed more than equally contributing women. Using two further between-subject treatments, we find no evidence that gender differences in altruism or in overconfidence explain the observed gender claim-gap. Further, the gender gap is present only among high contributors, and we show that the gap is particularly pronounced for large claims, which has potentially important consequences for gender equity in labour market outcomes.

Title: Entertainment-oriented or information-oriented streamers? retailers' streamer type choice with metaverse technology and consumer returns
Authors: Ke Bian, Guowei Hua, T. C. E. Cheng, Yadong Xu
Affiliations: Beijing Jiaotong University; The Hong Kong Polytechnic University; Beijing Technology and Business University

Title: Optimal multimodal transportation planning for precast modules used in modular construction under uncertainty
Authors: Wen Yi, Huiwen Wang, Bo Xiao, Ray Y. Zhong
Affiliations: The Hong Kong Polytechnic University; Michigan Technological University; The University of Hong Kong

Title: Correction
The economic impact of food loss reduction: an integrated food market and supply chain approach
Authors: Haitao Li, Hoa Hoang, Wyatt Thompson
Affiliations: Supply Chain & Analytics Department, Ed G. Smith College of Business, University of Missouri; Food and Agricultural Policy Research Institute, University of Missouri
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Supply chain equilibrium strategies under supply uncertainty: an analysis from a trust perspective
Authors: Xiao Fu, Jiahao Mao, Xinglong Qu, Guanghua Han
Affiliations: Zhejiang Informatization Development Institute, Hangzhou Dianzi University; School of Management, Hangzhou Dianzi University; School of International and Public Affairs, Shanghai Jiao Tong University
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Fuzzy radiotherapy optimization based on the surprise function: a comparative study of triangular and trapezoidal memberships
Authors: Nicole C. Cassimiro, Aurelio R. L. Oliveira
Affiliations: Universidade Estadual de Campinas, Institute of Applied Mathematics, Statistics and Scientific Computing
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Expected distances in grid networks: can the Manhattan metric be used in Manhattan?
Authors: Juliana Schulz, Okan Arslan, Gilbert Laporte
Affiliations: HEC Montréal; University of Bath
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Sustainable development goals and waste management in the wheat supply chain under uncertain conditions: implications from an emerging economy
Authors: Mahsa Rezaee Shirsavar, Misagh Rahbari, Mohammad Mohammadi
Abstract: Wheat, as one of the most fundamental crops, plays a strategic role in the food security of societies. The importance of wheat supply has been a critical issue in every society from the past to the present. Therefore, the aim of this research was to present a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model to optimize the wheat supply chain under uncertainty, which simultaneously incorporated the three main dimensions of sustainable development (economic, social, and environmental). In addition, various other features, such as wheat quality and supplier selection, were considered in this research. Furthermore, the chance-constrained programming (CCP) approach was employed to deal with the problem's uncertainty. To validate the problem practically, a real case study for the wheat supply chain in Iran was considered. Concerns about the generation of large volumes of waste throughout the wheat supply chain and the significant waste of production output led to the selection of the recycling (animal feed) method. This method not only combats waste disposal but also utilizes it as a potential source of profitability. Subsequently, an analysis of the employed waste management method was conducted by comparing it with the disposal (landfilling) method. Indeed, both waste management methods were applied in the model, and the results of each method were compared dimensionally. Finally, a sensitivity analysis was performed to validate the model and examine the impact of changes in key parameters on the problem's performance. Analysis of the results revealed that in the economic dimension, the highest profit earned was observed in the sale of processed products (40%), and also the highest cost incurred was related to wheat procurement costs (20%). In the social dimension, the largest share of job opportunities created was related to products transportation from silo to factory (29%). In the environmental dimension, the most significant negative impact was associated with the amount of electricity consumption for products production in factory (30%).

Title: Learning Dominant States in Elementary Resource Constrained Shortest Path Problems
Authors: Saverio Basso, Alessandro Minoli, Matteo Salani
Abstract: Abstract In this work, we investigate whether machine learning can be leveraged to identify promising states in dynamic programming algorithms, focusing on Elementary Resource Constrained Shortest Path Problems (ERCSPP). More in detail, we solved 41 single resource instances from SPPRCLIB using iterative relaxation techniques through the PathWyse library, systematically collecting all generated states (i.e. labels). We designed ad-hoc features computable in constant time and constructed two datasets: one containing all generated labels (G) and another with only those inserted into data pools (I), totaling several hundred million labels. Machine learning tools are then employed to explore these datasets, revealing significant patterns between successive relaxations. Leveraging these insights, we propose a normalization approach and apply supervised learning techniques to distinguish dominating states, both within subsequent relaxations of the same problem and in previously unseen instances. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach on Dataset G, while for Dataset I, performance varies, showing strong results within the same instance but declining for unseen ones. We therefore propose a data-driven policy that leverages trained models to prioritize the extension of promising labels during dynamic programming. Preliminary evaluation shows consistent reductions in the number of extended states across almost all instances, with speedups emerging on larger ones, supporting the viability of data-driven dynamic programming algorithms.

Title: High-Probability Polynomial-Time Complexity of Restarted Primal-Dual Hybrid Gradient Method for Linear Programming
Authors: Zikai Xiong
Affiliations: Department of Industrial Engineering and Management Sciences, Northwestern University, Evanston, Illinois 60208
Abstract: The restarted primal-dual hybrid gradient method (rPDHG) is a first-order method recently known for its computational effectiveness in solving linear programming (LP) problems. Despite its impressive practical performance, the theoretical iteration bounds for rPDHG can be exponentially poor. To investigate this gap from a probabilistic perspective, we show that rPDHG achieves polynomial-time complexity in a high-probability sense, under assumptions on the probability distribution from which the data instance is generated. We consider both Gaussian and more general sub-Gaussian distribution models. For standard-form LP instances with m constraints and n variables, our bounds take a particularly simple form when m is not too close to n: rPDHG iterates settle on the optimal basis in [Formula: see text] iterations, followed by [Formula: see text] iterations to compute an [Formula: see text]-optimal solution, with probability at least [Formula: see text] for [Formula: see text] that is not exponentially small. The Stage I bound further improves to [Formula: see text] in the Gaussian distribution model. Experimental results confirm the tail behavior and the polynomial-time dependence on problem dimensions of the iteration counts. As an application of our probabilistic analysis, we explore how the disparity among the components of the optimal solution bears on the performance of rPDHG, and we provide guidelines for generating challenging LP instances. Funding: Part of this work was performed at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and was supported by the Air Force Office of Scientific Research [Grant FA9550-22-1-0356]. Another part of this work was performed at the Georgia Institute of Technology and was supported by the Office of Naval Research [Award N00014-25-1-2088].

Title: Europe at the crossroads: trading strategic autonomy for resilience under degrowth
Authors: Oliver Kovacs
Abstract: This paper reviews the economic interpretations of strategic autonomy, which has been reintroduced, and sheds new light on it from the perspective of the European economy using a systems approach. The scientific conundrum is whether European strategic autonomy requires strengthening internal quantitative growth or whether it requires a shift towards degrowth – a transition that ultimately trades strategic autonomy for systemic resilience. The paper uses the zombie phenomenon to demonstrate the flawed nature of quantitative economic growth-based strategic autonomy and the necessity of a degrowth transition that replaces autonomy with resilience, which necessitates the fundamental reassessment of the role of zombies.

Title: AI-enabled traceability in the dairy supply chain: a technology-organisation-environment and acceptance model
Authors: Mohit Malik, Rahul S Mor, Vijay Kumar Gahlawat, Sarvjeet Ranjan, Ilias Vlachos
Abstract: The digital transformation in the dairy supply chain (SC) has enabled advanced innovations, including AI- and blockchain-based digital traceability systems that enhance transparency and efficiency. Despite these benefits, dairy stakeholders face significant barriers to adoption, including regulatory constraints, shifting consumer expectations, limited resources, and a lack of clear guidance for implementing digital innovations that support transparency and sustainability. To address these challenges, this research integrates the Technology-Organisation-Environment (TOE) framework with the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) to examine factors influencing the adoption of AI-enabled traceability systems in the dairy supply chain, offering policymakers and industry practitioners valuable insights. Survey data from 202 stakeholders in the dairy SC were analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling to examine an integrated TOE–TAM framework. The findings demonstrate that technological, organisational, and environmental factors strongly influence perceived usefulness and ease of use, which, in turn, influence stakeholders’ willingness to implement AI-enabled traceability systems. Competitive pressure does not significantly affect the adoption of AI-enabled traceability systems, suggesting that operational strategies and regulatory compliance outweigh competitive dynamics when making adoption decisions. This study contributes to the growing literature on traceability adoption and digital transformation by offering a multi-level TOE-TAM perspective on implementing the AI-enabled traceability in highly regulated food supply chains.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: An enhanced biased random-key genetic algorithm for solving the vulnerability envelope problem of urban rail transit networks
Authors: Zhiao Ma, Yu Gu, Yingying Xu, Anthony Chen, Xin Yang, Jianjun Wu
