Results from the other two experiments show that surprise promotes reciprocation only when trust reflects an intentional choice by the trustor and when cognitive load in the decision environment is not too high.

Title: Testing capacity-constrained learning
Authors: Andrew Caplin, Daniel Martin, Philip Marx, Anastasiia Morozova, Leshan Xu
Affiliations: New York University; University of California, Santa Barbara; Louisiana State University
Abstract: Abstract We introduce a general test of capacity-constrained learning models. Learning has capacity constraints when the set of possible ways to learn is exogenously fixed, as in the widely used fixed-capacity versions of rational inattention (Sims, 2003) and efficient coding (Woodford, 2012). With such models, changes in incentives do not alter the extent of attention, only how individuals decide to allocate their scarce attention. We show that choice data are consistent with capacity-constrained learning if and only if they satisfy a No Improving (Action or Attention) Switches (NIS) condition. Based on existing experiments in which the incentives for being correct are varied, we find strong evidence that participants fail NIS for a wide range of standard perceptual tasks: identifying the proportion of ball colors, recognizing shapes, and counting the number of balls. We further show that violations of NIS occur systematically in response to higher incentives, suggesting that incentives often expand attention beyond what capacity-constrained models allow. However, we find that this is not true for all existing perceptual tasks in the literature, which offers insights into settings where we do or do not expect incentives to impact the extent of attention.

Title: Platform financing and government subsidies for heterogeneous smallholder farmers under yield uncertainty
Authors: Shuchen Ni, Chun Feng
Affiliations: School of Transportation and Logistics, Southwest Jiaotong University; National United Engineering Laboratory of Integrated and Intelligent Transportation
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Exploring the distribution and evolution of decision-making autonomy for plants in international manufacturing networks: embedded case studies from the machinery industry
Authors: Yang Cheng, Tao Huang, John Johansen, Jan Olhager
Affiliations: Department of Materials and Production, Aalborg University; School of Business Administration, Jiangxi University of Finance and Economics; Department of Industrial and Mechanical Sciences, Lund University

Title: Generative artificial intelligence and international green supply chain performance: dynamic capabilities as strategic enablers
Authors: Shaofeng Wang, Hao Zhang
Affiliations: Fuzhou University of International Studies and Trade International Business School, , Fuzhou, , and School of Management, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, China; Zhejiang Shuren University School of Economics and Management, , Hangzhou
Abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how generative artificial intelligence (GAI) adoption is associated with international green supply chain performance and international competitive advantage in cross-border e-commerce enterprises. Drawing on dynamic capabilities theory and the Technology–Organization–Environment–Human framework, the authors examine absorptive capacity and transformative capacity as intermediate capability mechanisms and artificial intelligence turbulence as a contingency. Design/methodology/approach The authors use an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design. The quantitative strand combines survey data from 334 Chinese cross-border e-commerce enterprises with partial least squares structural equation modeling, fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis and importance-performance map analysis. The subsequent qualitative strand draws on semi-structured interviews with ten managers and executives directly involved in GAI implementation, which are integrated with the quantitative evidence at the interpretation stage. Findings GAI adoption is positively associated with absorptive and transformative capacities, which are in turn positively associated with international green supply chain performance and international competitive advantage. International green supply chain performance shows the largest estimated association with international competitive advantage. Artificial intelligence turbulence positively moderates the relationships between GAI adoption and both capacities, and the configurational analysis identifies five equifinal configurations sufficient for high international competitive advantage. Practical implications Managers should develop absorptive and transformative capacities alongside GAI implementation, integrate sustainability requirements into artificial intelligence-enabled supply chain decisions and pursue internally coherent implementation routes rather than a single ideal template. Originality/value This study integrates variance-based, configurational and qualitative evidence to explain the capability pathways through which GAI adoption is associated with environmental and competitive outcomes in cross-border supply chain settings rather than in dyadic buyer–supplier relationships.
Journal: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

Title: Geometric portfolio equilibria: constraint curvature and asset pricing
Authors: Massimiliano Ferrara
Abstract: Institutional investors optimise over feasible sets whose shape is dictated by regulation and mandate. This paper asks whether the intrinsic geometry of those sets, as distinct from the shadow cost of the constraints that define them, carries independent information for equilibrium prices. We answer the question in two steps. First, we show that the position limits and linear matching requirements most commonly invoked in this literature generate polyhedral feasible sets whose smooth strata are affine and therefore intrinsically flat, so that no curvature mechanism can be attributed to them; the correct analytical tools there are tangent and normal cones and Karush–Kuhn–Tucker multipliers. Second, we isolate a class of genuinely nonlinear constraints, of which the active boundary of a quadratic rebalancing budget is the leading case, whose transversal intersection with the wealth constraint is a smooth submanifold of dimension $$N-2$$ N - 2 with non-vanishing sectional curvature. On that class we formulate a competitive equilibrium with price impact, prove existence and uniqueness under an explicit curvature domination condition, and derive a three-term decomposition of expected excess returns into a zero-beta rate, a classical covariance premium, and a curvature term that is written explicitly as a second fundamental form contracted with the multiplier vector. A fully specified four-asset example computes every object in the decomposition in closed form and shows that the curvature term vanishes when the constraint is replaced by its tangent hyperplane, which separates it from the shadow cost of a binding constraint. An empirical exercise on S&P 500 index funds documents a priced constraint-proximity factor that is not spanned by the Fama–French–Carhart factors; we interpret this factor as a measure of crowding near regulatory limits rather than as an estimate of Riemannian curvature, and we state the conditions under which the two coincide.

Title: Kalman Filter Learning, Bounded Rationality and Informational Consistency
Authors: Szabolcs Deák, Paul Levine, Joseph Pearlman, Bo Yang
Affiliations: Department of Economics University of Exeter Exeter UK; School of Social Sciences, Economics University of Surrey Guildford UK; Department of Economics City St George's, University of London London UK; Department of Economics Swansea University Swansea UK
Abstract: ABSTRACT We develop a behavioural New Keynesian model with rational (RE) and boundedly rational (BR) agents. The latter are anticipated utility learners and use simple heuristic rules to forecast aggregate variables exogenous to their micro‐environment. For the RE agents, we study two information assumptions: standard perfect information and imperfect information (II‐involving Kalman‐filter learning). We show that a consistent set of II for the modeller and the private sector generates endogenous persistence of decisions in response to unobserved exogenous shocks and thus RE under II dominates the BR specifications in empirical comparisons. We reveal substantial evidence of composite RE(II)‐BR structure with estimated proportions of RE and BR agents. Our results highlight the importance of informational consistency for the analysis of behavioural heterogeneity.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: Childbirth Effects of the 2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami
Authors: Elizabeth Kayoon Hur, Seung‐hun Lee
Affiliations: Department of Economics Michigan State University East Lansing Michigan USA; Taipei School of Economics National Tsing Hua University Hsinchu Taiwan
Abstract: ABSTRACT This paper evaluates the effect of in utero exposure to the 2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami on birth outcomes in Indonesia. Exploiting variation in the timing of exposure, we find that the probability of a successful pregnancy drops by 5.4 percentage points (pp), while miscarriages increase by 5.0 pp for those exposed in the first trimester of pregnancy. Gestation length shortens by 0.28 months, and the likelihood of preterm birth rises by 5.4 pp. We find suggestive evidence that post‐disaster health investments by households may have shielded later cohorts from harmful effects, while measures of maternal health and socioeconomic status have limited explanatory power. Our results suggest the importance of considering fetal loss as a first‐order cost in natural disasters and highlight that facilitating household investment in health through various policies may mitigate negative birth effects in the aftermath.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: Scaffolding the void: Digital platforms as intermediaries in supply chain traceability
Authors: Quynh Do, Claudia Colicchia, Alessandro Creazza, Mark Stevenson, Stella Viscardi
Abstract: In response to the escalating regulatory and normative demands for supply chain traceability and transparency, digital platforms offer a novel solution that overcomes the limitations of the conventional, siloed approach to managing opaque, multi-tiered supply networks. However, little is known about how these third-party intermediaries help firms address supplier resistance and relational deficits inherent in multi-tier supply chains. This research addresses this gap by developing an empirically grounded framework that explains the scaffolding roles of digital platform organizations. Employing an abductive, multiple-case study approach, we analyze four use cases of traceability-oriented platforms within the garment and footwear sectors. Our findings first reveal that traceability challenges constitute an institutional void, a space where rapid legislative advancement outpaces existing norms and shared understandings in the industry. This in turn creates architectural, cognitive, and relational deficits that hinder traceability efforts. We then uncover three scaffolding mechanisms in which platforms enable firms to bridge these gaps: constructing interoperability layers, interpreting legislative demands to bridge cognitive gaps, and mediating relational trust. This study contributes to institutional theory and supply chain literature by showing how platforms scaffold socio-technical change to embed traceability practices in multi-tier settings. We also provide a strategic guide for managers to leverage platform networks to trace their supply chains.

Title: Material use and its relationship with per capita income. A panel data analysis at the global level
Authors: Tommaso Luzzati, Emilio Padilla Rosa, Bhavesh Gulati, Vicente Rios, Angela Parenti, Stefan Giljum
Abstract: Global use of materials has significantly increased over recent decades, causing a wide range of environmental and social concerns. In this study, we use the latest available data from the UN database on global material flows to investigate the Environmental Kuznets Curve (EKC) hypothesis for two widely used material flow indicators, Domestic Material Consumption and Material Footprint, for a dataset of 147 countries. Using both semiparametric and parametric methods over a longer period than any previous study (1970–2019), we find no evidence in support of the EKC hypothesis. A concerning result is that material-income elasticities are higher after 1989, implying that the situation has not improved. We conclude that major changes have not yet occurred in the income-material use relationship and that strong policy measures remain necessary to reduce material consumption.

Title: Channel competition in airline distribution: A game-theoretic analysis of Global Distribution System and New Distribution Capability
Authors: Yutao Guo, Changmin Jiang, Ruotian Chen, Hongwei Wang
Abstract: This paper examines how New Distribution Capability (NDC) reshapes the airline distribution value chain long dominated by Global Distribution Systems (GDS). We build a three-tier game-theoretic model of airline, technology provider, and travel agency across four structures—GDS monopoly, NDC monopoly, dual-channel competition, and incumbent-led integration—to identify the mechanisms of channel competition and incumbent transformation. Results show that GDS incentives are neutral in the benchmark model: fee adjustments and pass-through leave final prices and demand unchanged, helping explain the persistence of legacy models. Under an NDC monopoly, airlines have stronger incentives to invest in service quality, while agencies shift from rebate recipients to paying users. With GDS–NDC competition, platform fees fall and allocative efficiency improves; NDC’s technological edge is non-linear, as aggregators may employ penetration pricing once quality crosses a threshold. Incumbent-led integration—where a GDS operates both the legacy GDS and an NDC channel—internalizes inter-channel rivalry and restores monopoly pricing power. Welfare results reveal a trade-off: competition raises efficiency via lower fees, whereas incumbent-led integration can deliver higher dynamic welfare when technology-upgrade costs are low, despite stronger pricing power. Further extensions examine endogenous quality choice, fee rigidity, and NDC-exclusive ancillary bundling. They show how market structure shapes long-run airline quality investment, demonstrate that constrained GDS fees can turn agency incentives into a competitive instrument, and indicate that differentiated bundles strengthen NDC demand while making content access central to the welfare assessment of integration. Guided by these results, we propose a staged regulatory path: foster interoperability and entry when adoption costs are high; protect contestability during consolidation; and, at maturity, shift from price control to performance-based oversight.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: An energy-efficient coordinated procurement, production, and batch delivery scheduling system for sustainable operations with Net-Zero emissions
Authors: Sayem Ahmed, Ripon Kumar Chakrabortty, Alireza Abbasi, Tsan-Ming Choi
Abstract: Over the last decade, rising energy prices, global warming, the harmful effects of energy use, and carbon emissions have highlighted the importance of energy and carbon efficiency. In response to local energy regulations and carbon-sensitive markets, manufacturers and logistics organizations are actively seeking effective methods to improve energy and carbon efficiency. This research enhances supply chain planning and scheduling by combining procurement, production, and delivery decisions to support sustainable operations through simultaneously optimizing costs, energy consumption, and carbon emissions. An E nergy- E fficient C oordinated P roduction- D istribution S ystem ( EE-CPDS ) is designed, accounting for a flexible job-shop scheduling environment with inter-machine transport times and sequence-dependent setup times to reflect real production configurations. To address the computational challenge, we propose a novel multi-objective adaptive search memetic algorithm (MOASMA) that outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of solution quality, i.e., generating global solutions closer to true Pareto front with average hypervolume (HV) value of 0.7131 and Inverted Generational Distance Plus (IGD + ) value of 0.0249 across nine test instances, which is further endorsed by nonparametric statistical analysis. Among the instances solved by all competing algorithms, MOASMA provides better solutions for 77% of them. The correctness and effectiveness of the developed algorithm are verified by comparing the results with an exact solver (Gurobi), which is effective for small and medium-sized instances, while MOASMA proves efficient for larger-scale problems. The proposed system and algorithm will assist enterprises in solving practical-sized instances while rationalizing coordinated procurement, production, and distribution decisions that support sustainable operations and drive progress toward net-zero emissions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Defensive decoupling and resilience redistribution in the global power battery supply chain: A cascading failure framework with a context-dependent supplier rupture mechanism
Authors: Chao Wang, Sining Ma, Ming K. Lim
Abstract: Compliance and geopolitical pressures can destabilize supply relationships even when production capacity remains intact. Yet downstream continuity may reveal little about losses elsewhere in the supply chain. When interfirm transaction flows are unobserved, it is difficult to assess how defensive sourcing decisions and constrained reallocation shape these uneven outcomes. This study develops a cascading-failure framework integrating gravity-style flow reconstruction, context-dependent supplier rupture with nonlinear interference effects, constrained order reallocation, and overload and throughput-depletion exits. Flow reconstruction combines product–tier-normalized firm-scale proxies, technical coefficients, political alignment, and geographical distance. The framework is applied to a disclosed-core power-battery supply network of 295 firms and 615 directed relationships. Matched-edge Pearson and full-matrix QAP comparisons assess the reconstructed flows, while benchmarks, ablations, and sensitivity analyses examine cascade dynamics. In the focal reconstruction-origin stress test, eight of nine EU-facing terminal firms survive despite 75 firm exits, 70 caused by throughput depletion. Defensive rupture drives structural deterioration, while reallocation supports terminal-firm survival and network-wide survival. These asymmetric outcomes primarily reflect endogenous adjustment: the six initial compliance disconnections add approximately 0.07 percentage points to weighted flow loss. Separate interventions on model-stationary networks show that screening can induce additional exits, depending on behavioral settings, the pre-intervention network, and ESG-update rules. Sobol analysis identifies distinct parameter influences on modeled activity loss, fragmentation, and survival. The findings explain how relationship decisions and constrained adaptation produce uneven resilience across tiers, supporting whole-chain assessment that distinguishes ongoing network adjustment from the additional effects of compliance intervention.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Street-scale heat exposure mapping for urban cyclists: Integrating vision transformer-GAN with aggregated Strava cycling activity data
Authors: Jin Rui, Zhaowen Xu
Abstract: Street-scale variation in the thermal environment is difficult to represent using spatially coarse meteorological data, limiting the assessment of cycling environments during extreme heat. This study develops a street-scale heat-exposure mapping framework and applies it alongside aggregated cycling activity records in Melbourne. The framework combines street-view imagery and environmental metadata using a Vision Transformer and a conditional generative adversarial network to predict calibrated operative-temperature-equivalent fields. These fields serve as environmental heat-exposure proxies. Direct assessment of thermal comfort and physiological heat stress requires additional subjective and physiological observations. The model achieved a mean absolute error of 3.42°C against calibrated reference label fields on the independent test set. Analysis of 35,416 street-view images identified six landscape types, with higher predicted exposure in dense built-up environments and lower exposure in green-dominated environments. Multi-kernel support vector regression was used to examine the predictive importance of streetscape indicators, while aggregated Strava records from 4 to 13 March 2024 were used to compare cycling activity during the heatwave and adjacent comparison days. The principal contribution is a framework for characterising fine-scale environmental heat-exposure patterns and supporting their investigation alongside cycling activity. Its application informs the screening of potentially heat-vulnerable cycling environments, while the short observation window and aggregate data limit inference about individual adaptation and causal effects.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: “Made in heaven, matched by parents”: Can arranged marriage restrict labour market autonomy and participation of women?
Authors: Sugata Bag, Anirban Kar
Abstract: Female labour force participation in India has stagnated despite gains in other aspects. Do Indian women prefer to stay out of labour market voluntarily or do social norms prevent their participation? We identify parental involvement in partner choice during marriage as an important bottleneck. We first find that women who had some degree of involvement in partner choice enjoy significantly more autonomy in post-marriage labour market choices than those whose marriages were arranged solely by parents. We use a marriage tradition instrument to estimate causal effects. Since autonomy and participation affect each other, next, we estimate simultaneous equations for autonomy and participation for only rural women. We use parental involvement in marriage and district-level share of drought-affected villages as two exogenous variables the former for autonomy and the latter for participation. We find that autonomy significantly increases participation. We further explain the mechanism through a theoretical model. To distinguish between autonomy and participation; we introduce a new household delegation game. The main message of the theoretical model is that parental involvement in partner choice reduces women’s ability to screen partners leading to relatively more mismatches, i.e., women who are inclined to work mismatched with men who prefer

Title: Invisible bridge: Digital infrastructure, energy transition, and energy poverty
Authors: Shunlin Jin, Shuai Shao, Weidong Wang, Yuanren Zhou
Abstract: We study the effect of digital infrastructure on household energy poverty. We develop a theoretical framework in which digital infrastructure reduces labor-market and information frictions, raising household income and improving access to modern energy technologies. Using the rollout of China's largest national digital infrastructure program, the Broadband China Pilot (BCP) policy, and multiple micro-household tracking datasets, we find that the policy alleviates household energy poverty by approximately 2.7 percentage points in treated cities. The effect operates mainly through higher off-farm income and improved access to modern energy equipment, and is stronger in poorer and more remote markets. A distinctive rural survey dataset shows that digital connectivity also benefits older households with limited off-farm employment opportunities through neighbor-assisted transfer arrangements involving adult children and nearby connected households, while generating village-level information spillovers in modern energy equipment adoption. The findings highlight the role of digital infrastructure in promoting household energy transition and reducing energy poverty.

Title: When mortality jumps: Optimal portfolio design for defined contribution pension schemes
Authors: Davide Feleppa, Immacolata Oliva
Abstract: This paper analyzes optimal portfolio allocation in defined contribution pension schemes under joint exposure to mortality and financial jump risks. We develop a continuous-time framework in which both mortality intensity and financial asset prices follow jump–diffusion dynamics, extending standard pension models with continuous mortality and diffusion-based markets. The member’s objective combines expected terminal wealth maximization with downside risk control via Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR), generating a time inconsistent stochastic control problem. We reformulate the problem as a bilevel optimization structure: for a fixed CVaR threshold, the inner problem reduces to a standard stochastic control problem, while the outer problem becomes a one-dimensional convex minimization. Using inf-convolution regularization and a probabilistic gradient representation derived from Feynman–Kac theory, we establish existence, uniqueness, and differentiability properties of the value function, thereby ensuring analytical tractability of the model. These results provide a rigorous foundation for numerical implementation through semi-Lagrangian schemes combined with gradient-based optimization. Numerical experiments quantify the impact of mortality jumps and mortality-linked derivatives on optimal portfolio policies. In particular, short-maturity longevity derivatives enhance downside protection, and appropriately structured hedging of mortality jump risk improves tail risk measures without reducing expected terminal wealth.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: Identification of priority areas for inclusive automated vehicle infrastructure investment
Authors: Arkar Than Win, John D. Nelson, Chinh Ho
Abstract: Highly automated vehicles (AVs) have the potential to improve mobility for older adults and people with disabilities. Planning for AVs requires substantial infrastructure investments, but limited resources make simultaneous upgrades impractical. Understanding how potential mobility gains differ by locations is useful for targeting investments, yet little is known about these differences. To address this gap, this study uses propensity score matching with moderation analysis to examine how built environment characteristics moderate the potential impacts of AVs on trip frequencies of older adults and people with disabilities using two Australian datasets. Findings suggest that potential mobility gains vary by location. Potential mobility gains for people with disabilities are larger in areas with low density, public transport accessibility, diversity, and high cumulative accessibility; whereas those for older adults are greater in areas with high cumulative accessibility and road connectivity. These findings provide guidance for prioritising AV-related infrastructure investments to promote social inclusion.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: On the strategic benefits of diversity in teamwork and other aggregative games
Authors: Martin Kaae Jensen
Abstract: Can heterogeneity in team members’ ability levels confer benefits that enable heterogeneous teams to outperform homogeneous teams even when the latter are more skilled on average? Or do less capable individuals, as in Benabou (1996), drag down the productivities of more capable ones? This paper shows that, in aggregative games, such questions are fully tractable and that the answers depend on simple and economically interpretable conditions that weigh direct efficiency effects against individuals’ strategic adjustments to heterogeneity. The main results are qualitative and quantitative comparative statics results. The latter associate aggregate outcomes one-to-one with “diversity indices,” introduced here for the first time and shown always to exist given a reference population. These diversity indices turn out to be closely related to the inequality indices of Atkinson (1970) and Shorrocks (1980). In the main application to teamwork, heterogeneity in ability levels is shown to confer strategic benefits on teams under standard convexity assumptions.

Title: FOMC supply-side communication and long-term inflation expectations
Authors: Abhinay Mishra, Kshitij Bhalchandra Shingwekar
Abstract: We investigate whether topics emphasized in FOMC communication affect market inflation expectations beyond policy-rate decisions. Using Fed Chair statements from 2011 to 2026, we measure attention across six macroeconomic themes and examine meeting-day changes in the 5y-5y forward inflation break-even rate. Controlling for the two-year Treasury yield, we find that attention to supply-side risks raises inflation expectations, mainly through energy and supply-chain narratives, whereas demand-side attention has no significant effect. These findings suggest that market inflation expectations respond to risks emphasized in central bank communication, identifying narrative focus as a distinct monetary policy communication channel.

Title: Where is the Swiss safe haven? Geopolitical risk, bank deposits and custody portfolios
Authors: Dimitris Anastasiou, Athanasios Michairinas, Steven Ongena, Athanasios Sakkas
Abstract: Switzerland is the archetypal financial safe haven, yet its bank deposits do not behave like one. Using Swiss National Bank data, we find no robust positive deposit response to geopolitical risk. The clearer response appears in custody portfolios. After a one-standard-deviation rise in European geopolitical risk, the non-resident equity share falls by 1.16 p.p. relative to the resident share after two years, while the bond and money-market share rises by 0.78 p.p. after one year and 0.68 p.p. after two years. Global geopolitical threats and acts generate opposite relative-share responses, a pattern consistent with precautionary de-risking.

Title: A regional multi-criteria assessment of European education and training systems
Authors: Fernando J. Osório, Luís C. Dias
Abstract: This paper proposes a multi-criteria sorting and ranking approach based on ELECTRE TRI to assess educational performance across 200 European regions, across the 2020-2024 period. The analysis relies on criteria from early childhood education to adult learning within the European Union’s Education and Training 2030 (ET2030) framework. To address uncertainty in preference-related parameters, the worst and best categories each region can attain over an admissible parameter space are identified using linear programming. Rankings are obtained under pessimistic and optimistic perspectives, both derived to be consistent with the sorting results. The results are complemented with a SMAA-TRI analysis producing category acceptability indices, which are further aggregated to yield alternative compatible rankings. Through four modelling scenarios, the study examines the effects of imposing veto thresholds and a partial order on criteria weights favouring earlier education stages. The results reveal a persistent geographical divide, with lagging regions concentrated in Romania and southern Italy, and top performers mainly in Northern and Western Europe. The greatest improvements were observed across Ireland, Poland, Sweden, Hungary, and Croatia, while Romania remains stagnant and most German regions declined.

Title: A model-based systems engineering framework for integrated asset information modelling and simulation
Authors: Shouxuan Wu, Chao Yang, Yufan Liu, Haoxuan Zhang, Zhen Zhang, David B. Cameron, Foivos Psarommatis, Arild Waaler, Dimitris Kiritsis, Yuanwei Qu, Guoxin Wang, Jinzhi Lu
Affiliations: Beijing Institute of Technology; University of Oslo; Aalto University; École polytechnique fédérale de Lausanne; Beihang University

Title: Economics of ad-blocking: An analysis of customer incentivization and whitelisting content provider models
Authors: Ayesha Arora, Tarun Jain
Affiliations: Indian Institute of Management Calcutta; Indian Institute of Management Bangalore
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Revisiting the ordinal priority approach in multi-attribute decision-making: A centralized DEA-based preference voting interpretation
Authors: Renlong Wang
Affiliations: Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Rice University; School of Emergency Management Science and Engineering, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: The impact of AI investment on shipping outsourcing strategies for easing congestion under coastal piggybacking regulation
Authors: Naimeng Liu, Cheng Zhang, Bin Liu
Abstract: This paper examines the strategic interactions among AI adoption, shipping outsourcing mode selection, and coastal piggybacking (CPB) regulation in a multi-level shipping supply chain consisting of a cargo agent (CA), a liner shipping company (LS), a flag-of-convenience carrier (FOC), and a transshipment port (FOT). We develop a game-theoretic model in which AI serves dual roles: it enhances demand forecasting accuracy (information-precision effect) and reduces service time (service-time reduction effect). The cargo agent chooses between consignment and turnkey contracting under different information structures. We find that AI generates opposing effects on the CA’s outsourcing preference: the information-precision effect favors turnkey, while the service-time reduction effect favors consignment, leading to a counterintuitive outcome in which advanced AI makes consignment more attractive. The LS’s AI investment is profitable only under certain conditions and depends critically on the learning efficiency of the technology, revealing an asymmetry in how AI affects the LS versus the CA. Furthermore, AI improves social welfare only when congestion is sufficiently severe; otherwise, its demand-expansion effect may worsen congestion. CPB unambiguously reduces congestion and improves welfare, but its interaction with AI is conditional: complements when AI is immature, substitutes when mature. These findings challenge conventional wisdom and provide implications for the sequencing of regulatory and technology policies.

Title: Dynamic Programming-Compatible Uncertainty Sets in Robust Markov Decision Processes
Authors: Julien Grand-Clément, Nian Si, Shengbo Wang
Affiliations: Information Systems and Operations Management Department, Ecole des Hautes Etudes Commerciales de Paris, 78350 Jouy-en-Josas, France; Department of Industrial Engineering and Decision Analytics, Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Hong Kong; Daniel J. Epstein Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California 90007
Abstract: In this paper, we investigate the compatibility of robust Markov decision processes (RMDPs) with dynamic programming under various assumptions on the uncertainty set (i.e., we investigate when one can solve an RMDP by solving a fixed-point equation. We show that in all generality, s-rectangular and sa-rectangular uncertainty sets are the only models of uncertainty that are compatible with dynamic programming. Our analysis shows that existing nonrectangular models, including r-rectangularity, are only weakly compatible with dynamic programming as they require the assumption that rewards do not depend on the next state. In this case, our results imply that one can always construct a rectangular uncertainty set that is equivalent for both policy evaluation and optimization to the dynamic programming-compatible nonrectangular model. This highlights a key limitation; dynamic-programming-compatible nonrectangular uncertainty sets, although practically relevant for uncertainty quantification, do not provide a genuinely distinct assessment of policy performance. Interestingly, our proof techniques rely on identifying a novel simultaneous solvability property, which we show is central to several important properties of RMDPs, including the existence of stationary optimal policies and dynamic programming-based formulations. The simultaneous solvability property enables a unified approach to studying all existing models of uncertainty, rectangular and nonrectangular alike. Funding: The work described in this paper was partially supported by the Research Grants Council, University Grants Committee [Grant HKUST603/25] and the Agence Nationale de la Recherche [Grant HKUST603/25]. J. Grand-Clément was also supported by the Labex Ecodec [Grant ANR-11-LABEX-0047].

Title: Assessing the resilience of international multimodal container transport networks from a perspective of temporal accessibility
Authors: Yifan Zhu, Mengqiao Xu, Ran Yan, Adolf K.Y. Ng
Abstract: Multimodal container transport has become the predominant mode for international freight movement, but its supporting transport infrastructure is under threat from various risks. Therefore, accurately assessing the resilience of the international multimodal container transport network is critical to countries’ trade and economic development. This paper proposes a framework for assessing the resilience of international multimodal container transport networks (IMCTNs) that integrate road, inland rail, and international maritime shipping. First, an algorithm is developed to identify time-respecting international multimodal transport paths while considering transfer and schedule constraints. Based on these paths, the framework defines temporal accessibility metrics for international multimodal transport under two common multimodal modes (i.e., road-rail-sea and road-sea) at both the 10-km grid level and the city level. Second, the proposed accessibility metrics serve as performance indicators for evaluating the resilience of countries’ international multimodal transport networks against disruption risks. Finally, the effectiveness of this framework is illustrated through an application to a real IMCTN in Mainland China. The accessibility analysis reveals clear regional disparities, with a general decline from east to west and south to north under the two multimodal modes, and with clear daily variations in low-accessibility areas under the road-rail-sea mode. Analysis of this network’s resilience under a typical disaster scenario reveals that local disasters could have a nationwide impact, and areas with better infrastructure access, higher GDP, and greater distance from the disruption sources would exhibit higher resilience. These findings have important implications for enhancing the accessibility and improving the risk management of international multimodal container transport systems.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Policy strategies for improving multimodal freight transport: A two-stage framework for Thailand’s Eastern Economic Corridor (EEC) project
Authors: Sarawut Jansuwan, Zhuowei Wang, Anthony Chen
Abstract: The multimodal transportation network is critical to a country's economic development, acting as a lifeline for containerized cargo flows from domestic to international destinations and vice versa. Reliable infrastructure, such as railways, roadways, and seaports, allows for better cargo processing and speedier transit, all of which contribute significantly to the system's seamlessness and cost-effectiveness. Thailand's Eastern Economic Corridor (EEC) has been designated to promote the country's investment in advancing innovation and technology for future generations. However, as with many other freight routes, the EEC is currently experiencing congestion, accidents, and poor roadway service because of the widespread use of large container load vehicles, which limits capacity and leads to delays and subpar delivery performance. To address these issues, this paper develops a two-stage planning framework for assessing policy strategies for enhancing multimodal freight transport in EEC. The first stage uses a bi-level programming model to estimate the network's reserve capacity, while the second stage assesses travel time reliability (TTR) to determine the cost-effectiveness of infrastructure upgrades. The data reveal that the EEC network can only accommodate 78% of freight demand, with rail freight accounting for only 1.33% of total volume. Critical bottlenecks have been identified on Motorway 7, Highway 3, and Highway 36. The findings indicate that expanding these roadways and improving rail infrastructure, through initiatives such as the single rail transfer operator (SRTO), can dramatically reduce congestion and enhance dependability. It also suggests policy measures such as short-term operational optimizations, mid-term bottleneck reduction, and long-term integrated planning to improve network efficiency, support sustainable growth, and has the potential to position Thailand as a regional logistics hub in Southeast Asia. The two-stage planning framework and policy strategies can be used to broaden examples of multimodal freight transportation network expansion.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Institutions and social attitudes: The origin and impact of state ownership preferences in China
Authors: Pengfei Li, Ming Lu
Abstract: Historical institutions can shape contemporary social attitudes long after formal rules change. Combining the Chinese General Social Survey (CGSS) with historical city-level records on state-owned enterprises (SOEs), we examine whether exposure to China's planned economy is associated with contemporary preferences for state ownership. Using the allocation of civilian projects under the First Five-Year Plan as an instrument, we find that a one percentage point increase in the historical SOE output share is associated with a 1.076 percentage point increase in the probability of preferring the state-owned sector. The association remains positive after controlling for contemporary economic conditions and is statistically significant among respondents born by 1978 but not among those born later. The job-priority analysis offers suggestive evidence of a role for social prestige. Aggregating individual preferences to the city level, we find that the SOE subsidy advantage is larger in cities with stronger state ownership preferences, particularly when the local leader was born in the city. These results highlight the enduring impact of institutional legacies on social attitudes and policy outcomes, offering new insights into heterogeneous reform outcomes in transition economies.

Title: Time-varying impacts of government spending on CO2 emissions
Authors: Stefano Di Bucchianico, Mario Di Serio, Matteo Fragetta, Giovanni Melina
Abstract: A Bayesian factor-augmented interacted vector autoregression framework purified of expectations is employed to analyze how government spending shocks have impacted CO 2 emissions in the United States from the 1980s to the pre-pandemic period. Consumption-generated emissions are found to have generally risen following fiscal expansions, although their elasticity to government spending has declined substantially over time—with the five-year elasticity dropping from about 0.6 in the early 1980s to around zero by 2019. In contrast, positive government spending shocks increased production-generated emissions in the early 1980s — with a five-year elasticity near 0.5 — but reversed course by the end of the 1980s, eventually reaching an elasticity of −0.7 by the end of the sample. Examination of time-varying interaction variables suggests that environmental regulation, tertiarization, and a larger share of spending on public goods are associated with a mitigation — or even a reversal — of the emissions growth related to economic expansions driven by government spending. The income channel plays a more limited role, mostly confined to the earlier part of the sample. Furthermore, government consumption and investment are both associated with these shifts in emissions elasticities.

Title: Aggregation models with optimal weights for distributed Gaussian processes
Authors: Haoyuan Chen, Rui Tuo
Affiliations: Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Texas A&M University
Abstract: GP models have received increasing attention in recent years due to their superb prediction accuracy and modeling flexibility. To address the computational burdens of GP models for large-scale datasets, distributed learning for GPs are often adopted. Current aggregation models for distributed GPs is not time-efficient when incorporating correlations between GP experts. In this work, we propose a novel approach for aggregated prediction in distributed GPs. The technique is suitable for both the exact and sparse variational GPs. The proposed method incorporates correlations among experts, leading to better prediction accuracy with manageable computational requirements. As demonstrated by empirical studies, the proposed approach results in more stable predictions in less time than state-of-the-art consistent aggregation models.

Title: Privacy attack against federated tensor decomposition-based models
Authors: Yichen Ma, Michael Biehler, Jianjun Shi
Affiliations: H. Milton Stewart School of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Georgia Institute of Technology; Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, University of Wisconsin–Madison
Abstract: Federated adaptations of popular dimensionality reduction methods, such as tensor decomposition, have been widely implemented to address data transmission constraints and enable privacy-sensitive sharing across distributed systems. Federated learning (FL) typically involves training models collaboratively across multiple sites with a global server or aggregator while keeping raw data decentralized. While these methods often claim to preserve privacy through various mechanisms, we show that the shared information essential for FL can be exploited to reconstruct local sites’ private data. Furthermore, models that achieve better approximations to the true data and more effective FL approaches are increasingly vulnerable to attacks. We propose a novel attention-based privacy attack framework, along with theoretical analysis that quantifies privacy leakage using mutual information and entropy, to assess the vulnerability of federated tensor decomposition-based models, specifically Tucker decomposition. Simulations on synthetic three-dimensional point clouds and two case studies on healthcare correlation tensors and facial images demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, underscoring the need for stronger privacy measures in federated analytics.

Title: Modeling two-scale degradation with heterogeneity: A unified random-effects inverse Gaussian framework
Authors: Liangliang Zhuang, Yizhong Ma, Guanqi Fang, Ancha Xu
Affiliations: School of Economics and Management, Department of Management Science and Engineering, Nanjing University of Science and Technology; School of Statistics and Data Science, Zhejiang Gongshang University; Collaborative Innovation Center of Statistical Data Engineering, Technology & Application, Zhejiang Gongshang University; Laboratory for Statistical Monitoring and Intelligent Governance of Common Prosperity, Hangzhou, China
Abstract: Accurate modeling of product degradation is essential for reliable life prediction and maintenance planning. In many applications, degradation is jointly driven by age (calendar time) and usage (cumulative operation), and further complicated by unit-to-unit heterogeneity due to manufacturing or environmental variations. While existing models often focus on single-scale processes or assume homogeneous systems, few frameworks can flexibly accommodate both two scales and population-level variability. This paper proposes a unified two-scale degradation model based on additive reparameterized inverse Gaussian processes with random effects. The model captures monotonic degradation under the joint influence of age and usage, and introduces two forms of random effects to flexibly capture varying degrees of heterogeneity across units. It provides closed-form expressions for failure time distributions, enabling efficient reliability analysis. Two inference methods are developed: (i) a maximum likelihood estimator via an expectation-maximization algorithm with bootstrap intervals, and (ii) a Bayesian approach using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampling. Simulation studies confirm the accuracy and robustness of the proposed estimators and highlight the risks of model misspecification in reliability assessment. A real-world case study on outdoor coating degradation further demonstrates the model’s practical applicability. An open-source R package is provided to support implementation, with additional materials available online.

Title: A Bayesian jump model-based pathwise sampling approach for online anomaly detection
Authors: Dongmin Li, Miao Bai, Di Wang, Xiaochen Xian
Affiliations: H. Milton Stewart School of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Georgia Institute of Technology; Department of Operations and Information Management, University of Connecticut; Department of Industrial Engineering and Management, Shanghai Jiao Tong University
Abstract: Moving vehicle-based sensors (MVSs) have received growing attention for real-time anomaly detection in various applications such as wildfire and oil spill detection. To tackle challenges due to the spatial covariance structure among observations, uncertainties under partial observations, as well as the physical MVS movements, we propose a Bayesian jump model-based pathwise sampling approach to detect abrupt changes in an area of interest in real time using MVSs. Specifically, a jump-model based Bayesian scheme is proposed to exploit spatial correlation and real-time partial observations for status update, and to quantify uncertainties arising from noisy observations, limited observability, and anomaly occurrences. Based on the updated status, a Bayesian upper confidence bound is constructed as the sampling statistic to balance exploration and exploitation under noisy and partial observations. Guided by the sampling statistic, a route optimization model is then formulated to adaptively coordinate the routes of multiple MVSs for quick anomaly detection. We perform theoretical investigations and conduct simulations to confirm the exceptional effectiveness of the proposed method. A case study for early wildfire detection demonstrates that our proposed method outperforms benchmark methods, which contributes to the reduction of the area of affected land and wildfire-related costs.

Title: A stochastic defender-attacker-defender model for smart system resilience enhancement against hybrid cyber-physical risks
Authors: Zhaoyuan Yin, Chao Fang, Yiping Fang, Min Xie
Affiliations: Department of Systems Engineering, City University of Hong Kong; Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Hong Kong Polytechnic University; School of Management, Xi’an Jiaotong University; Laboratoire Génie Industriel, CentraleSupélec, Université Paris-Saclay
Abstract: With the advancement of digital and communication technology, modern critical infrastructure systems, e.g., power grids, tend to be controlled automatically and remotely through cyber systems. Such cyber-physical systems (CPS) promote more efficient operations but induce synergetic physical and cyber vulnerabilities in coupling network structures. These hybrid threats necessitate risk analysis and resilience enhancement of CPS from the cyber-physical perspective. We propose a stochastic defender-attacker-defender model with the consideration of both uncertain physical disruptions and malicious cyberattacks to secure CPS against hybrid risks. The developed model provides decision makers with resilient allocating and operating strategies for distributed energy resources and intelligent firewalls in CPS. The most threatening cyberattack scenario, which targets the availability and integrity of information systems simultaneously, is formulated with the consideration of incomplete knowledge to realistically simulate cyber risks. A column-constraints-generation based adaptive algorithm is developed to address the challenges that come from multilevel stochastic optimization and asymmetric information. Detailed case studies are conducted in the Hong Kong distribution system and Florida power grid with their communication systems to showcase the effectiveness of the proposed approach. The analytical results reveal the interactions and characteristics of concurrent cyber-physical threats and offer valuable managerial insights for decision makers to deploy defense strategies.

Title: Condition-based maintenance for production systems: Inferring degradation states from quality characteristics
Authors: Ziyu Wang, Shuguang He, Xiujie Zhao, Mengzi Zhen
Affiliations: College of Management and Economics, Tianjin University; School of Mechanical Engineering, Shanghai Jiao Tong University
Abstract: With the growing complexity of production systems, direct monitoring of system degradation has become increasingly challenging, posing difficulties for decision makers to plan appropriate maintenance actions. This paper presents a systematic framework that utilizes the quality characteristics of products to develop the optimal maintenance strategy for production systems. The degradation process of the system is modeled by a Wiener process. Product quality characteristics and underlying system states are mapped by a random function. The variability in the mapping mechanism is characterized by a normal distribution. Leveraging the partially observable Markov decision process, the optimal dynamic maintenance strategy is determined, and its structural properties are explored via in-depth stochastic analyses. Analytical results indicate that the optimal maintenance strategy is a control limit policy, with a threshold that divides the decision space into two mutually exclusive subspaces. Furthermore, numerical examples motivated by maintenance of vacuum molding machines are elaborated to illustrate the proposed model. Comparisons with common methods demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, whose performance outperforms that of the benchmarks under both finite and infinite horizons. It is also found that the increased uncertainty in the mapping mechanism between product quality and underlying states leads to a noticeable change in the optimal strategy and a higher maintenance cost.

Title: Robust condition-based fleet operations and maintenance: Integrating multi-asset degradation rate interactions and operations-induced degradation
Authors: Deniz Altinpulluk, Farnaz Fallahi, Murat Yildirim, Mohammad Javad Feizollahi
Affiliations: Industrial and Systems Engineering, Wayne State University; JP Morgan Chase
Abstract: Effective operations and maintenance (O&M) in modern production and service systems hinges on a careful orchestration of economic and degradation dependencies across a fleet of assets. While the economic dependencies are well studied, incorporating degradation dependencies and their impact on system operations remain an open challenge. In this article, we consider a general operations & maintenance problem, where a fleet of assets are utilized to satisfy the demand. Assets undergoing maintenance are temporarily unavailable for production. The degradation rate is influenced by two primary decision-dependent factors. First, higher production rates lead to faster degradation of assets. Second, a degrading asset can accelerate the degradation of related assets in the system. To address these dependencies, we model condition-based production and maintenance decisions for multi-asset systems with degradation interactions. We provide the first O&M model to optimize O&M in multi-asset systems with embedded decision-dependent degradation interactions. We formulate robust optimization models that inherently capture degradation and failure risks by embedding degradation signals via a set of constraints, and building condition-based uncertainty sets to model probable degradation scenarios. Our approach offers a seamless integration of data-driven degradation modeling and mathematical programming to bridge the gap across predictive and prescriptive models. Performance of the proposed O&M model is evaluated through extensive experiments, where the degradation is represented using vibration-based readings from a rotating machinery system. The proposed model provides significant improvements in terms of operation, maintenance, and reliability metrics.

Title: A communication-efficient distributed algorithm for online monitoring in big data systems
Authors: Miaomiao Yu, Wei Zhao, Fugee Tsung
Affiliations: Key Laboratory of Advanced Theory and Application in Statistics and Data Science-MOE, and School of Statistics and Academy of Statistics and Interdisciplinary Sciences, East China Normal University; Department of Statistics, Shanghai Polytechnic University; Department of Industrial Engineering and Decision Analytics, Hong Kong University of Science and Technology; The Information Hub, Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
Abstract: In the era of big data, the vast amounts of available information pose significant challenges to traditional monitoring algorithms. The sheer volume of data often results in its distribution across multiple machines, making full communication between these data points impractical due to prohibitive costs or privacy concerns. To address these challenges in constructing online monitoring statistics, we propose a communication-efficient distributed algorithm. Specifically, this algorithm transfers only summarized statistics between machines, rather than individual-level data. This approach not only mitigates the issue of large data volumes that cannot be centralized on a single machine but also overcomes the privacy concerns associated with direct data sharing. Furthermore, we introduce a divide-and-conquer scheme that enhances communication efficiency by focusing on the integration of gradient information for shift estimation. To further reduce communication costs, only vector-type information is exchanged, rather than matrix or more complex data. The proposed algorithm leads to an enhanced exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) control chart, thereby improving its monitoring capabilities. The reliability of the method is rigorously validated. Finally, simulation results and a practical example illustrate the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed scheme.

Title: Regional favoritism and educational attainment in Africa
Authors: Zareh Asatryan, Thushyanthan Baskaran, Patrick Hufschmidt, Alexander Stöcker
Abstract: Abstract We investigate the impact of regional favoritism on educational attainment in Africa. Using geocoded, individual-level survey data from the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS), we show that men who grew up in areas geographically linked to a national leader attain higher levels of education later in life. In contrast, we observe no beneficial effects of geographical leader connections for women on average; only a subset of women who have additional ethnic ties and are possibly from wealthier families experience such effects. We interpret these results using a discrete choice framework that models decisions regarding whether children continue schooling based on perceived returns to education versus the costs of that education. This framework suggests that preferential educational policies are unlikely to be the primary cause of the higher attainment observed for men and the subset of women mentioned previously. Instead, educational choices appear to respond to expectations of local economic booms in geographically connected regions. Additional evidence, such as regarding the likelihood of skilled employment later in life, supports this interpretation.

Title: Adaptive order allocation and cross-factory collaborative scheduling for distributed group manufacturing with heterogeneous resources
Authors: Weilong Li, Shunsheng Guo, Jun Guo, Baigang Du, Lei Wang, Yibing Li
Affiliations: Wuhan University of Technology

Title: A (32+ε)-approximation algorithm for three parallel machines scheduling with one vehicle job delivery coordination
Authors: Qihao Zheng, Longcheng Liu

Authors: Dan Luo, Simon Thevenin, Alexandre Dolgui
