The proposed framework offers a systematic way to combine existing formulations and to derive new ones. To illustrate its potential, we develop several new models for the Discrete Ordered Median Problem based on this concept. An extensive computational study is conducted to evaluate their performance against current state-of-the-art formulations. The results show that the proposed approach can lead to highly competitive and previously undiscovered models.

Title: Spatio-temporal graph reinforcement learning for multi-period supply chain synchronization: Joint procurement, warehousing, and multimodal routing with multiple 3PL providers
Authors: Jinjin Cai, Rui Song, Shiwei He, Jushang Chi, Kai Yan
Abstract: The multi-period supply chain synchronization problem (MP-SCSP) jointly coordinates procurement, inter-period warehousing, and multimodal transport across multiple third-party logistics providers under period-dependent constraints. To address the rapidly growing combinatorial complexity of the MP-SCSP, a mixed-integer linear programming formulation and a corresponding Markov decision process are established, together with STAGRL-PPO, a spatio-temporal-aware graph reinforcement learning framework based on proximal policy optimization. STAGRL-PPO combines an edge-attention graph neural network for multimodal topology encoding, temporal embeddings for period-dependent dynamics, and topology-aware action masking to ensure operational feasibility without heuristic post-processing. Experiments on Chicago-regional networks demonstrate strong computational performance. On small instances, STAGRL-PPO matches exact solutions while reducing computation time by 99.45%, with an average optimality gap of 1.33%. On large-scale instances where exact solvers fail within two hours, it obtains high-quality solutions in 10.24 s, with gaps of 8.4% to feasible upper bounds and 4.94% to theoretical lower bounds. On extreme-scale instances, the mean bound gap is 14.65% with a mean inference time of 24.79 s. Without additional training, the policy transfers to the unseen Manhattan-LION and Rhine–Alpine-40 networks with a mean objective difference of 2.50% relative to QMEA and a mean solution-time reduction of 94.92%. Ablation studies show that edge attention is critical to feasibility, whereas temporal embeddings accelerate convergence. Managerially, the framework adapts provider selection to price fluctuations, exploits intermodal routing to bypass capacity bottlenecks, and selects faster modes to satisfy strict delivery deadlines.

Title: Time–dependent manned–unmanned collaborative delivery routing with partial charging and locker configuration of unmanned ground vehicles
Authors: Wenheng Liu, Ge Feng, Weicun Zhang, Wenyan Zhao
Abstract: This paper focuses on the routing problem with collaborative delivery of manned delivery vehicles (MDVs) and unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) for urban last-mile logistics, subject to time windows, UGV’s locker and energy constraints, and traffic congestion. The objective is to minimize the total delivery cost. In the proposed collaborative delivery system, MDVs and UGVs operate in parallel, while UGVs perform multiple trips for small- to medium-sized parcels due to limited locker capacity, and partially recharge according to subsequent energy requirements. A mixed-integer nonlinear programming model is formulated for the problem. Given its NP–hard nature, an improved adaptive large neighborhood search algorithm incorporating arc–based path relinking (IALNS-APR) is developed. The algorithm features dedicated removal and insertion operators, and search strategies (e.g., multiplier–triggered operator selection, charging station number optimization, and elite set update). Extensive experiments on benchmark and tailored instances show that IALNS-APR outperforms Gurobi and other leading algorithms. Sensitivity analyses reveal that traffic congestion has a pronounced effect on the total cost, and partial charging reduces the total cost compared with full charging. Furthermore, optimizing locker configuration is critical for reducing travel cost and proves robust to collaborative delivery capacity.

Title: Optimal size and composition of government spending in small open economies
Authors: Qingyuan Du, Pedro Gomis-Porqueras, Solmaz Moslehi, Chung Tran
Abstract: We study optimal ﬁscal policy over the business cycle in a small open economy within a currency union that faces downward nominal wage rigidity. Government spending consists of public consumption and productive public investment, with investment accumulating into public capital subject to a time-to-build requirement. In this environment, we characterize the Ramsey allocation when the policymaker jointly chooses consumption taxes, public consumption, and public investment. Fiscal instruments operate through distinct but complementary margins. The consumption tax mitigates unemployment distortions when wage rigidity binds, while spending composition provides an additional intertemporal stabilization margin. Because public capital is subject to time-to-build and has limited short-run elasticity, counter-cyclical public investment smooths private consumption and stabilizes relative prices with modest contemporaneous distortions. Calibrating the model to France, we ﬁnd that coordinated ﬁscal policy substantially reduces unemployment risk and generates measurable welfare gains relative to regimes that rely solely on taxes or keep government spending composition ﬁxed. These results are robust to alternative calibrations and to an extension with government production of non-tradable public goods.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: Early Social Security claiming and slow asset decumulation: experimental evidence
Authors: John Duffy, Yue Li
Abstract: Retirement behavior in the U.S. exhibits two well-documented patterns: most individuals claim Social Security benefits early, before reaching their full retirement age, and retirees decumulate their assets more slowly than predicted by standard life-cycle models. This paper provides experimental evidence that these patterns emerge even in a controlled individual decision-making environment where early claiming and slow decumulation are not optimal. In a baseline treatment calibrated to current U.S. Social Security rules, participants display both early claiming and slower-than-optimal asset decumulation. Replacing larger annuities with lump-sum incentives in two alternative treatments, as has been proposed by the U.S. Congress, accelerates asset decumulation but does not lead to delayed claiming. These findings generalize from a convenience student sample to an older sample aged 45–55 and broadly resemble the observed behavior of similarly situated respondents in the Health and Retirement Study. We show that a wealth-preservation motive can jointly generate early claiming and slow asset decumulation, consistent with the experimental evidence.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: Corrigendum to “Equity markets and ESG dynamics: Assessing spillovers and portfolio strategies through time-varying parameters” [Energy Econ., 134 (2024), 107548]
Authors: Yi Wang, Shoaib Ali, Muhammad Ayaz

Title: Carbon mitigation potential of metro-based underground urban logistics under operational constraints
Authors: Bing Yan, Xiang Liu, Zhigang Liu, Chengcheng Yu
Abstract: Rising urban freight and decarbonization pressures raise an increasingly pressing question: can metros provide green freight mobility without harming passengers? We develop a policy-evaluation framework for metro-based underground logistics (MUL) that integrates multi-task demand forecasting, capacity-constrained freight realization, and emissions accounting under passenger-priority operations. Shanghai's empirical results have showed that freight demand peaks tend to occur outside passenger peaks, while high-volume freight OD flows are less concentrated along major passenger commuting corridors. Under our baseline setting, MUL realizes 66.69% of metro-replaceable demand on weekdays and 92.28% on weekends, with estimated net CO 2 reductions of 14.86% and 24.32%, respectively, after accounting for feeder travel, detours, and unrealized demand. The weekend estimate is more sensitive to freight-demand prediction uncertainty. Scenario comparisons identify station-proximate eligibility, direct routing, off-peak operation, and freight capacity allocation as the main operational levers shaping mitigation.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Is full disclosure always optimal? Strategic information design for vaccine campaigns via Bayesian persuasion
Authors: Letian Zhang, Tengfei Nie, Yizhen Li, Jianghua Zhang
Abstract: Timely disclosure of information on vaccine effectiveness is crucial in shaping public perceptions of its benefits, ultimately influencing vaccination decisions. This study employs a Bayesian persuasion framework to examine how a health organization can strategically design information campaigns on vaccine effectiveness to influence public vaccination choices. We derive the optimal strategies for both the health organization and the public and explore how factors such as vaccine externality affect the effectiveness of information design. Although it is commonly believed that full disclosure is the optimal strategy for maximizing social welfare, our findings challenge this view. In a scenario with a sufficient vaccine supply, moderate vaccination costs, and a relatively low public prior belief in high vaccine effectiveness, a partial disclosure strategy is more effective in improving vaccine coverage and enhancing social welfare. In a scenario with limited vaccine supply, the optimal information disclosure strategy for the health organization depends on the supply level. When the vaccination cost is low and the public's prior belief in high effectiveness is high, the health organization can strategically limit the frequency of signals indicating high vaccine effectiveness through partial disclosure to ensure efficient vaccine allocation and maximize social welfare. Additionally, we show that the value of information design is maximized when the public's prior belief is moderate. Our research offers practical insights for health organizations by providing guidance on how to effectively manage information disclosure, especially in the context of vaccine hesitancy.

Title: Beyond targeting women: Intrahousehold contexts and the effectiveness of food vouchers
Authors: Seollee Park, Yaeeun Han, Hyuncheol Bryant Kim
Abstract: Many transfer programs target women based on evidence that mothers are more likely than fathers to allocate resources toward child welfare. However, findings on gendered impacts remain mixed-likely because parental knowledge, preferences, and household decision-making roles differ across contexts. In this study, we experimentally vary the intrahousehold informational context itself through a randomized controlled trial in rural Ethiopia. Specifically, employing a factorial design, we cross-randomize two key dimensions: (1) which parent receives nutrition behavior change communication (BCC) - neither, mother only, or both; and (2) which parent receives a household food voucher - mother or father. We find that, pooled across settings in which fathers do not receive BCC, vouchers assigned to mothers generate larger improvements in child-feeding practices than vouchers assigned to fathers. The largest effects occur when mothers receive both BCC and the voucher. This maternal advantage attenuates and is no longer detectable when fathers also receive BCC. We provide suggestive evidence that when mothers have both a knowledge advantage and control over resources, they are better able to mobilize greater intrahousehold support. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for intrahousehold contexts, not just recipient gender, when designing nutrition interventions.

Title: Cognitive decline, education, and dynamic selection
Authors: Michael E. Darden
Abstract: I estimate a model of health investment, health, and sample participation, and I find substantially wider gaps in cognitive health by education relative to reduced-form estimators, even after accounting for the endogeneity of education. Selective exits (mortality or attrition) among less-educated respondents generate cross-sectional comparisons between highly educated individuals and the subset of healthier, less-educated individuals who survive. Furthermore, I find that education gaps widen at relatively early stages of cognitive decline—contrary to a large literature arguing that education affects levels but not slopes. Finally, I show that differential rates of cigarette smoking by education do not explain these gaps in cognitive health.

Title: A simulation-based framework for chronic disease management to improve health equity
Authors: Usame Yakutcan, Eren Demir, John R. Hurst
Affiliations: University of Hertfordshire; University College London
Abstract: Chronic diseases present a formidable global health challenge, with burdens unevenly distributed across populations, disproportionately affecting vulnerable and marginalised groups. A lack of established methods limits policymakers’ ability to design effective and equitable care pathways for individuals with chronic conditions. This study addresses this gap by introducing Chronic-Sim, a simulation-based framework tailored to the complexities of healthcare delivery. Chronic-Sim captures individual patient characteristics, demographics, socio-economic status (SES), and comorbidities. The framework presents a patient flow that is customisable for any chronic disease and supports multimorbidity by simulating multiple chronic conditions simultaneously. A novel hierarchical labelling approach is introduced to classify patients by SES, enabling the generation of outputs by deprivation category. The framework’s adaptability is demonstrated step-by-step within a chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) service at a major healthcare provider in the United Kingdom, incorporating cardiovascular disease to model multimorbidity. Interventions targeting access barriers are evaluated across SES categories, with outputs showing cost-effective improvements in patient-related (mortality, quality of life) and service-related metrics (admissions, service usage). Chronic-Sim offers a modular, data-driven decision-support tool adaptable to diverse health systems. Its novel contribution lies in empowering policymakers to test interventions, project inequities, and design fair and effective chronic disease care pathways.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Consumer-responsive sustainable supply chain management considering consumer behavior toward sustainability
Authors: Ikhyun Jo, Soongeol Kwon
Abstract: As consumer attention to sustainability grows in response to climate change concerns, firms face increasing pressure to align their supply chain strategies with evolving market responses. This study aims to support managerial decision-making by examining how firms should strategically design and manage their supply chains when consumer demand is shaped by cumulative, multidimensional, and uncertain responses to sustainability performance. To this end, we develop a consumer-responsive sustainable supply chain management framework, embedding a feedback loop between sustainability-driven operations and market demand. We formulate a multi-period mixed-integer linear programming model that links demand to consumers’ sustainability perception, which is formed cumulatively based on firms’ past sustainability performance. Sustainability performance is evaluated using carbon emissions, differentiated across emission scopes, and translated into an overall sustainability evaluation from the consumer perspective. To capture uncertainty in consumer behavior, the framework is extended to a two-stage stochastic programming model that reflects the evolution of sustainability-conscious consumers over time. Numerical experiments validate the proposed model and its internal feedback mechanism, illustrating how sustainability investments dynamically reshape consumer perception, demand realization, and subsequent supply chain decisions. The results show that incorporating consumer responsiveness can simultaneously increase profit and reduce total emissions, while sensitivity analyses reveal systematic shifts in optimal strategies with respect to consumer evaluation characteristics. Under uncertainty, the model favors precautionary sustainable capacity expansion and diversified parallel contracting as effective strategic hedges against evolving market conditions. These findings yield meaningful managerial implications and provide insights into how consumer-driven market mechanisms can support firms’ progress toward net-zero emission targets.

Title: Redistribution meets decarbonisation: Exploring universal basic income through an ecological macroeconomic integrated assessment model
Authors: Iñaki Arto, María Victoria Román, Simone D'Alessandro, Kurt Kratena, Guilherme Spinato Morlin, Manuel Tomás, Paola López-Muñoz, Ignacio Cazcarro, Ole van Allen
Abstract: The dual challenge of climate change and rising inequality calls for policies capable of delivering both ecological sustainability and social equity. Within the field of Ecological Macroeconomics (EM), integrated assessment models (IAM) with biophysical and socio-economic linkages provide a promising approach to explore policy trade-offs ex ante. This paper contributes to this literature by employing the Within Limits Integrated Assessment Model (WILIAM), an EM-IAM that combines a macroeconomic multi-regional input–output structure with explicit representations of energy and material flows, biophysical constraints, and climate damages. We assess a policy mix designed to support a just low-carbon transition in 21 European countries over the period 2025–2050, including a universal basic income (UBI) financed through a wealth tax, alongside a carbon tax aimed at internalising the external costs of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. We examine the interactions between redistribution and emissions within a unified modelling framework that accounts for household heterogeneity, economic rigidities and ecological limits. Our results show that the policy mix substantially reduces income inequality and improves social outcomes. However, the introduction of UBI generates rebound effects through increased consumption, which can be partially mitigated in the presence of carbon pricing. These findings highlight a potential trade-off between equity and environmental objectives. We discuss the mechanisms driving these dynamics and explore policy design implications, including the role of complementary measures to decouple well-being from material throughput. The paper illustrates the value of EM-IAMs for analysing complex policy interactions and advancing the integration of social and ecological dimensions in macroeconomic modelling.

Title: Obvious strategy-proofness with respect to a partition
Authors: R. Pablo Arribillaga, Jordi Massó, Alejandro Neme
Abstract: We define and study obvious strategy-proofness with respect to a partition of the set of agents. It encompasses strategy-proofness as a special case when the partition is the coarsest one and obvious strategy-proofness when the partition is the finest. For any partition, it falls between these two extremes. We establish two general properties of this new notion and apply it to the simple anonymous voting problem with two alternatives and strict preferences.

Title: Experience-based pairwise comparison dynamics
Authors: Jiabin Wu
Abstract: This paper introduces the experience-based pairwise comparison dynamics—a deterministic evolutionary process in which each agent, upon having the opportunity to revise her strategy, compares her realized payoff with that of another agent. The key departure from standard dynamics is that agents compare realized payoffs from actual matches rather than expected payoffs of strategies. Thus, agents need not know the population distribution of strategies and compute expected payoffs. In a uniformly random pairwise matching environment, this dynamic process is markedly more sensitive to the cardinality of the underlying game’s payoff structure than standard dynamics based on comparing the expected payoffs of different strategies. This heightened sensitivity yields equilibrium selection results in coordination games without the long waiting times typical of stochastic stability models. We further show that the strictly dominated strategy in the prisoner’s dilemma can survive.

Title: From pollution prevention to circular economy capabilities: The mediating role of absorptive capacity and moderating role of innovation orientation
Authors: Stephanie Graham, Trevor Cadden, Guangming Cao
Abstract: Recent studies have highlighted the need for firms to develop advanced capabilities to tackle the complex challenges of climate change. The purpose of this study is to examine a range of factors that support the development of circular economy capabilities (CEC). A theoretical framework grounded in the natural resource-based view (NRBV) and absorptive capacity theory (ACT) is developed to empirically test the antecedent role of preliminary capabilities (pollution prevention) in supporting the development of CEC. The role of other supporting mechanisms, such as absorptive capacity and cultural orientation, in the development of CEC is also considered. To test our hypotheses, data was collected via survey from 521 UK-based firms across a range of industries and analysed using structural equation modelling. The results provide support for the antecedent role or preliminary capabilities, such as pollution prevention, in supporting the development of CEC. This antecedent role is strengthened when mediated by absorptive capacity mechanisms. We also find support for the moderating role of sustainable innovation culture on the link between some, but not all, pollution prevention capabilities and CEC. Our study contributes to existing research in this area by highlighting a range of factors that can support the development of advanced environmental capabilities such as CEC. These insights are also useful for managers, who can draw on them to understand how to leverage their experience and cultural environment to support the development of advanced environmental capabilities.

Title: The timing fingerprint: A rank-based test of market timing
Authors: André A.P. Santos, Lorenzo Pascual Caneiro
Abstract: Traditional market-timing tests such as the Treynor–Mazuy and Henriksson–Merton tests are known to over-detect timing ability when fat tails and state-dependent volatility are present, and are based on rigid parametric assumptions about the timing payoff. We propose a test of market timing built on the concept of timing fingerprint, a rank-based test that presumes no functional form for the timing payoff and is calibrated to nominal size by a null-imposing wild bootstrap. We show that, while the same bootstrap restores the size of the classical tests, the fingerprint method identifies the direction and location of timing-like behavior across the entire benchmark distribution and is substantially more powerful against timing payoffs the classical tests do not span. We assess the finite-sample performance of the fingerprint test using Monte Carlo simulations and employ it to evaluate a large panel of U.S. equity mutual funds.

Title: Constant resource shares and Samuelson’s Shibboleth
Authors: Arthur Lewbel, Krishna Pendakur
Abstract: Suppose each individual in a community is given some fixed constant fraction of total available expenditures to spend. Samuelson (1948, 1954, 1956) argued that this would be a shibboleth (i.e., a procedure that doesn’t have meaning) because such a procedure cannot generally be rationalized by any social welfare function defined over the utilities of individuals. For modern collective household models, Samuelson’s shibboleth has been taken to imply that household resource shares (the fraction of a household’s budget allocated to each household member) cannot be constants. We show Samuelson’s claim depends on an assumption that is inappropriate for collective household models, and when that assumption is dropped, there is no shibboleth: resource shares can be any regular functions, including fixed constant fractions.

Title: Power outages, multi-product firms, and firm productivity: Theory and evidence from China
Authors: Jian Yu, Chen Zhao, Ying Li, Nan Wu
Abstract: This study develops a model of multi-product firms (MPFs) to examine their responses to power outages and the consequent effects on firm productivity. In the model, MPFs mitigate the adverse effects of power outages by discontinuing their less-productive products and focusing more on their core varieties. This buffering mechanism, however, comes at the cost of reduced product variety and a more concentrated product mix. We test this theory using firm–product-level export data from the Chinese metals and articles thereof industry from 2005 to 2015, combined with a text-based power outage index. Consistent with the model’s predictions, we find that a 1% increase in power outages reduces the productivity of single-product firms (SPFs) by 0.43%. MPFs experience a 0.31% smaller decline in productivity; however, this comes at the expense of a 0.20% reduction in product variety within these firms. We further calibrate the model and show that a 1% reduction in the observed 2005 outage level raises aggregate welfare by 0.017%, of which more than one-third is driven by MPF-specific within-firm reallocation and variety recovery. Our theory reconciles the findings on the impacts of power outages across countries, underscoring the critical role of the intra-firm extensive margin in economic loss assessments.

Title: Advanced tabu search for the multi-depot heterogeneous vehicle routing problem with backhauls
Authors: Wenjie Hu, Yang Wang, Rafael Martí, Anna Martínez-Gavara
Abstract: This work investigates the Multi-Depot Heterogeneous Vehicle Routing Problem with Backhauls (MD-VRPB), an important extension of the classical routing problem models that explicitly accounts for multiple depots and a heterogeneous fleet. The problem is motivated by large-scale distribution systems with multiple distribution centers and diverse vehicle types, where delivery and pickup operations must be jointly coordinated in a cost-effective manner. To address this problem, we propose a learning enhanced tabu search algorithm with long-term memory (LE-TS-LM). The proposed method embeds learning and long-term memory mechanisms into a tabu search framework and is built upon four complementary components: a greedy randomized construction procedure for generating diverse initial solutions throughout the iterative search process, a tabu search procedure with long-term memory for effective intensification and diversification, dedicated post-optimization techniques to refine route and vehicle-type decisions, and a probability updating and refinement mechanism that exploits historical high-quality solutions to guide future search. Extensive computational experiments are conducted on a total of 144 benchmark instances. The results demonstrate that LE-TS-LM consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods for this problem in terms of solution quality while maintaining competitive computational efficiency. In particular, the proposed algorithm identifies 120 new best known solutions, significantly advancing the current benchmarks for the MD-VRPB. Additional analyses further highlight the contribution of each algorithmic component to both performance improvement and solution robustness, extending in this way the scope of the paper since these successful elements and strategies proposed here can be adapted to solve other hard optimization problems.

Title: Adapting continuous metaheuristics to discrete problems: A taxonomy-oriented review
Authors: Ru Yang, Qiyuan Jiang, Ling Ding, Bo Zhang
Abstract: Continuous metaheuristics are difficult to apply directly to discrete optimization because their real-valued operations are incompatible with structured discrete solution spaces. Existing studies also lack a unified framework for classifying and comparing discretization strategies. Following a systematic multi-database search and mechanism-focused screening, this review constructs a purposively curated corpus of 299 studies published between 2008 and 2025. It develops a two-dimensional taxonomy of discretization logic and discrete problem structure, formally defines three mechanisms—Operator Replacement, Mapping, and Encoding Reconstruction—and clarifies their boundaries and strictly defined hybrid combinations. The review also identifies five non-exclusive solution structures and an additional Mixed-type label, and descriptively examines recurring method–problem associations within the curated corpus. The framework standardizes terminology and offers practice-informed, non-prescriptive considerations for selecting and designing discretization strategies for continuous metaheuristics.

Title: Heterogeneous manpower group scheduling in automotive RO–RO operations: Optimization models and algorithms
Authors: Ziqiao Mei, Zhou Xu, Feng Chen
Abstract: This paper investigates a loading and unloading routing problem in automotive Roll-On/Roll-Off (RO–RO) terminals, where drivers transport batches of cars between vessels and yard sections. Each batch is modeled as an arc-based task, and a manpower group can transport at most as many cars as it has drivers. Unlike previous studies, this work adopts a more flexible and practical problem setting by incorporating heterogeneous manpower groups and a non-exclusive transport mode, allowing multiple groups to jointly serve a single arc-based task. While this setting improves resource utilization and operational efficiency, it also increases the complexity of jointly deciding group assignment and visit frequency for each task. Consequently, different combinations of heterogeneous manpower groups for a task affect the number of required visits, thereby altering the path for these manpower groups. We prove that the problem is NP-hard and formulate it as both arc-based and path-based mixed integer linear programming models. To tackle this problem, we develop a hybrid bilevel memetic algorithm that combines a decomposition-based math-heuristic for generating initial solutions effectively and employs a bilevel variable neighborhood descent to improve solutions through local search. We conducted extensive experiments on instances generated based on real operational data. The results show that the path-based model excels on small-scale instances, while the hybrid bilevel memetic algorithm outperforms alternatives on medium- and large-scale instances. On average, the total group traveling cost of a rule-based heuristic derived from planner experience is 46.74% higher than that of our algorithm. Sensitivity analyses show that heterogeneous group sizes enable more efficient transport combinations, reducing idle drivers and extra visits.

Title: Hybrid mechanism and data driven active scheduling method for dynamic flexible job shop
Authors: Yang Yue, Guodong Sa, Mingjie Hou, Zhenyu Liu, Chan Qiu, Jianrong Tan
Abstract: Under the trend of personalized customization and intelligent manufacturing, the prevalence of uncertain disturbances and the flexibility of manufacturing systems significantly affect scheduling performance. Existing technologies heavily rely on heuristic rules or data driven deep learning methods in problem modeling and solving for dynamic flexible job shop (FJS), failing to fully exploit the structural knowledge embedded in scheduling mechanism. This leads to difficulties in model management and suboptimal scheduling performance. To this end, this paper proposes a hybrid mechanism and data driven active scheduling method for FJS under job insertion scenarios. A dual attention network model for FJS considering job insertions and a mechanism-based model are constructed to enable real-time and reliable representation of the workshop state. A self-attention-based phased policy network is proposed to capture the relationships among pending operations, thereby enabling active scheduling and extending the decision-making paradigm of completely reactive scheduling. Furthermore, a dual-layer phasic policy gradient optimization algorithm is introduced, which integrates dual state representation into the training process, thus ensuring efficient learning of both representation and decision-making models for FJS. Experiments on FJS instances with job insertions show that the proposed method achieves an enhanced performance over the state-of-the-art deep learning models and outperforms benchmark models across instances of different scales and properties, demonstrating strong research and practical value.

Title: Understanding heterogeneous green transitions: An evolutionary approach to policy, innovation, and technological change
Authors: Fausto Cavalli, Alessandra Mainini, Enrico Moretto, Ahmad Naimzada
Abstract: Economies facing similar environmental challenges and broadly comparable policy interventions can nevertheless follow very different green-transition paths: some quickly adopt clean technologies, while others remain locked into carbon-intensive production. To account for this puzzle, we develop an evolutionary model in which market selection between clean and dirty technologies coevolves with environmental policy. A welfare-maximizing regulator taxes emissions and allocates the revenues between current pollution abatement and investments that progressively improve the environmental performance of clean production. This links short-run environmental policy with long-run technological change. We characterize the possible long-run technological regimes and study their evolutionary stability. We find that the same policy stance can support multiple stable long-run outcomes: economies facing identical policies may converge to different regimes depending on their initial technological composition, providing a theoretical basis for understanding the observed heterogeneity across countries. We show that policy can promote innovation even when only dirty producers are active, thereby paving the way for a green transition. We also show that even a predominantly green economy may remain vulnerable to the re-entry of dirty technologies. Finally, we analyze the ability of a regulator to dynamically adapt the policy mix, in order to redirect the transition path toward a predetermined long-run environmental target. Although adaptive policies can mitigate lock-in and path dependence, they cannot completely eliminate them. Finally, simulations show that more stringent environmental targets may even lead to outcomes opposite to those intended because of scale effects.

Title: Time-of-use pricing and peak shifting in residential EV charging: a quasi-experimental study from China
Authors: Jingjing Li, Erik T. Verhoef, Shuai Chen, Yacan Wang
Abstract: The rapid growth of electric vehicles (EVs) has intensified peak load pressures on electricity systems. Time-of-use (TOU) pricing aims to alleviate this pressure by incentivizing intertemporal load shifting, yet causal evidence on its effectiveness, drawn from real-world, high-frequency charging data, remains scarce. This study employs a difference-in-differences (DID) model to evaluate the impact of TOU pricing on residential EV charging behavior, utilizing high-frequency hourly data from over 20,000 users in Shandong Province, China. Findings reveal that TOU pricing significantly reduces peak-period charging while increasing off-peak consumption, indicating a pronounced intertemporal substitution effect. Despite reduced peak demand, total charging volume marginally increases due to lower charging costs. CES model estimates detect weak own-price elasticity between peak and off-peak periods but significant cross-price elasticity. Welfare analysis indicates that TOU pricing enhances consumer surplus. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that users with higher peak-hour dependence and greater consumption volatility exhibit stronger adjustments. Overall, the findings demonstrate that TOU pricing not only mitigates peak load stress but also promotes EV usage and supports the electrification of transport. These results underscore the institutional value of TOU mechanisms in facilitating vehicle-grid integration and advancing coordinated development between the energy and transport sectors.

Title: Beyond traditional emissions modelling in high value manufacturing: a hybrid approach for net zero supply chains
Authors: Victoria Omeire, Okechukwu Okorie, Paul Mativenga, Maria Sharmina, Peter Hopkinson
Affiliations: The University of Manchester; University of Exeter
Abstract: Achieving net-zero emissions in high-value manufacturing requires more accurate ways of modelling emissions, particularly Scope 3 emissions across complex supply chains. This study conducts a systematic literature review to critically examine existing modelling approaches within production research and high-value manufacturing supply chains. The review shows that game theory, multi-regional input-output models, and simulation approaches such as system dynamics, discrete event simulation, and agent-based modelling are widely used to enhance emissions modelling. However, these approaches are still largely applied in isolation. This fragmentation limits their ability to capture the dynamic, behavioural, and macroeconomic complexities of global supply chains in high-value manufacturing contexts. Drawing on insights from the review, we propose a conceptual hybrid modelling framework for integrating complementary modelling approaches across production systems, supply chain management, and logistics contexts. We also highlight the enabling role of data analytics in strengthening model integration and supply chain transparency. Finally, we develop an agenda to guide future research in hybrid emissions modelling. This research provides a pathway for translating model outputs into industry-relevant insights, identifying key barriers, and exploring how emerging drivers can support a more adaptive and industry-informed transition to net-zero manufacturing.

Title: Mitigating supply chain transparency barriers with blockchain: a dynamic capabilities perspective
Authors: Eric Ragan, Mohammad H. Eslami
Affiliations: University of Gothenburg; University of Manitoba
Abstract: The complexity and risk uncertainty stemming from supply disruptions underscore the need for enhanced transparency in supply chain management. Although blockchain technologies offer promising solutions through secure, immutable ledgers, adoption rates remain low, and extant research focuses primarily on theoretical frameworks lacking empirical substantiation. Addressing this gap, the present study reconceptualises transparency barriers as capability frictions, systematic impediments that prevent firms from effectively deploying sensing, seizing, and transformation capabilities. Through an in-depth case study of a Swedish OEM and its suppliers, four transparency barriers are identified: information inaccuracy, risks of information sharing, lack of communication protocols, and future communications compatibility. Analysis demonstrates how these barriers create capability frictions by weakening sensing through information asymmetry, constraining seizing through limited collaboration, and restricting transformation through weak data governance. The findings reveal how blockchain's distinctive properties, immutability, transparency, and decentralised consensus, systematically reduce these frictions, enabling firms to transition from weakened to enhanced dynamic capabilities. Five propositions are developed theorising the mechanisms through which blockchain serves as a digital enabler for capability transformation, contributing to dynamic capabilities theory and supply chain management practice.

Title: Energy-efficient scheduling of unrelated parallel machines under time-of-use electricity pricing with release dates
Authors: Peng Wu, Jing Lu, Nan Li, Jintao Lu
Affiliations: Fuzhou University; Hebei Vocational University of Industry and Technology; Shanxi University of Electronic Science and Technology; Shanxi University; Taiyuan University of Science and Technology
Abstract: Time-of-use (TOU) electricity pricing is widely applied in industrial energy management, motivating manufacturers to adjust production schedules to time-varying tariffs. This study investigates an energy-efficient scheduling problem in an unrelated parallel-machine setting with job release dates under TOU pricing, aiming to minimise total electricity cost within a bounded planning horizon. The problem is first formulated as a period-indexed mixed-integer linear programming (P-MILP) model and strengthened by two valid inequalities. Given the NP-hard nature of the problem, we develop a two-stage heuristic (TSH) to solve practically sized instances efficiently. The method constructs an initial solution and then enhances it through a customised tabu search. Computational experiments on randomly generated instances show that the two valid inequalities reduce the average CPU time of the P-MILP model by up to 88.7%, while the TSH produces high-quality solutions within practical times and scales to instances with up to 800 jobs, with average optimality gaps below 0.4% relative to the lower bound in large-scale instances. Sensitivity analyses indicate that incorporating TOU pricing affects scheduling performance. Managers should adapt assignment and sequencing to price fluctuations by prioritising off-peak processing for long or energy-intensive jobs, while scheduling urgent or late-released jobs during high-price periods when necessary.

Title: Premarital migration and marriage payments: Evidence from Indonesian men
Authors: Hugues Champeaux, Elsa Gautrain, Karine Marazyan
Abstract: While bride price customs are widespread in many developing countries, little is known about their consequences on men’s decisions. In this paper, we exploit a quasi-natural experiment of a school-building program in Indonesia (INPRES) to investigate the relationship between marriage norms and the internal migrations of young men. Combining anthropological, administrative, and individual-based datasets, we implement a triple-difference approach. We show that the less advantaged young men, who have fewer resources to cope with rising marriage costs, are more likely to migrate out of their district of origin when the women they are expected to marry benefit from the program. These findings suggest that the interaction between marital norms and policies can result in unintended consequences, shaping major economic decisions such as premarital migration.

Title: Foreign aid and power play: Political cycles in world bank’s procurement allocation
Authors: Antoine Boucher, Lisa Chauvet, Marin Ferry
Abstract: This paper examines the existence of political cycles in the awarding of World Bank procurement contracts around elections. We analyze elections in the home country of firms winning these contracts, distinguishing between firms based in the aid recipient country (i.e., domestic firms) and those from other supplier countries (i.e., foreign firms). Our findings indicate that domestic firms are more likely to secure larger contracts around elections in their home country, especially when corporate donations to candidates are allowed. Additionally, our results reveal an increase in contract sizes awarded to foreign firms before elections in their home country. This cross-border political cycle appears to be driven by strong aid partnerships and historical colonial ties between the supplier and recipient countries. These findings reveal a political dimension in procurement dynamics with potential implications for development resource allocation. Understanding these patterns can help enhance the transparency and effectiveness of aid-funded contracting.

Title: Educational legacies of christian missions: Evidence from the Democratic Republic of the Congo
Authors: Pierre Donat-Bouillud, Coralie Hirschi, Etienne Le Rossignol
Abstract: This paper investigates the educational legacies of Christian missions established before independence, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, focusing on contemporary disparities in educational content, quality, access, and outcomes. Using georeferenced data from over 20,000 schools and two million students participating in the Examen National d’État (Exetat) between 2016 and 2019, as well as primary data from a phone survey of 624 school directors, we explore how proximity to Catholic and Protestant missions during the colonial period influences educational opportunities today. We find that schools near historical Christian missions offer a broader and higher-quality curriculum, with increased access to study tracks outside the basic Pedagogy section. Students attending these schools are more likely to pass the Exetat and achieve grades qualifying for university admission, although the magnitude of the effect is modest. Observable school-environment and quality characteristics attenuate the Catholic missionary-proximity coefficient by about half, while demand-side patterns point to additional differences in student composition. Our findings reveal that the strong partnership between missions and the colonial state entrenched spatial inequalities in educational access and quality, inequalities that persist to this day.

Title: Communication failure: The hidden face of the tragedy of the commons
Authors: Philippe Colo, Guillaume Pommey
Abstract: This paper studies communication failure regarding risks in the commons. It argues that strategic issues might explain why years of scientific reporting regarding future risks have failed to trigger sufficient climate awareness. We consider a game of contribution to a public bad, where there is uncertainty regarding the damage generated by externalities. Prior to the game, agents receive non-certifiable information regarding the damage from an informed utilitarian expert. We show that in large-scale public good problems information transmission usually fails. We compare this result with the cases of Rawlsian and anti-Rawlsian experts and discuss the implication for climate expert panels. We also investigate the influence of the value of information in our result, which provides us with some insight on the part played by deontology on scientific communication.

Title: Targeted bidders in government tenders
Authors: Matilde Cappelletti, Leonardo M. Giuffrida
Abstract: A set-aside promotes a more equitable procurement process by restricting participation in government tenders to small or disadvantaged businesses. Yet its micro-effects on tender outcomes (competition and contract efficiency) and targeted firm performance entail trade-offs, which we evaluate empirically using a decade of US federal procurement data. At the tender level, we employ a two-stage approach. First, we use random forest techniques to compute the propensity score for a tender being set aside based on rules implementation. Second, we employ the scores in an inverse probability weighting framework. We find that set-asides prompt more competition — implying that the rise in participation of targeted firms more than offsets the exclusion of untargeted ones — and contract inefficiency, measured by cost overruns and delays. We argue that adverse selection and moral hazard are mechanisms behind contract inefficiency. We then study the targeted firm behavior to uncover whether long-run benefits mitigate short-run drawbacks. We compare businesses differentially exposed to a set-aside spending shock through an event study framework. We find mixed evidence on firm growth.

Title: Biometric responses to unjustified and justified-envy in school choice allocations
Authors: Valon Vitaku, Alexander L. Brown, Marco A. Palma
Abstract: The two most prominent strategy-proof school choice mechanisms, Deferred Acceptance and Top Trading Cycles, offer a trade-off between eliminating justified-envy and Pareto efficiency, respectively. We introduce a novel, biometric approach to investigate how much individuals care about and physiologically react to each property. Using an experimental design that randomly varies whether subjects learn about others’ assignments in a school choice game, we measure arousal through galvanic skin response and valence through facial expressions when subjects experience envy with and without justification. We find increased arousal associated with receiving successively lower-ranked allocations, i.e., the (unjustified) envy of the allocation(s) of others. We note additional arousal when that envy is justified, but that result requires an explicit message to accentuate the justification. Eye-tracking data confirm that subjects do not notice markers of justified-envy until receiving this message. Facial-expression valence yields less conclusive results, but this may be due to the limitations of that method for anger detection.

Title: Machine Learning-Enhanced Rolling Horizon Optimization algorithm for dynamic scheduling in AGV-Supported rice production
Authors: Yaping Zhao, Weilei Feng, Xinyue Zhang, Lianmin Zhang, Jingyi Zhao
Abstract: The integration of machine learning and rolling horizon optimization provides a promising pathway for improving operational efficiency and sustainability in modern agriculture. This study investigates a dynamic scheduling problem in AGV-supported rice production, addressing two key challenges: (i) coordinating hybrid solar–main-grid energy usage under uncertainties in rice yield and solar irradiance, and (ii) dynamically synchronizing automated drying schedules with transportation logistics. To tackle these challenges, we develop a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)-based predictor to forecast uncertain variables, and integrate it into a Machine Learning-Enhanced Rolling Horizon Optimization (ML-RHO) framework. The framework continuously updates scheduling and routing decisions through rolling time windows, thereby combining AI-based forecasting with stochastic simulation and optimization. Using parameters calibrated from a large-scale rice farm in China together with controlled Monte Carlo scenarios, we benchmark ML-RHO against conventional methods and a perfect-foresight theoretical optimum. The results show that ML-RHO achieves near-optimal solutions (average deviation of 2.85%) while reducing computation time by more than 90%. This work demonstrates how AI and stochastic simulation can be jointly leveraged to develop scalable, energy-resilient scheduling frameworks for agriculture and related operations management domains.

Title: Robust qualification management in semiconductor manufacturing
Authors: Antoine Perraudat, Abdelkrim Yelles-Chaouche, Stéphane Dauzère-Pérès
Abstract: This paper studies a tactical/strategic (machine, operation) qualification management problem in semiconductor manufacturing systems, where demand uncertainty is a significant factor. To be eligible to process an operation on wafers, a machine must be qualified to ensure yield and quality requirements. Qualifying a machine for a specific operation is usually a time-consuming and costly process. Given a set of parallel non-identical machines in the work center of a semiconductor manufacturing facility, the problem solved in this paper consists in minimizing the combined cost of qualification and lost sales while considering demand uncertainty. New robust models and solution approaches are proposed. First, a deterministic mixed-integer linear program is introduced. Then, the demand uncertainty is modeled using a polyhedral uncertainty set. This modeling is used to define a static and affinely adjustable robust reformulations of the deterministic model. Subsequently, a two-stage solution approach, based on a column-and-constraint generation approach, is proposed. The different models and approaches are discussed and compared, notably through computational experiments on industrial data from a semiconductor manufacturer. The limits of the different solution approaches are also discussed, and recommendations are provided. The numerical results show that coping with demand uncertainty in semiconductor manufacturing does not require a large number of qualifications, but that it is critical to determine the relevant ones.

Title: Exact approach to joint order acceptance and non-permutation flow shop scheduling via logic-based benders decomposition
Authors: Gongjie Xu, Naiqi Wu, Yan Qiao, Siwei Zhang
Affiliations: Institute of Systems Engineering and Collaborative Laboratory for Intelligent Science and Systems, Macau University of Science and Technology
Abstract: In modern make-to-order (MTO) manufacturing, decision-makers face the critical challenge of simultaneously selecting profitable orders and scheduling them efficiently under finite capacity constraints. This paper studies the order acceptance and scheduling problem in a non-permutation flow shop (OAS-NPFS), maximising the normalised net contribution of accepted orders minus the makespan-related production cost. We formulate the problem using both mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) and constraint programming (CP), and exploit a classical dominance property to reduce the scheduling search space. An exact logic-based Benders decomposition (LBBD) framework is then developed, in which an MILP master selects orders and a CP subproblem evaluates the makespan of each accepted set and generates valid Benders cuts from certified lower bounds. The framework is strengthened by makespan-bounding inequalities, an iterated greedy (IG) warm start, and a branch-and-check (B&C) implementation. Experiments on instances with up to seven machines and 100 orders show that the proposed method achieves optimality for all 90 small-scale instances, 136 of 160 medium-scale instances, and 105 of 160 large-scale instances. Its average certified relative gaps are 0.0975% and 0.1325% for the medium- and large-scale sets, respectively. An industry-calibrated case further illustrates its ability to improve the acceptance–scheduling trade-off over benchmark policies.

Title: Control or co-creation: exploring ecosystem configurations based on power dynamics and sustainability focus
Authors: Taylan Kilinc, Wiebke Reim
Affiliations: Luleå University of Technology
Abstract: As manufacturing firms increasingly pursue sustainability and digital transformation, production systems are becoming more dependent on collaboration across industrial ecosystems. However, industrial ecosystems differ in governance, coordination, and steering, raising questions about why different arrangements produce divergent transition pathways in coordination, inclusiveness, and sustainability focus. While collaboration is widely emphasised as essential for sustainability transitions, less is known about how variations in power dynamics and sustainability focus shape ecosystem configurations and direction. This study examines how differences in power dynamics and sustainability focus generate distinct configurations and shape sustainability transitions. Drawing on 35 interviews across three industrial ecosystems in Northern Europe, we develop a typology based on two dimensions – power dynamics and sustainability focus – identifying four configurations: enforced efficiency, balanced optimisation, dominated innovation, and collaborative innovation. The findings show that sustainability transitions depend not only on sustainability focus but also on ecosystem coordination, creating trade-offs between control, collaboration, and transformation scope. By conceptualising configurations as outcomes of power dynamics and sustainability focus, the study explains why similar ambitions generate divergent pathways. The findings contribute to production research by showing how different ecosystem configurations influence coordination, collaboration, and sustainability implementation, while offering guidance for managers and policymakers supporting industrial sustainability transitions.

Title: Correction
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: The Value of an Attorney: Collateral Source Rule Changes as an Invalid Instrument
Authors: Eric Helland, Jungmo Yoon
Affiliations: Robert Day School of Economics and Finance Claremont McKenna College Claremont California USA; College of Economics and Finance Hanyang University Seoul Korea
Abstract: ABSTRACT The value of lawyers to their clients is notoriously difficult to estimate because of endogeneity. We utilize modifications to the collateral source (CS) rule that require reducing trial awards by the amount of payments from first‐party insurance as an instrument for hiring a lawyer. The problem with our instrument is that modifications to the CS rule have a direct effect on recovery and, hence, violate the exclusion restriction required for a valid instrument. We develop a new identification and estimation method that uses CS rule changes as an invalid instrument and bounds the impact of lawyers. We find that our estimated impact's upper and lower bounds are lower than estimates that do not correct for endogeneity. Our estimates of the impact of lawyers on total payment are consistently negative, although not precise enough to claim statistical significance. The upper bound of the effect of hiring a lawyer on total payment received is negative after fees in our preferred specification. This suggests that even in the most optimistic scenario, lawyers appear to reduce total recovery.

Title: A privacy-preserving distributed credit evaluation model based on blockchain
Authors: Xianhua Kuang, Chaoqun Ma, Konstantinos N. Baltas, Shiyu Jia, Yi-Shuai Ren
Abstract: Multi-source data fusion is crucial for improving the predictive performance of credit evaluation models. However, cross-organizational collaborative modeling faces challenges such as data privacy breaches, difficulty in verifying computational results, and a lack of transparency and auditability in the collaboration process. To address collaborative logistic regression modeling with vertically distributed data, this paper proposes a privacy-preserving method based on matrix transformation and further designs a trusted collaborative modeling mechanism integrating blockchain and trusted execution environment technologies. The results indicate that the proposed privacy-preserving method achieves lossless model accuracy while safeguarding data privacy and resisting collusion attacks. This method is more efficient for training and requires less communication than most federated learning schemes. The designed decentralized collaborative modeling mechanism provides a trust foundation for multiple parties without relying on a centralized trusted third party, ensuring the reliability of model results and enabling traceability and auditability throughout the entire collaborative modeling process.

Title: Benchmarking adaptive pricing policies for Mississippi River container-on-barge service
Authors: Alex Carroll
Abstract: Ports increasingly compete on the performance of their hinterland connections, where inland waterway transport (IWT) can provide high-capacity, lower-emission container flows but faces commercial uncertainty driven by volatile demand and shared asset constraints. This paper studies weekly pricing for an anonymized industry-proposed “fast barge” service serving five inland corridors on the Mississippi River system. We formulate a finite-horizon Markov decision process with stochastic, price-sensitive demand, corridor limits, and a shared fleet-hours allocation problem. Shipment manifests calibrate seasonality but contain no transaction prices, so reference tariffs and elasticities are explicit modeling assumptions. We compare transparent tariff, myopic, one-period, and shadow-price policies with proximal policy optimization (PPO), advantage actor–critic (A2C), and soft actor–critic (SAC), using common continuous actions, ten training seeds, and 200 paired evaluation seeds. A loose reference case remains price-boundary driven. A prespecified 300-hour benchmark has an interior unconstrained price and a positive deterministic capacity dual in 48.1% of weeks. In final evaluation, PPO and SAC improve on the validation-selected transparent benchmark by 0.089% (USD 51,800/year) and 0.362% (USD 211,100/year), respectively, with positive hierarchical intervals. Neither meets the prespecified 0.5% primary adoption screen, and the transparent benchmark retains 99.6% of SAC’s mean profit. The economic case for RL is therefore conditional on whether its annualized implementation and governance costs fall below the measured incremental value, rather than supporting an unconditional replacement recommendation.

Title: Randomized Subspace Gradient Method for Constrained Optimization
Authors: Ryota Nozawa, Pierre-Louis Poirion, Akiko Takeda
Affiliations: Graduate School of Information Science and Technology, The University of Tokyo, Tokyo 113-8656, Japan; Center for Advanced Intelligence Project, RIKEN, Tokyo 103-0027, Japan; and Center for Advanced Intelligence Project, RIKEN, Tokyo 103-0027, Japan
Abstract: We propose randomized subspace gradient methods for high-dimensional constrained optimization. Whereas there are related studies on unconstrained optimization problems, there are relatively few for constrained optimization problems because of the difficulty of handling constraints. Our algorithms project gradient vectors onto a subspace that is a random projection of the subspace spanned by the gradients of active constraints. We determine the worst case iteration complexity under linear and nonlinear settings and theoretically confirm that our algorithms can take a larger step size than their deterministic counterpart. From the advantages of taking longer steps and randomized subspace gradients, we show that our algorithms can be especially time-efficient when gradients are expensive to obtain. Furthermore, they perform well in cases in which gradients could not be obtained directly, and instead, gradients are obtained using directional derivatives. Funding: This work was partially supported by JSPS Grant-in-Aid for Scientific Research(B) [JP23H03351] and JST CREST [Grant JPMJCR24Q2].

Title: Reassessing REDD+ project effectiveness using multiple synthetic control methods: Evidence on additionality and location bias in the Brazilian Amazon
Authors: Etienne Wijler, Marina Friedrich, Thales A.P. West
Abstract: This study re-evaluates the impacts of the twelve voluntary REDD+ (Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and forest Degradation, plus other forest-related activities) projects in the Brazilian Amazon from West et al. (2020) on avoided deforestation and carbon credit generation. Although these initiatives are widely regarded as important tools for climate change mitigation, their effectiveness has come under increasing scrutiny. To shed light on this issue, we employ three causal inference methods—the original synthetic control method (SCM), Augmented SCM (ASCM), and Bayesian SCM (BSCM)—to construct counterfactual scenarios for the REDD+ projects and estimate their impact on avoided deforestation. Next to placebo tests, we employ conformal inference to evaluate statistical significance. In addition, we investigate adverse selection by developing two measures of deforestation threat and comparing the distribution of these between projects and control areas. Our objectives are three-fold: to compare the performance of the three methods, evaluate the robustness of the results across them, and to analyze potential location bias using our deforestation threat measures. Our findings corroborate the mounting literature indicating that most REDD+ projects overstate their climate impacts, consequently claiming more carbon credits than warranted. Moreover, the analysis reveals that most projects did not significantly reduce deforestation, with several more closely associated with increases in post-intervention deforestation than with decreases. Our findings also indicate that REDD+ projects are disproportionately located in areas facing relatively low deforestation pressure. These results highlight the need for more rigorous and transparent impact assessments of REDD+ projects to strengthen the credibility of carbon offsetting and have important implications for the integration of voluntary projects into regulated carbon markets under the Paris Agreement.

Title: Driving impact? How imperfect displacement shapes heterogeneous rebound in carsharing
Authors: Tamar Meshulam, Jozef Cossey, David Font Vivanco, Tamar Makov
Abstract: Green technologies, products, and services, such as carsharing, are commonly promoted as pathways to lower environmental impacts by increasing efficiency. Yet rebound effects, behavioral and economic responses to improved efficiency, may erode these environmental impact reductions. Many rebound studies assume perfect displacement, where a new technology or mode of service provision fully replaces an existing service on a one-to-one basis. While analytically convenient, this assumption overlooks real-world complexity and consumer heterogeneity. Using survey data from nearly 4500 Belgian carsharing users, we compare rebound estimates under perfect displacement with those based on reported shifts in mobility. Under the perfect displacement assumption, we find a 53% rebound effect. When accounting for imperfect displacement, however, rebound effects vary widely across users. While median effects remain positive (20%–46%), at the individual level rebound effects range from substantial net benefits to strong rebound (5th–95th percentile: −331% to 147%). A cluster analysis further reveals distinct user groups with systematically different impacts, underscoring that displacement patterns vary not only in scale but also in direction. These findings suggest that carsharing's environmental impact is highly user-dependent, and that relying on a single aggregate estimate may mask critical behavioral variations. As this case study demonstrates, accounting for imperfect displacement in rebound analysis is critical for advancing theory and for tailoring more effective policy interventions.

Title: Can natural capital accounting bring accountability for nature?
Authors: Rowan Alden Hull, Maree Fudge, Claire A. Horner, Leon A. Barmuta, Menna E. Jones, Elizabeth Pinkard, Emma tebrakunna country and Lee, Peat Leith
Abstract: With increasing global ecosystem degradation, new ways of governing the relationship between people and nature are needed. As Western societies increasingly turn to the emerging practice of Natural Capital Accounting (NCA), this is a critical time to consider its institutional role. In this paper we consider the effectiveness of NCA in bringing accountability for nature. This study theorises the link between accountability and NCA practice and explores this link empirically through quantitative and qualitative analyses of four methods of practice - the Capitals Coalition, Integrated Reporting, the System of Environmental Economic Accounting – Ecosystem Accounting, and Accounting for Nature®. The study found that NCA methods employ a range of technical mechanisms for delivering accountability, including data processes, external audit, and participation of, and transparency with, stakeholders; however, there were substantial limitations for their effectiveness. Our results highlight five challenges for NCA in delivering accountability for nature, underpinned by the broader governance environment in which this institution operates. We discuss governance options for bringing accountability for nature both with, and without, NCA. The findings of this study will help academics and policy makers to design institutional arrangements which are fit-for-purpose for bringing accountability for nature.

Title: Benefit-principle accounting of CO₂ emissions in the global textile and clothing value chain
Authors: Lila Ballav Bhusal
Abstract: Existing emission accounting frameworks assign CO₂ responsibility to producers or final consumers but do not identify factor-provider beneficiaries within bilateral trade flows. This study extends benefit-principle emissions (BPE) accounting by introducing a trade-pattern decomposition for the global textile and clothing (T&C) value chain. Using the multi-regional input-output table, the framework distinguishes producers, factor providers, final producers, and consumers, and separates final-goods, intermediate, and global value chain (GVC) trade. Consumer economies retain the largest single shares of their own T&C BPE. Developed-economy providers generally receive BPE above the consumption-based emissions (CBE) in their economies, while production-linked developing providers fall below. Bangladesh, the world's second-largest garment exporter, accounts for only 0.13% of EU-27 consumer T&C BPE despite its assembly role. Foreign factor-provider attribution rises in GVC-related trade, where assembly economies face higher CO₂ per dollar of factor-provider value added than in direct final-goods trade. Although final demand targets T&C products, emitted BPE concentrates in electricity, gas, and water, separating the consumer product from the emitting sector. Aggregate BPE-CBE ratios sit near parity for Bangladesh and selected developing-country pairs, while GVC-specific BPE exceeds CBE in most bilateral pairs. Bangladesh's economy-wide BPE exceeds its territorial emissions by 19%, showing that sectoral value capture and economy-wide balances can classify the same economy differently. Border carbon instruments based only on emission location or final-product origin can place compliance costs on actors capturing limited factor-provider benefit. Benefit-principle metrics give an additional diagnostic for border adjustment design, product-level disclosure, revenue recycling, and climate finance allocation.

Title: Livestock ownership and child nutrition: Empirical evidence from East Africa
Authors: Astewale Bimr Melaku, Bethelhem Legesse Debela
Abstract: Livestock keeping constitutes an integral component of smallholder livelihoods in developing countries, yet its linkages to child nutrition outcomes remain understudied. In this paper, we explore the relationship between ownership of different species of livestock and nutritional status of children using largescale cross-country household survey panel data from Ethiopia, Tanzania and Uganda, comprising over 19,000 child-year observations. We find that livestock ownership is positively associated with child height-for-age z-score (HAZ), with some variations across countries. Analyses of potential mechanisms reveal that the positive relationship between livestock ownership and child nutrition is channeled through increased household animal source food consumption, income, and food availability during food shortages. Further heterogeneity analyses show that the relationship varies widely across household income groups, agroecological and farming system classifications.

Title: Protected areas: questioning the development-conservation system. A socio-political-economic and ecological framework for a bottom-up approach
Authors: Mireille Razafindrakoto, François Roubaud, Florent Bédécarrats, Stéphanie M. Carrière, Emmanuel Pannier
Abstract: Despite repeated calls for urgent action to address biodiversity loss, the resounding verdict is that most conservation policies, in particular their main policy measure, Protected Areas (PAs), have failed to halt environmental degradation and achieve meaningful social outcomes. Yet, the international community has committed to extending PA coverage to 30% of the planet by 2030, and with one-third of the Global South’s population already living in or near a PA, this proportion is set to become a majority. In view of this, the current practice, which is supposed to promote sustainable development but is problematic, consists of juxtaposing socioeconomic policies and environmental policies, often regarded as mutually antagonistic, without considering a comprehensive view of governance issues. This article reviews the impact of PAs on biodiversity and the populations’ living conditions and identifies the knowledge gaps, before looking into why biodiversity conservation has been prioritised, inconclusively, to the detriment of local sociopolitical and economic dynamics and why the narrow principle of ‘inclusive governance’, more words than deeds, falls far short of the mark. The traditional approach, which is blind to the fact that conservation and development objectives are embedded within power relations and a broader sociopolitical dynamic, dominated by extractivist and capitalist logic, should be challenged. We propose a novel analytical framework with an operational methodological approach grounded in critical political ecology in order to take a bottom-up approach rooted in a territory and improve our understanding of the complex interactions between local socioecological, socioeconomic and sociopolitical concerns. This approach will help put in place more effective and inclusive policies consistent with local livelihoods, ways of life, equity and justice.

Title: The politics of environmental peacebuilding: global agendas, advocacy networks, and domestic policy arenas
Authors: Jacobo Grajales, Meryam El Bouhati, Benjamin Lévy, Toni-Giovanni Pegurri
Abstract: This article examines how environmental conflict narratives emerge and are used in peacebuilding policies. It advocates for a multi-level perspective that systematically connects global intervention agendas to political struggles in domestic policy arenas. Through a comparative analysis of four case studies—Liberia, Colombia, Côte d’Ivoire, and Lebanon—it investigates how environmental considerations are framed as security issues and incorporated into peacebuilding agendas. It explores how actors construct causal stories linking environmental issues to conflict, and how these narratives shape policy design, implementation, and resistance to change. It highlights how environmental conflict narratives are shaped by security concerns and donor-recipient relationships. While such narratives can support policy change by providing advocacy coalitions with a platform, their effects vary significantly depending on the domestic political context. This article contributes to environmental peacebuilding research by highlighting the strategic and contested nature of how environmental concerns enter peacebuilding discourse and practice.

Title: Income inequality as a barrier to the CO2-reducing potential of public investment: evidence from Latin America
Authors: Tainari Taioka, Marina da Silva Sanches, Gilberto Tadeu Lima
Abstract: This paper aims to empirically analyze the association between public investment and carbon emissions relative to Gross Domestic Product (GDP) for a panel of Latin American countries from 1994 to 2019. Given that reduced income inequality can enhance the effectiveness of environmental policies, the estimations are carried out under two income inequality regimes: higher and lower. A nonlinear Local Projections model with a threshold is employed, dividing the sample into two groups based on the Gini index. The results show that, during periods of relatively low income inequality, the estimated response of carbon-intensity growth to changes in public investment is negative over time. In contrast, under conditions of relatively high income inequality, the estimated association is not statistically significant at the 10% level. Our estimates suggest that a 10% increase in public investments is associated with an approximately 4.40% reduction in the growth rate of carbon intensity in the low-inequality regime, as measured by the Gini index, until the fourth year following the increase in public investment. These empirical findings support existing literature highlighting the positive association between income inequality and carbon emissions.

Title: Gender, risk aversion, and panic withdrawal in bank runs: Experimental evidence
Authors: Shaen Corbet, David Staunton, Steven Tucker
Abstract: Despite extensive evidence that women are more risk-averse than men, experimental bank run studies do not find consistent gender differentials across withdrawal behavior. We examine this puzzle using data from an incentivized laboratory experiment based on a two-bank Diamond–Dybvig game, with elicited risk preferences and variation in the banks’ portfolio-transparency policies. Results indicate that women are not more likely than men to withdraw early despite exhibiting greater risk aversion. We provide suggestive evidence that risk tolerance is related to beliefs about counterpart behavior among women while the corresponding relationship among men is small. Our findings indicate that beliefs about counterpart behavior, rather than risk preferences alone, are the dominant driver of withdrawal, and that the absence of gender differentials in the prior literature is a predictable consequence of effect size rather than evidence against a risk channel.

Title: Neutralizing hidden green protectionism: The efficiency of national treatment with internal taxes
Authors: Yaqiong Lin
Abstract: Does the National Treatment (NT) principle inevitably induce "hidden green protectionism"? While existing literature suggests that NT leads to inefficiently stringent product standards, we show that this distortion vanishes when governments can jointly deploy standards and internal taxes. Using an international oligopoly model, we find that the threshold for switching to cleaner standards under NT coincides with that under international cooperation. The availability of internal fiscal instruments allows governments to decouple environmental objectives from strategic trade motives, thereby restoring the regulatory efficiency of standard-setting under NT.

Title: Dynamic resource allocation with karma: An experimental study
Authors: Ezzat Elokda, Saverio Bolognani, Florian Dörfler, Heinrich H. Nax
Abstract: We perform a behavioral experiment of karma, a class of mechanisms for repeated resource allocation with attractive fairness and efficiency properties, in theory. Individuals in these mechanisms bid non-tradable credits that flow from resource consumers to yielders, like karma. Human subjects recruited on Amazon MTurk are repeatedly and randomly paired to bid karma according to time-varying and stochastic individual preferences or urgency to acquire resources. Treatments varied in the dynamic urgency process (frequent moderate urgency versus sporadic high urgency) and the richness of the bidding scheme (binary versus full range). Results are benchmarked against random allocation, and karma achieves a (almost) Pareto improvement over random, despite the MTurk subjects deviating significantly from the theoretically optimal Nash bidding policy. Maximum improvement is attained by subjects that deviate from Nash by up to one karma bid unit on average, and positive improvement is attained with average deviations of up to 3-4 bid units.
