These findings hold across all treatments, among which no significant differences are found, with the exception of the sporadic high urgency process with binary bidding treatment being (weakly) favorable over others. These results offer behaviorally robust lower bounds for the expected performance of karma in human populations. They also provide guidance for future testing and implementation of karma mechanisms in the real world.

Title: The latency location-or-routing problem
Authors: Alan Osorio-Mora, Eduardo Álvarez-Miranda, Francisco Saldanha-da-Gama
Abstract: This paper introduces the latency location-or-routing problem (LLoRP); a variant of the location-or-routing problem (LoRP) and an extension of the latency location-routing problem. The LLoRP consists of selecting (opening) a set of depots to serve a set of customers, which can be visited as part of routes also to be decided. The maximum number of depots to open is assumed to be exogenous. For the customers lying within a certain coverage range from an open depot, direct service is an alternative. A set of capacitated homogeneous vehicles is available to be assigned to the selected depots as needed. The goal is to minimize the sum of the waiting times of the customers for being served (latency). Several customer-centric applications of the LLoRP are discussed. Three mixed-integer-linear-programming formulations are developed and two lower bounds on the optimal latency value are devised. A tradeoff between LLoRP and LoRP is considered within a bi-objective modeling framework that is tackled using the ε − constrained method. An outcome of this analysis are compact formulations for the standard LoRP. This type of model is in itself a novelty for that problem. Finally, extensive computational results are discussed to assess the relevance of the LLoRP and the efficacy of the models and bounds proposed. The results highlight multiple distinguishing features of the LLoRP while identifying the most promising optimization models to use. They also provide strong evidence for the relevance of looking into tradeoff solutions when a cost-oriented objective becomes of interest in addition to latency.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Impacts of subway line extension on economic vitality and social cohesion: Evidence from Boston’s Green Line Extension through a double machine learning DID approach
Authors: Xinyi Huang, Yunhan Zheng, Dingyi Zhuang, Yuebing Liang, Jinhua Zhao
Abstract: Public transit has long been viewed as a great equalizer in urban life, expected to break down barriers among social groups and stimulate economic growth. However, empirical evidence on both dimensions remains limited to aggregated proxies such as property values, which may not capture actual and timely behavioral changes, particularly in the post-pandemic context. The Green Line Extension (GLX) in Somerville, Boston Metropolitan Area, which opened in December 2022, provides a natural experiment to examine these relationships. We analyze over 300,000 daily observations of points of interest (POIs) across three cities over 438 consecutive days, measuring economic vitality through daily visit counts and social cohesion through the income segregation of venue visitors. These two outcomes have rarely been studied together using granular behavioral data in the transit literature. We employ a double/debiased machine learning difference-in-differences (DMLDID) approach, which uses data-adaptive estimation to handle the nonlinear covariate-outcome relationships, where traditional linear DID would be misspecified. Our findings reveal a decoupling between the two outcomes. GLX significantly enhanced economic vitality, increasing average daily visits by approximately 23% per POI (95% CI: 13.4%–32.7%). The effects were strongest in retail trade and food service sectors. By contrast, its impact on income segregation at nearby venues was statistically insignificant, challenging the assumption that improved physical connectivity automatically promotes social mixing. The economic effects vary across sectors, while social cohesion effects are statistically insignificant in every sector examined, indicating that this decoupling holds across the sectoral composition of our study area rather than being confined to particular venue types. These findings suggest that, in this short- to mid-term post-pandemic window, transit investment alone did not advance social mixing, pointing to a potential role for complementary interventions alongside infrastructure expansion.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Are there similarities between the spatial patterns of autonomous and human-driven vehicle crashes? Evidence from a data-driven case study in California
Authors: Tianyi Chen, Kaidi Yang
Abstract: Comparisons between autonomous vehicles (AVs) and human-driven vehicles (HDVs) have been widely adopted as a means of assessing AV safety. This study provides a new data-driven perspective for such comparison-based assessments by quantitatively measuring the similarity between the spatial patterns of AV and HDV crashes. Using crash records of both vehicle types as inputs, the proposed method comprises three main steps: (1) reconstruction of investigated road network for in the absence of publicly disclosed AV operational routes; (2) crash hotspot identification using Network Kernel Density Estimation (NKDE); and (3) quantitative spatial similarity analysis based on multiple similarity indicators. The method is applied to case studies in two urban areas in California, San Francisco and the Silicon Valley area, across three time periods: 2016–2018, 2019–2021, and 2022–2024. The results reveal three key findings. First, the spatial patterns of AV crashes gradually become more similar to those of HDV crashes over time. Second, AV crash spatial patterns exhibit substantially greater temporal variability than their HDV counterparts. Third, notable differences are observed between the two urban areas in terms of the spatiotemporal patterns of vehicle crashes. These findings are plausibly attributable to the expanding scale and spatial coverage of AV operations, as well as ongoing advances in human-like AV control and decision-making mechanisms over time. This study provides practical insights for urban traffic management and AV manufacturers by improving understanding of how AV crash risks evolve relative to conventional traffic systems.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: A planning framework for enhancing power supply resilience from a climate risk perspective: evidence from the Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei region in China
Authors: Bowen Yi, Yulu Ji, Ying Fan
Abstract: Climate change is making extreme weather increasingly consequential for power systems, yet the economic implications of climate resilience under deep decarbonization pathways remain poorly quantified. This study develops an integrated climate stress-informed planning framework that links meteorological hazards, coupled supply-demand impacts, and long-term capacity investment, and applies it to China's Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region. Using meteorological records from 1980 to 2023, we construct four extreme-weather scenarios, including extreme cold, extreme heat, stagnation, and overcast, and further develop a compound extreme-weather scenario to capture combined climate stresses. These scenarios are embedded into a multi-stage generation-transmission expansion model with hourly dispatch over 2035–2055. Three findings emerge. First, short-duration extreme-weather events can substantially reshape long-term capacity portfolios, as the reliability of high-renewable systems is increasingly determined by a small number of critical hours rather than average conditions. Second, the nature of climate resilience evolves along the decarbonization pathway: early-stage impacts are dominated by demand-side operational adjustments, while later-stage resilience increasingly depends on renewable and storage investment, operational flexibility, and the spatial reallocation of capacity across regions. Third, interprovincial transmission undergoes functional differentiation, shifting from primarily continuous energy delivery toward complementary roles in energy supply and capacity support under climate stress. These findings highlight the importance of coordinated deployment of renewable resources, storage, and transmission infrastructure to maintain power system resilience during deep decarbonization.

Title: Reducing carbon emission by optimizing container liner fleet deployment and sailing speed
Authors: Siqi Yuan, Jian Gang Jin, Xiangdong Xu
Abstract: Facing stringent environmental regulations and an aging fleet, container liner shipping companies face mounting pressure to reduce fuel consumption and emissions. This paper optimizes tactical fleet deployment and sailing speed by explicitly incorporating vessel heterogeneity. A mixed integer nonlinear programming model is formulated, and a Velocity-Discretization-Based Dynamic Algorithm is developed to improve computational efficiency. Practical fleet adjustment constraints are further considered to evaluate the achievable benefits under limited vessel redeployment. Numerical experiments based on real-world operational data demonstrate that considering vessel heterogeneity and jointly optimizing deployment and speed can significantly reduce fuel consumption and CO 2 emissions. The proposed algorithm achieves reliable solutions with substantially shorter computational time than the direct solution, providing a practical decision-support tool for sustainable liner shipping operations.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Dynamic decarbonization pathways for inland shipping under energy system and policy uncertainties
Authors: Jun Yuan, Yuwei Zhang, Jian Gang Jin, Victor Nian, Xunpeng Shi
Abstract: Inland shipping decarbonization requires coordinated changes in fleets, fuels, infrastructure, and policy that static life cycle assessments cannot capture. This study develops a framework coupling Power-to-X pathways, dynamic hybrid life cycle assessment, a fleet digital twin, and multi-objective optimization. Applied to 2,100 weighted representative vessel records in the Yangtze River Delta from 2025 to 2050 under four policy scenarios, the selected integrated policy knee solution reduces diesel from 99.0% to 15.5% of fleet shaft energy demand. Battery electricity becomes the largest low-carbon pathway (30.3%), followed by hydrogen (22.1%), e-methanol (16.4%), and ammonia (15.6%). Cumulative life cycle emissions are 298.8 Mt CO 2 -eq, 10.4% below business as usual, while net present resource cost is 166.3 billion 2025 USD. Deep inland shipping decarbonization is feasible but back-loaded and depends on coordinated fleet renewal, infrastructure deployment, and fuel diversification.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Environmental impacts of development of railways in a road dominated infrastructure
Authors: Vinicius Donisete Lima Rodrigues Goulart, William Leles de Souza Costa, Rodrigo Affonso de Albuquerque Nóbrega
Abstract: Railway infrastructure plays a pivotal role in economic development, with well-documented environmental implications. However, emerging global agreements, and environmental policies introduce new dimensions that must be considered. The expansion of Brazil’s railway network has the potential to transform landscapes. This study evaluates the environmental effects of railway expansion, focusing on landcover conversion risk driven by proximity to infrastructure, population density, and agricultural potential. Spatial analysis and Random Forest modelling identified population and proximity to railways as the strongest contributors to landcover conversion risk revealing relevant environmental impacts, with overlap between estimated conversion risk and ecologically sensitive regions, and threatened species. While scenario-specific analyses highlight variations in potential impacts, the primary finding is: railways function as major drivers of landscape transformation, amplifying anthropogenic pressures on natural habitats. These results underscore the urgent need for proactive conservation planning to mitigate ecological impacts and ensure that infrastructure development aligns with global biodiversity goals.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Does Goliath help David? Anchor firms and startup clusters
Authors: Rahul R. Gupta
Abstract: Does attracting a “Goliath” firm to a county anchor the growth of regional industry clusters? Matching a hand-collected dataset of major corporate site selection contests to restricted-use U.S. Census microdata, I show that winning a Million Dollar Plant (MDP) generates 2515 net supply chain jobs in the first four years after announcement, declining to 1622 in the subsequent four years. Over the last four years of the panel between four and seven years after the MDP is announced, startups remain the largest contributor to job gains at 1694 jobs, more than offsetting a decline among other incumbents (-61% of the net total), with local incumbents (41%), and affiliated firms (15%) also contributing positively. Post-announcement startups are more numerous but smaller and slower-growing than comparable cohorts in runner-up counties. The two main sources of job creation draw on distinct segments of the local labor market: relative to those in finalist counties, startups in winning counties rely disproportionately on immigrant workers whereas local incumbents employ more local workers, and neither shows evidence of worker flows from the MDP’s corporate network.

Title: Opportunistic Upskilling in European Labour Markets—Evidence From a Wide Replication
Authors: Anil Yadav, John McHale, Jefferson R. B. Galetti
Affiliations: Central Bank of Ireland Ireland; University of Galway Ireland
Abstract: ABSTRACT We build on Modestino et al., who analysed “opportunistic upskilling” during the 2007 recession in the US, by extending their approach to European labour markets following recent economic shocks. Using a comprehensive dataset of online job postings (2019–2023) and an instrumental variable approach leveraging Ukrainian refugee inflows, we find that increases in labour supply have a significant positive effect on both education and experience requirements. Our findings reinforce the idea that employers opportunistically upskill labour demand in different but challenging macroeconomic contexts. The identification of such patterns, however, depends on the presence of a plausibly exogenous shock to labour markets.

Title: Multivariate Trend Inflation in the United States and the Euro Area
Authors: Max‐Sebastian Dovì
Affiliations: International Monetary Fund Washington DC USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT I provide a precision‐sampler‐based replication of the multivariate unobserved component stochastic volatility outlier‐adjusted model of Stock and Watson (2016) applied to inflation in the United States and the Euro Area (EA). I find a substantial post‐2020 increase in trend inflation for both the United States and the EA, and estimate end‐2024 trend inflation at 2.3 and 2.0 percent, respectively.

Title: Identifying Peer Effects in Networks with Unobserved Effort and Isolated Students
Authors: Aristide Houndetoungan, Cristelle Kouame, Michael Vlassopoulos
Affiliations: Department of Economics Laval University Quebec Canada; Education and Skills World Bank Group Washington DC USA; University of Southampton Southampton UK; Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) London UK; IZA@LISER Network, Esch‐sur‐Alzette/Belval Luxembourg
Abstract: ABSTRACT Peer influence on effort devoted to some activity is often studied when effort is unobserved, and the researcher instead observes an outcome that combines effort with other shocks. For instance, in education, achievement measures such as GPA reflect both effort and idiosyncratic GPA shocks. We propose an alternative approach that circumvents this approximation. Our framework distinguishes unobserved shocks to GPA that do not affect effort from preference shocks that do affect effort levels. We show that peer effects estimates obtained using our approach can differ significantly from classical estimates (where effort is approximated) if the network includes isolated students. Applying our approach to data on high school students in the United States, we find that peer effect estimates relying on GPA as a proxy for effort are 40% lower than those obtained using our approach.

Title: Fast Likelihood‐Free Parameter Estimation for Lévy Processes
Authors: Nicolas Coloma, William Kleiber
Affiliations: Department of Applied Mathematics University of Colorado Boulder Colorado USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT Lévy processes are widely used in financial modeling due to their ability to capture discontinuities and heavy tails, which are common in high‐frequency asset return data. However, parameter estimation remains a challenge when associated likelihoods are unavailable or costly to compute. We propose a fast and accurate method for Lévy parameter estimation using the neural Bayes estimation (NBE) framework—a simulation‐based, likelihood‐free approach that leverages permutation‐invariant neural networks to approximate Bayes estimators. We contribute new theoretical results, showing that NBE results in consistent estimators whose risk converges to that of the Bayes estimator under mild conditions. Moreover, through extensive simulations across several Lévy models, we show that NBE outperforms traditional methods in both accuracy and runtime, while also enabling two complementary approaches to uncertainty quantification. We illustrate our approach on a challenging high‐frequency cryptocurrency return dataset, where the method captures evolving parameter dynamics and delivers reliable and interpretable inference at a fraction of the computational cost of traditional methods. We investigate nearly a decade of high‐frequency Bitcoin returns, requiring less than one minute to estimate parameters under the proposed approach.

Title: Housing Supply Elasticities: A Structural Vector Autoregression Approach
Authors: Wesley A. Miller, Anthony W. Orlando, Christian L. Redfearn
Affiliations: University of Southern California Los Angeles California USA; California State Polytechnic University Pomona California USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT We estimate the first time‐varying, county‐level index of housing supply elasticities across the United States, using a structural vector autoregression model with sign restrictions to identify the effect of a positive demand shock. This index reveals four features of the supply curve in different local housing markets. First, supply elasticities are low, on average, generating faster price growth than housing unit growth for most of the country. Second, there is significant variation in elasticities across counties, both urban and rural. Third, elasticities have declined in more counties than they have risen over time, particularly in large urban markets. Fourth, these new estimates predict housing quantity growth better than previous models in the literature.

Title: A Smooth Specification Test for the Propensity Score
Authors: Shiyao Huang, Xiaojun Song
Affiliations: Department of Business Statistics and Econometrics Guanghua School of Management, Peking University Beijing China
Abstract: ABSTRACT This paper proposes a simple smooth specification test for the propensity score in the spirit of Neyman (1937). We derive a particular restriction on the propensity score and construct the specification test based on it. Using the density‐weighting method, we transform the original specification testing problem into a test of the joint significance of the generalized Fourier coefficients. We propose a novel projection method to eliminate the parameter estimation effect arising from estimating unknown nuisance parameters. The proposed test is shown to follow a standard distribution under the null hypothesis and to possess nontrivial asymptotic power against local alternatives that converge to the null at the parametric rate , where is the sample size. To enhance the practical applicability of the procedure, we further introduce a data‐driven selection method for determining the testing order, enabling automatic selection based on the observed data. Compared to existing methods, our test does not suffer from the “curse of dimensionality” faced by Shaikh et al. (2009); at the same time, our test is both asymptotically pivotal and more computationally efficient than that of Sant'Anna and Song (2019). Extensive simulations demonstrate that the proposed test yields satisfactory empirical size and power. Compared with previous tests, our test exhibits comparable overall performance and delivers clear improvements in some cases, especially for high‐frequency alternatives. Two empirical applications further illustrate the practical applicability of our proposal, examining propensity score specifications in the Soviet 156 Program and the US Job Corps Program.

Title: Labor Market Institutions, Fiscal Multipliers, and Macroeconomic Volatility
Authors: Maximilian Boeck, Jesús Crespo Cuaresma, Christian Glocker
Affiliations: Vienna University of Economics and Business Vienna Austria; Friedrich‐Alexander University Erlangen‐Nuremberg Nuremberg Germany; Wittgenstein Centre for Demography and Global Human Capital (IIASA, ÖAW, UniVie) Vienna Austria; Austrian Institute of Economic Research (WIFO) Vienna Austria; CESifo Munich Germany
Abstract: ABSTRACT How do labor market institutions shape the transmission of government spending shocks and macroeconomic volatility? We develop a theoretical model in which labor market institutions affect fiscal transmission through their effect on wage rigidity, job separation, and matching frictions. We estimate an interacted panel vector autoregressive model for 16 OECD economies and study how macroeconomic responses to government spending shocks vary with institutional labor market characteristics. In line with our theoretical predictions, we show that institutions that stabilize employment and wages tend to reduce output volatility and attenuate the response of output and employment to government spending shocks.

Title: Conditional Randomization Tests for the Specification of Interference Structure
Authors: Tadao Hoshino, Takahide Yanagi
Affiliations: School of Political Science and Economics Waseda University Shinjuku‐ku Japan; Graduate School of Economics Kyoto University Sakyo Japan
Abstract: ABSTRACT This study proposes specification tests for interference structure in causal inference with spillovers. We focus on experimental settings in which the treatment assignment mechanism is known. To test whether a given exposure mapping adequately summarizes the true interference structure, we develop conditional randomization tests by utilizing the hierarchical relationship between the null and alternative exposure mappings. When there are multiple candidate exposure mappings of interest, we propose a sequential specification testing procedure that controls the false discovery rate. Through extensive simulation exercises, we demonstrate that our tests have desirable size properties and satisfactory power. To illustrate the proposed methods, we revisit two existing social network experiments: One on farmers' insurance adoption and another on anti‐conflict education programs.

Title: Fiscal Policy Regimes in Resource‐Rich Economies
Authors: Hilde C. Bjørnland, Roberto Casarin, Marco Lorusso, Francesco Ravazzolo
Affiliations: BI Norwegian Business School Oslo Norway; Norges Bank Oslo Norway; CAMA Canberra Australia; Ca' Foscari University Venice Venice Italy; Department of Political Science University of Perugia Perugia Italy; Newcastle University Business School Newcastle upon Tyne UK; Free University of Bozen‐Bolzano Bolzano Italy
Abstract: ABSTRACT We analyse fiscal policy in resource‐rich economies using a novel Bayesian regime‐switching panel model. The identified regimes capture pro‐ or countercyclical fiscal behaviour by allowing regime‐specific shifts in the average fiscal stance, while the switches between the regimes have the interpretation of changes in fiscal policy. Applying the model to a panel of sixteen oil‐producing economies, we show that fiscal policy has alternated between a procyclical and countercyclical regime multiple times over the sample. Furthermore, we find that fiscal policy is more volatile in the procyclical regime and that the probability of being in the procyclical regime is higher for OPEC countries than for non‐OPEC countries. We also show that following either an increase or decrease in oil revenues, the growth in government expenditures is mostly increasing, suggesting an upward bias in expenditures in oil‐producing countries. These are new findings in the literature.

Title: Regularization of Synthetic Controls for Policy Evaluation
Authors: Yi‐Ting Chen
Affiliations: Department of Finance National Taiwan University Taipei Taiwan
Abstract: ABSTRACT We propose a unified framework for interpreting and comparing a broad class of synthetic control (SC) methods. Our framework is built on an analysis of a mean‐squared prediction error (MSPE) bound for the counterfactual predicted by a generic SC method, without imposing a specific outcome model. Using this framework, we develop a generalized SC method that provides a more comprehensive regularization of the MSPE bound than several existing SC methods. Through simulation studies and placebo analyses, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in predicting the counterfactual.

Title: Triply Robust Panel Estimators
Authors: Susan Athey, Guido Imbens, Zhaonan Qu, Davide Viviano
Affiliations: Stanford University Stanford USA; Columbia University New York USA; Harvard University Cambridge USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT This paper studies estimation of causal effects in a panel data setting. We introduce a new estimator, the Triply Robust Panel (TROP) estimator, that combines a flexible model for the potential outcomes based on a low‐rank factor structure on top of a two‐way‐fixed effect specification, with unit weights intended to upweight units similar to the treated units and time weights intended to upweight time periods close to the treated time periods. We study the performance of the estimator in a set of simulations designed to closely match several commonly studied real data sets. We find that there is substantial variation in the performance of the estimators across the settings considered. The proposed estimator outperforms Two‐Way‐Fixed‐Effect (TWFE) or Difference‐In‐Differences (DID), Synthetic Control (SC), Matrix Completion (MC) and Synthetic‐Difference‐In‐Differences (SDID) estimators. We investigate what features of the data generating process lead to this superior performance and assess the relative importance of the three components of the proposed estimator. We have two recommendations. Our preferred strategy is that researchers use simulations closely matched to the data they are interested in, along the lines discussed in this paper, to investigate which estimators work well in their particular setting. A simpler approach is to use more robust estimators such as SDID or the new TROP estimator, which we find to substantially outperform TWFE/DID estimators in many empirically relevant settings.

Title: Estimation of Heterogeneous Panel Data Models With Mixed Sampling Frequencies
Authors: Haoran Li, Haoyang Li, Naifu Xiao, Yimin Yang
Affiliations: School of Applied Economics Renmin University of China Beijing China; College of Economics and Management Nanjing Agricultural University Nanjing China; School of Public Finance and Taxation, Zhongnan University of Economics and Law Wuhan China; School of Finance Renmin University of China Beijing China
Abstract: ABSTRACT This paper studies heterogeneous mixed‐frequency panel data models, focusing on linear specifications that allow heterogeneity in both aggregation weights and slope coefficients. To address potential correlations between the heterogeneity and the covariates, we first show that, under additional normalization conditions, the mean‐group estimator delivers consistent and asymptotically normal slope estimates but biased weights estimators. As an alternative, we propose a correlated random effects estimator using a generalized Mundlak specification. We further discuss the implementation of these two estimators when covariates are observed at substantially higher sampling frequencies. Monte Carlo simulations are conducted to assess their finite‐sample properties. As an empirical illustration, we revisit the impact of temperature fluctuations on economic growth using the proposed framework.

Title: Issue Information
Exploring the application of statistical and symbolic AI in supply chain risk management: a systematic literature review
Authors: Zuha Shahid, Arnold Beckmann, Abdourahim Sylla, Gülgün Alpan, Cinzia Giannetti
Affiliations: Swansea University; University of Grenoble Alpes; Loughborough University
Abstract: Supply chains are increasingly facing risks and uncertainties due to globalisation, digitisation, and the complexity of interconnected networks. Recently, Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising tool for enhancing Supply Chain Risk Management (SCRM) through improved prediction and decision-making. This study presents a systematic literature review on two major AI paradigms, namely statistical and symbolic AI. Following the PRISMA methodology, a systematic search of the Scopus and Web of Science databases was conducted in April 2026. Based on a final synthesis of 87 primary research articles, this review analyses the literature across different risk types, risk management tasks, and knowledge and data sources. The findings reveal that statistical AI dominates with 68.97% of the reviewed papers, particularly in predictive tasks such as risk identification, risk assessment and proactive risk mitigation. Whereas symbolic AI, with 20.69% of the reviewed papers, remains critically underexplored. This comparative analysis underscores the need for hybrid approaches that combine the predictive capabilities of statistical AI with the interpretability and reasoning capabilities of symbolic AI. Such integration has the potential to enhance the effectiveness, robustness, transparency, and trustworthiness of SCRM systems, while also providing promising directions for future research and practical applications.

Title: Brand as a competitive lever: content provision and product pricing in live-streaming selling
Authors: Wenchao Cheng, Qiuyan Chen, Yiwen Bian, Jennifer Shang
Affiliations: Shanghai University; Jiangnan University; University of Pittsburgh
Abstract: Live-streaming selling (LSS) integrates real-time content, consumer interaction, and transactions, making content allocation a key strategic decision. This study examines how strong-brand firms should allocate limited live-streaming time between product-related and brand-related content when competing with weak-brand firms offering functionally similar but vertically differentiated products. Product-related content communicates experiential value but may spill over to comparable products through consumer perception and comparison. Brand-related content crowds out product demonstrations but builds loyal demand and reduces direct comparison. We develop a theoretical model with consumer-perception-based experiential information spillover. The strong-brand firm chooses between pure-product and mixed content strategies. We show that when brand value is sufficiently high and product differentiation is substantial, pure-product content is preferred. When products are close substitutes, mixed content becomes optimal because brand-related content expands loyal demand, softens price competition, and supports higher prices. Under certain conditions, mixed content can also benefit the weak-brand firm by relaxing competition despite reducing spillover gains, creating a win-win outcome. With endogenous content allocation, the strong-brand firm devotes more time to brand-related content as competition intensifies. Overall, this study highlights the strategic role of brand communication, which strengthens loyalty, shapes competitive outcomes, and sustains long-term profitability in live-streaming selling markets.

Title: Coordinated procurement for proactive shipment consolidation in project-based production systems
Authors: Najat Bara, Mohamed Nour Kitri, Onur Ozturk, Frédéric Gautier, Junkai He
Affiliations: Kedge Business School; Mohammed VI Polytechnic University; University of Ottawa; IAE Paris I Panthéon-Sorbonne (Sorbonne Business School)
Abstract: Effective production planning relies on the timely coordination of upstream procurement and transportation decisions to ensure material availability while controlling operational costs. In many supply chains, decentralised procurement practices hinder shipment consolidation opportunities and lead to inefficient transportation resource utilisation. This paper proposes a proactive shipment consolidation framework supporting production planning by coordinating procurement and transportation decisions upstream. Starting from production requirements, the approach anticipates consolidation opportunities by jointly determining supplier selection, delivery timing, and truck assignments for heterogeneous orders. Unlike the predominantly reactive and carrier-driven consolidation approaches in the literature, this framework adopts a proactive buyer-driven perspective that enables coordinated procurement decisions and improves transportation efficiency while ensuring the timely supply of materials for production. The problem is formulated as a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model minimising purchasing, transportation, and holding costs while accounting for ongoing orders already committed to suppliers and their shipment schedules. For large-scale instances, both a matheuristic and an Iterated Local Search (ILS) are developed. Computational experiments, based on data simulating historical industrial records, demonstrate the strong managerial value of proactive consolidation and confirm its scalability for real-world deployment.

Title: Optimising robotic pick-and-place operations and the application of RMS principles
Authors: Konstantinos Giannakos, Dimitrios Tsakoumis, Gregory Koronakos, Stathis Plitsos, Pavlos Eirinakis, Giulio Vivo, Angelo Nicotera
Affiliations: University of Piraeus; Centro Ricerche Fiat S.C.p.A; Iltar-Italbox Industrie Riunite Spa
Abstract: Robotic Pick-and-Place (PnP) kitting operations involve transferring components from storage locations to assembly positions under strict component-requirement compatibility constraints. In this work, this setting is formulated as a mapping-constrained Bipartite Travelling Salesman Problem (BTSP), systematically examined under three different industrially-driven graph cases. An Integer Programming (IP)-based exact solution method together with adjusted heuristics and reinforcement learning approaches are employed to generate feasible and optimal PnP sequences by explicitly enforcing compatibility and operational constraints. Notably, the IP approach achieves execution time reductions of up to 23.80% over the industrial baseline. To further improve system performance, a simulation-driven framework is introduced, where storage configuration is treated as a decision parameter and evaluated through repeated reconstruction of BTSP instances. This enables systematic exploration of layout alternatives, producing additional efficiency gains of 13.6% on average and up to 35.73%. The proposed framework is deployed within a Digital Twin-enabled architecture and validated in a real industrial environment, demonstrating how optimisation and simulation support the practical application of Reconfigurable Manufacturing Systems principles.

Title: Some innovative multivariate Bayesian schemes for monitoring the mean vector with applications to monitoring production processes
Authors: Hongxing Cai, Amitava Mukherjee, Tao Wang, Jiujun Zhang
Affiliations: Liaoning University; XLRI–Xavier School of Management; Huaiyin Normal University
Abstract: Bayesian approaches have gained popularity for addressing operational research and management problems, including process monitoring and product quality assessment. In particular, Bayesian approaches are often used to address complex multivariable processes. This paper analyses and evaluates a multivariate Bayesian generalised likelihood ratio (MBGLR) scheme, a multivariate Bayesian cumulative sum (MBCUSUM) scheme and a combination of two MBCUSUM (2MBCUSUM) schemes to monitor the mean vector of a multivariate Gaussian process distribution. Monte Carlo simulations are employed to evaluate the detection performance of these three schemes. Furthermore, they are compared with the multivariate generalised likelihood ratio (MGLR) scheme, the multivariate empirical Bayes (MEB) scheme, and a CUSUM-type multivariate empirical Bayes (CUSUM-MEB) scheme based on the steady-state average time to signal (SSATS). Simulation results show that the MBGLR scheme exhibits strong overall monitoring performance when suitable prior parameters and window sizes are selected. While the MBCUSUM and 2MBCUSUM schemes outperform the MBGLR scheme in detecting certain small shifts, the MBGLR scheme consistently outperforms the MGLR, MEB, and CUSUM-MEB schemes across all shift magnitudes for the different instances considered in this study. Finally, a lumber manufacturing dataset and a carbon-fibre tubing manufacturing dataset are used to illustrate the practical applicability of the proposed schemes.

Title: Research in memory of Professor William T. Ziemba
Authors: Sébastien Lleo, Leonard MacLean

Title: Outpatient appointment scheduling with decision‐dependent unpunctual arrivals
Authors: Shenghai Zhou, Shuo Pang, Haiyue Yu, Yushu Zeng
Affiliations: School of Business Central South University Changsha China; MOE Philosophy and Social Science Laboratory of Intelligent Governance for Complex Social Systems, Changsha, China; School of Management and Engineering Nanjing University Nanjing China; Shanghai Municipal Hospital of Traditional Chinese Medicine Shanghai University of Traditional Chinese Medicine Shanghai China; Antai College of Economics and Management Shanghai Jiao Tong University Shanghai China; Shanghai Municipal Hospital Disease Quality and Safety Sub‐Research Center Shanghai China; IESEG School of Management Lille France
Abstract: Abstract This article investigates appointment scheduling with stochastic service times (exogenous uncertainty) and schedule‐dependent unpunctual arrivals (endogenous uncertainty). First, our empirical study confirms that patients exhibit unpunctual behavior that varies across different age categories, visit types, and departments. More importantly, the empirical results document a statistically significant association between appointment time and patient unpunctuality. Second, we develop a mathematical formulation of the problem within a stochastic‐optimization framework considering schedule‐dependent uncertainties. The empirically observed appointment‐time‐specific arrival pattern is incorporated as a planning input. We confirm the differentiability property of the objective function and that its derivative is uniformly bounded. Building upon this result, we obtain an unbiased estimator of the gradient for the objective function, enabling us to design a gradient‐based optimization approach. To further enhance optimization performance and avoid local optima, we integrate gradient‐based local refinement with a curvature‐informed Variable Neighborhood Search (VNS) procedure, resulting in a hybrid solution method. Finally, numerical experiments demonstrate the computational efficiency of the proposed method and show that appointment‐time‐dependent unpunctuality can materially affect optimal schedule structures. In particular, different unpunctuality profiles can lead to distinct scheduling arrangements.

Title: Strategic inventory holdbacks: Managing waste and backlog in humanitarian operations
Authors: Nesim K. Erkip, Vera Tilson
Abstract: Humanitarian organizations distributing relief supplies must allocate limited inventory across multiple locations under uncertain demand, donation-constrained replenishment, heterogeneous lead times, and operational losses such as theft, displacement, and handling damage. Existing policies are often myopic and can perform poorly under variability or shifting supply conditions. We propose a non-myopic holdback heuristic for a two-echelon humanitarian distribution system in which warehouse inventory is strategically retained and released using a two-period decision rule. The policy leverages warehouse-level risk pooling and balances current allocations against future inventory availability under uncertainty. Using discrete-event simulation, we compare the heuristic against a no-holdback policy, a reactive “chase” policy, a loss-adjusted order-up-to policy, and a clairvoyant benchmark across a wide range of supply and demand conditions. Performance is evaluated using waste, fill rate, backlog age, and retailer-level fairness measures. Results show that the holdback policy substantially reduces waste while maintaining competitive service and fairness performance. In many settings, it also improves the balance of service across retailers. The approach is simple, data-light, and practical for humanitarian operations, and highlights the value of strategic inventory retention under uncertainty and operational loss risk.

Title: Dynamic subsidy design for coordinated emission abatement: A differential game with reference and delayed effects in low-carbon supply chain
Authors: Zixuan Hu, Yongguang Zhong, Tao Chu, Lei Wang, Jiaxin Zhang
Abstract: Within the low-carbon development paradigm, we examine the dynamic impacts of consumers' low-carbon reference effect and delayed effects of the manufacturer's product low-carbon level and the retailer's low-carbon publicity level on low-carbon goodwill. Through differential game modeling, we investigate long-term dynamic joint emission reduction and government subsidy strategies in a two-tier manufacturer–retailer supply chain. Specifically, by applying the maximum principle, we systematically compare member equilibrium strategies, discounted supply chain profits, and government input–output performance under the following three decision-making models: decentralized without cost-sharing, decentralized under the two-way cost-sharing contract, and centralized. Key findings indicate the following: (a) As consumers' low-carbon reference effect grows stronger, the government's optimal subsidy rate for manufacturer's low-carbon R&D increases accordingly; (b) Longer delays weaken the marginal input–output effectiveness of low-carbon subsidies, thereby reducing the government's optimal subsidy rates; (c) Delayed effects interact with the low-carbon reference effect. Changes in delay duration affect the dynamic updating of consumers' reference low-carbon levels, while the low-carbon reference effect makes the adverse impact of delays on the discounted supply chain profit more pronounced; (d) Under the joint influence of delayed effects and the low-carbon reference effect, centralized decision-making generates higher low-carbon effort levels but yields the lowest discounted supply chain profit, whereas the relative profits of decentralized models vary across delay intervals. From the perspective of government input–output performance, decentralized decision-making under the two-way cost-sharing contract performs best.

Title: Full in-house operation, partial outsourcing, or full outsourcing? A game-theoretic analysis of collaborative strategies for retired electric vehicle battery recycling
Authors: Jiumei Chen, Fenfang Sun, Manman Wang
Abstract: The circular utilization of retired electric vehicle batteries (EVBs) is essential for the sustainable development of the new energy vehicle industry. Establishing an efficient recycling system has become a key issue facing the industry. In view of this, this paper employs game theory to model and analyze three representative industrial configurations: (1) full in-house operation, where the battery manufacturer (BM) establishes its own recycling channel and invest in process innovation for recycling (PIR); (2) partial outsourcing, where recycling is outsourced while PIR investment remains with the BM; and (3) full outsourcing, where both recycling and PIR investment are delegated to the battery recycler (BR). The findings reveal that the BM's optimal recycling mode is jointly determined by the PIR cost and the operational effort level of the recycling channel. Moreover, the PIR cost has distinct impacts on the PIR level across modes. In addition, the operational effort level of the recycling channel and the PIR cost coefficient have non-monotonic effects on the recycling rate and transfer price, respectively, due to the interaction between cost pressure and profit redistribution effects. The results provide a theoretical basis for BMs' strategic decisions regarding recycling channel structure and the allocation of responsibility for PIR investment.

Title: The long-term effects of teachers’ gender stereotypes on labor outcomes
Authors: Joan J. Martínez
Abstract: This paper links a teacher-level measure of gender-stereotyped grading — validated against their Implicit Association Test (IAT) scores — to the later schooling and labor-market outcomes of 1.6 million Peruvian students. Exposure to a more stereotyped teacher widens the gender gaps in high-school completion, formal-sector employment, and earnings, driven by boys’ lasting gains rather than by girls’ smaller, short-lived losses. A single year with a math teacher one standard deviation more stereotyped than average raises boys’ on-time graduation by 0.9 percentage points and lowers girls’ by 0.6. Over the five years after high school (ages 17–22), it raises boys’ formal employment by 4%–12% of the mean employment rate and widens the gender pay gap by about 11% in the first two years, while girls’ losses fade thereafter. These effects run through high-school completion, not test scores or college enrollment. The widening gap in male-dominated industries mainly reflects men's entry rather than women's exit, and students show little sign of adopting the stereotypes themselves. Where structural barriers already constrain access to higher education, teachers’ stereotypes shape who finishes school and their early labor-market outcomes, rather than who reaches college.

Title: Standards and technology innovation with search
Authors: Lluís M. Granero, Santiago J. Rubio
Abstract: This paper examines optimal environmental regulation based on emission or performance standards in the presence of consumer search and firm innovation. With an exogenous market structure, we find that the emission and performance standards lead to the same equilibrium level of innovation, which decreases in the degree of competition in a Schumpeterian way, and these two policy tools are equivalent in terms of total welfare but not in distributional terms because they give rise to different levels of consumer and producer surplus. Here, low search costs can lead to price-increasing competition for concentrated industries and spillovers determine the time consistency of the standards. With an endogenous market structure, the two regulatory instruments lead to different levels of total welfare, they both yield excessive firm entry, and the magnitude of the inefficiency from excessive entry is relatively greater under the emission standard.
Journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

Title: The impact of import competition on gendered labor market outcomes
Authors: Leandro Freylejer, Liam D. Kelly
Abstract: Using a longitudinal random sample of 20% of tax filers in Canada and a triple-differences identification strategy, we study the effect of the rapid increase in Chinese imports on a multiplicity of labor market outcomes across genders. We find that the shock caused a small reduction in the gender gap in annual employment earnings relative to its negative impact on the earnings of workers of each gender separately. Furthermore, we find that the shock caused a larger share of male workers than female workers to transition to non-employment. On the other hand, estimates of differential transitions across locations and to self-employment were small and not statistically significant. Estimates of the probability of exiting wage employment for workers in different segments of the within-local-labor-market earnings distribution suggest that the shock had significant implications for within-gender earnings inequality.

Title: Green product co-design within cheap-talk information disclosure in a supply chain
Authors: Mengfan Li, Zhaofu Hong, Yunrong Zhang
Abstract: Green product co-design in supply chains has become an important practice, with information disclosure serving as a key facilitator for collaboration. However, the effectiveness of information disclosure, which may involve cheap talk (unverified information), on the collaboration of the supply chain remains unclear. Therefore, this study develops a game-theoretic model to investigate the strategic role of cheap talk in green product co-design, where the supplier determines and discloses its green design strategy, which may involve cheap talk, and the manufacturer subsequently sets its green design strategy based on the received information. Our analysis derives the optimal information disclosure strategy for the supplier and the optimal green design strategies for both parties. We identify two behavioral patterns that cheap talk can induce in the manufacturer: Green Idleness , whereby the manufacturer free-rides on the supplier’s green efforts upon receiving high-greenness disclosures, and Green Anxiety , whereby the manufacturer over-invests in response to low-greenness disclosures. Both Green Idleness and Green Anxiety become more pronounced when consumers are more sensitive to product greenness or when uncertainty about the supplier’s greenness is greater, while higher green investment costs for the manufacturer weaken both effects Importantly, our findings reveal that false disclosure can benefit both parties under certain conditions, and that strategic cheap talk can simultaneously improve both profitability and environmental performance in green supply chains. Furthermore, to enhance the robustness of the findings, we conduct a sensitivity analysis and develop a model extension incorporating the green halo effect into consumer utility, which further supports the main qualitative findings.

Title: Diagnosing silent errors in replication packages: Evidence from an AI agent
Authors: Leslie Tianyuan Zhang, Zeju Zhu
Abstract: We test whether an autonomous AI agent (Claude Code) can diagnose errors beyond rerunning code. The agent audits 40 AEA packages and reproduces results in all 26 with public data. We then seed a defect in each of 13 packages and conduct 39 blind sessions. It detects the defect in 37 sessions and provides the correct fix and statistical consequence in 34. Performance remains strong for silent defects that would pass a check based solely on matching reported regression estimates. Our results suggest that AI agents can add diagnostic value beyond re-execution and therefore lower the cost of computational reproduction.

Title: Structural shocks and political participation in the US
Authors: Marina Chugunova, Klaus Keller, Sampsa Samila
Abstract: This paper examines the impact of the large structural shocks—automation and import competition—on voter turnout during US federal elections from 2000 to 2016. Although the negative income effect of both shocks is comparable, we find that political participation decreases significantly in counties more exposed to industrial robots. In contrast, exposure to rising import competition does not reduce voter turnout and may even boost it in House elections. A survey experiment reveals that divergent beliefs about the effectiveness of government intervention drive this contrast. Our study highlights the role of beliefs in shaping consequences of structural shocks.

Title: Constrained reinforcement learning for the dynamic inventory routing problem under stochastic supply and demand
Authors: Umur Hasturk, Kees Jan Roodbergen, Evrim Ursavas, Albert H. Schrotenboer
Abstract: Green hydrogen has multiple use cases and is produced from renewable energy, such as solar or wind energy. It can be stored in large quantities, decoupling renewable energy generation from its use, and is therefore considered essential for achieving a climate-neutral economy. The intermittency of renewable energy generation and the stochastic nature of demand are, however, challenging factors for the dynamic planning of hydrogen storage and transportation. This holds particularly in the early-adoption phase when hydrogen distribution occurs through vehicle-based networks. We therefore address the Dynamic Inventory Routing Problem (DIRP) under stochastic supply and demand with direct deliveries for the vehicle-based distribution of hydrogen. To solve this problem, we propose a Constrained Reinforcement Learning (CRL) framework that integrates constraints into the learning process and incorporates parameterized post-decision state value predictions. Additionally, we introduce Lookahead-based CRL (LCRL), which improves decision-making over a multi-period horizon to enhance short-term planning while maintaining the value predictions. Our computational experiments demonstrate the efficacy of CRL and LCRL across diverse instances. Our learning methods provide near-optimal solutions on small scale instances that are solved via value iteration. Furthermore, both methods outperform typical deep learning approaches such as Proximal Policy Optimization, as well as classical inventory heuristics, such as (s,S)-policy-based and Power-of-Two-based heuristics. Furthermore, LCRL achieves a 10% improvement over CRL on average, albeit with higher computational requirements. Analyses of optimal replenishment policies reveal that accounting for stochastic supply and demand influences these policies, showing the importance of our addition to the DIRP.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Control irreducibility in coupled ground-aerial logistics networks: A multi-configuration simulation study
Authors: Yue Chen
Abstract: The rapid deployment of drone-based logistics introduces a critical risk: cascading failures in coupled ground-aerial networks. This study investigates whether runtime adaptive control can prevent systemic collapse when vertiports become functionally isolated due to ground traffic congestion, and where the boundary of control effectiveness lies. An integrated co-simulation framework coupling SUMO with a custom aerial logistics model is developed. Three control strategies are evaluated across 11 network configurations, complemented by a healthy baseline search and gradual stress experiments. A no-disturbance benchmark confirms operation at > 99% completion, indicating that collapse is disturbance-triggered rather than inherently infeasible. Results reveal a “Control Irreducibility” regime under strong coupling and limited capacity: none of the runtime strategies produced statistically significant improvement over baseline (paired t -test, p > .05 across all comparisons), with completion rates remaining below 4% in the stressed regime. Gradual stress experiments identify a demand-dominated transition ( λ ≈ 2.0) from healthy to irreducible operation, with no intermediate controllable regime. This finding holds under alternative metrics, including effective throughput rate. Cascading collapse is consistently triggered by functional isolation, followed by overload propagation. In contrast, structural design interventions — capacity redundancy and topology-aware vertiport placement — achieve a sixfold improvement in completion rate and, when combined with adaptive control, extend network survival time by over 900 s, demonstrating design–control synergy. Validated across regular and real-world road networks, these findings establish that resilience must be embedded in network design, with runtime control serving as a complementary safety buffer.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Berth and yard space allocation optimization with mobile shore power under two carbon policies
Authors: Shumin Lin, Yinchen Zhu, Lu Zhen, Chunfeng Liu, Wencheng Wang
Abstract: Against the backdrop of increasingly stringent global decarbonization requirements, ports, as key nodes in global trade, have attracted growing academic and industrial attention regarding both operational efficiency and carbon emissions. To improve operational efficiency and reduce carbon emissions, this study proposes a comprehensive optimization model for berth allocation, quay crane (QC) allocation, yard space allocation, and mobile shore power scheduling under two carbon policies: a carbon tax policy, which imposes a predetermined tax on carbon emissions, and a carbon trading policy, under which emission allowances can be purchased or sold relative to an allocated emission quota. The model aims to balance port operational efficiency and carbon emissions, thereby minimizing the total cost of the port. A hybrid meta-heuristic algorithm, QL-ALNS, combining Q-learning with adaptive large neighborhood search is designed to solve large-scale optimization problems. By employing Q-learning as an intelligent decision-making mechanism to adaptively select removal and repair operators, the algorithm achieves a balance between efficient exploration and exploitation of complex solution spaces. In numerical experiments, the effectiveness and efficiency of the algorithm are validated by comparing it with Gurobi and the adaptive large neighborhood search algorithm. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model and algorithm can effectively improve port operational efficiency and reduce carbon emissions. Several managerial insights are also derived from the sensitivity analyses. For example, carbon pricing promotes emission reduction, while excessively high carbon prices or scheduling costs may increase costs without proportional environmental benefits; carbon quotas mainly affect trading costs rather than operating decisions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Unified threshold strategies for online conversion problems with transaction costs
Authors: Wenming Zhang, Na Shu, Xiangyue Zhang, Chenlu Zhang
Abstract: Online conversion problems study how a trader should sell a given amount of asset over a finite horizon in order to maximize revenue under price uncertainty and fixed transaction costs. This paper develops a unified threshold optimization framework for both the continuous online conversion problem with transaction costs ((Formula presented) ) and the discrete online conversion problem with transaction costs ((Formula presented) ) under the competitive difference. For (Formula presented), we propose an optimal strategy (Formula presented) (Optimal Selling Continuous). For (Formula presented), we introduce an integer block selling structure and propose an optimal strategy (Formula presented) (Optimal Selling Discrete). When the transaction cost (Formula presented), (Formula presented) recovers the competitive difference performance achieved by (Formula presented) in Wang et al. (2022). For (Formula presented), the zero transaction cost case shows that (Formula presented) is less conservative than (Formula presented) in Zhang et al. (2011). Numerical experiments under simulated price sequences and real EUR/USD exchange rate data demonstrate that the proposed strategies achieve strong numerical revenue performance in the tested settings and provide implementable threshold rules for online trading environments with fixed transaction costs.

Title: What can we gain from pooling VAR and local projection impulse response functions?
Authors: Viet Hoang Dinh
Abstract: I show that pooling Vector Autoregression (VAR) and Local Projection (LP) impulse response functions (IRFs) may address the bias-variance trade-off in IRF estimation. I also propose a sequence-of-block bootstrap method, designed to construct confidence intervals for the pooled IRFs. I document three main findings: (i) Monte Carlo exercises suggest that the pooled estimator generally yields lower root mean squared error than both VAR and LP at short and medium horizons. (ii) Using the sequence-of-block bootstrap, inference based on the pooled estimator delivers coverage rates that are slightly lower than those under LP and more accurate than those based on VAR, while producing substantially shorter average interval lengths than LP. (iii) The pooling approach combined with the sequence-of-block bootstrap produces sensible results in an empirical application to monetary policy.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: Forecasting the price of carbon with macroeconomic and financial variables
Authors: Andrea Bastianin, Elisabetta Mirto, Yan Qin, Luca Rossini
Abstract: We tackle the issue of producing point, sign, and density forecasts for the monthly real price of carbon in the European Union Emissions Trading System (EU ETS). We show that Bayesian Vector Autoregressive (BVAR) models augmented with factors based on macroeconomic and financial variables yield improvements in point and density forecasting performance, with the largest point-forecast gains emerging at intermediate and longer horizons. In particular, the one-factor BVAR model provides lowest values at six and nine months ahead, while the baseline BVAR performs best at the one-year horizon. By contrast, a large BVAR including all predictors individually does not improve point forecast accuracy, supporting the use of parsimonious model specifications. Simple forecast pooling delivers modest gains from medium horizons onward, but does not mitigate the time variation in relative forecast performance. We also provide a qualitative comparison of model-based forecasts with survey expectations and forecasts released by data providers, which further highlights that relative forecast performance varies over time. Moreover, we consider verified emissions and show that stochastic volatility improves point forecasts, with reductions of about 6.5–7.1% at the one-year horizon. Lastly, we use model-based forecasts to construct market monitoring tools that track demand and price pressure in the EU ETS.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: Do women comply more than men? Experimental evidence from a general population sample
Authors: Müge Süer, Nicola Cerutti, Jana Friedrichsen, Gyula Seres
Abstract: Women are typically perceived as more compliant than men; however, the literature provides inconclusive evidence. Using a novel experimental design comprising two complementary experiments, we test this claim in online samples representative of the German adult population. The first experiment (N = 1600) features a probabilistic social dilemma game (PDG) in which participants can increase their individual payoff at the expense of exposing themselves and their group to probabilistic losses. In two treatment conditions, they receive either a recommendation on socially optimal behavior or the same recommendation plus information on weakly non-compliant peer behavior. We find that the recommendation strongly affects behavior, but more so for women than for men. The welfare improvement is substantial. Information on the non-compliant behavior of others erodes compliance with recommendation but does not induce significantly different responses in men and women. In the second experiment (N = 522), we elicit empirical and normative expectations about behavior in the PDG with a behavioral recommendation, in order to study the role of norms in adhering to it. While men and women are expected to hold similar normative beliefs, men are expected to follow the recommendation less often, suggesting that compliance is a (strong) female social norm.

Title: Day-ahead market scheduling strategy of a virtual power plant under the single imbalance pricing scheme via stochastic robust optimization
Authors: Álvaro García-Cerezo, Petra Miljan, Hrvoje Pandžić
Abstract: The high integration of renewable energy technologies in power systems represents a challenge due to the uncertainty in their production. In most European markets, producers should comply with their scheduled operation or face the penalties imposed through an imbalance mechanism. Renewable energy sources can be coordinated along with other technologies within a virtual power plant to mitigate the imbalance penalties. To mitigate this issue, in this paper a day-ahead market scheduling strategy of a virtual power plant under the single imbalance pricing scheme is determined using a novel two-stage formulation. The first stage comprises the day-ahead market scheduling, while the second stage involves rescheduling of the assets once the deviations in the renewable production availability, modeled using scenarios, are known. Novelty of this work lies in the combination of scenario-based stochastic programming and robust optimization to model uncertainty in the imbalance price deviations. The risk of the decision maker is controlled using the conditional value-at-risk for a given confidence level. The presented case study is based on data from the Croatian power system. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed formulation outperforms the formulation of previous works in reducing the arbitrage between the day-ahead market and the imbalance settlement. Moreover, in-sample and out-of-sample simulations lead to similar profits. Furthermore, the benefits of changing the risk-aversion level of the decision maker at the different stages of the problem are evaluated.

Title: Measuring efficiency and abatement costs in waste-to-energy: A nonparametric shadow pricing approach
Authors: Zuyao Liu, Bin Zhang, Fawaz Baddar ALHussan, Zhaohua Wang, Zhiyang Shen
Abstract: Waste-to-energy (WTE) has become a crucial component of the circular economy and has attracted growing attention from environmental economists. In the waste-to-energy process, municipal solid waste plays a dual role: it is conceptually an output of human economic activities and an input for electricity generation. This dual nature makes the characterization of production technology particularly challenging. To address this issue, we develop a network by-production analytical framework and its corresponding multiplier model to evaluate the two operationally observable stages of WTE systems: energy conversion and pollution abatement. A distinctive feature of our approach is that the shadow prices of the equality-constrained linking input, municipal solid waste, are allowed to take either positive or negative values. The sign of the ratio between the shadow price of municipal solid waste and that of electricity provides an operational interpretation: for instance, when excessive waste input causes operational overload, the ratio becomes negative, indicating how much electricity output could increase if one unit of waste input were reduced. Furthermore, undesirable outputs such as carbon emissions and other pollutants are incorporated into production technology to assess the environmental performance of waste-to-energy generation. The proposed model is applied to a panel dataset of 167 Chinese cities over the period 2000–2022, yielding new insights into the efficiency of waste-to-energy plants and the marginal abatement costs of pollutants.

Title: Research on critical chain project buffer monitoring based on activity resilience
Authors: Junguang Zhang, Jiaqi Zhang, Jianfei Cui, Shanshan Guo
Abstract: As complex projects face frequent and diverse risk-induced disturbances, critical activities, which serve as key nodes for mitigating localized risks, have begun to play an increasingly important role in critical chain project buffer management. To address these dynamic risk disturbances effectively and enhance the resilience of critical activities, we propose a buffer allocation and control method for critical chain projects based on activity resilience theory. First, activity resilience is evaluated along two dimensions, namely resistance to disturbances and functional recovery capacity, and buffer allocation is determined accordingly. Second, to address different types of risk disturbances, buffer monitoring zones are streamlined, and differentiated monitoring strategies are implemented according to the resilience levels of the target activities. Finally, by integrating activity resilience indicators with the monitoring zone framework, buffer trigger points and corresponding response plans are established to facilitate the and precise real-time monitoring of critical chain project buffers. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method effectively enhances the resilience of project activities, improves the efficiency of risk early warning, and increases project completion performance, thereby providing novel insights and strategies for critical chain project buffer management.

Title: A clustering-based framework for preference inference in inverse multiobjective optimization
Authors: Emilio Carrizosa, Nuria Gómez-Vargas, Veronica Piccialli
Abstract: Decision-making in real-world applications often involves multiple competing objectives, with decision-makers applying their own preferences to balance trade-offs. Inverse Multiobjective Optimization (IMO) aims to infer both the underlying objective functions and the implicit preferences that drive observed decisions. In this work, we propose an approach that integrates clustering into inverse optimization to group decision-makers based on their preference structures rather than their observed decisions. Our method is an optimization-based clustering IMO framework that minimizes regrets, which is the difference between the objective value of observed decisions and the optimal value under the inferred preference structure, resulting in Mixed-Integer Quadratic Programs (MIQPs). Additionally, we incorporate interpretability requirements to ensure that inferred preferences are meaningful and align with domain knowledge. To enhance computational efficiency, we derive a heuristic that provides a warm-start solution for the global optimization algorithms, improving convergence and solution quality. We validate our approach on synthetic datasets and a diet recommendation problem, demonstrating its ability to uncover interpretable and robust decision-making patterns.

Title: Convergence to collusion in algorithmic pricing
Authors: Kevin Michael Frick
Abstract: Artificial intelligence algorithms are increasingly used by firms to set prices. Previous research shows that they can learn to collude, but how quickly and reliably they can do so has remained an open question. I study average-reward soft actor-critic algorithms that set continuous prices in the workhorse environment of this literature: a repeated Bertrand duopoly with symmetric firms, deterministic logit demand, and constant marginal costs, where agents observe only market prices and their own profits. The algorithms can converge to a collusive outcome within 50,000 periods, and in 36% of simulations learned punishments make one-period deviations unprofitable, so that high prices are mutual best responses. Successful simulations show cooperative behaviour supported by reward-punishment schemes that discourage deviations. When high prices are not supported by punishments, profitable deviations are typically on the order of hundredths of a percent.

Title: Off the clock? Working time misperceptions and labour market outcomes
Authors: Thomas Breda, Vladimir Pecheu, Baptiste Roux
Abstract: This paper documents a gap between workers’ formal working time arrangements and their own reports of them, and examines what this gap reveals about informal working time flexibility. Combining administrative and survey data at the individual level, we construct a new and unique data set which shows that nearly 20% of the workforce mistakenly report that they work under day contracts, with no monitoring of hours, while they are actually paid through a standard hours contract. This reveals that many workers with various profiles may be misinformed about the legal environment governing something as fundamental as their working time. We show that these misreporting workers differ from classic workers in terms of working conditions: they perform more unpaid overtime hours but have a higher wage rate per contractual hour, so that their true compensation per hour worked is similar. Working time rules appear not to be fully applied to misreporters, but we find no evidence that employers use the discrepancy to extract rents. Non-compliance seems to operate as an informal working time arrangement facilitating a gradual transition between standard hours contracts and day contracts.

Title: Trends and structure of educational assortative mating
Authors: Edoardo Ciscato
Abstract: I study the structure and evolution of educational assortative mating in the U.S. using 1962–2025 Current Population Survey data. From observed marital patterns, I recover the full matrix of marital gains across educational groups within the equilibrium matching framework of Choo and Siow ( 2006 ) and provide a novel characterization of its complementarity structure using Singular Value Decomposition. This approach allows me to infer the number of relevant sorting dimensions, to describe how different educational attainments are valued along each dimension, and to develop aggregate measures of assortative mating based on local odds ratios. I show that the first dimension explains more than 90% of total sorting in all periods and ranks individuals monotonically by educational attainment, consistent with the presence of human capital complementarities à la Becker. However, higher-order dimensions capture homogamous preferences that help explain the prevalence of same-education couples in the data. I document evidence of a long-run increase in educational assortative mating, with a marked slowdown since the 1990s, although the magnitude of the long-run increase is sensitive to how educational categories are defined, partly due to a coding change in the CPS educational variable in 1992. I also show that high-school dropouts have become increasingly isolated, college and postgraduate groups have converged, and gender asymmetries in returns from sorting have declined.

Title: Will new transportation technologies increase urban density?
Authors: Edward L. Glaeser
Abstract: Will 21st century transportation innovations work against urban density, as the car did in the 20th century, or promote urban centralization, as the railroad did in the 19th century? Reducing the cost of commuting always reduces urban centralization in the classic Alonso-Muth-Mills model but that result reverses if the number of trips is endogenous and the elasticity of trips with respect to their costs is greater than one. That elasticity may have increased over time, as an increasing share of daily trips seems to be discretionary and city centers increasingly provide entertainment. This paper asks discusses the urbanizing effects of four trends in transportation technology: shared mobility (such as Uber), autonomy (such as Waymo), vertical travel and green mobility, as provided by bike lane. As people spend more time traveling in denser, large areas, innovations that reduce the time cost of travel, such as autonomous cars, seem likely to complement urban living, as long as they don't excessively increase traffic. Sharing is also easier in big cities, so technologies that involve sharing are also centripetal. The other trends seem less likely to have major effects. Moreover, the forces of inertia, which include both regulation and legacy infrastructure, are likely to limit the impact of any new technologies in Europe and the U.S., so that the biggest changes in urban form are likely to appear in east Asia and the developing world.

Title: A simulation–optimisation framework for front-warehouse location planning in instant retail
Authors: Ruijing Wu, Cheng Zhang, Wei Xiao, Zhenyang Shi
Affiliations: Shanghai International Studies University; Hohai University; Zhejiang University of Technology
Abstract: The instant retail model that provides ultra-fast on-demand delivery service from local front warehouses is gaining increasing popularity. However, its profitability is constrained by escalating costs due to system characteristics like temporal and spatial concentration of demand, time-varying courier availability, interdependence among consecutive orders, and the consequent cascading order delays. This paper develops a simulation-optimisation framework to solve the front-warehouse location problem in instant retail, which integrates a discrete-event simulation model that captures system characteristics and micro-level system dynamics, and proposes a ranking-and-selection algorithm that identifies the best location strategy with high statistical confidence via adaptive sampling. Extensive numerical studies using both synthetic and real data demonstrate that this approach consistently selects the optimal solution with over 99% probability while maintaining high computational efficiency even for large-scale problems. This approach outperforms classical facility location models and simulation-based genetic algorithms in terms of both profitability and service timeliness, and the advantage is primarily driven by the feature of temporal demand concentration arising in instant retail. We further find that under constrained courier capacity, light order batching can effectively improve profits and service responsiveness, and off-peak pricing may mitigate cascading order delays when demand peaks coincide with traffic congestion.

Title: Bill of sustainability: integrating life cycle assessment into bill of materials and operations for sustainable manufacturing
Authors: Bening Mayanti, Petri Helo, Linda L. Zhang, Roger Jiao
Affiliations: University of Vaasa; Univ. Lille, CNRS, UMR 9221 – LEM – Lille Economie Management; Georgia Institute of Technology
Abstract: Managing sustainability-related data for a wide range of products systematically and efficiently is a challenge for manufacturing companies. While manufacturing execution systems (MES) and enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems maintain up-to-date information on process and raw material batches, this data is traditionally disconnected from environmental impact quantification. This paper presents the concept of the bill of sustainability (BOS), a framework that integrates a generic bill of materials and operations with life cycle assessment (LCA) to enable a product-portfolio-level system that can report product-instance-level sustainability data.
